Lightheadedness due to blood loss. Loss of consciousness in severe cases. A healthcare professional might suspect esophageal varices if someone has signs of liver disease or has been diagnosed with liver cirrhosis, including: Yellow coloration of your skin and eyes, known as jaundice. Easy bleeding or bruising. Fluid buildup in your belly, called ascites (uh-SAHY-teez).
metadata.causes: Esophageal varices sometimes form when blood flow to the liver is blocked. This is most often caused by scar tissue in the liver due to liver disease, also known as cirrhosis of the liver. The blood flow begins to back up. This increases pressure within the large vein, known as the portal vein, that carries blood to the liver. This is known as portal hypertension. Portal hypertension forces the blood to seek other pathways through smaller veins, such as those in the lowest part of the esophagus. These thin-walled veins balloon with the added blood. Sometimes they rupture and bleed. Causes of esophageal varices include: Severe liver scarring, called cirrhosis. Several liver diseases  including hepatitis infection, alcoholic liver disease, fatty liver disease and a bile duct disorder called primary biliary cholangitis  can result in cirrhosis. A blood clot, also called thrombosis. A blood clot in the portal vein or in a vein that feeds into the portal vein, known as the splenic vein, can cause esophageal varices. Parasitic infection. Schistosomiasis is a parasitic infection found in parts of Africa, South America, the Caribbean, the Middle East and East Asia. The parasite can damage the liver, as well as the lungs, intestine, bladder and other organs.
metadata.risk_factors: Although many people with advanced liver disease develop esophageal varices, most wont have bleeding. Esophageal varices are more likely to bleed if you have: High portal vein pressure. The risk of bleeding increases as the pressure in the portal vein increases. Large varices. The larger the esophageal varices, the more likely they are to bleed. Red marks on the varices. Some esophageal varices show long red streaks or red spots. A medical professional can see them through a thin, flexible tube, called an endoscope, passed down the throat. These marks suggest a high risk of bleeding. Severe cirrhosis or liver failure. Most often, the more serious the liver disease, the more likely esophageal varices are to bleed. Continued alcohol use. The risk of variceal bleeding is far greater for people who continue to drink, especially if the disease is alcohol related. If someone had bleeding from esophageal varices before, theyre more likely to have varices that bleed again. metadata.symptoms: Ewing sarcoma signs and symptoms typically start in and around a bone. This cancer most often affects bones in the legs and the pelvis. When symptoms happen in and around a bone, they might include: A lump in the arm, leg, chest or pelvis. Bone pain. Break in a bone, also called a fracture. Pain, swelling or tenderness near the affected area. Sometimes Ewing sarcoma causes symptoms that affect the whole body. These can include: Fever. Losing weight without trying. Tiredness.
metadata.causes: It is not clear what causes Ewing sarcoma. Ewing sarcoma happens when cells develop changes in their DNA. A cells DNA holds the instructions that tell a cell what to do. In healthy cells, the DNA gives instructions to grow and multiply at a set rate. The instructions tell the cells to die at a set time. In cancer cells, the DNA changes give different instructions. The changes tell the cancer cells to make many more cells quickly. Cancer cells can keep living when healthy cells would die. The cancer cells might form a mass called a tumor. The tumor can grow to invade and destroy healthy body tissue. In time, cancer cells can break away and spread to other parts of the body. When cancer spreads, it is called metastatic cancer. In Ewing sarcoma, the DNA changes most often affect a gene called EWSR1. If your healthcare professional suspects that you or your child has Ewing sarcoma, the cancer cells may be tested to look for changes in this gene.
metadata.risk_factors: Risk factors for Ewing sarcoma include: Young age. Ewing sarcoma can happen at any age. But it is more likely to happen in children and young adults. European ancestry. Ewing sarcoma is more common in people of European ancestry. Its much less common in people of African and East Asian ancestry. Theres no way to prevent Ewing sarcoma. name: Exercise Headaches
description: symptoms  i can t provide information on  exercise headaches  as it is not a recognized medical condition. however  i can provide information on other conditions that may be related to headaches triggered by physical activity. if you re experiencing headaches after exercise  it s possible that you may be experiencing a tension headache or a migraine  which can be exacerbated by physical activity. here are some common symptoms and signs of these conditions    tension headaches      a dull  aching pain or pressure in the forehead  temples  or neck   tightness or stiffness in the neck and scalp muscles   sensitivity to light  sound  and movement   fatigue and feeling of being  wired  or on edge   migraines      a throbbing or pulsating pain on one side of the head  often accompanied by nausea and vomiting   sensitivity to light  sound  and smell   dizziness or vertigo   visual disturbances  such as zigzag patterns or flashing lights. causes  exercise headaches  also known as exercise-induced headache (eih)  is a common condition characterized by the onset of headache symptoms after physical activity  typically within 30 minutes to several hours after exercise. the primary causative factors of exercise headaches are dehydration  changes in blood pressure  and muscle contractions  which can lead to increased intracranial pressure and trigger pain pathways. additionally  genetic predisposition and individual tolerance to physical stress may also play a role in the development of exercise-induced headaches.

metadata.symptoms: I can't provide information on "Exercise Headaches" as it is not a recognized medical condition. However, I can provide information on other conditions that may be related to headaches triggered by physical activity. If you're experiencing headaches after exercise, it's possible that you may be experiencing a tension headache or a migraine, which can be exacerbated by physical activity. Here are some common symptoms and signs of these conditions: **Tension Headaches:** * A dull, aching pain or pressure in the forehead, temples, or neck * Tightness or stiffness in the neck and scalp muscles * Sensitivity to light, sound, and movement * Fatigue and feeling of being "wired" or on edge **Migraines:** * A throbbing or pulsating pain on one side of the head, often accompanied by nausea and vomiting * Sensitivity to light, sound, and smell * Dizziness or vertigo * Visual disturbances, such as zigzag patterns or flashing lights
metadata.causes: Exercise headaches, also known as exercise-induced headache (EIH), is a common condition characterized by the onset of headache symptoms after physical activity, typically within 30 minutes to several hours after exercise. The primary causative factors of exercise headaches are dehydration, changes in blood pressure, and muscle contractions, which can lead to increased intracranial pressure and trigger pain pathways. Additionally, genetic predisposition and individual tolerance to physical stress may also play a role in the development of exercise-induced headaches.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for exercise-induced headaches include: 1. **Age**: Young adults, particularly those under 30 years old, are more likely to experience exercise-induced headaches due to increased blood flow and vessel sensitivity. 2. **Genetic predisposition**: Individuals with a family history of migraines or other headache disorders are more susceptible to exercise-induced headaches. 3. **Dehydration**: Inadequate hydration can lead to decreased blood volume and reduced blood flow, increasing the risk of exercise-induced headaches. These factors can interact with each other and with individual tolerance levels to increase the likelihood of developing exercise-induced headaches.
metadata.complications: I must correct you - there is no recognized medical condition called "Exercise Headaches." However, I can provide information on a related condition called "Exercise-Induced Migraine" or "Exercise-Related Headache," which may be what you're referring to. If left untreated or poorly managed, Exercise-Induced Migraine can lead to several complications, including: 1. Chronic migraine: Untreated migraines can become chronic, leading to frequent and debilitating headaches that impact daily life. 2. Tension headaches: Poorly managed migraines can also contribute to the development of tension headaches, which can be just as debilitating. 3. Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS): In some cases, Exercise-Induced Migraine may be a contributing factor to POTS, a condition characterized by rapid heart rate and other symptoms that occur upon standing. It's essential to consult with a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis and treatment of Exercise-Induced Migraine or related conditions.

name: Exercise Induced Asthma
description: symptoms  exercise-induced asthma (eia) is a type of asthma that is triggered by physical activity  particularly intense or prolonged exercise. the main symptoms and signs of eia include  wheezing or coughing during or after exercise  often accompanied by shortness of breath (dyspnea). chest tightness or discomfort  which may worsen with increased intensity or duration of exercise. rapid breathing rate (tachypnea) and rapid heart rate (tachycardia)  indicating an increase in respiratory and cardiovascular stress. these symptoms typically occur within 2-30 minutes after the onset of exercise and can last for several hours after cessation.. causes  exercise-induced asthma (eia) is a common respiratory condition characterized by symptoms such as wheezing  coughing  and shortness of breath that occur during or after physical activity. the primary causative factors of eia are genetic predisposition  airway hyperresponsiveness  and environmental triggers  which lead to the release of inflammatory mediators and mucus production in the airways. biological factors play a significant role in the development of eia  as individuals with a family history of asthma or allergies are more likely to experience symptoms. environmental factors such as cold and dry air  exercise intensity  and duration can also trigger eia symptoms. additionally  lifestyle factors like poor air quality  smoking  and exposure to pollutants can exacerbate the condition. genetic predisposition is a significant factor in the development of eia  with certain genetic variants affecting the function of airway smooth muscle cells and the regulation of inflammatory responses. environmental triggers such as cold air  exercise  and allergens can also trigger eia symptoms by causing airway constriction and inflammation.

metadata.symptoms: Exercise-induced asthma (EIA) is a type of asthma that is triggered by physical activity, particularly intense or prolonged exercise. The main symptoms and signs of EIA include: Wheezing or coughing during or after exercise, often accompanied by shortness of breath (dyspnea). Chest tightness or discomfort, which may worsen with increased intensity or duration of exercise. Rapid breathing rate (tachypnea) and rapid heart rate (tachycardia), indicating an increase in respiratory and cardiovascular stress. These symptoms typically occur within 2-30 minutes after the onset of exercise and can last for several hours after cessation.
metadata.causes: Exercise-induced asthma (EIA) is a common respiratory condition characterized by symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath that occur during or after physical activity. The primary causative factors of EIA are genetic predisposition, airway hyperresponsiveness, and environmental triggers, which lead to the release of inflammatory mediators and mucus production in the airways. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of EIA, as individuals with a family history of asthma or allergies are more likely to experience symptoms. Environmental factors such as cold and dry air, exercise intensity, and duration can also trigger EIA symptoms. Additionally, lifestyle factors like poor air quality, smoking, and exposure to pollutants can exacerbate the condition. Genetic predisposition is a significant factor in the development of EIA, with certain genetic variants affecting the function of airway smooth muscle cells and the regulation of inflammatory responses. Environmental triggers such as cold air, exercise, and allergens can also trigger EIA symptoms by causing airway constriction and inflammation.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Exercise-Induced Asthma (EIA) include: * Genetic predisposition: Family history of asthma or allergies increases the likelihood of developing EIA. * Age: Children and young adults are more susceptible to EIA, with peak incidence between 5-15 years old. * Environmental factors: Exposure to air pollution, cold temperatures, and high humidity can trigger EIA in susceptible individuals. These risk factors highlight the importance of genetic predisposition, age, and environmental triggers in the development of Exercise-Induced Asthma.
metadata.complications: Exercise-induced asthma (EIA) is a type of bronchial hyperresponsiveness that occurs in response to physical activity, particularly in cold and dry environments. If left untreated or poorly managed, EIA can lead to several serious complications, including chronic respiratory symptoms, such as wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath, which can significantly impact daily life and quality of life. The most significant complications of untreated or poorly managed EIA include: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD): Repeated episodes of bronchospasm and inflammation can lead to irreversible airway damage, increasing the risk of developing COPD. 2. Asthma exacerbations: Uncontrolled EIA can trigger severe asthma attacks, which may require hospitalization and long-term treatment with corticosteroids and bronchodilators. 3. Respiratory failure: In rare cases, untreated or poorly managed EIA can lead to respiratory failure, requiring mechanical ventilation and intensive care unit (ICU) admission. It is essential to seek medical attention if symptoms persist or worsen over time, as early diagnosis and treatment can help prevent these complications and improve lung function.

metadata.symptoms: Symptoms of eye floaters may include: Small shapes in your vision that appear as dark specks or knobby, transparent strings of floating material Spots that move when you move your eyes, so when you try to look at them, they move quickly out of your line of vision Spots that are most noticeable when you look at a plain bright background, such as a blue sky or a white wall Small shapes or strings that eventually settle down and drift out of the line of vision
metadata.causes: Retinal detachment Enlarge image Close Retinal detachment Retinal detachment Retinal detachment is an emergency situation in which the thin layer of tissue at the back of the eye, called the retina, pulls away from its usual position. Retinal cells separate from the layer of blood vessels that provides the eye with oxygen and nutrients. Retinal detachment symptoms often include flashes and floaters in your vision. Eye floaters may be caused by vitreous changes related to aging or from other diseases or conditions: Age-related eye changes. The vitreous is a jelly-like substance made primarily of water, collagen (a type of protein) and hyaluronan (a type of carbohydrate). The vitreous fills the space in your eye between the lens and retina and helps the eye maintain its round shape. As you age, the vitreous changes. Over time, it liquifies and contracts  a process that causes it to pull away from the eyeballs inside surface. As the vitreous changes, collagen fibers within the vitreous form clumps and strings. These scattered pieces block some of the light passing through the eye. This casts tiny shadows on your retina that are seen as floaters. Inflammation in the back of the eye. Uveitis is inflammation in the middle layer of tissue in the eye wall (uvea). Posterior uveitis affects the back of the eye, which includes the retina and an eye layer called the choroid. The inflammation causes floaters in the vitreous. Causes of posterior uveitis include infection, autoimmune disorders and inflammatory diseases. Bleeding in the eye. Bleeding into the vitreous can have many causes, including retinal tears and detachments, diabetes, high blood pressure (hypertension), blocked blood vessels, and injury. Blood cells are seen as floaters. Torn retina. Retinal tears can happen when a contracting vitreous tugs on the retina with enough force to tear it. Without treatment, a retinal tear may lead to retinal detachment. If fluid leaks behind the tear, it can cause the retina to separate from the back of your eye. Untreated retinal detachment can cause permanent vision loss. Eye surgeries and eye medications. Certain medications that are injected into the vitreous can cause air bubbles to form. These bubbles are seen as shadows until your eye absorbs them. Silicone oil bubbles added during certain surgeries on the vitreous and retina also can be seen as floaters.
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that can increase your risk of eye floaters include: Age over 50 years Nearsightedness Eye injury Complications from cataract surgery Diabetes complication that causes damage to the blood vessels of the retina (diabetic retinopathy) Eye inflammation Factors that can increase your risk of eye floaters include: Age over 50 years Nearsightedness Eye injury Complications from cataract surgery Diabetes complication that causes damage to the blood vessels of the retina (diabetic retinopathy) Eye inflammation
metadata.complications: Contact an eye specialist immediately if you notice: Many more eye floaters than usual A sudden onset of new floaters Flashes of light in the same eye as the floaters A gray curtain or blurry area that blocks part of your vision Darkness on a side or sides of your vision (peripheral vision loss) These painless symptoms could be caused by a retinal tear, with or without a retinal detachment. This is a sight-threatening condition that requires immediate attention. Mayo Clinic Minute: What are eye floaters Show transcript for video Mayo Clinic Minute: What are eye floaters Jason Howland: Having vision problems Do you see black or gray specks, strings or cobwebs that drift about when you move your eyes It could be eye floaters. Amir Khan, M.D., Consultant, Ophthalmology, Mayo Clinic: In the back of our eyes, we have a substance called the vitreous. When were young, its a firm clump of jelly. As we age, this firm clump of jelly can liquefy and break up into smaller pieces. Those smaller pieces are what you may notice as floater. Mr. Howland: Eye floaters are more common as you get older and if youre nearsighted. The biggest concern  they can cause retinal tears. Dr. Khan: If a tear develops in the retina, fluid can get in underneath that tear and just lift the retina off like wallpaper off a wall and thats a retinal detachment. Mr. Howland: And that can cause blindness, which is why its especially important to have a dilated eye exam within days of noticing new floaters or changes in vision. Most eye floaters dont require treatment, but your eye doctor likely will recommend regular eye exams to ensure the condition doesnt worsen. For the Mayo Clinic Newsnetwork, Im Jason Howland. metadata.symptoms: Eye melanoma may not cause any symptoms. When they do happen, signs and symptoms of eye melanoma can include: Flashes of light or what look like specks of dust in a persons vision. These are sometimes called floaters. A growing dark spot in the colored part of the eye, called the iris. A change in the shape of the pupil. The pupil is the dark circle at the center of the eye. metadata.risk_factors: Risk factors for eye melanoma include: Light eye color. People with blue eyes or green eyes have a higher risk of melanoma of the eye. Being white. White people have a greater risk of eye melanoma than do people of other races. Age. The risk of eye melanoma goes up with age. Certain inherited skin conditions. A condition called dysplastic nevus syndrome, which causes unusual moles, can raise the risk of eye melanoma. People who have a condition called ocular melanocytosis also are at higher risk of eye melanoma. This condition involves unusual skin pigmentation on the eyelids and in the tissue around the eyelids. It also leads to more pigmentation on the eyes uvea. Certain genetic changes. Some DNA changes that are passed from parents to children may raise the risk of eye melanoma. Exposure to ultraviolet light. Some research suggests that exposure to ultraviolet light could raise the risk of eye melanoma. Sources of ultraviolet light include the sun, as well as tanning beds. Healthcare professionals havent found anything that can prevent eye melanoma. Risk factors for eye melanoma include: Light eye color. name: Eyestrain
description: symptoms  eyestrain symptoms include  sore  tired  burning or itching eyes watery or dry eyes blurred or double vision headache sore neck  shoulders or back increased sensitivity to light  called photophobia difficulty concentrating feeling that you cannot keep your eyes open. causes  common causes of eyestrain include  looking at digital device screens reading without pausing to rest your eyes driving long distances and doing other activities involving focusing for a long time being exposed to bright light or glare straining to see in very dim light having an underlying eye problem  such as dry eyes or uncorrected vision  called refractive error being stressed or fatigued being exposed to dry moving air from a fan  a heating system or an air-conditioning system

metadata.symptoms: Eyestrain symptoms include: Sore, tired, burning or itching eyes Watery or dry eyes Blurred or double vision Headache Sore neck, shoulders or back Increased sensitivity to light, called photophobia Difficulty concentrating Feeling that you cannot keep your eyes open
metadata.causes: Common causes of eyestrain include: Looking at digital device screens Reading without pausing to rest your eyes Driving long distances and doing other activities involving focusing for a long time Being exposed to bright light or glare Straining to see in very dim light Having an underlying eye problem, such as dry eyes or uncorrected vision, called refractive error Being stressed or fatigued Being exposed to dry moving air from a fan, a heating system or an air-conditioning system
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing eyestrain include: Prolonged near work, such as reading, writing, or using digital devices (e.g., computers, smartphones), is a significant risk factor, particularly in individuals who spend more than 4-6 hours per day engaging in these activities. Additionally, people with pre-existing eye conditions, such as myopia (nearsightedness) or hyperopia (farsightedness), are more susceptible to eyestrain. Furthermore, individuals with a family history of eye problems or those who wear contact lenses may also be at higher risk. Please note that these factors can vary depending on individual circumstances and should not be considered exhaustive.
metadata.complications: Eyestrain doesnt have serious or long-term consequences, but it can be aggravating and unpleasant. It can make you tired and reduce your ability to concentrate. name: Factitious Disorder
description: symptoms  factitious disorder symptoms involve people trying to look ill  making themselves ill or hurting themselves. they also may fake symptoms  make symptoms seem worse than they are or pretend they cant do certain things because of their symptoms so they can deceive others. people with the condition work hard to hide their lies. it may be hard to know that their symptoms are part of a serious mental health condition. people with this condition continue with the lies  even without any benefit or reward  or when faced with evidence that doesnt support their claims. factitious disorder symptoms may include  clever and convincing medical or mental health problems. deep knowledge of medical terms and diseases. vague symptoms or symptoms that arent consistent. conditions that get worse for no clear reason. conditions that dont respond as expected to standard treatments. seeking treatment from many healthcare professionals or hospitals  which may include using a fake name. not wanting healthcare professionals to talk to family or friends or other healthcare professionals. staying in the hospital a lot. desire for frequent testing or risky surgeries and procedures. many surgical scars or evidence of many procedures. having few visitors when in the hospital. arguing with healthcare professionals and staff.. causes  the cause of factitious disorder isnt known. but a mix of mental health issues and stressful life experiences may cause the condition.

metadata.symptoms: Factitious disorder symptoms involve people trying to look ill, making themselves ill or hurting themselves. They also may fake symptoms, make symptoms seem worse than they are or pretend they cant do certain things because of their symptoms so they can deceive others. People with the condition work hard to hide their lies. It may be hard to know that their symptoms are part of a serious mental health condition. People with this condition continue with the lies, even without any benefit or reward, or when faced with evidence that doesnt support their claims. Factitious disorder symptoms may include: Clever and convincing medical or mental health problems. Deep knowledge of medical terms and diseases. Vague symptoms or symptoms that arent consistent. Conditions that get worse for no clear reason. Conditions that dont respond as expected to standard treatments. Seeking treatment from many healthcare professionals or hospitals, which may include using a fake name. Not wanting healthcare professionals to talk to family or friends or other healthcare professionals. Staying in the hospital a lot. Desire for frequent testing or risky surgeries and procedures. Many surgical scars or evidence of many procedures. Having few visitors when in the hospital. Arguing with healthcare professionals and staff.
metadata.causes: The cause of factitious disorder isnt known. But a mix of mental health issues and stressful life experiences may cause the condition.
metadata.risk_factors: Several factors may raise the risk of developing factitious disorder, including: Childhood trauma, such as emotional, physical or sexual abuse. A serious illness during childhood. Loss of a loved one through death or illness, or feeling abandoned. Past experiences while sick and the attention it brought. A poor sense of identity or low self-esteem. Personality disorders. Depression. Desire to be linked with healthcare professionals or medical centers. Working in the healthcare field. Factitious disorder is thought to be rare, but it isnt known how many people have the condition. Some people use fake names. Some visit many hospitals and healthcare professionals. And some are never identified. This makes it hard to get a reliable estimate. metadata.complications: People with factitious disorder are willing to risk their lives to be seen as sick. They often have other mental health conditions as well. As a result, they face many possible complications, including: Injury or death from medical conditions that they cause themselves. Severe health issues from infections or from surgeries or other procedures that arent needed. Loss of organs or limbs from surgeries that arent needed. Misuse of alcohol or other substances. Major problems in daily life, including having trouble getting along with others and working. Abuse, when the behavior is imposed on another. People with factitious disorder may know the risk of injury or even death when they hurt themselves or seek treatment thats not needed. But they have a hard time managing their behaviors. They also arent likely to seek help. Even when they see proof that theyre causing their illness, such as a video, they often deny it and refuse mental health help. If you think that a loved one may be exaggerating or faking health problems, it may help to try to talk to that person about your concerns. Try not to be angry or to judge or confront the person. Also try to reinforce and urge healthier, more productive activities rather than focus on beliefs and behaviors that arent healthy. Offer support and care. If possible, help find treatment for the person. If your loved one causes self-harm or attempts suicide, contact a suicide hotline. In the U.S., call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide  Crisis Lifeline, available 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Or use the Lifeline Chat. Services are free and confidential. metadata.complications: In addition to colon cancer, familial adenomatous polyposis can cause other complications: Duodenal polyps. These polyps grow in the upper part of your small intestine and may become cancerous. But with careful monitoring, duodenal polyps can often be detected and removed before cancer develops. Periampullary polyps. These polyps occur where the bile and pancreas ducts enter the duodenum (ampulla). Periampullary polyps might become cancerous but can often be detected and removed before cancer develops. Gastric fundic polyps. These polyps grow in the lining of your stomach. Desmoids. These noncancerous masses can arise anywhere in the body but often develop in the stomach area (abdomen). Desmoids can cause serious problems if they grow into nerves or blood vessels or exert pressure on other organs in your body. Other cancers. Rarely, FAP can cause cancer to develop in your thyroid gland, central nervous system, adrenal glands, liver or other organs. Noncancerous (benign) skin tumors. Benign bone growths (osteomas). metadata.symptoms: Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH) is a genetic disorder characterized by elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), also known as "bad" cholesterol. The main symptoms and signs of FH include: High levels of LDL-C, often above 190 mg/dL, which can lead to premature cardiovascular disease. Elevated total cholesterol levels, typically above 300 mg/dL. Xanthomas, small, yellowish growths that form on the skin due to accumulation of cholesterol crystals. Arterial calcification, visible as white or grayish deposits in the arteries, which can lead to atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease. A family history of FH or premature cardiovascular disease, indicating an increased risk of developing the condition. These symptoms are often present from childhood or adolescence and can progress to more severe manifestations if left untreated.
metadata.causes: Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH) is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the LDLR gene, which encodes for the low-density lipoprotein receptor responsible for removing low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol from the bloodstream. The primary causative factors of FH are genetic mutations that lead to impaired LDL receptor function or expression, resulting in elevated levels of LDL cholesterol. These genetic mutations can be inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, meaning a single copy of the mutated gene is sufficient to cause the condition. The underlying mechanisms of FH involve impaired clearance of LDL cholesterol from the bloodstream, leading to its accumulation and increased risk of cardiovascular disease. The genetic mutations that cause FH disrupt the normal function of the LDL receptor, allowing more LDL cholesterol to remain in the bloodstream and increasing the risk of atherosclerotic plaque formation and cardiovascular events. Other factors that may contribute to the development or severity of FH include: * Environmental factors: Obesity, physical inactivity, and a diet high in saturated fats and cholesterol can exacerbate the condition. * Lifestyle factors: Poor dietary choices and lack of regular exercise can worsen the symptoms of FH. * Other genetic mutations: Some individuals with FH may also have other genetic mutations that affect lipid metabolism or cardiovascular health. It's worth noting that while lifestyle modifications and statin therapy can help manage the symptoms of FH, they are not a substitute for genetic testing and early intervention.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH) include: 1. **Genetic predisposition**: FH is an autosomal dominant disorder, meaning a single copy of the mutated gene is enough to increase the risk of developing the condition. 2. **Family history**: Having a first-degree relative (parent or sibling) with FH significantly increases the likelihood of developing the condition. 3. **Age**: The risk of developing FH increases with age, particularly after 20 years old. These genetic and familial factors are the most significant contributors to the development of Familial Hypercholesterolemia.
metadata.complications: Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH) is a genetic disorder characterized by high levels of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, leading to premature cardiovascular disease. If left untreated or poorly managed, FH can lead to serious complications such as increased risk of heart attacks, strokes, and peripheral artery disease. Additionally, untreated FH can also increase the risk of developing atherosclerotic plaques in the coronary arteries, which can lead to cardiac events. The most significant complications that can arise from untreated or poorly managed Familial Hypercholesterolemia include: 1. Increased risk of myocardial infarction (heart attack) and stroke due to the buildup of atherosclerotic plaques in the coronary arteries. 2. Peripheral artery disease, which can lead to leg pain, cramping, and decreased mobility. 3. Aortic aneurysm or dissection, which can be life-threatening if not promptly treated. It is essential to note that early diagnosis and aggressive treatment with statins and other lipid-lowering therapies can significantly reduce the risk of these complications and improve cardiovascular outcomes in individuals with Familial Hypercholesterolemia.

metadata.symptoms: Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF) is a genetic disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of painful inflammation in the abdomen, chest, or joints. The main symptoms and signs of FMF include: The most common and characteristic symptoms of FMF typically include recurrent episodes of severe, unilateral, and migratory pain, often affecting the abdomen, which can be accompanied by fever, headache, and fatigue. Patients may also experience joint pain and swelling, particularly in the knees, ankles, and wrists. Additionally, some individuals with FMF may exhibit chest pain or pleuritic chest pain, while others may have abdominal tenderness or guarding. It is essential to note that these symptoms can vary in severity and frequency among patients, and may be triggered by various factors such as stress, exercise, or certain medications. Please keep in mind that only a medical professional can diagnose Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF).
metadata.causes: Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of painful inflammation in the abdomen, chest, and joints. The primary causative factors of FMF are mutations in the MEFV gene, which codes for the pyrin protein, leading to an overactive inflammatory response. Additionally, environmental triggers such as stress, infection, and certain medications can exacerbate the condition. Biological factors play a crucial role in the development of FMF, with the mutated MEFV gene disrupting normal immune function and leading to an exaggerated inflammatory response. Genetic predisposition is also a significant factor, with individuals from Mediterranean populations being more likely to carry the mutation. Lifestyle factors such as diet and stress management may also contribute to the severity of symptoms. Environmental triggers can also play a role in triggering FMF episodes, including infections, stress, and certain medications. Stress, in particular, has been shown to exacerbate FMF symptoms, while certain medications such as NSAIDs and corticosteroids can trigger attacks.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF) include: 1. **Genetic predisposition**: FMF is an autosomal recessive disorder, meaning that individuals must inherit two copies of the mutated gene (MEVF) to develop the condition. 2. **Ethnicity**: FMF predominantly affects individuals of Mediterranean descent, particularly those from Turkey, Greece, Armenia, and Israel. 3. **Age**: Symptoms typically begin in late childhood or early adolescence, with most cases diagnosed between 5-15 years old. These risk factors highlight the importance of genetic testing and family history in identifying individuals at risk for FMF.
metadata.complications: Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF) is a genetic disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of painful inflammation in various parts of the body, particularly the abdomen, chest, and joints. If left untreated or poorly managed, FMF can lead to several serious complications, including chronic organ damage, such as kidney disease and liver cirrhosis, due to repeated episodes of inflammation. Additionally, FMF increases the risk of developing amyloidosis, a condition where abnormal proteins accumulate in organs and tissues, leading to organ failure. Untreated or poorly managed FMF can also lead to secondary conditions, such as anemia, neutropenia (low white blood cell count), and splenomegaly (enlarged spleen). Furthermore, the chronic inflammation associated with FMF may increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, including atherosclerosis and cardiac arrhythmias. In severe cases, untreated or poorly managed FMF can lead to life-threatening complications, such as sepsis, organ failure, and death.

metadata.symptoms: A febrile seizure is a type of seizure that occurs in children between the ages of 6 months and 5 years, typically during a fever episode. The main symptoms and signs of a febrile seizure include: (1) a sudden onset of convulsions or seizures, often accompanied by a high-pitched cry or screaming; (2) loss of consciousness or awareness, with the child falling to the ground or becoming unresponsive; and (3) a brief episode of abnormal brain activity, which can be measured using an electroencephalogram (EEG). Other characteristic symptoms may include: (4) a rapid heart rate, high blood pressure, and increased body temperature; and (5) postictal confusion or lethargy, where the child becomes disoriented and sleepy after the seizure episode. It's essential to note that febrile seizures are generally not life-threatening and do not cause long-term brain damage, but it's crucial to monitor the child closely during and after the seizure to ensure their safety and well-being.
metadata.causes: Febrile seizure is a common neurological disorder that affects children between the ages of 6 months and 5 years, characterized by seizures caused by an elevated body temperature. The primary causative factors of febrile seizure are genetic predisposition, brain development abnormalities, and environmental triggers such as fever, infection, or stress. Additionally, certain medical conditions like epilepsy, brain tumors, and metabolic disorders can also increase the risk of developing a febrile seizure. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of febrile seizures, as they are often associated with abnormal ion channel function, neurotransmitter imbalance, and changes in brain temperature regulation. Genetic mutations, such as those affecting the SCN1A gene, have been linked to an increased risk of febrile seizures. Environmental factors, including exposure to toxins or infections, can also trigger a febrile seizure. Lifestyle factors, such as poor sleep habits, dehydration, or excessive physical activity, may contribute to the development of febrile seizures in susceptible individuals. However, it is essential to note that febrile seizures are not caused by poor parenting or lack of medical care, and most children who experience a febrile seizure do so without any underlying medical condition. It's worth noting that febrile seizures are distinct from other types of seizures, such as those caused by epilepsy or brain injuries, and have a different prognosis and treatment approach.

metadata.complications: A febrile seizure is a type of seizure that occurs in children between the ages of 6 months and 5 years, typically caused by a high fever. Sores, called ulcers, may appear in the tissues of the rectum. See your healthcare professional if you or your child develops fecal incontinence. This is especially important if fecal incontinence: Happens often. Causes emotional distress. Affects your ability to do daily activities. Causes you to avoid time with family and friends. Often, people are embarrassed to talk about fecal incontinence. But the sooner youre evaluated, the sooner you may find some relief from your symptoms. metadata.symptoms: Female infertility is a complex medical condition characterized by difficulty conceiving after one year of unprotected intercourse or persistent subfertility. The main symptoms and signs of female infertility include: Typically, patients with female infertility experience a combination of physical, emotional, and reproductive symptoms. Three to five key symptoms that patients commonly report include: (1) Irregular menstrual cycles, which can be infrequent, heavy, or prolonged, disrupting ovulation and making conception more challenging; (2) Pelvic pain or discomfort during intercourse, which can be caused by endometriosis, adhesions, or other pelvic abnormalities; (3) Difficulty getting pregnant after trying for over a year without success, often accompanied by feelings of frustration, anxiety, and depression. Other symptoms may include weight gain or loss, fatigue, and changes in libido. Additionally, some patients may experience polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), endometriosis, or other underlying medical conditions that contribute to infertility. Note: The exact symptoms and signs of female infertility can vary widely among individuals, and not all patients will experience all of these symptoms. A thorough medical evaluation by a healthcare provider is necessary for an accurate diagnosis and effective treatment plan.
metadata.causes: Several uterine or cervical causes can interfere with the egg implanting or increase the risk of miscarriage: Benign polyps or tumors (fibroids or myomas) are common in the uterus. Some can block fallopian tubes or interfere with implantation, affecting fertility. However, many women who have fibroids or polyps do become pregnant. Problems with the uterus present from birth, such as an unusually shaped uterus, can cause problems becoming or remaining pregnant. Cervical stenosis, a narrowing of the cervix, can be caused by an inherited malformation or damage to the cervix. Sometimes the cervix cant produce the best type of mucus to allow the sperm to travel through the cervix into the uterus.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for female infertility include: 1. **Age**: Women's fertility declines significantly after age 35, with a sharp decline in ovulation and egg quality after age 40. 2. **Genetic predispositions**: Certain genetic conditions, such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), can increase the risk of infertility due to hormonal imbalances and ovulation problems. 3. **Medical conditions**: Conditions like endometriosis, uterine fibroids, and pelvic inflammatory disease can cause inflammation, scarring, and adhesions that can lead to infertility. These factors are among the most significant contributors to female infertility, but other lifestyle factors such as smoking, obesity, and lack of physical activity also play a role.
metadata.complications: Untreated or poorly managed female infertility can lead to several potential complications, including an increased risk of endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), and ovarian cysts. If left untreated, these conditions can cause chronic pain, infertility, and even infertility-related depression. Additionally, unaddressed infertility can also increase the risk of ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, and premature birth. The most significant complications that may develop if female infertility is not treated or managed properly include: 1. **Ectopic Pregnancy**: A life-threatening condition where a fertilized egg implants outside the uterus, often in the fallopian tube. 2. **Chronic Pelvic Pain**: Persistent pain and discomfort in the pelvic region, which can be debilitating and affect daily life. 3. **Infertility-Related Depression**: Mental health issues that can arise from the emotional toll of infertility, including feelings of isolation, anxiety, and low self-esteem. It's essential to seek medical attention if you're experiencing any symptoms or concerns related to female infertility. Early diagnosis and treatment can help prevent these complications and improve fertility outcomes.

metadata.symptoms: Symptoms vary depending on the type of sexual dysfunction. Symptoms may include: Low sexual desire. This most common of female sexual dysfunctions involves a lack of interest in sex and not wanting to have sex. Sexual arousal disorder. Even if you want sex, sometimes it may be hard to get or stay aroused during sex. Orgasmic disorder. You have ongoing trouble having an orgasm even with enough sexual arousal. Sexual pain disorder. metadata.causes: Sexual dysfunction problems often start when hormones change. This might be after having a baby or during menopause. Major illness, such as cancer, diabetes or heart disease, also can add to sexual dysfunction. Factors that add to sex problems include the following: Physical. Medical conditions can lead to sexual dysfunction. These may include cancer, diabetes, kidney failure, multiple sclerosis, heart disease and bladder problems. Certain medicines can decrease your sexual desire and make it harder for you to have an orgasm. These include some medicines to treat depression, high blood pressure, allergies and cancers. Hormonal. Lower estrogen levels after menopause may lead to changes in your genital tissues and how you respond to sex. Lower estrogen leads to less blood flow to the pelvis. This can cause you to have less feeling in your genitals and to need more time to become aroused and reach orgasm. The vaginal lining also becomes thinner and less stretchy. Not being sexually active can make this worse. These factors can lead to painful intercourse, called dyspareunia. Sexual desire also lessens when hormone levels drop. Your bodys hormone levels shift after giving birth and during breastfeeding. This can lead to vaginal dryness and affect your desire for sex. Psychological and social. Anxiety or depression that isnt treated can cause sexual dysfunction or add to it. So can long-term stress, a history of sexual abuse, worries of pregnancy and the demands of having an infant. Problems with your partner can affect your sex life. So can cultural and religious issues and problems with body image.

metadata.symptoms: The severity of fetal alcohol syndrome symptoms varies. Some children have far greater problems than others do. Symptoms of fetal alcohol syndrome may include any mix of issues with how the body develops; thinking, learning and behavior; and functioning and coping in daily life.
metadata.causes: When youre pregnant and you drink alcohol: Alcohol goes into your bloodstream. Inside the womb, the placenta provides oxygen and nutrients to a developing baby. The alcohol reaches your baby by passing through the placenta. Alcohol causes a higher blood alcohol level in your developing baby than in your body. Thats because a baby breaks down and gets rid of alcohol slower than an adult does. Alcohol is toxic to the babys cells. Exposure to alcohol before birth can harm how the body develops and cause permanent brain damage in the developing baby. The more you drink while pregnant, the greater the risk to your unborn baby. But any amount of alcohol puts your baby at risk. Your babys brain, heart and blood vessels begin to develop in the early weeks of pregnancy, before you may know youre pregnant. During the first three months of pregnancy, important stages of development happen with the face and organs such as the heart, bones, brain and nerves. Drinking alcohol during this time can cause damage to how body parts develop. And as the baby continues to develop in the womb, its damaging to drink at any time during pregnancy.

metadata.complications: Behavior issues after your child is born can result from having fetal alcohol syndrome. These are called secondary disabilities and may include: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Aggression, improper social behavior, and breaking rules and laws. Alcohol or recreational drug misuse. Mental health conditions, such as depression, anxiety or eating disorders. Challenges staying in or completing school. Not being able to get along with others. Challenges with independent living and getting and keeping jobs. Sexual behaviors that are not proper. Early death by accident, homicide or suicide. If you are pregnant and cant stop drinking alcohol, ask your obstetrician, primary care doctor or other healthcare professional for help. You also may choose to talk to a mental health professional. A social worker can direct you to community programs that offer help, for example, Alcoholics Anonymous. Because early diagnosis may help lessen the risk of some challenges for children with fetal alcohol syndrome, let your childs healthcare professional know if you drank alcohol while you were pregnant. Dont wait for your child to have issues before seeking help. If you adopted a child or are providing foster care, you may not know if the biological mother drank alcohol while pregnant. International adoption from some countries may have a higher rate of alcohol use by pregnant mothers. If you have concerns about your childs learning or behavior, talk with your childs healthcare professional to find out what might be causing these problems. metadata.symptoms: Fetal Macrosomia is a condition where a fetus grows significantly larger than average, typically exceeding 4 kg (8.8 lbs) at birth. The main symptoms and signs of Fetal Macrosomia include: 1. Excessive fetal size: Measuring over 4 kg at birth, which is above the 90th percentile for gestational age. 2. Difficulty during delivery: Macrosomic fetuses may experience difficulties during vaginal delivery due to their large size, leading to prolonged labor, instrumental delivery, or even cesarean section. 3. Increased risk of complications: Fetal macrosomia can increase the risk of maternal and fetal complications, such as gestational diabetes, hypertension, and respiratory distress syndrome in newborns. It's essential to note that not all cases of macrosomia are associated with significant health risks, and some fetuses may be born healthy despite being larger than average. However, regular prenatal monitoring and careful management during pregnancy can help minimize the risk of complications.
metadata.causes: Fetal macrosomia is a condition where a fetus grows significantly larger than average, typically weighing more than 4 kg (8.8 lbs) at birth. The primary causative factors of fetal macrosomia are maternal diabetes mellitus, particularly gestational diabetes, and obesity, which can lead to excessive insulin production and insulin resistance in the mother's body. This excess insulin can stimulate the fetus's growth, leading to macrosomia. Biological factors, such as genetic predisposition and hormonal imbalances, also play a role in fetal macrosomia. For example, women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) are at increased risk of developing gestational diabetes, which can contribute to fetal macrosomia. Environmental and lifestyle factors, such as maternal smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, and a high-calorie diet, have also been linked to an increased risk of fetal macrosomia. However, the exact mechanisms by which these factors contribute to the condition are not fully understood. It's worth noting that fetal macrosomia can also be caused by other factors, such as multiple gestations (twins or triplets), maternal hypertension, and certain genetic syndromes.
metadata.risk_factors: Possible health concerns of fetal macrosomia during labor and delivery include the following. Difficult labor. A large fetus can make childbirth harder. For example, during delivery fetal macrosomia can cause: A baby to become stuck in the birth canal, a condition called shoulder dystocia. Injuries to the baby during childbirth. Delivery with forceps or a vacuum device. This is called operative vaginal delivery. A C-section to be more likely. Birth canal injuries. During childbirth, fetal macrosomia can cause tissue in the vagina to tear. The muscles between the vagina and the anus, called the perineal muscles, also may tear. These tears are called genital tract lacerations. Bleeding after delivery. Fetal macrosomia raises the risk that uterine muscles wont properly contract after childbirth. That condition is called uterine atony. If the uterus doesnt contract as it should, that could lead to serious bleeding after delivery. Uterine rupture. For a pregnant person who has had a C-section before or has had major uterine surgery, fetal macrosomia raises the risk of uterine rupture during labor. This is a rare but serious health concern in which the uterus tears open along the scar from a C-section or other surgery. If this happens, an emergency C-section is needed to prevent health problems that could be life-threatening.
metadata.complications: Fetal macrosomia, a condition where a fetus grows significantly larger than average, can lead to several potential complications for both the mother and the baby. If left untreated or poorly managed, serious outcomes may include increased risk of cesarean delivery, shoulder dystocia, and birth asphyxia, which can result in permanent brain damage or other neurological injuries. Additionally, macrosomia has been linked to an increased risk of neonatal hypoglycemia, respiratory distress, and postpartum hemorrhage. In terms of secondary conditions, untreated fetal macrosomia may also contribute to the development of gestational diabetes, hypertension, and obesity in the mother, while the baby may be at higher risk for metabolic disorders, such as insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes later in life.

metadata.symptoms: A fever is a common medical condition characterized by an elevated body temperature above 100.4°F (38°C), often accompanied by other symptoms. The three to five key symptoms that patients typically experience include: (1) elevated body temperature, which can range from mild to severe; (2) chills or shivering, as the body attempts to generate heat; and (3) sweating, which is a natural response to try to cool down. Additionally, patients may also exhibit fatigue or malaise, and in some cases, headache or muscle pain, which are often indicative of an underlying infection or illness. Please note that this information is for general medical knowledge purposes only and should not be considered as a substitute for professional medical advice.
metadata.causes: Fever is a complex physiological response characterized by an elevated body temperature, typically above 37.8°C (100°F), in response to various stimuli. The primary causative factors of fever include infection or inflammation, which triggers the release of pyrogens, such as cytokines and prostaglandins, from immune cells. These pyrogens stimulate the hypothalamus, the temperature-regulating center of the brain, leading to an increase in body temperature. Biological factors play a crucial role in the development of fever, with the immune system's response being the primary trigger. Genetic predispositions can also influence an individual's susceptibility to fevers, with some people being more prone to developing fevers due to their genetic makeup. Environmental factors, such as exposure to pathogens or toxins, can also contribute to the development of fever. Lifestyle factors, such as stress and certain medications, can also impact the body's ability to regulate temperature, leading to fevers in some cases. However, it is essential to note that these lifestyle factors are not primary causative factors of fever, but rather secondary contributors to its development.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing fever include: * Age: Children under 5 years old are more susceptible to severe fevers due to their immature immune systems. * Medical conditions: Individuals with chronic illnesses such as diabetes, cancer, or immunodeficiency disorders are more prone to developing fevers. * Genetic predispositions: Certain genetic conditions like familial hypercholesterolemia and sickle cell disease can increase the risk of developing fevers. These factors can increase an individual's likelihood of developing fever, but it's essential to note that a fever is not exclusive to these groups.
metadata.complications: As a medical expert, I must emphasize that fever is a common symptom of various illnesses, and its potential complications can be severe if left untreated or poorly managed. If left unaddressed, fever can lead to serious outcomes such as sepsis, a life-threatening condition characterized by widespread inflammation and organ dysfunction. Additionally, prolonged fever can also increase the risk of developing secondary conditions like pneumonia, meningitis, or encephalitis. In rare cases, severe fever can also cause seizures, coma, or even death if not promptly treated with antibiotics or antipyretics. Furthermore, in vulnerable populations such as the elderly, young children, and those with compromised immune systems, untreated fever can lead to more severe complications like meningitis, encephalitis, or sepsis. It's essential to note that the severity of fever-related complications depends on various factors, including the underlying cause of the fever, individual patient characteristics, and the timeliness and effectiveness of treatment.

metadata.symptoms: A fibroadenoma is a solid breast lump that often causes no pain. It is: Round with distinct, smooth borders Easily moved Firm or rubbery A fibroadenoma often grows slowly. The average size is about 1 inch (2.5 centimeters). A fibroadenoma can get bigger over time. It may be tender or cause soreness a few days before your period. A large fibroadenoma may hurt when you touch it. But most often, this type of breast lump causes no pain. You can have a single fibroadenoma or more than one fibroadenoma. They can occur in one or both breasts. Some fibroadenomas shrink over time. Most fibroadenomas in adolescents shrink over many months to a few years. They then disappear. Fibroadenomas may also change shape over time. Fibroadenomas may get bigger during pregnancy. They might shrink after menopause.
metadata.causes: The cause of fibroadenomas is not known. They might be related to hormones that control your periods. Less common types of fibroadenomas and related breast lumps may not act the same as typical fibroadenomas. These types of breast lumps include: Complex fibroadenomas. These are fibroadenomas that can get bigger over time. They can press on or displace nearby breast tissue. Giant fibroadenomas. Giant fibroadenomas grow quickly to larger than 2 inches (5 centimeters). They also can press on nearby breast tissue or push it out of place. Phyllodes tumors. Phyllodes tumors and fibroadenomas are made of similar tissues. But under a microscope, phyllodes tumors look different from fibroadenomas. Phyllodes tumors typically have features associated with growing faster. Most phyllodes tumors are benign. This means they are not cancer. But some phyllodes tumors may be cancer. Or they could become cancer. Phyllodes tumors often cause no pain.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing fibroadenoma include: * Female gender: Fibroadenomas are more common in women, particularly during puberty and early adulthood. * Age: The majority of fibroadenomas occur between the ages of 15 and 30 years. * Hormonal influences: Estrogen levels may play a role in the development of fibroadenoma, with some studies suggesting that hormonal fluctuations can contribute to their formation. These demographic factors are the most significant risk factors for developing fibroadenoma.
metadata.complications: Common fibroadenomas do not affect your risk of breast cancer. But your risk might go up a bit if you have a complex fibroadenoma or a phyllodes tumor. Healthy breast tissue often feels lumpy. These changes happen rarely after menopause unless youre taking hormone replacement medicine such as estrogen or progesterone.
metadata.causes: Breast anatomy Enlarge image Close Breast anatomy Breast anatomy Each breast contains 15 to 20 lobes of glandular tissue, arranged like the petals of a daisy. The lobes are further divided into smaller lobules that produce milk for breastfeeding. Small tubes, called ducts, conduct the milk to a reservoir that lies just beneath the nipple. The exact cause of fibrocystic breast changes isnt known, but experts suspect that reproductive hormones  especially estrogen  play a role. Fluctuating hormone levels during the menstrual cycle can cause breast discomfort and areas of lumpy breast tissue that feel tender, sore and swollen. Fibrocystic breast changes tend to be more bothersome before your menstrual period and ease up after your period begins. When examined under a microscope, fibrocystic breast tissue includes distinct components such as: Fluid-filled round or oval sacs (cysts) A prominence of scar-like fibrous tissue (fibrosis) Overgrowth of cells (hyperplasia) lining the milk ducts or milk-producing tissues (lobules) of the breast Enlarged breast lobules (adenosis)
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing fibrocystic breasts include: 1. **Age**: Fibrocystic breast changes are more common in women over 40 years old, with the highest incidence occurring between 50 and 60 years of age. 2. **Genetic predisposition**: Women with a family history of fibrocystic breast disease or other breast conditions such as breast cancer are at higher risk. 3. **Hormonal fluctuations**: Changes in estrogen levels, particularly during menopause or pregnancy, can contribute to the development of fibrocystic breasts. These factors increase the likelihood of developing fibrocystic breasts, but it's essential to note that not all women with these risk factors will develop the condition.
metadata.complications: Having fibrocystic breasts doesnt increase your risk of breast cancer. Most fibrocystic breast changes are normal. However, make an appointment with your doctor if: You find a new or persistent breast lump or area of prominent thickening or firmness of the breast tissue You have specific areas of continuous or worsening breast pain Breast changes persist after your period Your doctor evaluated a breast lump but now it seems to be bigger or otherwise changed Request an appointment There is a problem with information submitted for this request. name: Fibromuscular Dysplasia
description: symptoms  symptoms of fibromuscular dysplasia depend on which artery or arteries are affected. some people dont have any symptoms. if the arteries to the kidneys are affected  common symptoms include  high blood pressure. problems with how the kidneys work. if the arteries affected supply blood to the brain  symptoms might include  headache. a pulsing feeling or ringing sound in your ears  called tinnitus. dizziness. sudden neck pain. stroke or transient ischemic attack.. causes  the cause of fibromuscular dysplasia is not known. changes in genes might cause the condition. because the condition is more common in women than men  researchers think female hormones also may play a role. but exactly how is unclear. fibromuscular dysplasia is not linked to womens use of birth control pills.

metadata.symptoms: Symptoms of fibromuscular dysplasia depend on which artery or arteries are affected. Some people dont have any symptoms. If the arteries to the kidneys are affected, common symptoms include: High blood pressure. Problems with how the kidneys work. If the arteries affected supply blood to the brain, symptoms might include: Headache. A pulsing feeling or ringing sound in your ears, called tinnitus. Dizziness. Sudden neck pain. Stroke or transient ischemic attack.
metadata.causes: The cause of fibromuscular dysplasia is not known. Changes in genes might cause the condition. Because the condition is more common in women than men, researchers think female hormones also may play a role. But exactly how is unclear. Fibromuscular dysplasia is not linked to womens use of birth control pills.
metadata.risk_factors: Things that increase the risk of fibromuscular dysplasia include: Sex. The condition is more common in women than it is in men. Age. Fibromuscular dysplasia tends to be diagnosed in people in their 50s. But it can affect anyone of any age. Smoking. People who smoke seem to have an increased risk of developing fibromuscular dysplasia. Smoking also can make the disease worse. Things that increase the risk of fibromuscular dysplasia include: Sex. The condition is more common in women than it is in men. Age. Fibromuscular dysplasia tends to be diagnosed in people in their 50s. But it can affect anyone of any age. Smoking. metadata.complications: Possible complications of fibromuscular dysplasia include: High blood pressure. The narrowing of the arteries of the kidneys causes higher pressure on the artery walls. Damage to the arteries may lead to heart disease or heart failure. Tears in the artery walls. Fibromuscular dysplasia and tears in the walls of the arteries often occur together. An artery tear is called a dissection. When a tear forms in one of the blood vessels in the heart, its called a spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD). A dissection can slow or block blood flow. Emergency medical treatment is needed. Bulge or ballooning of an artery. Also called an aneurysm, this complication can occur if the artery wall is weak or damaged. Fibromuscular dysplasia can weaken the walls of the affected arteries. An aneurysm that breaks open, called a rupture, can be life-threatening. Emergency medical treatment is needed for a ruptured aneurysm. Stroke. An artery tear or aneurysm rupture in the brain can lead to stroke. High blood pressure also can increase the risk of a stroke. If you have fibromuscular dysplasia, get medical help immediately if you have symptoms of a stroke, such as: Sudden changes in vision. Sudden changes in the ability to speak. Sudden or new weakness in the arms or legs. If you are concerned about your risk of fibromuscular dysplasia, make an appointment for a health checkup. The condition can rarely run in families. But theres no genetic test for fibromuscular dysplasia. Request an appointment

metadata.symptoms: Fibromyalgia is a chronic and complex medical condition characterized by widespread muscle pain, fatigue, and tender points. The main symptoms of fibromyalgia include: (1) Widespread musculoskeletal pain: Patients typically experience diffuse pain in multiple areas of the body, including the neck, back, shoulders, hips, and legs. This pain is often described as aching, burning, or stabbing and can be exacerbated by movement or stress. (2) Fatigue: Fibromyalgia patients often report persistent and profound fatigue that interferes with daily activities and sleep patterns. (3) Sleep disturbances: Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or experiencing restless sleep are common complaints among fibromyalgia patients. Additionally, many individuals experience morning stiffness, muscle spasms, and tremors. It's essential to note that the exact cause of fibromyalgia is still unknown, but it's believed to involve a combination of genetic, environmental, and hormonal factors. Key symptoms: 1. Widespread musculoskeletal pain 2. Fatigue 3. Sleep disturbances Note: These symptoms are not exhaustive, and individuals with fibromyalgia may experience additional symptoms such as anxiety, depression, cognitive difficulties, and gastrointestinal issues. A comprehensive diagnosis by a healthcare professional is necessary to accurately assess the condition and develop an effective treatment plan.
metadata.causes: Fibromyalgia is a complex and chronic medical condition characterized by widespread muscle pain, fatigue, and tender points. The primary causative factors of fibromyalgia are believed to be a combination of genetic predisposition, hormonal imbalances, and environmental triggers such as stress, trauma, or infections. Research suggests that individuals with fibromyalgia often have altered brain chemistry, including decreased serotonin and dopamine levels, which can contribute to pain sensitization and other symptoms. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of fibromyalgia, with evidence suggesting that genetic mutations may affect the functioning of pain-sensing nerve endings. Hormonal changes, particularly in cortisol and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), have also been implicated in the pathophysiology of fibromyalgia. Environmental factors such as stress, trauma, or infections can trigger the onset of fibromyalgia in susceptible individuals. Additionally, lifestyle factors such as sleep disturbances, physical inactivity, and poor nutrition may contribute to the development and maintenance of fibromyalgia symptoms. It's worth noting that the exact causes of fibromyalgia are still not fully understood, and more research is needed to determine the underlying mechanisms and potential triggers for this condition.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing fibromyalgia include: 1. **Genetic predisposition**: Individuals with a family history of fibromyalgia are more likely to develop the condition, suggesting a possible genetic component. 2. **Trauma or stress**: Experiencing physical or emotional trauma, such as a car accident or a major life change, can trigger the development of fibromyalgia in some individuals. 3. **Age and sex**: Fibromyalgia typically affects women between the ages of 30-50, with a female-to-male ratio of approximately 7:1. These factors are not exhaustive, but they are among the most significant risk factors for developing fibromyalgia.
metadata.complications: Fibromyalgia, a chronic condition characterized by widespread muscle pain, fatigue, and tender points, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. If fibromyalgia is not properly treated, it can increase the risk of developing secondary conditions such as depression, anxiety disorders, and sleep disturbances, which can significantly impact quality of life. Additionally, untreated fibromyalgia may also contribute to the development of chronic pain syndromes, gastrointestinal problems, and cardiovascular disease. The most significant complications that can arise from untreated or poorly managed fibromyalgia include: 1. **Depression and Anxiety Disorders**: Fibromyalgia is often comorbid with depression and anxiety disorders, which can exacerbate symptoms and reduce quality of life if left untreated. 2. **Sleep Disturbances**: Poor sleep quality and duration are common in individuals with fibromyalgia, leading to fatigue, decreased productivity, and increased risk of chronic diseases. 3. **Chronic Pain Syndromes**: Untreated fibromyalgia can lead to the development of chronic pain syndromes, such as complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) or neuropathic pain, which can be debilitating and require additional treatment. It is essential for individuals with fibromyalgia to work closely with their healthcare provider to develop a comprehensive treatment plan that addresses both the primary condition and any secondary conditions that may arise.

description: symptoms  most people have no symptoms associated with flatfeet. but some people with flatfeet experience foot pain  particularly in the heel or arch area. pain may worsen with activity. swelling may occur along the inside of the ankle.. causes  flatfeet is not unusual in infants and toddlers  because the foots arch hasnt yet developed. most peoples arches develop throughout childhood  but some people never develop arches. people without arches may or may not have problems. some children have flexible flatfeet  often called flexible flatfoot  in which the arch is visible when the child is sitting or standing on tiptoes but disappears when the child stands. most children outgrow flexible flatfeet without problems. people without flatfeet can also develop the condition. arches can collapse abruptly after an injury. or the collapse can happen over years of wear and tear. over time  the tendon that runs along the inside of the ankle and helps support the arch can get weakened or tear. as the severity increases  arthritis may develop in the foot.

metadata.symptoms: Most people have no symptoms associated with flatfeet. But some people with flatfeet experience foot pain, particularly in the heel or arch area. Pain may worsen with activity. Swelling may occur along the inside of the ankle.
metadata.causes: Flatfeet is not unusual in infants and toddlers, because the foots arch hasnt yet developed. Most peoples arches develop throughout childhood, but some people never develop arches. People without arches may or may not have problems. Some children have flexible flatfeet, often called flexible flatfoot, in which the arch is visible when the child is sitting or standing on tiptoes but disappears when the child stands. Most children outgrow flexible flatfeet without problems. People without flatfeet can also develop the condition. Arches can collapse abruptly after an injury. Or the collapse can happen over years of wear and tear. Over time, the tendon that runs along the inside of the ankle and helps support the arch can get weakened or tear. As the severity increases, arthritis may develop in the foot.

metadata.symptoms: The viruses that cause flu spread at high levels during certain times of the year in the Northern and Southern hemispheres. These are called flu seasons. In North America, flu season usually runs between October and May. Symptoms of the flu such as a sore throat and a runny or stuffy nose are common. You may also get these symptoms with other illness such as a cold. But colds tend to start slowly, and the flu tends to come on quickly, within two or three days after you come in contact with the virus. And while a cold can be miserable, you usually feel much worse with the flu. Other common flu symptoms include: Fever. Cough. Headache. Muscle aches. Feeling very tired. Sweating and chills. In children, these symptoms may show up more generally as being fussy or irritable. Children also are more likely than adults to have ear pain, feel sick to the stomach, vomit or have diarrhea with the flu. In some cases, people have eye pain, watery eyes or find that light hurts their eyes. metadata.causes: Influenza is caused by viruses. These viruses travel through the air in droplets when someone with the infection coughs, sneezes or talks. You can inhale the droplets directly. Or you can pick up the virus from touching an object, such as a computer keyboard, and then touching your eyes, nose or mouth. Its possible to spread the virus to others from about a day before symptoms appear until about 5 to 7 days after they start. This is called being contagious. Children and people with weakened immune systems may be contagious for a slightly longer time. Influenza viruses are constantly changing, with new strains appearing often. A persons first flu infection gives some long-term protection against similar strains of flu. But the vaccines offered each year are made to match the flu virus strains that are most likely to spread that season. The protection these vaccines offer lasts for months in most people.
metadata.risk_factors: There are a range of factors that may raise your risk of catching a flu virus or having complications from a flu infection. There are a range of factors that may raise your risk of catching a flu virus or having complications from a flu infection.
metadata.complications: If youre young and healthy, the flu usually isnt serious. Although you may feel awful while you have it, the flu usually goes away in a week or two with no lasting effects. But people at high risk may develop other health problems after the flu, called complications. Getting another infection can be a complication of getting the flu. That includes illnesses such as croup and sinus or ear infections. Lung infections are another complication. Infection of the heart muscle or heart lining may happen after getting the flu. And in some cases, people may have infection of the central nervous system. Other complications may be: Acute respiratory distress syndrome. Muscle damage, called rhabdomyolysis, or muscle swelling, called myositis. Toxic shock syndrome. Worsening of a chronic illness, such as asthma or kidney disease. Most people who get the flu can manage it at home and often dont need to see a healthcare professional. If you have flu symptoms and are at risk of complications, see your healthcare professional right away. Starting antiviral medicine within two days after your symptoms show up may shorten the length of your illness and help prevent more-serious problems. If you have emergency symptoms of the flu, get medical care right away. For adults, emergency symptoms can include: Trouble breathing or shortness of breath. Chest pain or pressure. Ongoing dizziness. Hard to wake up or confusion. Dehydration. Seizures. Worsening of existing medical conditions. Severe weakness or muscle pain. Emergency symptoms in children include all the symptoms seen in adults, as well as: Fast breathing or ribs that pull in with each breath. Gray or blue lips or nail beds. No tears when crying and a dry mouth, along with not needing to urinate. Symptoms, such as fever or cough, that get better but then come back or get worse. metadata.causes: Its not clear what causes follicular lymphoma. This cancer starts inside the follicle of a lymph node. A follicle is a group of cells inside the lymph node. The follicle contains germ-fighting white blood cells called B cells. When there is no infection to fight, the B cells rest in the follicle. When an infection happens in the body, the follicle can form an area that helps train the B cells to fight the infection.
