metadata.symptoms: Lactose intolerance is a common condition characterized by the inability to digest lactose, a sugar found in milk and other dairy products, due to a deficiency of the enzyme lactase. The main symptoms and signs of lactose intolerance include: * Bloating and gas: Patients typically experience discomfort, bloating, and gas after consuming lactose-containing products, which can be uncomfortable and embarrassing. * Diarrhea: Lactose intolerance often leads to loose, watery stools, which can be accompanied by abdominal cramps, nausea, and vomiting. * Stomach cramps: Painful stomach cramps are a common symptom of lactose intolerance, especially after consuming dairy products that contain high levels of lactose. * Nausea and vomiting: Some patients may experience nausea and vomiting after consuming lactose-containing products, which can be severe in some cases. It's essential to note that lactose intolerance is not the same as a milk allergy or sensitivity. If you suspect you have lactose intolerance, consult with your healthcare provider for proper diagnosis and treatment.
metadata.causes: Lactose intolerance is a common condition characterized by the inability to digest lactose, a sugar found in milk and other dairy products, due to a deficiency of the enzyme lactase. The primary causative factors of lactose intolerance are genetic mutations that affect the production or function of lactase, leading to reduced lactase activity in individuals who consume large amounts of lactose-containing foods. Additionally, environmental factors such as diet and gut microbiome composition can also contribute to the development of lactose intolerance. Biological factors play a significant role in lactose intolerance, as it is often inherited from one's parents. People with lactose intolerance have a lower number of lactase-producing cells in their small intestine, which are responsible for breaking down lactose into easily absorbed sugars. This reduced enzyme activity leads to the accumulation of undigested lactose in the gut, resulting in symptoms such as bloating, gas, and diarrhea. Environmental factors can also contribute to the development of lactose intolerance, particularly if an individual consumes large amounts of lactose-containing foods at a young age. A diet that is high in lactose can lead to increased pressure on the small intestine to produce more lactase, which can result in a decrease in lactase activity over time. Lifestyle factors such as diet and gut microbiome composition also play a role in lactose intolerance. Individuals who consume lactose-containing foods regularly may experience a decline in lactase production, leading to symptoms of intolerance. Additionally, an imbalance of the gut microbiome, which is composed of trillions of microorganisms that help break down food, can contribute to lactose intolerance by reducing the production of lactase. In summary, lactose intolerance is primarily caused by genetic mutations that affect lactase production or function, with environmental and lifestyle factors contributing to its development. Understanding these underlying mechanisms is essential for developing effective treatments and management strategies for individuals with lactose intolerance.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for lactose intolerance include: 1. **Genetic predisposition**: Individuals of African, Asian, or Native American descent are more likely to be lactose intolerant due to a lower production of lactase enzyme in adulthood. 2. **Age**: Lactose intolerance often develops after weaning, typically between 3-6 years old, and may increase with age as the body's ability to digest lactose declines. 3. **Dietary habits**: A diet high in dairy products or those who consume large amounts of lactose-containing foods can exacerbate symptoms of lactose intolerance. These factors highlight the importance of genetic background, age, and dietary choices in determining an individual's likelihood of developing lactose intolerance.
metadata.complications: Lactose intolerance occurs when individuals with a deficiency of lactase, the enzyme that breaks down lactose, a sugar found in milk and other dairy products, cannot properly digest it. If left untreated or poorly managed, lactose intolerance can lead to several serious complications, including malnutrition, weight loss, and gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea, bloating, and abdominal pain. The most significant complications of untreated or poorly managed lactose intolerance include: 1. Malabsorption of essential nutrients: Lactose intolerance can lead to the malabsorption of calcium, vitamin D, and other essential nutrients found in dairy products, which can cause a range of health problems. 2. Increased risk of osteoporosis: The malabsorption of calcium can increase the risk of osteoporosis, particularly in individuals with lactose intolerance who are also deficient in vitamin D. 3. Gastrointestinal damage: Chronic exposure to undigested lactose can lead to inflammation and damage in the small intestine, potentially causing long-term gastrointestinal problems. It's essential for individuals with lactose intolerance to follow a lactose-free diet or take lactase enzyme supplements to manage their symptoms and prevent these complications.

metadata.symptoms: Laryngitis is an inflammation or irritation of the larynx (voice box), which can cause a range of symptoms. The most common and characteristic symptoms of laryngitis include hoarseness, a raspy or gravelly voice, and a decrease in vocal pitch. Patients typically experience difficulty speaking or singing, with a strained or effortful voice that may be accompanied by a cough or sore throat. In some cases, patients may also experience shortness of breath, chest tightness, or a feeling of constriction in the throat. These symptoms can vary in severity and duration, but laryngitis is typically characterized by persistent hoarseness and vocal fatigue, which can last from a few days to several weeks if left untreated.
metadata.causes: Acute and chronic laryngitis have some causes in common. These include: Irritating substances that can be breathed in, such as chemical fumes, allergens and smoke. Acid reflux due to GERD. Repeated overuse of the voice, such as when you sing, talk loudly or shout a lot. Smoking.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing laryngitis include: 1. **Age**: Laryngitis is more common in children and young adults (under 40 years old), with the peak incidence between 5-15 years old. 2. **Recurring respiratory infections**: Individuals with a history of recurrent viral or bacterial infections, such as streptococcal pharyngitis, are at higher risk of developing laryngitis. 3. **Smoking and vocal abuse**: Prolonged exposure to smoke and excessive vocal strain can cause inflammation and irritation of the vocal cords, leading to laryngitis. These factors increase the likelihood of developing laryngitis, but it's essential to note that anyone can develop the condition, regardless of age or background.
metadata.complications: Laryngitis, an inflammation of the vocal cords, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. If not treated promptly, laryngitis can cause chronic hoarseness, breathing difficulties, and even lead to respiratory failure in severe cases. Additionally, untreated laryngitis can increase the risk of developing secondary conditions such as pneumonia, bronchitis, and vocal cord paralysis. In severe cases, if left untreated for an extended period, laryngitis can also lead to: * Vocal cord scarring and permanent voice loss * Aspiration pneumonia, where food or liquids enter the lungs * Respiratory failure, requiring mechanical ventilation It is essential to seek medical attention if symptoms persist or worsen over time.

metadata.symptoms: If youre allergic to latex, youre likely to have symptoms after touching latex rubber products, such as gloves or balloons. You also can have symptoms if you breathe in latex particles that are released into the air when someone removes latex gloves. Latex allergy symptoms range from mild to serious. A reaction depends on how sensitive you are to latex and the amount of latex you touch or inhale. Your reaction can become worse with each additional latex exposure.
metadata.causes: In a latex allergy, the immune system identifies latex as a harmful substance and triggers certain antibodies to fight it off. The next time there is a latex exposure, these antibodies tell the immune system to release histamine and other chemicals into the bloodstream. This process produces a range of allergy symptoms. The more times someone is exposed to latex, the more strongly their immune system is likely to respond. This is called sensitization. Latex allergy can happen in these ways: Direct contact. The most common cause of latex allergy involves touching latex-containing products, including latex gloves, condoms and balloons. Inhalation. Latex products, especially gloves, release latex particles. You can breathe in these particles when they become airborne. The amount of airborne latex from gloves differs greatly depending on the brand of glove used. Its possible to have other skin reactions when using latex. They include: Allergic contact dermatitis. This reaction results from the chemical additives used during manufacturing. The main symptom is a skin rash with formation of blisters 24 to 48 hours after exposure, similar to poison ivy. Irritant contact dermatitis. Not an allergy, this skin irritation is caused by wearing rubber gloves or exposure to the powder inside them. Symptoms include dry, itchy, irritated areas, usually on the hands. Not all latex products are made from natural sources. Products containing synthetic materials, such as latex paint, are unlikely to cause a reaction.
metadata.risk_factors: Certain people are at greater risk of developing a latex allergy: People with spina bifida. The risk of latex allergy is highest in people with spina bifida  a birth defect that affects the development of the spine. People with this disorder often are exposed to latex products through early and frequent healthcare. People with spina bifida should always avoid latex products. People who undergo multiple surgeries or medical procedures. Repeated exposure to latex gloves and medical products increases your risk of developing latex allergy. Healthcare workers. metadata.symptoms: Lazy eye, also known as amblyopia, is a common vision disorder where one eye fails to develop proper depth perception due to misalignment or weakness of the muscles controlling eye movement. The main symptoms and signs of lazy eye include: (1) Strabismus, or crossed eyes, which can be detected by observing how the eyes move when looking at an object; (2) Diplopia, or double vision, where the patient sees two images of a single object; (3) Difficulty judging distances and depth perception, leading to problems with spatial awareness and navigation; (4) Head tilting or turning to compensate for blurred vision in one eye, which can lead to postural difficulties and fatigue; and (5) Decreased visual acuity in the affected eye, often measured as a lower than normal Snellen fraction. It's essential to note that lazy eye is typically diagnosed in children, but it can also occur in adults due to various factors such as cataracts, glaucoma, or brain injuries. metadata.causes: Lazy eye, also known as amblyopia, is a common vision disorder that affects approximately 2-3% of children worldwide. The primary causes of lazy eye are biological and genetic factors, including anisometropia (a significant difference in refractive error between the two eyes) and strabismus (misalignment of the eyes). Additionally, environmental factors such as prolonged near work or poor visual development can contribute to the development of lazy eye. Biological factors play a crucial role in the development of lazy eye, as anisometropia can lead to uneven visual input to the brain, causing one eye to become dominant over the other. Genetic predisposition can also increase the risk of developing lazy eye, as some families may have a higher incidence of this condition. Environmental factors, such as prolonged near work or poor visual development, can contribute to the development of lazy eye by reducing the opportunity for normal binocular vision and depth perception.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing "Lazy Eye" (also known as Amblyopia) include: * Young age at onset: Children under 7 years old are more susceptible to developing amblyopia, with the highest risk between 2-5 years old. * Family history: Individuals with a family history of amblyopia or strabismus (crossed eyes) are more likely to develop the condition. * Premature birth or low birth weight: Babies born prematurely or with low birth weight may be at higher risk for developing amblyopia due to their brain's incomplete development. These factors can increase an individual's likelihood of developing Lazy Eye, but it's essential to note that many cases are not caused by a single factor and may require comprehensive evaluation and treatment.
metadata.complications: Lazy eye, also known as amblyopia, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. If left uncorrected, lazy eye can cause permanent vision loss in the affected eye, with the risk of blindness increasing significantly. Additionally, lazy eye can increase the risk of developing other eye problems, such as cataracts, glaucoma, and retinal detachment. In particular, the most significant complications include: * Amblyopia can lead to decreased visual acuity, reduced depth perception, and impaired binocular vision, making everyday activities challenging. * Untreated lazy eye can result in permanent vision loss, with some studies suggesting that up to 20% of children with untreated amblyopia may become completely blind in the affected eye by adulthood. * Poor management of lazy eye can also increase the risk of developing secondary conditions such as cataracts, which are a clouding of the lens in the eye that can lead to vision loss.

metadata.causes: Lead poisoning is a medical condition caused primarily by exposure to lead, which can occur through ingestion, inhalation, or skin contact with lead-based substances. The primary biological factor contributing to lead poisoning is the toxic effects of lead on the body's physiological processes, particularly its impact on the nervous system and hematopoietic (blood-forming) cells. Genetic predisposition may also play a role in an individual's susceptibility to lead poisoning. Environmental factors such as contaminated water, soil, or air can expose individuals to lead, while lifestyle factors like poor hygiene, inadequate housing conditions, and occupational exposure to lead-based products can also increase the risk of developing lead poisoning. Lifestyle factors that contribute to lead poisoning include: * Ingestion of lead-contaminated food or water * Inhalation of lead dust or fumes from old paint, pipes, or other sources * Skin contact with lead-based products, such as cosmetics or household cleaners Biological factors that contribute to lead poisoning include: * The body's inability to effectively remove lead through excretion * Lead's interference with the production of hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen * Lead's impact on the nervous system, including damage to brain development and function. Genetic factors that may contribute to lead poisoning include: * Genetic variations that affect an individual's ability to metabolize or excrete lead * Family history of lead exposure or poisoning Overall, lead poisoning is a preventable condition that can be caused by a combination of biological, genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for lead poisoning include: 1. Age: Children under 6 years old are at highest risk due to their developing brains and bodies, which can be more susceptible to lead's toxic effects. 2. Occupation: Workers in industries that use lead-based products, such as construction, mining, or manufacturing, are at increased risk of exposure. 3. Geographic location: Residents living in areas with high levels of lead contamination in soil, water, or air, such as urban areas with old housing stock or industrial sites, are also at higher risk. These demographic factors can significantly increase an individual's likelihood of developing lead poisoning.
metadata.complications: Lead poisoning can lead to severe and potentially life-threatening complications, including organ damage, neurological impairment, and cardiovascular problems. If left untreated or poorly managed, lead poisoning can cause permanent brain damage, kidney failure, and anemia, which can significantly impact a person's quality of life and increase the risk of mortality. Additionally, lead exposure has been linked to an increased risk of stroke, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease. In terms of specific complications, some of the most significant outcomes include: * Encephalopathy: Lead poisoning can cause damage to the brain, leading to cognitive impairment, seizures, and coma. * Nephropathy: Chronic kidney damage can lead to kidney failure, requiring dialysis or transplantation. * Anemia: Lead exposure can disrupt red blood cell production, leading to anemia, which can increase the risk of infections and other complications. It's essential to seek medical attention immediately if you suspect lead poisoning, as early treatment can help prevent these complications and improve outcomes.

metadata.symptoms: Left ventricular hypertrophy usually develops gradually. Some people do not have symptoms, especially during the early stages of the condition. Left ventricular hypertrophy itself doesnt cause symptoms. But symptoms may occur as the strain on the heart worsens. They may include: Shortness of breath, especially while lying down. Swelling of the legs. Chest pain, often when exercising. Sensation of rapid, fluttering or pounding heartbeats, called palpitations. Fainting or a feeling of lightheadedness.
metadata.causes: Anything that puts stress on the hearts lower left chamber can cause left ventricular hypertrophy. The lower left chamber is called the left ventricle. As the strain on the lower left chamber increases, the muscle tissue in the chamber wall thickens. Sometimes, the size of the heart chamber itself also increases. Left ventricular hypertrophy also may be caused by gene changes that affect the heart muscles structure. Things that can cause the heart to work harder and may possibly lead to left ventricular hypertrophy include: High blood pressure. Also called hypertension, this is the most common cause of left ventricular hypertrophy. Long-term high blood pressure strains the left side of the heart, causing it to grow bigger. Treating high blood pressure can help reduce left ventricular hypertrophy symptoms and may even reverse it. Narrowing of the aortic valve. The aortic valve is between the lower left heart chamber and the bodys main artery, called the aorta. Narrowing of the valve is called aortic stenosis. When the valve is narrowed, the heart must work harder to pump blood into the aorta. Intensive athletic training. Intense, long-term strength and endurance training causes changes in the heart. The changes help the heart handle the extra physical workload. But the changes can make the heart muscle grow larger. Sometimes this is called athletes heart or athletic heart syndrome. Its unclear whether the increased heart size in athletes can lead to stiffening of the heart muscle and disease. Certain conditions passed down through families, called genetic conditions, can make the heart thicker. They include: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. This condition is caused by changes in genes that cause the heart muscle to thicken. The thickening makes it harder for the heart to pump blood. It can occur even without high blood pressure. People with one parent with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy have a 50 chance of having the changed gene that causes the disease. Amyloidosis. Proteins build up around the organs, including the heart. The collection of proteins interferes with how the organs work. When the condition is passed down through families, it is called familial amyloidosis. It also may affect the nerves and kidneys.
metadata.risk_factors: Things that increase the risk of left ventricular hypertrophy include: Age. Left ventricular hypertrophy is more common in older people. So is high blood pressure, which can cause heart muscle thickening. Weight. Being overweight increases the risk of high blood pressure and left ventricular hypertrophy. Family history. Changes in genes passed down through families may lead to left ventricular hypertrophy. Diabetes. Having diabetes increases the risk of left ventricular hypertrophy. Female gender. Women with high blood pressure are more likely to get the condition than are men with similar blood pressure measurements. Things that increase the risk of left ventricular hypertrophy include: Age. metadata.complications: Left ventricular hypertrophy changes the structure of the heart and how the heart works. The thickened left ventricle becomes weak and stiff. This prevents the lower left heart chamber from filling properly with blood. As a result, blood pressure in the heart increases. Complications of left ventricular hypertrophy include: Heart failure. Irregular heart rhythms, called arrhythmias. Too little oxygen to the heart, called ischemic heart disease. Sudden, unexpected loss of heart function, breathing and consciousness, called sudden cardiac arrest. Seek emergency care if: You feel chest pain that lasts more than a few minutes. You have severe difficulty breathing. You have severe lightheadedness or lose consciousness. You have a sudden, severe headache, difficulty speaking, or weakness on one side of your body. If you have mild shortness of breath or other symptoms, such as palpitations, see your healthcare professional. If you have high blood pressure or another condition that increases the risk of left ventricular hypertrophy, your healthcare team is likely to recommend regular health checkups to check your heart. metadata.symptoms: Symptoms of Perthes disease include: Limping. Pain or stiffness in the hip, groin, thigh or knee. Limited range of motion of the hip joint. Pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest. Perthes disease usually involves just one hip. Both hips can be affected, but they usually are affected at different times.
metadata.causes: Perthes disease occurs when too little blood reaches the ball portion of the hip joint for a short time. Without enough blood, this bone becomes weak and collapses. The cause of the reduced blood flow is unknown.
metadata.risk_factors: Risk factors for Perthes disease include: Age. Perthes disease can affect children of nearly any age, but it most commonly begins between ages 4 and 10. Your childs sex. Perthes disease can affect children of nearly any age, but it most commonly begins between ages 4 and 10. Your childs sex. Perthes is about four times more common in boys than in girls.
metadata.complications: Children who have had Perthes disease are at higher risk of developing hip arthritis in adulthood  especially if the hip joint has poor healing. If the ball-and-socket joint doesnt fit together well after healing, the joint can wear out early. In general, children who are diagnosed with Perthes disease after age 6 are more likely to develop hip conditions later in life. The younger the child is at the time of diagnosis, the better the chances for the hip joint to heal in a typical, round shape. Make an appointment with your healthcare professional if your child begins limping or complains of hip, groin or knee pain. metadata.symptoms: Legionnaires' disease is a type of pneumonia caused by the Legionella bacteria, which can be found in contaminated water sources such as cooling towers, hot tubs, and plumbing systems. The main symptoms and signs of Legionnaires' disease include: High fever (usually above 103°F), often accompanied by chills, shaking, and muscle weakness; Coughing, which may produce yellow or greenish mucus; Shortness of breath, chest pain, and difficulty breathing; Headache, fatigue, and confusion.
metadata.causes: Legionnaires' disease is a type of pneumonia caused by the Legionella bacteria, which is typically found in water systems such as cooling towers, air conditioning units, and plumbing fixtures. The primary causative factors are contaminated water sources, particularly those with high levels of organic matter, nutrients, and pH imbalances, which allow the bacteria to thrive. Additionally, genetic predisposition and weakened immune systems can increase susceptibility to Legionnaires' disease. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of Legionnaires' disease, as the Legionella bacteria can cause infection when inhaled into the lungs. The bacteria produce toxins that trigger an inflammatory response, leading to symptoms such as fever, cough, and pneumonia. Environmental factors also contribute to the spread of Legionnaires' disease, particularly in settings with poor water quality management, such as hospitals, hotels, and other public buildings. Lifestyle factors, such as smoking and underlying health conditions, can also increase the risk of developing Legionnaires' disease. Genetic predisposition may play a role in susceptibility to Legionnaires' disease, as some individuals may have genetic variations that affect their immune response to the bacteria. Weakened immune systems, such as those seen in people with HIV/AIDS or undergoing chemotherapy, also increase the risk of developing the condition. It's worth noting that Legionnaires' disease is typically spread through aerosolized water droplets, which can be generated by contaminated water systems, making it essential to maintain proper water quality management and hygiene practices.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Legionnaires' disease include: 1. **Age**: Older adults (65 years and older) are more susceptible to severe illness and mortality from Legionnaires' disease. 2. **Immunocompromised individuals**: Those with weakened immune systems, such as HIV/AIDS patients or those undergoing chemotherapy, are more likely to develop severe illness and complications. 3. **Smoking**: Smoking can increase the risk of developing Legionnaires' disease by impairing lung function and making it harder for the body to fight off the infection. These demographic factors significantly increase an individual's likelihood of developing Legionnaires' disease.
metadata.complications: Legionnaires' disease, a type of pneumonia caused by the Legionella bacteria, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is respiratory failure, which can require mechanical ventilation support and may be life-threatening. Additionally, Legionnaires' disease can also cause secondary conditions such as acute kidney injury (AKI), sepsis, and multi-organ failure, which can significantly impact patient outcomes. In severe cases, untreated or poorly managed Legionnaires' disease can lead to serious outcomes, including: 1. Respiratory failure: This is a life-threatening condition that requires immediate medical attention. 2. Acute kidney injury (AKI): This can occur due to the infection causing inflammation and damage to the kidneys. 3. Sepsis: A potentially fatal condition that occurs when the body's response to an infection becomes uncontrolled. These complications highlight the importance of prompt diagnosis, treatment, and close monitoring of patients with Legionnaires' disease to prevent serious outcomes.

metadata.causes: Its not clear what causes leiomyosarcoma. This cancer starts when something changes the cells in the smooth muscles. Many areas of the body have smooth muscle tissue. These include the digestive system, urinary system, blood vessels and uterus. Leiomyosarcoma happens when smooth muscle cells develop changes in their DNA. In time, cancer cells can break away and spread to other parts of the body. When cancer spreads, its called metastatic cancer.

metadata.symptoms: Leukoplakia usually occurs on the gums, the insides of the cheeks, the bottom of the mouth under the tongue and, sometimes, the tongue. Usually it is not painful and it may not be noticed for a while. Leukoplakia may appear as: White or gray patches that cannot be wiped away. Patches with a rough, ridged, wrinkled or smooth surface, or a combination of these. Patches with shapes and edges that are not regular. Thick or hard patches. White patches of leukoplakia may appear along with raised, red areas called erythroplakia (uh-rith-roe-PLAY-key-uh). This combination is called speckled leukoplakia. These patches are more likely to show changes that may lead to cancer.
metadata.causes: The exact cause of leukoplakia is not known. But long-term irritation from tobacco use  smoked and smokeless  appears to be strongly related to many cases. Often, regular users of smokeless tobacco products get leukoplakia in places where they hold the tobacco between their gums and cheeks. The use of betel nut, also called an areca nut, may be a cause of leukoplakia. A betel nut packet, like smokeless tobacco, is held between the gum and cheek. Other possible causes may include ongoing irritation from: Long-term, heavy alcohol use. Jagged, broken or sharp teeth rubbing on tongue surfaces. Broken dentures or dentures that do not fit well. Your doctor or other healthcare professional can talk with you about what may be causing leukoplakia.
metadata.risk_factors: Tobacco use, particularly smokeless tobacco, puts you at high risk of leukoplakia and mouth cancer. Long-term, heavy alcohol use increases your risk. Drinking alcohol combined with using tobacco increases your risk even more. Tobacco use, particularly smokeless tobacco, puts you at high risk of leukoplakia and mouth cancer. Long-term, heavy alcohol use increases your risk. Drinking alcohol combined with using tobacco increases your risk even more.
metadata.complications: Leukoplakia usually does not cause permanent damage to the inside of the mouth. But leukoplakia increases the risk of mouth cancer. Mouth cancers often form near leukoplakia patches. And the patches themselves may show cancerous changes. Even after leukoplakia patches are removed, the risk of mouth cancer remains. Even though leukoplakia does not usually cause discomfort, sometimes it can suggest a more serious condition. See your doctor or other healthcare professional if you have any of these: White patches or sores in the mouth that do not heal on their own within two weeks. Lumps in the mouth. White, red or dark patches in the mouth. Changes in the inside of the mouth that do not go away. Ear pain. Problems swallowing. Problems opening the jaw. metadata.symptoms: A lipoma is a benign fatty tumor that can occur anywhere in the body, but it's most commonly found under the skin. The main symptoms of a lipoma are typically related to its size, location, and potential discomfort or irritation. Patients often experience: (1) a palpable lump or mass under the skin, which may be tender to the touch; (2) a feeling of heaviness or fullness in the affected area; and (3) occasional pain or discomfort, especially if the lipoma is located near a joint or nerve. In some cases, patients may also notice a slight swelling or redness around the lipoma due to inflammation or irritation. It's worth noting that lipomas are usually painless and don't typically cause any significant symptoms, but in rare cases, they can become infected or inflamed if not properly cared for.
metadata.causes: A lipoma is a benign tumor composed of fat cells that grow in the skin or under the skin. The main causes of lipoma are related to biological factors, such as genetic predisposition and hormonal influences. Additionally, certain environmental factors, such as exposure to radiation and certain chemicals, may also contribute to the development of lipoma. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of lipoma, as it is often associated with mutations in genes that regulate cell growth and differentiation. For example, mutations in the PTEN gene have been linked to an increased risk of developing lipomas. Hormonal influences, such as exposure to estrogen and testosterone, can also contribute to the growth of fat cells and lead to the development of lipoma. Environmental factors, such as radiation exposure and certain chemical exposures, may also increase the risk of developing lipoma. For example, studies have shown that workers in industries that involve high levels of radiation exposure are at a higher risk of developing lipomas. Additionally, some chemicals, such as pesticides and heavy metals, have been linked to an increased risk of developing lipoma. Lifestyle factors, such as obesity and physical inactivity, may also contribute to the development of lipoma. However, it is essential to note that these factors are not direct causes of lipoma but rather potential contributing factors that may increase the risk of developing this condition. It's worth noting that lipomas are relatively common and often benign, with most cases being small and asymptomatic. Treatment options for lipoma typically involve surgical removal or observation, as they do not pose a significant health risk.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing lipomas include: * Age: Lipomas are more common in adults over 40 years old, with a peak incidence between 50-70 years. * Obesity: Individuals with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher are at increased risk of developing lipomas due to chronic inflammation and insulin resistance. * Family history: Having a first-degree relative with a lipoma increases the likelihood of developing one, suggesting a possible genetic predisposition. These factors contribute significantly to the development of lipomas, although other lifestyle and medical conditions may also play a role.
metadata.complications: A lipoma, a benign tumor composed of fat cells, can potentially lead to several complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is nerve compression, which can cause numbness, tingling, pain, and weakness in the affected area. Additionally, lipomas can also lead to skin irritation, infection, and even cancer-like growths (liposarcomas) in rare cases. In rare instances, a lipoma can become large enough to compress nearby organs or structures, such as nerves, blood vessels, or joints, leading to serious outcomes like chronic pain, limited mobility, and decreased quality of life.

metadata.symptoms: During pregnancy, a listeria infection is likely to cause only mild symptoms in the pregnant person. But the effects on the baby can be devastating. The baby can die in the womb or have a life-threatening infection within a few days of birth. Symptoms of a listeria infection in a newborn can be subtle. But they can include: Little interest in feeding. Crankiness. High temperature, called fever, or low temperature, called hypothermia. Vomiting. Trouble breathing. Little to no energy. Low birth weight.
metadata.causes: Listeria infection is primarily caused by the bacterium Listeria monocytogenes, which can be found in various environments, including soil, water, and food products. The primary causative factors are contaminated food and water sources, particularly those that have not been properly refrigerated or handled, such as soft cheeses, unpasteurized dairy products, and deli meats. Additionally, individuals with weakened immune systems, such as pregnant women, older adults, and those with underlying medical conditions, are also at increased risk of developing listeria infection. Underlying mechanisms: The bacteria Listeria monocytogenes can cause infection through several routes, including ingestion, inhalation, or skin contact. Once ingested, the bacteria can colonize the gut and spread to other parts of the body, causing a systemic infection. The bacteria's ability to survive in refrigerated environments and its virulence factors, such as the listeriolysin O toxin, contribute to its pathogenicity. Biological and genetic factors: Listeria monocytogenes is a gram-positive bacterium that can cause infection in humans due to its unique biological characteristics, including its ability to form biofilms and survive in low-oxygen environments. The bacteria's virulence factors are also influenced by genetic mutations, which can affect its ability to invade host cells and evade the immune system. Environmental and lifestyle factors: Contaminated food and water sources, as well as poor hygiene practices, contribute to the spread of listeria infection. Pregnant women, older adults, and individuals with weakened immune systems are at increased risk due to their compromised health status. Additionally, individuals who work in high-risk environments, such as food processing plants or hospitals, may also be exposed to listeria bacteria. It's worth noting that listeria infection can be prevented by following proper food handling and storage practices, such as refrigerating perishable foods promptly and avoiding cross-contamination.
metadata.risk_factors: If youre pregnant or you have a weak immune system, be extra cautious about listeria. Take added safety measures with these types of foods: Soft cheeses and Mexican-style cheeses. Dont eat these, even if they were made using pasteurized milk. Some examples of soft cheeses are feta, brie, Camembert and blue cheese. Mexican-style cheeses include queso blanco and queso fresco. Hot dogs and deli meats. Stay away from these unless theyre reheated until steaming hot. Keep fluid from hot dog packages away from other foods, utensils and surfaces on which food is prepared. Wash your hands after handling these products. Use any opened hotdog packages in the refrigerator within one week. Use closed packages within two weeks. When you refrigerate lunch and deli meats or meat sliced at your deli, use opened packages within 3 to 5 days. Use closed packages of factory-sealed lunch and deli meats within two weeks of storing in the refrigerator. Meat spreads. Dont eat refrigerated meat spreads sold at a deli or meat counter, or from a stores refrigerated section. Canned meat spreads are OK. So are shelf-stable spreads, which can be safely stored at room temperature. Refrigerate after opening though. Smoked seafood. These products can be labeled as nova style, lox, kippered or jerky. Its OK to eat them in cooked dishes. Canned or shelf-stable smoked seafood also is OK. Raw or lightly cooked sprouts. Cook sprouts of any kind thoroughly. Cut melon. Eat the fruit right away or refrigerate it. Keep it refrigerated at 41 degrees Fahrenheit or lower, and use it within seven days. Throw out any cut melon thats left at room temperature for over four hours. Raw milk or milk products, also called unpasteurized milk. Do not use these at all. Only use pasteurized milk and milk products. Make sure the products label says pasteurized.
metadata.complications: Listeria infection, caused by the bacterium Listeria monocytogenes, can lead to severe complications if left untreated or poorly managed. The most significant complications include meningitis, sepsis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), which can result in long-term disability, organ failure, and even death. Untreated listeriosis can also cause fetal loss, stillbirth, and neonatal sepsis, making prompt medical attention crucial to prevent these outcomes.

metadata.causes: Liver cancer happens when liver cells develop changes (mutations) in their DNA. A cells DNA is the material that provides instructions for every chemical process in your body. DNA mutations cause changes in these instructions. One result is that cells may begin to grow out of control and eventually form a tumor  a mass of cancerous cells. Sometimes the cause of liver cancer is known, such as with chronic hepatitis infections. But sometimes liver cancer happens in people with no underlying diseases and its not clear what causes it.
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that increase the risk of primary liver cancer include: Chronic infection with HBV or HCV. Chronic infection with the hepatitis B virus (HBV) or hepatitis C virus (HCV) increases your risk of liver cancer. Cirrhosis. This progressive and irreversible condition causes scar tissue to form in your liver and increases your chances of developing liver cancer. Certain inherited liver diseases. Liver diseases that can increase the risk of liver cancer include hemochromatosis and Wilsons disease. Diabetes. People with this blood sugar disorder have a greater risk of liver cancer than those who dont have diabetes. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. An accumulation of fat in the liver increases the risk of liver cancer. Exposure to aflatoxins. Aflatoxins are poisons produced by molds that grow on crops that are stored poorly. Crops, such as grains and nuts, can become contaminated with aflatoxins, which can end up in foods made of these products. Excessive alcohol consumption. Consuming more than a moderate amount of alcohol daily over many years can lead to irreversible liver damage and increase your risk of liver cancer. metadata.symptoms: A liver hemangioma is a benign vascular tumor composed of abnormally large blood vessels, typically found in the liver. The main symptoms and signs of liver hemangioma are often asymptomatic or mild, making diagnosis challenging. However, some patients may experience the following characteristic symptoms: 1. **Abdominal discomfort or pain**: A dull ache or tenderness in the upper right abdomen is a common complaint among patients with liver hemangiomas. 2. **Weight loss and fatigue**: As the tumor grows, it can cause weight loss due to decreased appetite and fatigue resulting from decreased liver function. 3. **Nausea and vomiting**: Some patients may experience nausea and vomiting, particularly if the tumor is large enough to compress adjacent organs or structures. It's essential to note that many liver hemangiomas are discovered incidentally during imaging studies for unrelated reasons, such as abdominal pain or other medical conditions. In most cases, liver hemangiomas do not cause symptoms or complications, and treatment is usually reserved for symptomatic patients or those with large tumors.
metadata.causes: A liver hemangioma is a benign tumor composed of blood vessels that can occur in people of all ages. The primary causative factors for liver hemangioma are thought to be related to genetic mutations, with some studies suggesting a link between familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) and liver hemangiomas. Additionally, exposure to certain environmental toxins, such as vinyl chloride, has also been identified as a potential risk factor. Biological mechanisms underlying liver hemangioma involve the abnormal proliferation of endothelial cells, which line blood vessels, leading to the formation of a benign tumor. The exact mechanism is not fully understood, but it is thought to be related to mutations in genes involved in cell growth and differentiation, such as the PTEN gene. There is no clear evidence linking lifestyle factors or environmental exposures to liver hemangioma development. However, some studies suggest that individuals with a family history of FAP may be at increased risk of developing liver hemangiomas.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing liver hemangiomas include: 1. **Age**: Liver hemangiomas are more common in women, particularly those over 40 years old. 2. **Genetic predisposition**: Individuals with a family history of hemangiomas or other vascular malformations are at increased risk. 3. **Hormonal influences**: Women taking oral contraceptives or hormone replacement therapy may be more likely to develop liver hemangiomas. These factors contribute significantly to the overall risk, but it's essential to note that many cases of liver hemangioma occur in individuals without any known risk factors.
metadata.complications: A liver hemangioma, also known as a hepatic hemangioma, is a benign tumor composed of blood vessels that can cause potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is bleeding, which can occur due to rupture of the tumor, leading to hematemesis (vomiting blood) and potentially life-threatening hemorrhage. Another serious outcome is liver dysfunction, where the tumor can compress surrounding liver tissue, impairing its function and leading to jaundice, ascites, and other symptoms. Untreated or poorly managed liver hemangiomas may also lead to secondary conditions such as portal hypertension, which can cause varices (enlarged veins) in the esophagus, stomach, or intestines. Additionally, the tumor can grow and distort the surrounding liver tissue, potentially leading to cirrhosis, a condition characterized by scarring and damage to liver cells. It's worth noting that most liver hemangiomas are asymptomatic and do not require treatment, but if symptoms persist or worsen, medical attention is necessary to prevent these complications.

name: Loblastoma
description: symptoms  ameloblastoma often causes no symptoms  but signs and symptoms may include pain and a lump or swelling in the jaw. if left untreated  the tumor can grow very large  distorting the shape of the lower face and jaw and shifting teeth out of position.. causes  ameloblastoma begins in the cells that form the protective enamel lining on your teeth. rarely  it may start in gum tissue. the exact cause of the tumor is unclear  but several genetic changes (mutations) may be involved in the development of ameloblastoma. these changes may impact the location of the tumor  the type of cells involved and how fast the tumor grows. ameloblastomas are generally classified by type  but they can also be classified by cell type. the four main types include  conventional ameloblastoma. this is the most common type and grows aggressively  usually in the lower jawbone  and approximately 10 recur after treatment. unicystic ameloblastoma. this type is less aggressive  but typically occurs at a younger age. the tumor is often in the back of the lower jawbone at the molars. recurrence is possible after treatment. peripheral ameloblastoma. this type is rare and affects the gums and oral tissue in the upper or lower jaw. the tumor has a low risk of recurrence after treatment. metastasizing ameloblastoma. this type is very rare and is defined by tumor cells that occur away from the primary site in the jaw.

metadata.symptoms: Ameloblastoma often causes no symptoms, but signs and symptoms may include pain and a lump or swelling in the jaw. If left untreated, the tumor can grow very large, distorting the shape of the lower face and jaw and shifting teeth out of position.
metadata.causes: Ameloblastoma begins in the cells that form the protective enamel lining on your teeth. Rarely, it may start in gum tissue. The exact cause of the tumor is unclear, but several genetic changes (mutations) may be involved in the development of ameloblastoma. These changes may impact the location of the tumor, the type of cells involved and how fast the tumor grows. Ameloblastomas are generally classified by type, but they can also be classified by cell type. The four main types include: Conventional ameloblastoma. This is the most common type and grows aggressively, usually in the lower jawbone, and approximately 10 recur after treatment. Unicystic ameloblastoma. This type is less aggressive, but typically occurs at a younger age. The tumor is often in the back of the lower jawbone at the molars. Recurrence is possible after treatment. Peripheral ameloblastoma. This type is rare and affects the gums and oral tissue in the upper or lower jaw. The tumor has a low risk of recurrence after treatment. Metastasizing ameloblastoma. This type is very rare and is defined by tumor cells that occur away from the primary site in the jaw.
metadata.risk_factors: I must inform you that there is no such medical condition as "Lobastoma." It's possible that you may be referring to a different term, such as "Glioblastoma," which is a type of brain cancer. If that's the case, here are some significant risk factors for developing Glioblastoma: * Age: Glioblastoma typically affects adults over 50 years old, with most cases occurring in people between 55 and 75. * Genetic predisposition: Individuals with a family history of glioblastoma or other brain tumors may be at increased risk. * Radiation exposure: People who have received radiation therapy to the head or brain, especially at a young age, are more likely to develop glioblastoma later in life. Please note that these risk factors do not guarantee the development of Glioblastoma, and many people without these risk factors can still develop the condition.
metadata.complications: Rarely, ameloblastoma can become cancerous (malignant). Very rarely, ameloblastoma cells can spread to other areas of the body (metastasize), such as the lymph nodes in the neck and lungs. Ameloblastoma may recur after treatment. metadata.causes: Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS) is a non-invasive, pre-cancerous condition characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the breast lobules. The primary causative factors of LCIS include genetic mutations, particularly in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, which increase the risk of developing breast cancer. Additionally, environmental factors such as radiation exposure and certain hormone replacement therapies may also contribute to the development of LCIS. Biological mechanisms underlying LCIS involve the disruption of normal cell growth and division patterns, leading to the formation of abnormal cell clusters that can potentially progress to invasive cancer if left untreated. Genetic predisposition plays a significant role in the development of LCIS, with women having a higher risk of developing the condition if they have a family history of breast cancer or other genetic mutations. Environmental factors such as radiation exposure and certain hormone replacement therapies may also contribute to the development of LCIS by causing DNA damage and disrupting normal cell growth patterns. Lifestyle factors, such as obesity and physical inactivity, may also increase the risk of developing LCIS, although the evidence is less clear-cut. It's worth noting that LCIS is not a true cancer, but rather a marker for increased breast cancer risk. Women with LCIS are at higher risk of developing invasive breast cancer, but the condition itself does not progress to cancer without further genetic mutations or other factors.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS) include: Age: Women over 40 years old are at higher risk of developing LCIS, with the majority of cases occurring in women between 50-70 years old. Genetic predisposition: Family history and genetic mutations such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 increase the likelihood of developing LCIS. Lifestyle factors: Exposure to radiation and certain hormonal therapies may also contribute to the development of LCIS.
metadata.complications: I must correct you that Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS) is not a cancer, but rather a non-invasive condition where abnormal cells are present in the lobules of the breast tissue. However, if left untreated or poorly managed, LCIS can increase the risk of developing invasive breast cancer. If LCIS is untreated or poorly managed, potential complications include: Invasive breast cancer: The abnormal cells in LCIS can progress to invasive cancer, which can spread to other parts of the body and lead to serious outcomes such as metastatic disease, bone pain, and organ failure. Secondary conditions like lymphedema (swelling of the arms) or chronic pain may also develop due to the growth of new breast tissue or scarring from surgery. Additionally, LCIS can increase the risk of developing ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), a non-invasive cancer that can progress to invasive cancer if left untreated. Please note that LCIS is not a guarantee of future cancer development, and most women with LCIS will not develop breast cancer. However, it's essential for individuals with LCIS to work closely with their healthcare provider to monitor the condition and reduce the risk of developing invasive cancer.

metadata.symptoms: The most common symptom of long QT syndrome is fainting, also called syncope. A fainting spell from LQTS can happen with little to no warning. Fainting happens when the heart beats in an irregular way for a short time. You might faint when youre excited, angry or scared, or during exercise. If you have LQTS, things that startle you can cause you to pass out, such as a loud ringtone or an alarm clock. Before fainting happens, some people with long QT syndrome might have symptoms such as: Blurred vision. Lightheadedness. Pounding heartbeats called palpitations. Weakness. Long QT syndrome also can cause seizures in some people. Babies born with LQTS may have symptoms during the first weeks to months of life. Sometimes the symptoms start later in childhood. Most people born with LQTS have symptoms by age 40. Symptoms of long QT syndrome sometimes happen during sleep. Some people with long QT syndrome (LQTS) do not notice any symptoms. The disorder may be found during a heart test called an electrocardiogram. Or it may be discovered when genetic tests are done for other reasons.
metadata.causes: Chambers and valves of the heart Enlarge image Close Chambers and valves of the heart Chambers and valves of the heart A typical heart has two upper and two lower chambers. The upper chambers, the right and left atria, receive incoming blood. The lower chambers, the more muscular right and left ventricles, pump blood out of the heart. The heart valves are gates at the chamber openings. They keep blood flowing in the right direction. Long QT syndrome (LQTS) is caused by changes in the hearts electrical signaling system. It doesnt affect the shape or form of the heart. To understand the causes of LQTS, it may help to know how the heart usually beats. In a typical heart, the heart sends blood out to the body during each heartbeat. The hearts chambers squeeze and relax to pump the blood. The hearts electrical system controls this coordinated action. Electrical signals called impulses move from the top to the bottom of the heart. They tell the heart when to squeeze and beat. After each heartbeat, the system recharges to prepare for the next heartbeat. But in long QT syndrome, the hearts electrical system takes longer than usual to recover between beats. This delay is called a prolonged QT interval. Long QT syndrome usually falls into two groups. Congenital long QT syndrome. Youre born with this type of LQTS. Its caused by changes in DNA that are passed down through families. That means it is inherited. Acquired long QT syndrome. This type of LQTS is caused by another health condition or medicine. It usually can be reversed when the specific cause is found and treated.
metadata.risk_factors: Things that may raise the risk of long QT syndrome (LQTS) include: A history of cardiac arrest. Having a parent, brother, sister or child with long QT syndrome. Using medicines known to cause prolonged QT intervals. People who are assigned female at birth who take certain heart medicines. A lot of vomiting or diarrhea, which can cause changes in body minerals such as potassium. Eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa, which also cause changes in the levels of body minerals. If you have long QT syndrome and want to become pregnant, tell your healthcare professional. Your care team carefully checks you during pregnancy to help prevent things that can trigger LQTS symptoms. metadata.complications: Usually after an episode of long QT syndrome (LQTS), the heart goes back to a regular rhythm. But sudden cardiac death can happen if the heart rhythm isnt quickly corrected. The heart rhythm may reset on its own. Sometimes, treatment is needed to reset the heart rhythm. Complications of long QT syndrome may include: Torsades de pointes (twisting of the points). This is a life-threatening fast heartbeat. The hearts two lower chambers beat fast and out of rhythm. The heart pumps out less blood. The lack of blood to the brain causes sudden fainting, often without warning. If a long QT interval lasts for a long time, fainting can be followed by a full-body seizure. If the dangerous rhythm does not correct itself, then a life-threatening arrhythmia called ventricular fibrillation follows. Ventricular fibrillation. This type of irregular heartbeat causes the lower heart chambers to beat so fast that the heart trembles and stops pumping blood. Unless a device called a defibrillator is quickly used to correct the hearts rhythm, brain damage and death can happen. Sudden cardiac death. This is the swift and not expected ending of all heart activity. Long QT syndrome has been linked to sudden cardiac death in young people who otherwise appear healthy. LQTS might be responsible for some unexplained events in children and young adults, such as unexplained fainting, drownings or seizures. Proper medical treatment and lifestyle changes can help prevent complications of long QT syndrome. Make an appointment for a health checkup if you faint or if you feel like you have a pounding or fast heartbeat. Tell your healthcare team if you have a parent, brother, sister or child with long QT syndrome. Long QT syndrome can run in families, which means it can be inherited. Request an appointment

metadata.symptoms: Low blood pressure symptoms can include: Blurred or fading vision. Dizzy or lightheaded feelings. Fainting. Fatigue. Trouble concentrating. Upset stomach. For some people, low blood pressure may be a symptom of an underlying health condition. Thats especially so when blood pressure drops suddenly or when low blood pressure occurs with symptoms. A sudden fall in blood pressure can be dangerous. A change of just 20 mm Hg can make you feel dizzy or faint. For example, those symptoms could happen after a drop in systolic pressure from 110 mm Hg to 90 mm Hg. And big drops can be life-threatening. These can happen for reasons such as serious bleeding, serious infections or allergic reactions. Extreme low blood pressure can lead to a condition known as shock. Symptoms of shock include: Confusion, especially in older people. Cold, clammy skin. Decrease in skin color, also called pallor. Rapid, shallow breathing. Weak and rapid pulse.
metadata.causes: Low blood pressure has various causes. Some health conditions and the use of certain medicines can cause it. Other factors affect blood pressure as well. Blood pressure is determined by the amount of blood the heart pumps and the amount of resistance to blood flow in the arteries. A blood pressure reading has two numbers: Top number, called systolic pressure. The top number is the pressure in the arteries when the heart beats. Bottom number, called diastolic pressure. The bottom number is the pressure in the arteries when the heart rests between beats. The American Heart Association classifies healthy blood pressure as normal. Normal blood pressure usually is lower than 120/80 mm Hg. Blood pressure varies throughout the day. It depends on: Body position. Breathing. Food and drink. Medicines. Physical condition. Stress. Time of day. Blood pressure usually is lowest at night and rises sharply on waking.
metadata.risk_factors: Anyone can have low blood pressure. Risk factors for hypotension include: Age. Drops in blood pressure when standing up or after eating occur mainly in adults older than 65. Neurally mediated hypotension mainly affects children and younger adults. Medications. Certain medicines have the potential to cause low blood pressure. These include all medicines that treat high blood pressure. Certain diseases. Parkinsons disease, diabetes and some heart conditions can lead to low blood pressure. Alcohol or illegal drugs. Either of these may raise the risk of low blood pressure. Anyone can have low blood pressure. Risk factors for hypotension include: Age. metadata.complications: Complications of low blood pressure can include: Dizzy feeling. Weakness. Fainting. Injury from falls. Severely low blood pressure can lower the bodys oxygen levels, which can lead to heart and brain damage. If you have symptoms of extreme low blood pressure or shock, call 911 or your local emergency number. Most healthcare professionals consider blood pressure to be too low only if it causes symptoms. Minor dizzy or lightheaded feelings from time to time can be caused by many things. Causes could include spending too much time in the sun or in a hot tub. Its important to see a healthcare professional to find out the cause of your symptoms. If you often have low blood pressure readings but feel fine, you might not need treatment. Instead, your healthcare professional tracks your health during routine checkups. It can help to keep a record of your symptoms, when they occur and what youre doing at the time. metadata.symptoms: The main symptom of a low sperm count is not being able to start a pregnancy. There might be no other clear symptoms. In some people, an underlying health condition causes a low sperm count along with other symptoms. Depending on the condition, these other symptoms can include: Trouble with sexual function  for example, some people have low sex drive. Others have trouble getting or keeping an erection thats firm enough for sex, also called erectile dysfunction. Pain, swelling or a lump in the testicle area. Less facial or body hair or other symptoms of a chromosome or hormone condition.
metadata.causes: For the body to make sperm, the testicles and certain organs in the brain that produce hormones need to work properly. Once sperm are made in the testicles, sperm travel in delicate tubes until they mix with semen. Then semen is released from the penis, usually during an orgasm. Issues with any of these systems can lower the number of sperm in semen. When sperms movement or shape is irregular, that also can lessen fertility. Still, the cause of low sperm count often cant be found.
metadata.risk_factors: Many risk factors are linked with low sperm count and other issues that can cause low sperm count. Some risk factors are lifestyle choices, including: Smoking tobacco. Drinking alcohol. Using certain illicit drugs. Some health conditions can be risk factors, such as: Being overweight. Being very stressed. Having certain past or present infections. Having had trauma to the testicles. Being born with a fertility disorder or having a blood relative with a fertility disorder. Having certain health conditions, including tumors and long-term illnesses. Having a history of undescended testicles. Some treatments for health conditions also can be risk factors, including: Cancer treatments, such as radiation. Certain medicines. Vasectomy or major abdominal or pelvic surgery. Some things in a persons environment also may raise the risk of a low sperm count. These include being exposed to toxins. name: Lung Cancer
description: symptoms  lung cancer typically doesnt cause symptoms early on. symptoms of lung cancer usually happen when the disease is advanced. signs and symptoms of lung cancer that happen in and around the lungs may include  a new cough that doesnt go away. chest pain. coughing up blood  even a small amount. hoarseness. shortness of breath. wheezing. signs and symptoms that happen when lung cancer spreads to other parts of the body may include  bone pain. headache. losing weight without trying. loss of appetite. swelling in the face or neck.. causes  lung cancer happens when cells in the lungs develop changes in their dna. a cells dna holds the instructions that tell a cell what to do. in healthy cells  the dna gives instructions to grow and multiply at a set rate. the instructions tell the cells to die at a set time. in cancer cells  the dna changes give different instructions. the changes tell the cancer cells to make many more cells quickly. cancer cells can keep living when healthy cells would die. this causes too many cells. the cancer cells might form a mass called a tumor. the tumor can grow to invade and destroy healthy body tissue. in time  cancer cells can break away and spread to other parts of the body. when cancer spreads  its called metastatic cancer. smoking causes most lung cancers. it can cause lung cancer in both people who smoke and in people exposed to secondhand smoke. but lung cancer also happens in people who never smoked or been exposed to secondhand smoke. in these people  there may be no clear cause of lung cancer.

metadata.symptoms: Lung cancer typically doesnt cause symptoms early on. Symptoms of lung cancer usually happen when the disease is advanced. Signs and symptoms of lung cancer that happen in and around the lungs may include: A new cough that doesnt go away. Chest pain. Coughing up blood, even a small amount. Hoarseness. Shortness of breath. Wheezing. Signs and symptoms that happen when lung cancer spreads to other parts of the body may include: Bone pain. Headache. Losing weight without trying. Loss of appetite. Swelling in the face or neck.
metadata.causes: Lung cancer happens when cells in the lungs develop changes in their DNA. A cells DNA holds the instructions that tell a cell what to do. In healthy cells, the DNA gives instructions to grow and multiply at a set rate. The instructions tell the cells to die at a set time. In cancer cells, the DNA changes give different instructions. The changes tell the cancer cells to make many more cells quickly. Cancer cells can keep living when healthy cells would die. This causes too many cells. The cancer cells might form a mass called a tumor. The tumor can grow to invade and destroy healthy body tissue. In time, cancer cells can break away and spread to other parts of the body. When cancer spreads, its called metastatic cancer. Smoking causes most lung cancers. It can cause lung cancer in both people who smoke and in people exposed to secondhand smoke. But lung cancer also happens in people who never smoked or been exposed to secondhand smoke. In these people, there may be no clear cause of lung cancer.

metadata.symptoms: Lupus, also known as Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by widespread inflammation and damage to various organs and tissues in the body. The main symptoms of lupus can vary widely among patients, but some common and characteristic signs include: Fever, fatigue, and malaise are typical initial symptoms, often accompanied by joint pain and swelling, particularly in the hands and feet. Skin rashes, such as a butterfly-shaped rash on the face, chest, or back, are also common, while kidney problems, including proteinuria (excess protein in the urine) and hematuria (blood in the urine), can occur due to lupus nephritis. Additionally, patients with lupus may experience headaches, muscle pain, and swelling of the lymph nodes. Other symptoms can include hair loss, mouth sores, and a low platelet count, which can increase the risk of bleeding.
metadata.causes: Lupus is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by inflammation and damage to various tissues in the body. The primary causative factors of lupus are genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, and hormonal influences. Research suggests that genetic mutations in genes such as MHC class II, TNF-alpha, and IL-6 contribute to the development of lupus, while environmental factors like UV radiation, infections, and certain medications may trigger or exacerbate the condition. Biological mechanisms underlying lupus involve a complex interplay between immune cells, cytokines, and hormones. The immune system mistakenly attacks healthy tissues, leading to inflammation and tissue damage. This is often triggered by an imbalance in the immune response, where pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha and IL-6 dominate over anti-inflammatory cytokines. Environmental factors, such as exposure to sunlight, infections, or certain medications, can also contribute to the development of lupus. Additionally, hormonal influences, particularly during pregnancy or menstruation, may trigger lupus flares in susceptible individuals.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) include: 1. **Genetic predisposition**: Individuals with a family history of SLE, particularly first-degree relatives, are more likely to develop the disease. 2. **Age**: SLE typically affects women between the ages of 15 and 44, with the peak incidence occurring in young adulthood. 3. **Autoimmune disorders**: Having other autoimmune conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis or thyroid disease, increases the risk of developing SLE. These factors highlight the importance of genetic predisposition, age, and co-existing autoimmune disorders in increasing the likelihood of developing Lupus.
metadata.complications: Having lupus also increases your risk of: Infection. People with lupus are more vulnerable to infection because both the disease and its treatments can weaken the immune system. Cancer. Having lupus appears to increase your risk of cancer; however, the risk is small. Bone tissue death. This occurs when the blood supply to a bone declines, often leading to tiny breaks in the bone and eventually to the bones collapse. Pregnancy complications. Women with lupus have an increased risk of miscarriage. Lupus increases the risk of high blood pressure during pregnancy and preterm birth. To reduce the risk of these complications, doctors often recommend delaying pregnancy until your disease has been under control for at least six months.

metadata.risk_factors: Your risk for getting Lyme disease depends on if you spend time where they are likely to live. This includes the: Region. Deer ticks that carry Lyme disease are widespread. They are mostly found in the upper Midwest, the northeastern and mid-Atlantic states, and in south central and southeastern Canada. The castor bean tick is found throughout Europe. Habitat. Ticks live in wooded, shrubby or grassy areas. Time of year. The risk of infection is greater in the spring, summer and fall. But ticks can be active any time the temperature is above freezing. metadata.complications: Some people with Lyme disease report symptoms that continue after treatment. These longer-lasting symptoms may include: Arthritis that begins with Lyme disease and doesnt improve. Body aches and pains. Constant or frequent tiredness. Memory complaints. These conditions are not clearly understood. Some people with these symptoms may be diagnosed with post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, or PTLDS. These long-lasting problems may be caused by: Incomplete treatment. Reinfection with Lyme disease. Immune system response to fragments of killed bacteria. Immune system activity that harms healthy tissues, also called autoimmunity. Conditions other than Lyme disease that have not been diagnosed. Most people who get Lyme disease dont remember having a tick bite. And many symptoms of Lyme disease relate to other conditions. See your health care provider if you have Lyme disease symptoms. An early diagnosis and proper treatment can improve outcomes. If you know you had a tick bite or might have been around ticks, watch for symptoms. metadata.symptoms: Parts of the immune system Enlarge image Close Parts of the immune system Parts of the immune system The lymphatic system is part of the bodys immune system, which protects against infection and disease. The lymphatic system includes the spleen, thymus, lymph nodes and lymph channels, as well as the tonsils and adenoids. Leg lymphedema Enlarge image Close Leg lymphedema Leg lymphedema Lymphedema is swelling in an arm or a leg. In rare circumstances, it affects both arms or both legs. It can also affect the chest wall and abdomen. Lymphedema signs and symptoms include: Swelling of part or all of the arm or leg, including fingers or toes A feeling of heaviness or tightness Restricted range of motion Recurring infections Hardening and thickening of the skin (fibrosis) Signs and symptoms can range from mild to severe. Lymphedema caused by cancer treatment may not occur until months or years after treatment.
metadata.causes: The lymphatic system is a network of vessels that carry protein-rich lymph fluid throughout the body. Its part of your immune system. Lymph nodes act as filters and contain cells that fight infection and cancer. The lymph fluid is pushed through the lymph vessels by muscle contractions as you move through the tasks of your day and small pumps in the wall of the lymph vessels. Lymphedema occurs when the lymph vessels are not able to adequately drain lymph fluid, usually from an arm or leg. The most common causes of lymphedema include: Cancer. If cancer cells block lymph vessels, lymphedema may result. For instance, a tumor growing near a lymph node or lymph vessel could enlarge enough to block the flow of the lymph fluid. Radiation treatment for cancer. Radiation can cause scarring and inflammation of lymph nodes or lymph vessels. Surgery. In cancer surgery, lymph nodes are often removed to see if the disease has spread. However, this doesnt always result in lymphedema. Parasites. In developing countries in the tropics, the most common cause of lymphedema is infection with threadlike worms that clog the lymph nodes. Less commonly, lymphedema results from inherited conditions in which the lymphatic system doesnt develop properly.
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that may increase the risk of developing lymphedema include: Older age Excess weight or obesity Rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis Factors that may increase the risk of developing lymphedema include: Older age Excess weight or obesity Rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis
metadata.complications: Lymphedema complications may include: Skin infections (cellulitis). The trapped fluid provides fertile ground for germs, and the smallest injury to the arm or leg can be an entry point for infection. Affected skin appears swollen and red and is typically painful and warm to the touch. Your doctor may prescribe antibiotics to keep on hand so that you can start taking them immediately. Sepsis. Untreated cellulitis can spread into the bloodstream and trigger sepsis  a potentially life-threatening condition that occurs when the bodys response to an infection damages its own tissues. Sepsis requires emergency medical treatment. Leakage through the skin. With severe swelling, the lymph fluid can drain through small breaks in the skin or cause blistering. Skin changes. In some people with very severe lymphedema, the skin of the affected limb can thicken and harden so it resembles the skin of an elephant. Cancer. A rare form of soft tissue cancer can result from the most-severe cases of untreated lymphedema. Make an appointment with your doctor if you notice persistent swelling in your arm or leg. If youve already been diagnosed with lymphedema, see your doctor if there is a sudden dramatic increase in the size of the involved limb. metadata.symptoms: Swollen lymph nodes Enlarge image Close Swollen lymph nodes Swollen lymph nodes One of the most common places to find swollen lymph nodes is in the neck. This image shows three swollen lymph nodes below the lower jaw. Symptoms of lymphoma vary depending on the type you have and what part of the body it affects. Early-stage lymphomas may not cause symptoms. When they happen, symptoms of lymphoma may include: Swollen lymph nodes, which might feel like a lump under the skin. They happen most often in the neck, armpit and groin. Fever. Drenching night sweats. Fatigue. Weight loss without trying. Pain in the chest, abdomen or bones. Itchy skin. Cough. Lymphoma of the skin, also known as cutaneous lymphoma, can cause symptoms such as: A rash, patch or plaque on the skin. Itchy skin. A change in skin color. This change may be a shade of red, purple or brown depending on your skin color. Skin that is peeling and painful. A mass, also called a tumor, on the skin. If lymphoma involves the brain and spinal cord, also called the central nervous system, symptoms may include: Confusion. Double vision. Headaches. Hearing loss. Nausea. Vomiting. Weakness in the arms or legs.
metadata.causes: Its not clear what causes lymphoma. Cancer happens when cells develop changes in their DNA. A cells DNA holds the instructions that tell the cell what to do. In healthy cells, the DNA gives instructions to grow and multiply at a set rate. The instructions tell the cells to die at a set time. In cancer cells, the DNA changes give different instructions. The changes tell the cancer cells to make many more cells quickly. Cancer cells can keep living when healthy cells would die. This causes too many cells. In lymphoma, the cancer cells can build up in the lymph nodes, blood, bone marrow, spleen and other tissues throughout the body. Lymphoma gets its name from the kind of cell that makes up these cancers. These cancers start in germ-fighting white blood cells called lymphocytes.
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that can increase the risk of lymphoma include: A family history of lymphoma. Having a blood relative, such as a parent or sibling, with lymphoma may increase your risk of lymphoma. A weakened immune system or an autoimmune condition. Having a condition that affects the immune system can increase the risk of lymphoma. Conditions may include rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, inflammatory bowel disease and others. The immune system also may be weakened after organ transplant. Some infections. Some infections have been linked to lymphoma. These infections include human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), Epstein-Barr virus, human T-lymphotropic virus 1 (HTLV-1), Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), hepatitis C and others. metadata.complications: Complications of lymphoma may include: Relapse. Even after successful treatment, lymphoma may come back. This is called a relapse. Sometimes the relapse happens years later.
