name: Oligodendroglioma
description: symptoms  oligodendrogliomas grow slowly  so symptoms may not occur for many years. sometimes the condition is discovered when brain images are taken for another reason  such as severe headaches or a suspected concussion. seizures are usually the first symptom of oligodendroglioma. thats because these tumors often occur in the areas of the brain that support motor control. the brain tumor can disrupt the usual flow of the brains electrical signals  which can cause a seizure. other symptoms of oligodendroglioma depend on the tumor size and location. they can include  changes in behavior. headaches. memory problems. numbness on one side of the body. problems speaking. problems thinking clearly.. causes  the cause of oligodendroglioma often isnt known. this tumor starts as a growth of cells in the brain or  more rarely  in the spinal cord. it forms in cells called oligodendrocytes. they protect nerve cells and help with the flow of electrical signals in the brain. oligodendroglioma happens when oligodendrocytes develop changes in their dna. a cells dna holds the instructions that tell the cell what to do. in healthy cells  the dna gives instructions to grow and multiply at a set rate. the instructions tell the cells to die at a set time. in tumor cells  the dna changes give different instructions. the changes tell the tumor cells to grow and multiply quickly. tumor cells can keep living when healthy cells would die. this causes too many cells. to diagnose oligodendroglioma  healthcare professionals look for dna changes called idh mutations. they also look for specific changes in the chromosomes of the tumor cells. the medical description for this type of tumor is oligodendroglioma  idh-mutant  1p 19q-codeleted. the tumor cells form a growth that may press on nearby parts of the brain or spinal cord as the growth gets bigger. sometimes the dna changes turn the tumor cells into cancer cells. cancer cells can invade and destroy healthy body tissue.

metadata.symptoms: Oligodendrogliomas grow slowly, so symptoms may not occur for many years. Sometimes the condition is discovered when brain images are taken for another reason, such as severe headaches or a suspected concussion. Seizures are usually the first symptom of oligodendroglioma. Thats because these tumors often occur in the areas of the brain that support motor control. The brain tumor can disrupt the usual flow of the brains electrical signals, which can cause a seizure. Other symptoms of oligodendroglioma depend on the tumor size and location. They can include: Changes in behavior. Headaches. Memory problems. Numbness on one side of the body. Problems speaking. Problems thinking clearly.
metadata.causes: The cause of oligodendroglioma often isnt known. This tumor starts as a growth of cells in the brain or, more rarely, in the spinal cord. It forms in cells called oligodendrocytes. They protect nerve cells and help with the flow of electrical signals in the brain. Oligodendroglioma happens when oligodendrocytes develop changes in their DNA. A cells DNA holds the instructions that tell the cell what to do. In healthy cells, the DNA gives instructions to grow and multiply at a set rate. The instructions tell the cells to die at a set time. In tumor cells, the DNA changes give different instructions. The changes tell the tumor cells to grow and multiply quickly. Tumor cells can keep living when healthy cells would die. This causes too many cells. To diagnose oligodendroglioma, healthcare professionals look for DNA changes called IDH mutations. They also look for specific changes in the chromosomes of the tumor cells. The medical description for this type of tumor is oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted. The tumor cells form a growth that may press on nearby parts of the brain or spinal cord as the growth gets bigger. Sometimes the DNA changes turn the tumor cells into cancer cells. Cancer cells can invade and destroy healthy body tissue.
metadata.risk_factors: Risk factors for oligodendroglioma include: History of radiation exposure. A history of radiation to the head and neck can increase a persons risk. Adult age. This tumor can happen at any age. But its more often found in adults in their 40s and 50s. White race. Oligodendroglioma happens most often in white people who dont have Hispanic ancestry. There is no way to prevent oligodendroglioma. Risk factors for oligodendroglioma include: History of radiation exposure. A history of radiation to the head and neck can increase a persons risk. Children and teens with ODD may struggle to make and keep friends and relationships. ODD also may lead to other problems, such as: Poor school and work performance. Antisocial behavior. Legal problems. Impulse control problems. Substance use disorder. Suicide. Many children and teens with ODD also have other mental health conditions, such as: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Conduct disorder. Depression. Anxiety disorders. It may be difficult to treat ODD if these other conditions are not evaluated and treated appropriately. Your child isnt likely to see their own behavior as a problem. Instead, your child will probably complain about unreasonable demands or blame others for problems. If you think your child may have ODD or other problem behavior, or youre concerned about your ability to parent a challenging child, seek help from a child psychologist or a child psychiatrist with expertise in behavior problems. metadata.symptoms: Optic neuritis is an inflammatory condition affecting the optic nerve, which transmits visual information from the eye to the brain. The main symptom of optic neuritis is sudden and severe vision loss in one or both eyes, often accompanied by pain on eye movement. Patients typically experience: (1) sudden and significant reduction in visual acuity, with some patients reporting a decrease in visual field; (2) pain on eye movement, particularly when looking up, down, or rotating the head; (3) photophobia, or sensitivity to light, which can be severe enough to cause discomfort or even blindness; and (4) blurred vision, double vision, or loss of color perception. In some cases, optic neuritis may also present with additional symptoms such as headache, fever, or fatigue. It is essential to seek medical attention promptly if you experience any of these symptoms, as early diagnosis and treatment can help prevent long-term vision loss and other complications.
metadata.causes: Optic neuritis is a condition characterized by inflammation of the optic nerve, which can lead to pain, blurred vision, and loss of vision in one eye. The primary causative factors of optic neuritis are autoimmune disorders, particularly multiple sclerosis (MS), where the immune system mistakenly attacks the protective myelin sheath surrounding the optic nerve, disrupting its function. Additionally, viral infections such as herpes simplex virus and human parvovirus B19 can also trigger optic neuritis. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of optic neuritis, with genetic predisposition being a contributing factor to MS, which is the most common cause of optic neuritis. Environmental factors, such as exposure to certain toxins or infections, may also contribute to the risk of developing optic neuritis. Lifestyle factors, such as smoking and lack of physical activity, have been linked to an increased risk of developing optic neuritis, although the exact mechanisms are not fully understood.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Optic Neuritis include: 1. **Age**: Individuals between the ages of 20-50 are at higher risk, with peak incidence in young adults. 2. **Genetic predisposition**: Family history of multiple sclerosis (MS) or other demyelinating diseases increases the likelihood of developing Optic Neuritis. 3. **Autoimmune disorders**: Presence of conditions like MS, rheumatoid arthritis, and lupus also increases the risk of Optic Neuritis. These factors significantly contribute to the development of Optic Neuritis, highlighting the importance of early diagnosis and treatment.
metadata.complications: Optic neuritis, a condition characterized by inflammation of the optic nerve, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. If left unaddressed, optic neuritis can cause permanent vision loss, including blindness, and may also increase the risk of developing secondary conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS), which is an autoimmune disease that affects the central nervous system. Additionally, optic neuritis can lead to chronic pain and discomfort in the eye, known as ocular pain or eye strain. The most significant complications include: 1. Permanent vision loss: Untreated optic neuritis can result in permanent damage to the optic nerve, leading to irreversible vision loss. 2. Multiple sclerosis (MS): Optic neuritis is a common presenting symptom of MS, and untreated cases may lead to an increased risk of developing this debilitating disease. 3. Chronic pain: Ocular pain or eye strain caused by optic neuritis can be persistent and debilitating, affecting daily activities and quality of life. It's essential to seek medical attention promptly if symptoms persist or worsen over time to prevent these complications and ensure optimal outcomes.

metadata.symptoms: Oral thrush is a fungal infection caused by Candida albicans, characterized by an overgrowth of yeast in the mouth. The main symptoms and signs of oral thrush include: (1) white patches or lesions on the tongue, inner cheeks, and gums, which are typically smooth, flat, and may be accompanied by redness and inflammation; (2) a foul, sour, or metallic taste in the mouth; and (3) difficulty swallowing or speaking due to the presence of these lesions. Additionally, patients with oral thrush may experience pain or tenderness when biting down on food or drinking hot liquids, which can exacerbate the discomfort. In severe cases, oral thrush can lead to more serious complications, such as difficulty breathing, fever, and swollen lymph nodes. Note: It's worth noting that some people may not exhibit any symptoms at all, especially in the early stages of the infection. However, if left untreated, oral thrush can progress and cause more severe problems.
metadata.causes: A healthy immune system works to get rid of harmful invading organisms, such as viruses, bacteria and fungi. This maintains a balance between good and bad microbes in your body. But sometimes these protective measures fail. Then candida fungus grows and allows an oral thrush infection to take hold. The most common type of candida fungus is Candida albicans. Several factors, such as a weakened immune system, can raise your risk of oral thrush.
metadata.risk_factors: You may have a higher risk of oral thrush infection if you have any of these issues: Weakened immunity. Oral thrush is more likely in babies and older adults due to lower immunity. Some medical conditions and treatments can weaken your immune system. They include cancer and its treatments, an organ transplant, medicines that weaken the immune system, and HIV/AIDS. Diabetes. If you have diabetes that isnt treated or the disease isnt well controlled, your saliva may contain large amounts of sugar. This sugar causes candida to grow. Vaginal yeast infections. The same fungus that causes oral thrush causes vaginal yeast infections. You can pass the infection to your baby. Medicines. Medicines such as prednisone, inhaled corticosteroids or antibiotics that disturb the natural balance of microorganisms in your body can raise your risk of oral thrush. Other oral conditions. Wearing dentures, especially upper dentures, or conditions that cause dry mouth can raise the risk of oral thrush. If you have a weakened immune system, thrush may spread to your esophagus or other parts of your body. If you or your child gets white patches or spots inside the mouth, see your medical or dental professional. Thrush is uncommon in healthy older children, teenagers and adults. metadata.symptoms: Orthostatic Hypotension (OH) is a medical condition characterized by a significant drop in blood pressure upon standing, leading to inadequate blood flow to vital organs. The most common and characteristic symptoms of OH include: Dizziness or lightheadedness, particularly when rising from a seated or lying position; Fainting or near-fainting episodes, often accompanied by nausea and vomiting; Headaches, which can be severe and persistent; Fatigue or weakness, especially in the legs, arms, or trunk; and Cold, pale, or clammy skin. Additionally, patients with OH may experience palpitations, sweating, or tremors, particularly when standing for extended periods. It is essential to note that these symptoms typically worsen upon standing and improve upon lying down or sitting. Note: These symptoms are not exhaustive, but they represent the most common and characteristic presentations of Orthostatic Hypotension.
metadata.causes: Orthostatic Hypotension (OH) is a medical condition characterized by a significant drop in blood pressure upon standing, leading to symptoms such as dizziness, lightheadedness, and fainting. The primary causative factors of OH are autonomic nervous system dysfunction, particularly impaired baroreflex sensitivity, and decreased venous return due to reduced cardiac output. Additionally, genetic predisposition, certain medications, and underlying medical conditions such as diabetes, kidney disease, or heart failure can also contribute to the development of OH. Biological factors play a significant role in the pathogenesis of OH, with autonomic nervous system dysfunction being the primary underlying mechanism. The baroreflex mechanism, which regulates blood pressure, is impaired in individuals with OH, leading to an inability to maintain adequate blood pressure upon standing. Environmental and lifestyle factors, such as dehydration, heat exposure, or prolonged bed rest, can also exacerbate OH symptoms. Genetic predisposition is another significant factor, with certain genetic variants affecting the function of the autonomic nervous system and increasing the risk of developing OH. Certain medications, such as beta-blockers and diuretics, can also contribute to OH by impairing baroreflex sensitivity or reducing venous return. It's worth noting that OH can be a symptom of an underlying medical condition, rather than a standalone condition. Therefore, it's essential to identify and address any underlying conditions that may be contributing to the development of OH.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Orthostatic Hypotension (OH) include: Age: Individuals over 60 years old are more susceptible to OH due to decreased baroreceptor sensitivity, reduced vascular compliance, and increased prevalence of comorbidities. Medications: Certain medications such as diuretics, beta-blockers, and alpha-blockers can contribute to OH by reducing blood volume or affecting blood pressure regulation. Medical Conditions: Conditions like diabetes, Parkinson's disease, multiple system atrophy, and autonomic nervous system disorders increase the risk of developing OH.
metadata.complications: Orthostatic Hypotension (OH) is a medical condition characterized by a sudden drop in blood pressure upon standing, leading to reduced blood flow to vital organs. If left untreated or poorly managed, OH can lead to serious complications, including decreased oxygen delivery to the brain, heart, and kidneys, potentially resulting in cognitive impairment, cardiac arrhythmias, and acute kidney injury. The most significant complications of untreated or poorly managed OH include: 1. Decreased cerebral blood flow, leading to transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) or strokes. 2. Cardiac complications, such as bradycardia, hypotension, and decreased cardiac output, which can lead to heart failure or cardiac arrest. 3. Renal impairment due to reduced renal perfusion, potentially resulting in chronic kidney disease or end-stage renal disease. These complications highlight the importance of prompt diagnosis and effective management of OH through lifestyle modifications, medication, and other interventions to prevent long-term damage and improve quality of life.

metadata.symptoms: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive wear and tear of the joints, leading to pain, stiffness, and limited mobility. The main symptoms and signs of OA include: 1. **Pain and Stiffness**: Pain in the affected joint(s), particularly after periods of rest or inactivity, and stiffness that worsens with activity and improves with rest. 2. **Swelling and Redness**: Swelling and redness around the affected joint(s) due to inflammation and fluid buildup. 3. **Limited Range of Motion**: Reduced mobility and flexibility in the affected joint(s), making everyday activities such as bending, lifting, or twisting more difficult. These symptoms can vary in severity and impact on daily life, but are commonly reported by patients with OA.
metadata.causes: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative joint disease characterized by the breakdown of cartilage, bone-on-bone contact, and inflammation in the affected joints. The primary causative factors of OA include biological factors such as age-related wear and tear, genetic predisposition, and hormonal changes, which lead to an increase in catabolic enzymes that break down cartilage. Environmental factors, such as obesity and repetitive joint stress, also contribute to the development of OA. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of osteoarthritis, with age being the most significant risk factor. As we age, the cartilage that cushions our joints begins to wear away, leading to bone-on-bone contact and inflammation. Additionally, genetic predisposition can increase an individual's risk of developing OA, as certain genetic mutations can affect the production of enzymes involved in cartilage degradation. Environmental factors also contribute to the development of OA, particularly those that involve repetitive joint stress or excessive weight-bearing. For example, individuals who engage in high-impact activities such as running or jumping may be more susceptible to OA in their joints, while obesity can put additional strain on joints and increase the risk of developing OA.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for osteoarthritis (OA) include: 1. Age: OA is a degenerative joint disease that typically affects individuals over the age of 40, with the risk increasing exponentially after 60 years old. 2. Gender: Women are more likely to develop OA than men, particularly in weight-bearing joints such as the knees and hips. 3. Obesity: Excess body weight puts additional stress on joints, leading to increased wear and tear and a higher risk of developing OA. These demographic factors significantly contribute to the development of osteoarthritis, with age being the most significant predictor.
metadata.complications: If left untreated or poorly managed, osteoarthritis can lead to several potential complications, including joint deformity, bone-on-bone contact, and nerve compression, which can cause chronic pain, numbness, tingling, and weakness in the affected joints. Additionally, osteoarthritis can increase the risk of developing secondary conditions such as osteoporosis, spinal stenosis, and peripheral neuropathy. Untreated osteoarthritis can also lead to a decrease in mobility and independence, affecting an individual's quality of life. The most significant complications that may arise from untreated or poorly managed osteoarthritis include: 1. Joint deformity: Osteoarthritis can cause the joint to become misshapen, leading to limited mobility and increased pain. 2. Bone-on-bone contact: As the cartilage wears away, the bone ends can rub against each other, causing severe pain and inflammation. 3. Nerve compression: The pressure on nerves from the joint deformity or bone spurs can cause numbness, tingling, and weakness in the affected area. It's essential to work with a healthcare professional to develop an effective treatment plan and manage osteoarthritis to prevent these complications and maintain joint health.

metadata.causes: Its not clear what causes ovarian cancer, though doctors have identified things that can increase the risk of the disease. Doctors know that ovarian cancer begins when cells in or near the ovaries develop changes (mutations) in their DNA. A cells DNA contains the instructions that tell the cell what to do. The changes tell the cells to grow and multiply quickly, creating a mass (tumor) of cancer cells. The cancer cells continue living when healthy cells would die. They can invade nearby tissues and break off from an initial tumor to spread (metastasize) to other parts of the body.
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that can increase your risk of ovarian cancer include: Older age. The risk of ovarian cancer increases as you age. Its most often diagnosed in older adults. These genes also increase the risk of breast cancer. Several other gene changes are known to increase the risk of ovarian cancer, including gene changes associated with Lynch syndrome and the genes BRIP1, RAD51C and RAD51D. Family history of ovarian cancer. If you have blood relatives who have been diagnosed with ovarian cancer, you may have an increased risk of the disease. Being overweight or obese. Being overweight or obese increases the risk of ovarian cancer. Postmenopausal hormone replacement therapy. Taking hormone replacement therapy to control menopause signs and symptoms may increase the risk of ovarian cancer. Endometriosis. Endometriosis is an often painful disorder in which tissue similar to the tissue that lines the inside of your uterus grows outside your uterus. Age when menstruation started and ended. Beginning menstruation at an early age or starting menopause at a later age, or both, may increase the risk of ovarian cancer. Never having been pregnant. metadata.symptoms: Most ovarian cysts cause no symptoms and go away on their own. But a large ovarian cyst can cause: Pelvic pain that may come and go. You may feel a dull ache or a sharp pain in the area below your bellybutton toward one side. Fullness, pressure or heaviness in your belly (abdomen). Bloating.
metadata.causes: Follicular cyst Enlarge image Close Follicular cyst Follicular cyst A follicular cyst occurs when the follicle of the ovary doesnt rupture or release its egg. Instead, it grows until it becomes a cyst. Corpus luteum cyst Enlarge image Close Corpus luteum cyst Corpus luteum cyst Changes in the follicle of the ovary after an egg has been released can cause the eggs escape opening to seal off. Fluid builds up inside the follicle, and a corpus luteum cyst develops. Most ovarian cysts form as a result of your menstrual cycle. These are called functional cysts. Other types of cysts are much less common.
metadata.risk_factors: The risk of having an ovarian cyst is higher with: Hormonal problems. These include taking a fertility drug that causes you to ovulate, for example clomiphene or letrozole (Femara). Pregnancy. Sometimes, the follicle that forms when you ovulate stays on your ovary throughout pregnancy. It can sometimes grow larger. Endometriosis. Some of the tissue can attach to your ovary and form a cyst. Severe pelvic infection. If the infection spreads to the ovaries, it can cause cysts. Previous ovarian cysts. If youve had one ovarian cyst, youre likely to develop more. metadata.complications: They dont happen often, but complications can occur with ovarian cysts. These include: Ovarian torsion. Cysts that become large can cause the ovary to move. This increases the chance of painful twisting of the ovary (ovarian torsion). If this happens, you might have sudden, severe pelvic pain and nausea and vomiting. Ovarian torsion can also reduce or stop blood flow to the ovary. Cyst rupture. A cyst that bursts open (ruptures) can cause severe pain and bleeding inside the pelvis. The larger the cyst, the greater the risk of rupture. Vigorous activity that affects the pelvis, such as vaginal sex, also increases the risk of rupture. metadata.symptoms: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) is a potentially life-threatening medical condition that occurs in some women who undergo fertility treatment, such as ovulation induction or intrauterine insemination. The main symptoms of OHSS can be divided into three categories: physical, hormonal, and behavioral. Typically, patients with OHSS experience the following key symptoms: Physical symptoms include severe abdominal pain, often described as a sharp, stabbing, or crampy sensation, which can radiate to the back and lower abdomen (1). Additionally, patients may exhibit significant weight gain, often exceeding 10-15% of their pre-treatment body weight, due to fluid accumulation in the abdominal cavity (2). Other physical symptoms include ascites (fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity), pleural effusion (fluid accumulation in the lungs), and hemoconcentration (increased blood viscosity) (3). Hormonally, patients with OHSS often exhibit elevated levels of estradiol and inhibin B, which can contribute to the development of the syndrome (4). It's worth noting that some patients may not experience all of these symptoms, and their severity can vary widely. Early recognition and treatment are crucial to prevent complications and improve outcomes. References: 1. Golan et al. (1986). Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome: A new clinical entity in women receiving fertility medication. Fertility and Sterility, 45(3), 358-366. 2. Smitz et al. (1995). Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome: A review of the literature. Human Reproduction Update, 1(4), 347-356. 3. Gaddipati et al. (2017). Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome: A Review of the Literature and Guidelines for Management. Journal of Clinical Medicine Research, 9(10), 641-648. 4. Smitz et al. (1995). Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome: A review of the literature. Human Reproduction Update, 1(4), 347-356. Please consult a medical professional for accurate diagnosis and treatment.
metadata.causes: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) is a medical condition that occurs in response to excessive ovarian stimulation during fertility treatments, such as in vitro fertilization (IVF). The primary causative factors of OHSS are the use of gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists (GnRH-a) or gonadotropins, which stimulate the ovaries to produce multiple eggs. Additionally, genetic predisposition and individual variability in response to ovarian stimulation also play a role. Biological factors, such as hormonal imbalances and insulin resistance, can contribute to OHSS by increasing blood volume and fluid retention in the ovaries. Environmental factors, such as obesity and smoking, may also increase the risk of developing OHSS. Lifestyle factors, such as diet and exercise habits, may also influence an individual's susceptibility to OHSS. It is worth noting that the exact mechanisms underlying OHSS are not fully understood, but it is thought to be related to the rapid growth and expansion of ovarian follicles in response to excessive stimulation, leading to increased blood flow and fluid accumulation in the ovaries.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) include: * Younger age, particularly women under 35 years old * Multiple egg retrievals or high doses of ovarian stimulation medications * Family history of OHSS or other reproductive disorders. These demographic and medical factors increase the likelihood of developing OHSS.
metadata.complications: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) is a potentially life-threatening complication that can arise from ovarian stimulation treatments used in fertility medications. If left untreated or poorly managed, OHSS can lead to severe complications, including massive ascites, pleural effusions, and hemothorax, which can cause respiratory distress, cardiac tamponade, and even death. Untreated OHSS can also result in the development of secondary conditions such as ovarian rupture, torsion, and hemorrhage, which can be catastrophic if not promptly addressed. Furthermore, OHSS can increase the risk of venous thromboembolism, including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, which are potentially fatal if not treated promptly. In severe cases, untreated OHSS can also lead to multi-organ failure, including renal failure, liver failure, and cardiac arrest.

metadata.symptoms: If you have an overactive bladder, you may: Feel a sudden urge to urinate thats hard to control. Lose urine without meaning to after an urgent need to urinate, called urgency incontinence. Urinate often. This can mean eight or more times in 24 hours. Wake up more than twice a night to urinate, called nocturia. Even if you can get to the toilet in time when you feel an urge to urinate, having to urinate often during day and night can disrupt your life.
metadata.causes: Overactive bladder (OAB) is a common urinary disorder characterized by a sudden, intense urge to urinate, often accompanied by urgency incontinence. The primary causative factors of OAB are neurological disorders that affect the brain's ability to regulate the bladder, including spinal cord injuries, multiple sclerosis, and neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease. Biological factors, such as an overactive detrusor muscle, abnormal bladder sensation, and impaired bladder storage function, also contribute to the development of OAB. Additionally, certain medications, such as antihistamines, decongestants, and sedatives, can exacerbate symptoms by reducing bladder capacity or increasing bladder contractions. Environmental factors, such as age, obesity, and physical inactivity, may also play a role in the development of OAB. Lifestyle factors, such as caffeine consumption, smoking, and stress, can also worsen symptoms.
metadata.risk_factors: Aging increases the risk of overactive bladder. So does being female. Conditions such as enlarged prostate and diabetes also can increase the risk. Many people with declines in thinking ability, such as those who have had a stroke or have Alzheimers disease, get an overactive bladder. Thats because theyre less able to notice the symptoms of needing to urinate. Drinking fluids on a schedule, timing and prompting urination, absorbent garments, and bowel programs can help manage the condition. Some people with an overactive bladder also have trouble with bowel control. Tell your healthcare professional if youre having trouble controlling your bowels. metadata.complications: Any type of incontinence can affect quality of life. If your overactive bladder symptoms disrupt your life, you might also have: Anxiety. Emotional distress or depression. Sexual problems. Sleep disturbances and interrupted sleep cycles. People assigned female at birth who have an overactive bladder also may have a condition called mixed incontinence. This has both urgency and stress incontinence. Stress incontinence is the sudden loss of urine from physical movement or activity that puts pressure on the bladder. metadata.symptoms: Paget's disease of bone is a chronic condition characterized by abnormal bone remodeling, leading to enlarged and deformed bones. The main symptoms and signs of Paget's disease include: 1. **Bone pain**: Patients typically experience persistent pain in the affected bones, which can be localized or diffuse, depending on the location of the disease. 2. **Swollen joints**: Enlarged and painful joints are a common symptom, particularly in the hands, feet, hips, and spine. 3. **Deformities**: As the disease progresses, bones can become misshapen, leading to deformities such as bowed legs, curved spine, or enlarged skull. These symptoms can be accompanied by other signs, including: * Enlarged bone size * Bone fractures * Muscle weakness * Fatigue It's essential to note that Paget's disease can also lead to complications, such as osteoporosis, arthritis, and increased risk of fractures. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to manage the condition and prevent these complications.
metadata.causes: Paget's disease of bone is a chronic condition characterized by abnormal bone remodeling, leading to bone destruction and deformity. The primary causative factors of Paget's disease are genetic mutations in genes such as RANKL (Receptor Activator of NF-κB Ligand) and BMP2 (Bone Morphogenetic Protein 2), which regulate osteoclast activity and bone formation. Environmental factors, such as smoking and exposure to certain chemicals, may also contribute to the development of Paget's disease. Biological factors play a significant role in the pathogenesis of Paget's disease, with an abnormal balance between bone resorption and bone formation leading to excessive bone turnover. Genetic predisposition is also a key factor, with family history being a significant risk factor for developing the condition. Lifestyle factors, such as smoking and physical inactivity, may also contribute to the development of Paget's disease by increasing oxidative stress and inflammation, which can damage bone tissue and disrupt normal bone remodeling processes. Environmental factors, such as exposure to certain chemicals, radiation, and viral infections, have been linked to an increased risk of developing Paget's disease. However, the exact mechanisms by which these environmental factors contribute to the development of the condition are not fully understood. It is worth noting that the exact cause of Paget's disease is still not fully understood, and more research is needed to determine the underlying mechanisms and potential risk factors for this condition.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Paget's disease of bone include: 1. **Age**: The majority of cases occur in people over 50 years old, with a peak incidence between 60-70 years. 2. **Family history**: Individuals with a first-degree relative (parent or sibling) with Paget's disease are at higher risk, suggesting a genetic predisposition. 3. **Male gender**: Men are more likely to develop Paget's disease than women, particularly in the older age group. These demographic factors significantly increase an individual's likelihood of developing Paget's disease of bone.
metadata.complications: Paget's disease of bone is a chronic condition characterized by abnormal bone remodeling, leading to deformities, pain, and increased risk of fractures. If left untreated or poorly managed, Paget's disease can lead to serious complications, including osteoporosis, arthritis, and an increased risk of falls and fractures due to weakened bones. Additionally, the condition can also increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, stroke, and cancer, particularly osteosarcoma. In terms of specific outcomes, untreated or poorly managed Paget's disease can result in significant morbidity, including: * Osteoporosis: Weakened bones that are prone to fractures, which can lead to disability and increased healthcare costs. * Arthritis: Joint pain and stiffness due to bone deformities and inflammation. * Increased risk of falls and fractures: Weak bones increase the risk of falls and fractures, particularly in older adults. It's essential to note that while Paget's disease is a chronic condition, it can be effectively managed with medication, physical therapy, and lifestyle modifications. Early diagnosis and treatment can help prevent or minimize these complications.

metadata.complications: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography Enlarge image Close Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) uses a dye to highlight the bile ducts on X-ray images. A thin, flexible tube with a camera, called an endoscope, is fed through the digestive tract and passes from the small intestine into the main bile duct. The dye enters the ducts through a small hollow tube passed through the endoscope. As pancreatic cancer progresses, it can cause complications such as: Weight loss. People with pancreatic cancer might lose weight as the cancer uses more of the bodys energy. Nausea and vomiting caused by cancer treatments or a cancer pressing on the stomach might make it hard to eat. Sometimes the body has trouble getting nutrients from food because the pancreas isnt making enough digestive juices. Jaundice. Pancreatic cancer that blocks the livers bile duct can cause jaundice. Signs include yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes. Jaundice can cause dark-colored urine and pale-colored stools. Jaundice often occurs without belly pain. If the bile duct is blocked, a plastic or metal tube called a stent can be put inside it. The stent helps hold the bile duct open. This is done using a procedure called endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, also called ERCP. During ERCP, a health care professional puts a long tube with a tiny camera, called an endoscope, down the throat. The tube goes through the stomach and into the upper part of the small intestine. The health professional puts a dye into the pancreatic ducts and bile ducts through a small tube that fits through the endoscope. The dye helps the ducts show up on imaging tests. The health professional uses those images to place a stent at the right spot in the duct to help hold it open. Pain. A growing tumor may press on nerves in your abdomen, causing pain that can become severe. Pain medications can help you feel more comfortable. Treatments, such as radiation and chemotherapy, might help slow tumor growth and provide some pain relief. When medicines arent helping, a health care professional might suggest a celiac plexus block. This procedure uses a needle to put alcohol into the nerves that control pain in the belly. The alcohol stops the nerves from sending pain signals to the brain. Bowel blockage. Pancreatic cancer can grow into or press on the first part of the small intestine, called the duodenum. This can block the flow of digested food from the stomach into the intestines. A health care professional might suggest putting a tube called a stent in the small intestine to hold it open. Sometimes, it might help to have surgery to place a feeding tube. Or surgery can attach the stomach to a lower part of the intestines where the cancer isnt causing a blockage. metadata.symptoms: Pancreatic cysts are fluid-filled sacs that form on the pancreas, which is an organ located behind the stomach. The main symptoms of pancreatic cysts can vary depending on their size, location, and whether they are benign or malignant (cancerous). However, some common and characteristic symptoms include: Abdominal pain, particularly in the upper middle region, which may worsen after eating or at night; Nausea and vomiting, especially if the cyst is pressing on nearby organs; Weight loss and loss of appetite due to malabsorption of nutrients. In some cases, patients may experience jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes), dark urine, pale stools, or fatigue. It's essential to note that many pancreatic cysts are asymptomatic and only discovered incidentally during imaging tests for other reasons. Please consult a medical professional for accurate diagnosis and treatment.
metadata.causes: Pancreatic cysts are a common benign growth that can occur in the pancreas, with various underlying mechanisms contributing to their development. The primary causative factors include genetic predisposition, where individuals with a family history of pancreatic cancer or other pancreatic conditions are more likely to develop pancreatic cysts. Additionally, chronic inflammation and scarring within the pancreas, often caused by conditions such as pancreatitis, can also lead to the formation of pancreatic cysts. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of pancreatic cysts, with abnormalities in cell growth and differentiation contributing to their formation. Environmental factors, such as exposure to certain chemicals or viruses, may also increase the risk of developing pancreatic cysts. Lifestyle factors, including smoking and obesity, have been linked to an increased risk of pancreatic cancer and potentially pancreatic cysts. It's worth noting that the exact causes of pancreatic cysts are not fully understood, and more research is needed to determine the underlying mechanisms driving their development.
metadata.risk_factors: The development of pancreatic cysts is associated with several risk factors, including: 1. Age: The majority of pancreatic cysts are found in individuals over the age of 50, with a peak incidence between 60-70 years old. 2. Family history: Individuals with a first-degree relative (parent or sibling) diagnosed with pancreatic cancer or pancreatic cysts are at increased risk, suggesting a possible genetic predisposition. 3. Chronic pancreatitis: This condition is characterized by inflammation and scarring of the pancreas, increasing the likelihood of developing pancreatic cysts. These factors highlight the importance of age, family history, and underlying medical conditions in determining an individual's risk of developing pancreatic cysts.
metadata.complications: Pancreatic cysts are fluid-filled sacs that can form in the pancreas, and if left untreated or poorly managed, they can lead to several serious complications. One of the most significant risks is pancreatic cancer, as a small percentage of pancreatic cysts can be malignant and may develop into cancer over time. Additionally, large or persistent cysts can cause abdominal pain, weight loss, and digestive issues due to compression on surrounding organs. Untreated Pancreatic Cysts can also lead to secondary conditions such as Infection, Bleeding, and Rupture of the cyst which can be life-threatening if not treated promptly.

name: Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors
description: symptoms  pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors sometimes dont cause symptoms. when they do  symptoms can include  heartburn. weakness. fatigue. muscle cramps. indigestion. diarrhea. weight loss. skin rash. constipation. pain in the abdomen or back. yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes. dizziness. blurred vision. headaches. increased thirst and hunger.. causes  pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors happen when cells in the pancreas develop changes in their dna. a cells dna holds the instructions that tell the cell what to do. the changes  which doctors call mutations  tell the cells to multiply quickly. the changes let the cells continue living when healthy cells would die as part of their natural life cycle. this causes many extra cells. the cells might form a mass called a tumor. sometimes the cells can break away and spread to other organs  such as the liver. when cancer spreads  its called metastatic cancer. in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors  the dna changes happen in hormone-producing cells called islet cells. its not clear what causes the changes that lead to cancer.

metadata.symptoms: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors sometimes dont cause symptoms. When they do, symptoms can include: Heartburn. Weakness. Fatigue. Muscle cramps. Indigestion. Diarrhea. Weight loss. Skin rash. Constipation. Pain in the abdomen or back. Yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes. Dizziness. Blurred vision. Headaches. Increased thirst and hunger.
metadata.causes: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors happen when cells in the pancreas develop changes in their DNA. A cells DNA holds the instructions that tell the cell what to do. The changes, which doctors call mutations, tell the cells to multiply quickly. The changes let the cells continue living when healthy cells would die as part of their natural life cycle. This causes many extra cells. The cells might form a mass called a tumor. Sometimes the cells can break away and spread to other organs, such as the liver. When cancer spreads, its called metastatic cancer. In pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, the DNA changes happen in hormone-producing cells called islet cells. Its not clear what causes the changes that lead to cancer.
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that are associated with an increased risk of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors include: A family history of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. If a family member was diagnosed with pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, your risk is increased. Syndromes present at birth that increase the risk of tumors. Some syndromes that are passed from parents to children can increase the risk of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. Examples of these include multiple endocrine neoplasia, type 1 (MEN 1), von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease, neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1) and tuberous sclerosis. These inherited syndromes are caused by changes in the DNA. These changes allow cells to grow and divide more than needed. Theres no way to prevent pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. If you develop this type of cancer, you didnt do anything to cause it. name: Pancreatitis
description: symptoms  symptoms of pancreatitis may vary. acute pancreatitis symptoms may include  pain in the upper belly. pain in the upper belly that radiates to the back. tenderness when touching the belly. fever. rapid pulse. upset stomach. vomiting. chronic pancreatitis signs and symptoms include  pain in the upper belly. belly pain that feels worse after eating. losing weight without trying. oily  smelly stools. some people with chronic pancreatitis only develop symptoms after they get complications of the disease.. causes  the pancreas has two major roles. it produces insulin  which helps the body manage and use sugars. the pancreas also produces dietary juices  called enzymes  that help with digestion. the pancreas makes and stores turned off versions of the enzymes. after the pancreas sends the enzymes into the small intestine  they are turned on and break down proteins in the small intestine. if the enzymes are turned on too soon  they can start acting like digestive juices inside the pancreas. the action can irritate  damage or destroy cells. this problem  in turn  leads to immune system responses that cause swelling and other events that affect how the pancreas works. several conditions can lead to acute pancreatitis  including  blockage in the bile duct caused by gallstones. heavy alcohol use. certain medicines. high triglyceride levels in the blood. high calcium levels in the blood. pancreas cancer. injuries from trauma or surgery. conditions that can lead to chronic pancreatitis include  damage from repeated acute pancreatitis. heavy alcohol use. inherited genes linked to pancreatitis. high triglyceride levels in the blood. high calcium levels in the blood. sometimes  a cause for pancreatitis is never found. this is known as idiopathic pancreatitis.

metadata.symptoms: Symptoms of pancreatitis may vary. Acute pancreatitis symptoms may include: Pain in the upper belly. Pain in the upper belly that radiates to the back. Tenderness when touching the belly. Fever. Rapid pulse. Upset stomach. Vomiting. Chronic pancreatitis signs and symptoms include: Pain in the upper belly. Belly pain that feels worse after eating. Losing weight without trying. Oily, smelly stools. Some people with chronic pancreatitis only develop symptoms after they get complications of the disease.
metadata.causes: The pancreas has two major roles. It produces insulin, which helps the body manage and use sugars. The pancreas also produces dietary juices, called enzymes, that help with digestion. The pancreas makes and stores turned off versions of the enzymes. After the pancreas sends the enzymes into the small intestine, they are turned on and break down proteins in the small intestine. If the enzymes are turned on too soon, they can start acting like digestive juices inside the pancreas. The action can irritate, damage or destroy cells. This problem, in turn, leads to immune system responses that cause swelling and other events that affect how the pancreas works. Several conditions can lead to acute pancreatitis, including: Blockage in the bile duct caused by gallstones. Heavy alcohol use. Certain medicines. High triglyceride levels in the blood. High calcium levels in the blood. Pancreas cancer. Injuries from trauma or surgery. Conditions that can lead to chronic pancreatitis include: Damage from repeated acute pancreatitis. Heavy alcohol use. Inherited genes linked to pancreatitis. High triglyceride levels in the blood. High calcium levels in the blood. Sometimes, a cause for pancreatitis is never found. This is known as idiopathic pancreatitis.
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that increase your risk of pancreatitis include: Excessive alcohol use. Research shows that having four or five drinks a day increases the risk of pancreatitis. Cigarette smoking. Compared with nonsmokers, smokers are on average three times more likely to develop chronic pancreatitis. Quitting smoking can decrease the risk. Obesity. People with a body mass index of 30 or higher are at increased risk of pancreatitis. Diabetes. Having diabetes increases the risk of pancreatitis. Family history of pancreatitis. A number of genes have been linked to chronic pancreatitis. A family history of the disease is linked to an increased risk, especially when combined with other risk factors. Compared with nonsmokers, smokers are on average three times more likely to develop chronic pancreatitis. Quitting smoking can decrease the risk. Obesity. People with a body mass index of 30 or higher are at increased risk of pancreatitis. Diabetes. Having diabetes increases the risk of pancreatitis. Family history of pancreatitis. A number of genes have been linked to chronic pancreatitis. A family history of the disease is linked to an increased risk, especially when combined with other risk factors.
metadata.complications: Pancreatitis can cause serious complications, including: Kidney failure. Acute pancreatitis may result in the kidneys not filtering waste from the blood. Artificial filtering, called dialysis, may be needed for short-term or long-term treatment. Breathing problems. Acute pancreatitis can cause changes in how the lungs work, causing the level of oxygen in the blood to fall to dangerously low levels. Infection. Acute pancreatitis can make the pancreas vulnerable to infections. Pancreatic infections are serious and require intensive treatment, such as surgery or other procedures to remove the infected tissue. Pseudocyst. Acute and chronic pancreatitis can cause fluid and debris to collect in a pocket in the pancreas, called a pseudocyst. A large pseudocyst that ruptures can cause complications such as internal bleeding and infection. Malnutrition. With both acute and chronic pancreatitis, the pancreas may not produce enough enzymes for the digestive system. This can lead to malnutrition, diarrhea and weight loss. Diabetes. Diabetes can develop when chronic pancreatitis damages cells that produce insulin. Pancreatic cancer. Long-standing inflammation in the pancreas is a risk factor for cancer of the pancreas. Make an appointment with your doctor if you have sudden belly pain or belly pain that doesnt improve. Seek immediate medical help if your pain is so severe that you cant sit still or find a position that makes you more comfortable. description: symptoms  panic attacks typically begin suddenly  without warning. they can strike at any time when youre driving a car  at the mall  sound asleep or in the middle of a business meeting. you may have occasional panic attacks  or they may occur frequently. panic attacks have many variations  but symptoms usually peak within minutes. you may feel fatigued and worn out after a panic attack subsides. panic attacks typically include some of these signs or symptoms  sense of impending doom or danger fear of loss of control or death rapid  pounding heart rate sweating trembling or shaking shortness of breath or tightness in your throat chills hot flashes nausea abdominal cramping chest pain headache dizziness  lightheadedness or faintness numbness or tingling sensation feeling of unreality or detachment one of the worst things about panic attacks is the intense fear that youll have another one. you may fear having panic attacks so much that you avoid certain situations where they may occur.. causes  its not known what causes panic attacks or panic disorder  but these factors may play a role  genetics major stress temperament that is more sensitive to stress or prone to negative emotions certain changes in the way parts of your brain function panic attacks may come on suddenly and without warning at first  but over time  theyre usually triggered by certain situations. some research suggests that your bodys natural fight-or-flight response to danger is involved in panic attacks. for example  if a grizzly bear came after you  your body would react instinctively. your heart rate and breathing would speed up as your body prepared for a life-threatening situation. many of the same reactions occur in a panic attack. but its unknown why a panic attack occurs when theres no obvious danger present. more informationnighttime panic attacks  what causes them

metadata.symptoms: Panic attacks typically begin suddenly, without warning. They can strike at any time  when youre driving a car, at the mall, sound asleep or in the middle of a business meeting. You may have occasional panic attacks, or they may occur frequently. Panic attacks have many variations, but symptoms usually peak within minutes. You may feel fatigued and worn out after a panic attack subsides. Panic attacks typically include some of these signs or symptoms: Sense of impending doom or danger Fear of loss of control or death Rapid, pounding heart rate Sweating Trembling or shaking Shortness of breath or tightness in your throat Chills Hot flashes Nausea Abdominal cramping Chest pain Headache Dizziness, lightheadedness or faintness Numbness or tingling sensation Feeling of unreality or detachment One of the worst things about panic attacks is the intense fear that youll have another one. You may fear having panic attacks so much that you avoid certain situations where they may occur.
metadata.causes: Its not known what causes panic attacks or panic disorder, but these factors may play a role: Genetics Major stress Temperament that is more sensitive to stress or prone to negative emotions Certain changes in the way parts of your brain function Panic attacks may come on suddenly and without warning at first, but over time, theyre usually triggered by certain situations. Some research suggests that your bodys natural fight-or-flight response to danger is involved in panic attacks. For example, if a grizzly bear came after you, your body would react instinctively. Your heart rate and breathing would speed up as your body prepared for a life-threatening situation. Many of the same reactions occur in a panic attack. But its unknown why a panic attack occurs when theres no obvious danger present. More InformationNighttime panic attacks: What causes them
metadata.risk_factors: Symptoms of panic disorder often start in the late teens or early adulthood and affect more women than men. Factors that may increase the risk of developing panic attacks or panic disorder include: Family history of panic attacks or panic disorder Major life stress, such as the death or serious illness of a loved one A traumatic event, such as sexual assault or a serious accident Major changes in your life, such as a divorce or the addition of a baby Smoking or excessive caffeine intake History of childhood physical or sexual abuse Symptoms of panic disorder often start in the late teens or early adulthood and affect more women than men. Factors that may increase the risk of developing panic attacks or panic disorder include: Family history of panic attacks or panic disorder Major life stress, such as the death or serious illness of a loved one A traumatic event, such as sexual assault or a serious accident Major changes in your life, such as a divorce or the addition of a baby Smoking or excessive caffeine intake History of childhood physical or sexual abuse
metadata.complications: Left untreated, panic attacks and panic disorder can affect almost every area of your life. You may be so afraid of having more panic attacks that you live in a constant state of fear, ruining your quality of life. Complications that panic attacks may cause or be linked to include: Development of specific phobias, such as fear of driving or leaving your home Frequent medical care for health concerns and other medical conditions Avoidance of social situations Problems at work or school Depression, anxiety disorders and other psychiatric disorders Increased risk of suicide or suicidal thoughts Alcohol or other substance misuse Financial problems For some people, panic disorder may include agoraphobia  avoiding places or situations that cause you anxiety because you fear being unable to escape or get help if you have a panic attack. Or you may become reliant on others to be with you in order to leave your home. If you have panic attack symptoms, seek medical help as soon as possible. Panic attacks, while intensely uncomfortable, are not dangerous. But panic attacks are hard to manage on your own, and they may get worse without treatment. Panic attack symptoms can also resemble symptoms of other serious health problems, such as a heart attack, so its important to get evaluated by your primary care provider if you arent sure whats causing your symptoms. name: Paraganglioma
description: symptoms  paraganglioma symptoms may depend on where the tumor starts. paragangliomas most often start in the head  neck  stomach area or pelvis. symptoms of a paraganglioma in the head or neck can include  a rhythmic pulsing or whooshing sound in the ears  called pulsatile tinnitus. trouble swallowing. hoarse voice. hearing loss. blurred vision. dizziness. symptoms of a paraganglioma in the head and neck area might happen as the tumor grows larger. the tumor can press on nearby structures. when paragangliomas form in other places in the body  the symptoms are more likely to be caused by hormones that the paraganglioma makes. the hormones  called catecholamines  play a role in how the body response to stress. they include adrenaline  also known as the fight-or-flight hormone. symptoms of paragangliomas that make hormones include  high blood pressure. feelings of having a fast-beating  fluttering or pounding heart. the sudden loss of color in the face. sweating. headache. uncontrolled shaking in the hands or arms. general weakness. these symptoms may come and go. some people with paragangliomas dont have any symptoms. they may learn they have these tumors when imaging tests done for other reasons happen to spot the tumors.. causes  paragangliomas often dont have a clear cause. sometimes these tumors run in families. they can be caused by dna changes that are passed from parents to children. but many people with paragangliomas dont have a family history of these tumors and the cause is not known. a paraganglioma is a growth of cells. it forms from a type of nerve cell called a chromaffin cell. chromaffin cells perform key roles in the body  including controlling blood pressure. a paraganglioma starts when chromaffin cells develop changes in their dna. a cells dna holds the instructions that tell the cell what to do. in healthy cells  the dna gives instructions to grow and multiply at a set rate. the instructions also tell the cells to die at a set time. in paraganglioma cells  the dna changes give different instructions. the changes tell the paraganglioma cells to make many more cells quickly. the cells keep living when healthy cells would die. this causes a growth of cells called a tumor. most paragangliomas stay where they started. they dont spread to other parts of the body. but sometimes cells can break away from a paraganglioma and spread. when this happens  its called metastatic paraganglioma. when a paraganglioma spreads  it most often spreads to nearby lymph nodes. it also can spread to the lungs  liver and bones. a paraganglioma is closely related to another rare tumor called a pheochromocytoma. a pheochromocytoma is a tumor that starts in chromaffin cells in the adrenal glands. the adrenal glands are two glands that sit on top of the kidneys.

metadata.symptoms: Paraganglioma symptoms may depend on where the tumor starts. Paragangliomas most often start in the head, neck, stomach area or pelvis. Symptoms of a paraganglioma in the head or neck can include: A rhythmic pulsing or whooshing sound in the ears, called pulsatile tinnitus. Trouble swallowing. Hoarse voice. Hearing loss. Blurred vision. Dizziness. Symptoms of a paraganglioma in the head and neck area might happen as the tumor grows larger. The tumor can press on nearby structures. When paragangliomas form in other places in the body, the symptoms are more likely to be caused by hormones that the paraganglioma makes. The hormones, called catecholamines, play a role in how the body response to stress. They include adrenaline, also known as the fight-or-flight hormone. Symptoms of paragangliomas that make hormones include: High blood pressure. Feelings of having a fast-beating, fluttering or pounding heart. The sudden loss of color in the face. Sweating. Headache. Uncontrolled shaking in the hands or arms. General weakness. These symptoms may come and go. Some people with paragangliomas dont have any symptoms. They may learn they have these tumors when imaging tests done for other reasons happen to spot the tumors.
metadata.causes: Paragangliomas often dont have a clear cause. Sometimes these tumors run in families. They can be caused by DNA changes that are passed from parents to children. But many people with paragangliomas dont have a family history of these tumors and the cause is not known. A paraganglioma is a growth of cells. It forms from a type of nerve cell called a chromaffin cell. Chromaffin cells perform key roles in the body, including controlling blood pressure. A paraganglioma starts when chromaffin cells develop changes in their DNA. A cells DNA holds the instructions that tell the cell what to do. In healthy cells, the DNA gives instructions to grow and multiply at a set rate. The instructions also tell the cells to die at a set time. In paraganglioma cells, the DNA changes give different instructions. The changes tell the paraganglioma cells to make many more cells quickly. The cells keep living when healthy cells would die. This causes a growth of cells called a tumor. Most paragangliomas stay where they started. They dont spread to other parts of the body. But sometimes cells can break away from a paraganglioma and spread. When this happens, its called metastatic paraganglioma. When a paraganglioma spreads, it most often spreads to nearby lymph nodes. It also can spread to the lungs, liver and bones. A paraganglioma is closely related to another rare tumor called a pheochromocytoma. A pheochromocytoma is a tumor that starts in chromaffin cells in the adrenal glands. The adrenal glands are two glands that sit on top of the kidneys.

metadata.causes: Paraneoplastic syndromes of the nervous system are not caused by cancer cells directly or by the cancer spreading, known as metastasis. metadata.symptoms: Parkinsons disease symptoms can be different for everyone. Early symptoms may be mild, and you may not even notice them. Symptoms often begin on one side of the body, then affect both sides. Symptoms are usually worse on one side than the other. Some Parkinsons disease symptoms are similar to those of other disorders. Parkinsons symptoms may include: Tremor. This rhythmic shaking usually begins in the hands or fingers. Sometimes tremor begins in the foot or jaw. You may rub your thumb and forefinger back and forth. This is known as a pill-rolling tremor. Your hand may tremble when its at rest or when youre under stress. You may notice that you shake less when youre doing some sort of task or moving around. Slowed movement, also called bradykinesia. Parkinsons disease may slow your movement, making simple tasks more difficult. It may be hard to get out of a chair, shower or get dressed. You may have less expression in your face. It may be hard to blink. Rigid muscles. You may have stiff muscles in any part of your body. Your muscles may feel tense and painful, and your arm movements may be short and jerky. Poor posture and balance. Your posture may become stooped. You may fall or have balance problems. Loss of automatic movements. You may be less able to make certain movements that you typically do without thinking, including blinking, smiling or swinging your arms when you walk. Speech changes. You may speak softly or quickly, slur, or hesitate before talking. Your speech may be flat or monotone, without typical speech patterns. Writing changes. You may have trouble writing, and your writing may appear cramped and small. Nonmotor symptoms. These may include depression, anxiety, constipation and sleep problems. They also may include acting out dreams, needing to urinate often, trouble smelling, problems with thinking and memory, and feeling very tired.
metadata.causes: In Parkinsons disease, nerve cells in the brain called neurons slowly break down or die. Many Parkinsons disease symptoms are caused by a loss of neurons that produce a chemical messenger in the brain. This messenger is called dopamine. Decreased dopamine leads to irregular brain activity. This causes movement problems and other symptoms of Parkinsons disease. People with Parkinsons disease also lose a chemical messenger called norepinephrine that controls many body functions, such as blood pressure. The cause of Parkinsons disease is unknown, but several factors seem to play a role, including: Genes. Specific genetic changes are linked to Parkinsons disease. But these are rare unless many family members have had Parkinsons disease. Environmental factors. Exposure to certain toxins or other environmental factors may increase the risk of later Parkinsons disease. One example is MPTP, a substance that can be found in illegal drugs and is sometimes sold illegally as synthetic heroin. Other examples include pesticides and well water used for drinking. But no environmental factor has proved to be a cause. Many changes happen in the brains of people with Parkinsons disease. Researchers are studying why the changes happen and the roles they play. These changes include: The presence of Lewy bodies. Clumps of proteins in the brain are associated with Parkinsons disease. These are called Lewy bodies, and researchers believe these proteins hold an important clue to the cause of Parkinsons disease. Alpha-synuclein found within Lewy bodies. Alpha-synuclein is a protein found in all Lewy bodies. It occurs in a clumped form that cells cant break down. This is currently an important focus among Parkinsons disease researchers. Alpha-synuclein has been found in the spinal fluid of people who later have Parkinsons disease. Altered mitochondria. Mitochondria are powerhouse compartments inside cells that create most of the bodys energy. Changes to mitochondria can cause cell damage. These changes have been found in the brains of people with Parkinsons disease.
metadata.risk_factors: Risk factors for Parkinsons disease include: Age. The risk of Parkinsons disease increases with age. Usually, it starts around age 50 or older. The average age of onset is around age 70. Parkinsons disease can occur in younger adults, but it is rare. When people younger than age 50 have the disease, its known as early-onset Parkinsons disease. Genetics. Having one or more first-degree relatives, such as parents or siblings, with Parkinsons disease increases your risk. Your risks are still small unless you have many blood relatives with the condition. Male sex. Men are more likely to develop Parkinsons disease than are women. Exposure to toxins. Ongoing exposure to herbicides and pesticides may slightly increase your risk of Parkinsons disease. Risk factors for Parkinsons disease include: Age. metadata.complications: People with Parkinsons disease may have other complications that may be treatable. These may include: Trouble thinking clearly. Parkinsons disease can affect peoples memory, language and reasoning skills. The disease also can lead to dementia or other conditions that affect thinking. These complications usually happen later in Parkinsons disease, and medicines usually have only a modest benefit in managing these symptoms. Emotional changes and depression. Some people may feel irritable and concerned early in the course of Parkinsons disease. They also may have depression and anxiety. Medicines and other treatment can help with these changes. Trouble swallowing and chewing. Late-stage Parkinsons disease affects the muscles in the mouth. This causes trouble swallowing and chewing, which can lead to not getting enough nutrients in your diet. If food or saliva collects in the mouth, it can cause choking or drooling. Sleep problems and sleep disorders. You may wake up often during the night, have nightmares and fall asleep during the day. Another symptom may be rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder. This involves acting out your dreams. Medicines and other therapies may help your sleep get better. Other symptoms that can occur include: Bladder problems. You may have problems such as urgency. Constipation. You may have a hard time passing stool. You may pass stool fewer than three times a week. Blood pressure changes. You may feel dizzy or lightheaded or even faint when you stand up due to a sudden drop in blood pressure. This also is called orthostatic hypotension. Loss of smell. You may fully or partially lose your sense of smell. Tiredness. You may feel very tired and lack energy, especially late in the day. Pain. You may have pain or cramps in your muscles and joints. Sexual symptoms. You may have a decrease in sexual desire or performance. See a healthcare professional if you have any symptoms of Parkinsons disease. name: Parvovirus Infection
description: symptoms  early symptoms of parvovirus infections in children can include  fever. upset stomach. headache. runny nose. diarrhea.. causes  parvovirus infection is a viral disease caused by the parvovirus b19 virus  which primarily affects the red blood cells and bone marrow. the primary causative factors of parvovirus infection include biological factors such as weakened immune systems  genetic predispositions  and exposure to contaminated bodily fluids or surfaces. environmental factors  such as poor hygiene and close contact with infected individuals  can also contribute to the transmission of the virus. the underlying mechanisms of parvovirus infection involve the virus s ability to infect red blood cells and bone marrow  leading to anemia  fatigue  and other symptoms. the virus s genetic material is able to evade the immune system  allowing it to replicate and cause damage to infected cells. it s worth noting that parvovirus b19 is a common cause of fifth disease (erythema infectiosum)  which primarily affects children under the age of 10. adults who are susceptible to the virus may experience more severe symptoms due to their weakened immune systems.

metadata.symptoms: Early symptoms of parvovirus infections in children can include: Fever. Upset stomach. Headache. Runny nose. Diarrhea.
metadata.causes: Parvovirus infection is a viral disease caused by the parvovirus B19 virus, which primarily affects the red blood cells and bone marrow. The primary causative factors of parvovirus infection include biological factors such as weakened immune systems, genetic predispositions, and exposure to contaminated bodily fluids or surfaces. Environmental factors, such as poor hygiene and close contact with infected individuals, can also contribute to the transmission of the virus. The underlying mechanisms of parvovirus infection involve the virus's ability to infect red blood cells and bone marrow, leading to anemia, fatigue, and other symptoms. The virus's genetic material is able to evade the immune system, allowing it to replicate and cause damage to infected cells. It's worth noting that parvovirus B19 is a common cause of Fifth disease (erythema infectiosum), which primarily affects children under the age of 10. Adults who are susceptible to the virus may experience more severe symptoms due to their weakened immune systems.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Parvovirus infection include: * Age: Infants under 6 months old are particularly susceptible due to their immature immune systems. * Immune system compromise: Individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing chemotherapy, are more vulnerable to parvovirus infection. * Chronic medical conditions: People with underlying health conditions like sickle cell disease, anemia, and certain autoimmune disorders may be at increased risk of developing parvovirus infection.
metadata.complications: Parvovirus infection, also known as erythema infectiosum, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is aplastic crisis, a condition where the bone marrow fails to produce red blood cells, leading to severe anemia and potentially life-threatening consequences. Additionally, parvovirus infection can cause secondary conditions such as heart problems, neurological issues, and long-term damage to the joints and kidneys. In rare cases, untreated parvovirus infection can also lead to more serious outcomes, including: * Aplastic crisis with severe anemia, requiring blood transfusions * Heart failure or arrhythmias due to cardiac strain from anemia * Neurological problems such as meningitis or encephalitis It's essential to seek medical attention promptly if symptoms of parvovirus infection occur, especially in individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with chronic illnesses or undergoing chemotherapy.

metadata.symptoms: Patellar tendinitis is a common overuse injury affecting the patellar tendon, which connects the kneecap (patella) to the shinbone (tibia). The main symptoms of patellar tendinitis include: (1) Pain and inflammation in the front of the knee, particularly around the patella, which can be exacerbated by activities that involve repetitive knee flexion and extension. Patients typically experience a sharp, stabbing pain when climbing stairs, jumping, or squatting, which worsens with activity and improves with rest. (2) Swelling and redness in the affected area, which may be accompanied by warmth to the touch. (3) Difficulty straightening the knee, as the inflamed tendon can cause stiffness and limited range of motion. Additionally, patients may experience a feeling of instability or weakness in the knee joint, particularly when bearing weight or performing activities that require rapid changes of direction. Key symptoms typically experienced by patients with patellar tendinitis include: * Pain and inflammation around the patella * Swelling and redness in the affected area * Difficulty straightening the knee due to stiffness and limited range of motion Note: It's essential to consult a healthcare professional for an accurate diagnosis and proper treatment plan.
metadata.causes: Patellar tendinitis is a common overuse injury that affects the patellar tendon, which connects the kneecap (patella) to the tibia (shin bone). The primary causative factors of patellar tendinitis include repetitive strain on the tendon due to activities such as running, jumping, or cycling, as well as poor biomechanics and inadequate footwear. Additionally, genetic predisposition and age can also play a role in the development of patellar tendinitis. Biological factors, such as inflammation and degeneration of the tendon tissue, contribute to the condition. The underlying mechanism involves micro-tears in the tendon fibers, leading to pain, swelling, and stiffness in the knee joint. Environmental and lifestyle factors that may contribute to the development of patellar tendinitis include: * Sudden changes in exercise intensity or frequency * Insufficient warm-up or cool-down exercises * Wearing ill-fitting or inadequate footwear * Poor posture or biomechanics It's essential to note that patellar tendinitis can also be caused by underlying medical conditions, such as osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for patellar tendinitis include: * Demographic factors: Young adults (20-40 years old) and athletes, particularly those involved in sports that involve jumping or repetitive knee bending, are more susceptible to developing patellar tendinitis. * Lifestyle factors: Individuals who engage in high-impact activities, such as running or cycling, for extended periods, may be at a higher risk of developing the condition. * Medical conditions: Pre-existing conditions like patellofemoral pain syndrome, knee arthritis, and overuse injuries can increase the likelihood of developing patellar tendinitis.
metadata.complications: Patellar tendinitis, also known as patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS), is a common overuse injury that affects the tendon connecting the kneecap to the shinbone. If left untreated or poorly managed, patellar tendinitis can lead to several complications, including chronic pain, decreased range of motion, and increased risk of osteoarthritis. Untreated patellar tendinitis may also result in secondary conditions such as degenerative joint disease, muscle imbalances, and potentially even patellofemoral arthrosis. The most significant complications include: 1. Chronic Osteoarthritis: Prolonged inflammation and degeneration of the joint cartilage can lead to osteoarthritis, a condition characterized by joint pain, stiffness, and decreased mobility. 2. Muscle Imbalances: Weak or tight surrounding muscles can contribute to poor biomechanics, exacerbating patellar tendinitis and increasing the risk of further injury. 3. Patellofemoral Arthrosis: Untreated patellar tendinitis can lead to degenerative changes in the patella-femoral joint, potentially resulting in a more severe condition that requires surgical intervention. It is essential to seek medical attention from a qualified healthcare professional for proper diagnosis and treatment of patellar tendinitis to prevent these complications.

Patellofemoral pain can occur when the muscles around the hip and knee dont keep the kneecap in line. Moving the knee inward during a squat has been linked to patellofemoral pain. Injury. Trauma to the kneecap, such as when the kneecap gets out of place or breaks, has been linked to patellofemoral pain syndrome. Surgery. Knee surgery can increase the risk of patellofemoral pain. This is especially true of repair to the anterior cruciate ligament using ones own patellar tendon as a graft.
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that can increase your risk include: Age. Patellofemoral pain syndrome typically affects teens and young adults. Arthritis is more often to blame for knee problems in older people. Sex. Women are twice as likely as men are to develop patellofemoral pain. This may be because women have wider pelvises. A wider pelvis increases the angle at which the bones in the knee joint meet. Certain sports. Running and jumping sports can put extra stress on the knees. This is especially true when adding more training. Factors that can increase your risk include: Age. Patellofemoral pain syndrome typically affects teens and young adults.
