metadata.symptoms: Newborns with PKU initially dont have any symptoms. However, without treatment, babies usually develop signs of PKU within a few months. Signs and symptoms of untreated PKU can be mild or severe and may include: A musty odor in the breath, skin or urine, caused by too much phenylalanine in the body Nervous system (neurological) problems that may include seizures Skin rashes, such as eczema Lighter skin, hair and eye color than family members, because phenylalanine cant transform into melanin  the pigment responsible for hair and skin tone Unusually small head size (microcephaly) Hyperactivity Intellectual disability Delayed development Behavioral, emotional and social problems Mental health disorders
metadata.causes: Autosomal recessive inheritance pattern Enlarge image Close Autosomal recessive inheritance pattern Autosomal recessive inheritance pattern To have an autosomal recessive disorder, you inherit two changed genes, sometimes called mutations. You get one from each parent. Their health is rarely affected because they have only one changed gene. Two carriers have a 25 chance of having an unaffected child with two unaffected genes. They have a 50 chance of having an unaffected child who also is a carrier. They have a 25 chance of having an affected child with two changed genes. A gene change (genetic mutation) causes PKU, which can be mild, moderate or severe. In a person with PKU, a change in the phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) gene causes a lack of or reduced amount of the enzyme thats needed to process phenylalanine, an amino acid. A dangerous buildup of phenylalanine can develop when a person with PKU eats protein-rich foods, such as milk, cheese, nuts or meat, or grains such as bread and pasta, or aspartame, an artificial sweetener.
metadata.risk_factors: Risk factors for inheriting PKU include: Having both parents with a gene change that causes PKU. Two parents must pass along a copy of the changed gene for their child to develop the condition. Being of a certain racial or ethnic descent. PKU affects people from most ethnic backgrounds worldwide. But in the United States, its most common in people of European ancestry and much less common in people of African ancestry. metadata.complications: Untreated PKU can lead to complications in infants, children and adults with the disorder. When women with PKU have high blood phenylalanine levels during pregnancy, it can harm their unborn baby. Untreated PKU can lead to: Irreversible brain damage and marked intellectual disability beginning within the first few months of life Neurological problems such as seizures and tremors Behavioral, emotional and social problems in older children and adults Major health and developmental problems Talk to your health care provider in these situations: Newborns. If routine newborn screening tests show that your baby may have PKU, your childs health care provider will want to start dietary treatment right away to prevent long-term problems. Women of childbearing years. Its especially important for women with a history of PKU to see a health care provider and maintain the PKU diet before becoming pregnant and during pregnancy. This reduces the risk of high blood phenylalanine levels harming their unborn babies. Adults. People with PKU need to receive lifelong care. Adults with PKU who have stopped the PKU diet in their teens may benefit from a visit with their health care providers. Returning to the diet may improve mental functioning and behavior and prevent further damage to the central nervous system that can result from high phenylalanine levels. name: Pheochromocytoma
description: symptoms  a pheochromocytoma often causes the following symptoms  high blood pressure. headache. heavy sweating. rapid heartbeat. some people with pheochromocytomas also have symptoms such as  nervous shaking. skin that turns a lighter color  also called pallor. shortness of breath. panic attack-type symptoms  which can include sudden intense fear. anxiety or a sense of doom. vision problems. constipation. weight loss. some people with pheochromocytomas have no symptoms. they dont realize they have the tumor until an imaging test happens to find it.. causes  endocrine system enlarge image close endocrine system endocrine system the endocrine system is made up of glands and organs that make hormones. the endocrine system includes the pituitary gland  thyroid gland  parathyroid glands  adrenal glands  pancreas  and ovaries or testicles. researchers dont know exactly what causes a pheochromocytoma. the tumor forms in cells called chromaffin cells. these cells are located in the center of an adrenal gland. they release certain hormones  mainly adrenaline and noradrenaline. these hormones help control many body functions  such as heart rate  blood pressure and blood sugar. adrenaline and noradrenaline trigger the bodys fight-or-flight response. that response happens when the body thinks there is a threat. the hormones cause blood pressure to rise and the heart to beat faster. they also prepare other body systems so you can react quickly. a pheochromocytoma causes more of these hormones to be released. and it causes them to be released when youre not in a threatening situation. most of the chromaffin cells are in the adrenal glands. but small clusters of these cells also are in the heart  head  neck  bladder  stomach area and along the spine. chromaffin cell tumors located outside of the adrenal glands are called paragangliomas. they may cause the same effects on the body as a pheochromocytoma.

metadata.symptoms: A pheochromocytoma often causes the following symptoms: High blood pressure. Headache. Heavy sweating. Rapid heartbeat. Some people with pheochromocytomas also have symptoms such as: Nervous shaking. Skin that turns a lighter color, also called pallor. Shortness of breath. Panic attack-type symptoms, which can include sudden intense fear. Anxiety or a sense of doom. Vision problems. Constipation. Weight loss. Some people with pheochromocytomas have no symptoms. They dont realize they have the tumor until an imaging test happens to find it.
metadata.causes: Endocrine system Enlarge image Close Endocrine system Endocrine system The endocrine system is made up of glands and organs that make hormones. The endocrine system includes the pituitary gland, thyroid gland, parathyroid glands, adrenal glands, pancreas, and ovaries or testicles. Researchers dont know exactly what causes a pheochromocytoma. The tumor forms in cells called chromaffin cells. These cells are located in the center of an adrenal gland. They release certain hormones, mainly adrenaline and noradrenaline. These hormones help control many body functions, such as heart rate, blood pressure and blood sugar. Adrenaline and noradrenaline trigger the bodys fight-or-flight response. That response happens when the body thinks there is a threat. The hormones cause blood pressure to rise and the heart to beat faster. They also prepare other body systems so you can react quickly. A pheochromocytoma causes more of these hormones to be released. And it causes them to be released when youre not in a threatening situation. Most of the chromaffin cells are in the adrenal glands. But small clusters of these cells also are in the heart, head, neck, bladder, stomach area and along the spine. Chromaffin cell tumors located outside of the adrenal glands are called paragangliomas. They may cause the same effects on the body as a pheochromocytoma.
metadata.risk_factors: Multiple endocrine neoplasia, type 2B (MEN 2B) Enlarge image Close Multiple endocrine neoplasia, type 2B (MEN 2B) Multiple endocrine neoplasia, type 2B (MEN 2B) People with MEN 2B have tumors of nerves in the lips, mouth, eyes and digestive tract. They also may have a tumor on the adrenal gland, called pheochromocytoma, and medullary thyroid cancer. A persons age and certain medical conditions can raise the risk of a pheochromocytoma. Most pheochromocytomas are found in people between the ages of 20 and 50. But the tumor can form at any age. People who have certain rare genetic conditions have a higher risk of pheochromocytomas. The tumors usually are not cancer and havent spread in the body. This type of tumor is called benign or nonmetastatic pheochromocytoma. Rarely, the tumors are cancer and are spreading in the body. This type of tumor is called malignant or metastatic pheochromocytoma. Often, benign tumors related to these rare genetic conditions form in both adrenal glands. Genetic conditions linked with pheochromocytoma include: Multiple endocrine neoplasia, type 2 (MEN 2). This condition can cause tumors in more than one part of the bodys hormone-making system, called the endocrine system. There are two types of MEN 2, including type 2A and type 2B. Both can involve pheochromocytomas. Other tumors linked with this condition can appear in other parts of the body. These body parts include the thyroid, parathyroid glands, lips, mouth and digestive system. Von Hippel-Lindau disease. This condition can cause tumors in many parts of the body. Possible sites include the brain and spinal cord, endocrine system, pancreas and kidneys. Neurofibromatosis 1. This condition causes tumors in the skin called neurofibromas. It also can cause tumors of the nerve at the back of the eye that connects to the brain, called the optic nerve. Hereditary paraganglioma syndromes. These conditions are passed down in families. They can result in pheochromocytomas or paragangliomas. metadata.complications: A pheochromocytoma can lead to other health problems. The high blood pressure linked with a pheochromocytoma can damage organs, especially tissues of the heart and blood vessel system, brain and kidneys. This damage can cause dangerous conditions, including: Heart disease. Stroke. Kidney failure. Vision loss. High blood pressure is one of the main symptoms of a pheochromocytoma. But most people who have high blood pressure dont have an adrenal tumor. Talk to your healthcare professional if any of these factors apply to you: Spells of symptoms linked with pheochromocytoma, such as headaches, sweating and a fast, pounding heartbeat. Trouble controlling high blood pressure with your current treatment. High blood pressure that starts before the age of 20. Recurring large rises in blood pressure. A family history of pheochromocytoma. A family history of a related genetic condition. These include multiple endocrine neoplasia, type 2 (MEN 2), von Hippel-Lindau disease, inherited paraganglioma syndromes and neurofibromatosis 1. Request an appointment

name: Pilocytic Astrocytoma
description: symptoms  symptoms of pilocytic astrocytoma can vary depending on the tumors size and where its growing in the brain. these tumors grow slowly  so symptoms may develop over weeks or months and get worse over time. many of the signs and symptoms of pilocytic astrocytoma are caused by increased pressure in the brain or by the tumor pressing on nearby structures. children with tumors near the cerebellum or brainstem may show signs earlier because those areas control balance  coordination and vital functions. pilocytic astrocytoma symptoms in children usually are not different from pilocytic astrocytoma symptoms in adults. the location of the tumor  rather than age  determines the type of symptoms you have.. causes  the exact cause of pilocytic astrocytomas isnt known. most of these tumors happen without a known trigger. however  scientists have found certain factors in genes and the environment that may play a role in the growth of pilocytic astrocytoma tumors. many pilocytic astrocytomas are linked to changes in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (mapk) pathway. this pathway is a system that helps cells communicate and controls how cells grow and divide. these changes can trigger growth signals in brain cells and may lead to tumor growth. at this time  theres no proven link between pilocytic astrocytomas and environmental factors such as cellphone use  diet or chemical exposure.

metadata.symptoms: Symptoms of pilocytic astrocytoma can vary depending on the tumors size and where its growing in the brain. These tumors grow slowly, so symptoms may develop over weeks or months and get worse over time. Many of the signs and symptoms of pilocytic astrocytoma are caused by increased pressure in the brain or by the tumor pressing on nearby structures. Children with tumors near the cerebellum or brainstem may show signs earlier because those areas control balance, coordination and vital functions. Pilocytic astrocytoma symptoms in children usually are not different from pilocytic astrocytoma symptoms in adults. The location of the tumor, rather than age, determines the type of symptoms you have.
metadata.causes: The exact cause of pilocytic astrocytomas isnt known. Most of these tumors happen without a known trigger. However, scientists have found certain factors in genes and the environment that may play a role in the growth of pilocytic astrocytoma tumors. Many pilocytic astrocytomas are linked to changes in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway. This pathway is a system that helps cells communicate and controls how cells grow and divide. These changes can trigger growth signals in brain cells and may lead to tumor growth. At this time, theres no proven link between pilocytic astrocytomas and environmental factors such as cellphone use, diet or chemical exposure.
metadata.risk_factors: While experts dont know exactly what causes pilocytic astrocytoma, researchers have found some risk factors that may raise a persons chances of developing this kind of tumor: While experts dont know exactly what causes pilocytic astrocytoma, researchers have found some risk factors that may raise a persons chances of developing this kind of tumor:
metadata.complications: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a type of brain tumor that can cause various potential complications, including increased intracranial pressure, seizures, and hydrocephalus (fluid accumulation in the brain). If left untreated or poorly managed, pilocytic astrocytoma can lead to serious outcomes such as cerebral edema, herniation, and even death. Additionally, secondary conditions like meningitis, abscesses, and radiation-induced necrosis can also occur if the tumor is not properly treated. However, in most cases, with appropriate treatment, including surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, the prognosis for pilocytic astrocytoma is generally good, and the risk of serious complications is significantly reduced.

name: Pilonidal Cyst
description: symptoms  a pilonidal cyst may not cause symptoms. but if its infected  the skin around the cyst may be swollen and painful. symptoms of an infected pilonidal cyst include  a pit near the top of the buttocks crease. pain. inflamed  swollen skin. pus or blood leaking from an opening in the skin. an odor from draining pus.. causes  the cause of most pilonidal cysts is loose hairs that puncture the skin. friction and pressure from rubbed skin  tight clothing  cycling or long periods of sitting can force hair into the skin. the body creates a cyst around the hair to try to push it out. most pilonidal cysts form on the tailbone. people who groom animals or cut hair can develop a cyst between their fingers.

metadata.symptoms: A pilonidal cyst may not cause symptoms. But if its infected, the skin around the cyst may be swollen and painful. Symptoms of an infected pilonidal cyst include: A pit near the top of the buttocks crease. Pain. Inflamed, swollen skin. Pus or blood leaking from an opening in the skin. An odor from draining pus.
metadata.causes: The cause of most pilonidal cysts is loose hairs that puncture the skin. Friction and pressure from rubbed skin, tight clothing, cycling or long periods of sitting can force hair into the skin. The body creates a cyst around the hair to try to push it out. Most pilonidal cysts form on the tailbone. People who groom animals or cut hair can develop a cyst between their fingers.
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that might increase your risk of a pilonidal cyst include: Being a young adult white male. Being overweight. Having an inactive lifestyle. Sitting for long periods at a time. Having thick, stiff body hair. Factors that might increase your risk of a pilonidal cyst include: Being a young adult white male. Being overweight. Having an inactive lifestyle. Sitting for long periods at a time. Having thick, stiff body hair.
metadata.complications: Some people have pilonidal cysts that become infected again and again over a long time. Without treatment, these people may be at increased risk of a type of skin cancer called squamous cell carcinoma. If you notice any symptoms of a pilonidal cyst, see your health care provider. metadata.symptoms: Pinched nerve symptoms include: Numbness or less feeling in the area supplied by the nerve. Sharp, aching or burning pain, which may radiate outward. Tingling, or a pins and needles feeling. Muscle weakness in the affected area. Often feeling as if a foot or hand has fallen asleep. Symptoms related to a pinched nerve may be worse when youre sleeping.
metadata.causes: Pinched nerve due to herniated disk Enlarge image Close Pinched nerve due to herniated disk Pinched nerve due to herniated disk A herniated disk in the lower spine may pinch a nerve root. This can cause pain that radiates down the back of the leg, known as sciatica. Pinched median nerve Enlarge image Close Pinched median nerve Pinched median nerve A pinched median nerve in the wrist can lead to pain, numbness and weakness in the hand and fingers, known as carpal tunnel syndrome. A pinched nerve occurs when too much pressure, known as compression, is applied to a nerve by surrounding tissues. This tissue might be bone or cartilage, such as when a herniated spinal disk compresses a nerve root. Or muscle or tendons may compress a nerve. In carpal tunnel syndrome, a variety of tissues may be responsible for compression of the carpal tunnels median nerve in the wrist. It can be caused by swollen tendon sheaths within the tunnel, enlarged bone that narrows the tunnel, or a thickened and degenerated ligament. A number of conditions may cause tissue to compress a nerve or nerves, including: Injury. Rheumatoid or wrist arthritis. Stress from repetitive work. Hobbies or sports. Obesity. If a nerve is pinched for only a short time, theres often no permanent damage. Once the pressure is relieved, nerve function returns. However, if the pressure continues, chronic pain and permanent nerve damage can occur.
metadata.risk_factors: The following factors may increase your risk of experiencing a pinched nerve: Sex assigned at birth. Women are more likely to develop carpal tunnel syndrome, possibly due to having smaller carpal tunnels. Bone spurs. Trauma or a condition that causes bone thickening, such as osteoarthritis, can cause bone spurs. Bone spurs can stiffen the spine as well as narrow the space where your nerves travel, pinching nerves. Rheumatoid arthritis. Inflammation caused by rheumatoid arthritis can compress nerves, especially in your joints. Thyroid disease. People with thyroid disease are at higher risk of carpal tunnel syndrome. Other risk factors include: Diabetes. People with diabetes are at higher risk of nerve compression. Overuse. Jobs or hobbies that require repetitive hand, wrist or shoulder movements increase the risk of a pinched nerve. This includes assembly line work. Obesity. Excess weight can add pressure to nerves. Pregnancy. Water and weight gain associated with pregnancy can swell nerve pathways, compressing your nerves. Prolonged bed rest. metadata.causes: The cause of pineoblastoma often isnt known. This cancer starts as a growth of cells in the pineal gland. The pineal gland is located in the center of the brain. metadata.causes: Causes of pink eye include: Viruses. Bacteria. Allergies. A chemical splash in the eye. A foreign object in the eye. In newborns, a blocked tear duct.
metadata.risk_factors: Risk factors for pink eye include: Exposure to someone infected with the viral or bacterial form of conjunctivitis. Exposure to something youre allergic to, for allergic conjunctivitis. Using contact lenses, especially extended-wear lenses. metadata.complications: In both children and adults, pink eye can cause inflammation in the cornea that can affect vision. Prompt evaluation and treatment by your healthcare professional can reduce the risk of complications. See your professional if you have: Eye pain. A feeling that something is stuck in the eye. Blurred vision. Light sensitivity. There are serious eye conditions that can cause eye redness. These conditions may cause eye pain, a feeling that something is stuck in your eye, blurred vision and light sensitivity. If you experience these symptoms, seek urgent care. People who wear contact lenses need to stop wearing their contacts as soon as pink eye symptoms begin. metadata.symptoms: Pinworm, also known as Enterobius vermicularis, is a highly contagious parasitic infection caused by the pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis) that affects the intestines. The main symptom of pinworm is anal itching, which is often described as a persistent and intense burning sensation in the perianal region. This itching typically occurs at night, leading to scratching and discomfort. Other common symptoms include: (1) excessive scratching around the anus, which can lead to skin irritation, bleeding, and secondary infections; (2) small, thin, white or yellowish worms may be visible on toilet paper, bedding, or clothing, particularly after bowel movements; and (3) abdominal pain, diarrhea, or constipation in some cases. In rare instances, pinworm infection can also lead to more severe complications such as perianal fissures, abscesses, or even intestinal blockages if left untreated for an extended period.
metadata.causes: Pinworm, also known as Enterobius vermicularis infection, is a common parasitic gastrointestinal disorder caused primarily by the pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis) parasite. The main biological factor leading to pinworm infection is the ingestion of contaminated food or water containing the parasite's eggs, which are highly resistant to environmental factors and can survive for weeks outside the human body. Genetic predisposition may also play a role in susceptibility to pinworm infection. Environmental factors such as poor hygiene, inadequate handwashing, and contaminated food handling practices contribute to the spread of pinworms. Lifestyle factors like poor diet, stress, and lack of sleep may also increase the risk of developing pinworm infection. The primary causative factor leading to pinworm infection is the ingestion of contaminated food or water containing the parasite's eggs, which are highly resistant to environmental factors and can survive for weeks outside the human body.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing pinworm infection include: 1. Age: Children under the age of 6 are more susceptible to pinworm infection due to their curiosity and tendency to put objects in their mouths. 2. Gender: Females are more likely to develop pinworm infection, particularly during menstruation or pregnancy. 3. Poor hygiene and sanitation: Infrequent handwashing, inadequate toilet cleaning, and sharing personal items can increase the risk of transmission. These factors significantly contribute to the likelihood of developing pinworm infection.
metadata.complications: Pinworm, also known as Enterobius vermicularis, is a common parasitic infection that can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is intestinal obstruction, where the pinworms can cause inflammation and scarring in the intestines, leading to bowel blockages. Additionally, chronic pinworm infestations can increase the risk of developing colonic cancer and rectal prolapse.

metadata.symptoms: Pityriasis rosea is a skin condition characterized by an initial herald patch followed by a widespread eruption of pink to reddish-brown patches, often with a scaly texture. The main symptoms and signs of pityriasis rosea include: (1) A characteristic herald patch, typically oval in shape and 2-5 cm in diameter, which appears on the trunk or limbs before the onset of other lesions; (2) Widespread involvement of the skin, with patches often appearing in a symmetrical distribution; and (3) Scaling and erythema (redness) of the affected areas. Additionally, patients may experience pruritus (itching), which can be intense, especially during the initial stages of the condition. Please note that pityriasis rosea is typically self-limiting, meaning it will resolve on its own without treatment, but in some cases, antihistamines or topical corticosteroids may be prescribed to alleviate symptoms.
metadata.causes: Pityriasis rosea is a skin condition characterized by an itchy, scaly rash that typically appears as a single large patch (herald patch) followed by smaller patches of lesions. The primary causative factors of pityriasis rosea are thought to be viral infections, with the most commonly implicated viruses being human herpesviruses 6 and 7 (HHV-6 and HHV-7). These viruses trigger an immune response that leads to the characteristic rash. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of pityriasis rosea, as the condition is thought to be triggered by reactivation of latent viral infections. Genetic predisposition may also contribute to the risk of developing the condition, with some studies suggesting that individuals with a family history of pityriasis rosea are more likely to develop it. Environmental and lifestyle factors have not been identified as primary causes of pityriasis rosea, although stress and hormonal changes may exacerbate symptoms. The exact mechanisms underlying the development of pityriasis rosea are still not fully understood, but research suggests that the condition is associated with an abnormal immune response and inflammation in the skin. It's worth noting that pityriasis rosea can also be triggered by other factors such as: * Stress * Hormonal changes * Sun exposure * Certain medications * Weakened immune system However, these factors are not considered primary causes of the condition.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing Pityriasis Rosea include: * Age: Individuals between 5 and 35 years old are more likely to develop Pityriasis Rosea, with a peak incidence in late childhood and early adulthood. * Genetic predisposition: Family history plays a significant role, with first-degree relatives of individuals with Pityriasis Rosea being at increased risk. * Weakened immune system: Individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with autoimmune disorders or taking immunosuppressive medications, are more susceptible to developing Pityriasis Rosea.
metadata.complications: Pityriasis rosea is a skin condition characterized by an itchy, scaly rash that can be accompanied by fever, fatigue, and swollen lymph nodes. If left untreated or poorly managed, pityriasis rosea can lead to several potential complications, including secondary infections, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH), and the development of psoriasis or other skin conditions. The most significant complications of untreated or poorly managed pityriasis rosea include: 1. Secondary bacterial or fungal infections: The rash can become infected with bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus or fungi like Malassezia, leading to more severe symptoms and potentially life-threatening conditions. 2. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH): The rash can leave behind patches of discoloration that may take months or even years to fade, affecting the patient's self-esteem and quality of life. 3. Development of psoriasis: Pityriasis rosea is often considered a precursor to psoriasis, with some studies suggesting that up to 10% of patients will develop psoriasis within two years of their initial diagnosis. It is essential for individuals with pityriasis rosea to seek medical attention if symptoms persist or worsen over time, as early treatment can help prevent these complications and improve outcomes.

The most significant complications of placenta accreta include: * Severe postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), which is bleeding that occurs after delivery and can be life-threatening if not treated promptly. * Uterine rupture, which can lead to severe abdominal pain, organ damage, and potentially fatal consequences for both the mother and fetus. * Maternal mortality, which can occur due to severe blood loss, cardiac arrest, or other complications related to PPH. metadata.symptoms: Placenta previa is a pregnancy complication characterized by the placenta partially or completely covering the internal cervical os (the opening of the uterus into the vagina). The main symptoms and signs of placenta previa include: Typically, patients with placenta previa experience three to five key symptoms. These include: 1. **Abnormal vaginal bleeding**: This is often the most concerning symptom, as it can be a sign of significant bleeding from the placenta. The bleeding may be heavy and prolonged, and can be accompanied by clotting or spotting. 2. **Painful contractions**: Women with placenta previa may experience painful uterine contractions, which can be a sign that the placenta is separating from the uterus and causing bleeding. 3. **Severe abdominal pain**: Patients may also experience severe abdominal pain, which can be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and fever. It's essential to note that these symptoms can vary in severity and presentation from one patient to another. In some cases, patients may not experience any noticeable symptoms until the placenta separates from the uterus, leading to a sudden and severe bleed.
metadata.causes: Placenta previa is a pregnancy complication characterized by the placenta partially or completely covering the cervix, which can lead to bleeding during pregnancy or after delivery. The primary causative factors of placenta previa are biological in nature, specifically related to the abnormal implantation of the placenta on the uterine wall. This occurs when the placenta implants too low in the uterus, often due to a previous uterine scar from cesarean section or other surgical procedures. The underlying mechanisms involve the placenta's attachment to the uterine lining, which can be disrupted by various factors such as: * Abnormal implantation of the placenta * Uterine scarring or adhesions * Hormonal influences during pregnancy Environmental and lifestyle factors are not typically considered primary causes of placenta previa.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for placenta previa include: 1. **Multiparity**: Women who have had multiple pregnancies are at higher risk of developing placenta previa. 2. **Advanced maternal age**: Women over 35 years old, especially those over 40, are more likely to experience placenta previa due to decreased uterine elasticity and increased risk of placental implantation issues. 3. **History of placenta previa or other pregnancy complications**: Women who have had previous placenta previa or other pregnancy-related complications, such as preeclampsia or fetal growth restriction, are at higher risk of developing the condition again. These factors increase the likelihood of placenta previa by affecting uterine shape and function, leading to abnormal placental implantation.
metadata.complications: Placenta previa is a pregnancy complication where the placenta partially or completely covers the cervix, which can lead to severe bleeding during delivery. If left untreated or poorly managed, serious outcomes may include maternal hemorrhage, shock, and even death. Additionally, preterm labor and fetal distress are also potential complications if the condition is not properly addressed. The most significant complications of placenta previa include: 1. Maternal hemorrhage: Severe bleeding can lead to shock, organ failure, and even death. 2. Fetal distress: The lack of oxygen and nutrients can cause the baby to become distressed, leading to potential long-term health issues or even stillbirth. 3. Premature birth: Untreated placenta previa can lead to preterm labor, which can increase the risk of complications for both the mother and the baby. It's essential to note that prompt medical attention and proper management are crucial in preventing these serious outcomes.

metadata.complications: Placental abruption, also known as placental separation, is a serious medical condition that occurs when the placenta separates from the uterus before childbirth. If left untreated or poorly managed, placental abruption can lead to severe complications, including fetal distress, respiratory distress syndrome, and cardiac arrest. Additionally, maternal hemorrhage, shock, and organ failure are also potential life-threatening outcomes if the condition is not promptly and effectively treated. Fetal death: The separation of the placenta can deprive the fetus of oxygen and nutrients, leading to fetal demise. 2. Maternal hemorrhage: Excessive bleeding from the uterus can lead to shock, organ failure, and even maternal death. 3. Organ failure: Severe bleeding and hypotension can cause damage to vital organs such as the kidneys, liver, and lungs. It's essential to seek immediate medical attention if symptoms of placental abruption occur, including severe abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and fetal distress. Prompt treatment with medications, surgical intervention, or other interventions may help prevent these complications and ensure a better outcome for both the mother and the fetus.

metadata.causes: The plantar fascia is a band of tissue, called fascia, that connects your heel bone to the base of your toes. It supports the arch of the foot and absorbs shock when walking. Tension and stress on the fascia can cause small tears. Repeated stretching and tearing of the facia can irritate or inflame it, although the cause remains unclear in many cases of plantar fasciitis.
metadata.risk_factors: Even though plantar fasciitis can develop without an obvious cause, some factors can increase your risk of developing this condition. They include: Age. Plantar fasciitis is most common in people between the ages of 40 and 60. Certain types of exercise. Activities that place a lot of stress on your heel and attached tissue  such as long-distance running, ballet dancing and aerobic dance  can contribute to the onset of plantar fasciitis. Foot mechanics. Flat feet, a high arch or even an atypical pattern of walking can affect the way weight is distributed when youre standing and can put added stress on the plantar fascia. Obesity. Excess pounds put extra stress on your plantar fascia. Occupations that keep you on your feet. Factory workers, teachers and others who spend most of their work hours walking or standing on hard surfaces can be at increased risk of plantar fasciitis. metadata.symptoms: Plexiform neurofibromas can cause different symptoms based on where they grow, how big they are, and how they press on nearby nerves and tissues. Some people have no symptoms at first. Others may notice changes in how their bodies look, feel or move. Common signs and symptoms of plexiform neurofibroma include: Pain. Ongoing pain, which may be moderate to severe, is common in people with plexiform neurofibroma. Pain from plexiform neurofibroma can make it difficult to do daily activities and affect movement. Swelling or soft lumps. Tumors can cause growths that can be seen or felt under the skin. These may grow over time and may be soft, spongy or thickened. Changes in appearance. Tumors in visible areas such as the face or limbs can cause disfigurement, leading to emotional or social concerns. Movement changes. Tumors pressing on nerves or muscles can make it harder to walk, grasp objects or perform everyday tasks. Vision changes. Tumors near the eyes or the optic nerve can cause blurred vision, drooping eyelids or other changes in how the eyes look or work. Numbness or tingling. These symptoms may occur when the tumor interferes with how a nerve works  either by pressing on it or growing into it. Bladder or bowel changes. Plexiform neurofibromas near the pelvis or lower spine can affect the nerves that control the bladder and bowel. This can lead to symptoms such as urgency, frequent urination, leakage or trouble emptying, as well as constipation or stool leakage. High blood pressure. Some tumors may affect nearby structures or organs in a way that leads to high blood pressure, especially if they press on blood vessels or involve the kidneys or adrenal glands. Emotional changes. Children may feel anxious, sad or lonely due to their symptoms, appearance or ongoing pain. Request an appointment
metadata.causes: Most plexiform neurofibromas occur in people with a condition called neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). NF1 is caused by a change in the NF1 gene, which is located on chromosome 17. This gene typically helps control how cells grow. When it isnt working properly, cells that support nerves may grow too much and form tumors like plexiform neurofibromas.
metadata.risk_factors: Plexiform neurofibromas are linked to a genetic condition called neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Anyone with NF1 has a risk of developing these tumors. The number, size and location of tumors can vary from person to person. Having NF1 is the main risk factor for plexiform neurofibroma. Up to 50 of people with NF1 will develop one or more plexiform neurofibromas during their lives. Plexiform neurofibromas are linked to a genetic condition called neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). metadata.complications: Plexiform neurofibroma is a type of benign nerve sheath tumor that can cause significant complications if left untreated or poorly managed. If left untreated, plexiform neurofibroma can lead to compression of surrounding nerves, resulting in chronic pain, numbness, tingling, and weakness in the affected limb. Additionally, this condition can increase the risk of developing secondary conditions such as nerve damage, muscle atrophy, and decreased range of motion. Untreated or poorly managed plexiform neurofibroma can also lead to serious complications, including: 1. Nerve damage: Compression of nerves by the tumor can cause permanent nerve damage, leading to chronic pain, numbness, and weakness. 2. Muscle atrophy: Prolonged compression of nerves can lead to muscle wasting and weakness in the affected limb. 3. Decreased range of motion: Chronic compression of joints and surrounding tissues can lead to decreased range of motion and stiffness in the affected limb. It's essential to seek medical attention from a qualified neurosurgeon or orthopedic specialist for proper diagnosis and treatment of plexiform neurofibroma to prevent these complications and improve outcomes.

Mild signs and symptoms often are similar to those of a cold or flu, but they last longer. Signs and symptoms of pneumonia may include: Chest pain when you breathe or cough Confusion or changes in mental awareness (in adults age 65 and older) Cough, which may produce phlegm Fatigue Fever, sweating and shaking chills Lower than normal body temperature (in adults older than age 65 and people with weak immune systems) Nausea, vomiting or diarrhea Shortness of breath Newborns and infants may not show any sign of the infection. metadata.causes: Many germs can cause pneumonia. The most common are bacteria and viruses in the air we breathe. Your body usually prevents these germs from infecting your lungs. But sometimes these germs can overpower your immune system, even if your health is generally good. Pneumonia is classified according to the types of germs that cause it and where you got the infection.
metadata.risk_factors: Pneumonia can affect anyone. But the two age groups at highest risk are: Children who are 2 years old or younger People who are age 65 or older Other risk factors include: Being hospitalized. Youre at greater risk of pneumonia if youre in a hospital intensive care unit, especially if youre on a machine that helps you breathe (a ventilator). Chronic disease. Youre more likely to get pneumonia if you have asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or heart disease. Smoking. Smoking damages your bodys natural defenses against the bacteria and viruses that cause pneumonia. Weakened or suppressed immune system. People who have HIV/AIDS, whove had an organ transplant, or who receive chemotherapy or long-term steroids are at risk. Pneumonia can affect anyone. metadata.complications: Even with treatment, some people with pneumonia, especially those in high-risk groups, may experience complications, including: Bacteria in the bloodstream (bacteremia). Bacteria that enter the bloodstream from your lungs can spread the infection to other organs, potentially causing organ failure. Difficulty breathing. If your pneumonia is severe or you have chronic underlying lung diseases, you may have trouble breathing in enough oxygen. You may need to be hospitalized and use a breathing machine (ventilator) while your lung heals. Fluid accumulation around the lungs (pleural effusion). Pneumonia may cause fluid to build up in the thin space between layers of tissue that line the lungs and chest cavity (pleura). If the fluid becomes infected, you may need to have it drained through a chest tube or removed with surgery. Lung abscess. An abscess occurs if pus forms in a cavity in the lung. An abscess is usually treated with antibiotics. Sometimes, surgery or drainage with a long needle or tube placed into the abscess is needed to remove the pus. See your doctor if you have difficulty breathing, chest pain, persistent fever of 102 F (39 C) or higher, or persistent cough, especially if youre coughing up pus. metadata.symptoms: Symptoms of pneumonitis may develop quickly or slowly and can worsen over time. At times symptoms may suddenly get worse or better. Also, symptoms vary greatly among people with the condition and include: Trouble breathing. Dry cough that usually doesnt bring up any mucus. Extreme tiredness. Loss of appetite. Fever. Joint and muscle pain. Headache. Weight loss.
metadata.causes: Bronchioles and alveoli in the lungs Enlarge image Close Bronchioles and alveoli in the lungs Bronchioles and alveoli in the lungs In your lungs, the main airways, called bronchi, branch off into smaller and smaller passageways. The smallest airways, called bronchioles, lead to tiny air sacs called alveoli. Pneumonitis happens when an irritating substance causes inflammation in the tiny air sacs called alveoli in your lungs. Inflamed lung tissue makes it hard for oxygen to pass through the alveoli into the bloodstream. Many causes have been linked to pneumonitis. But its not clear why some people have a strong immune system response to certain substances that cause pneumonitis, while others do not. For many people, the specific substance causing the inflammation is never identified. Some types of pneumonitis include hypersensitivity pneumonitis, drug-induced pneumonitis and radiation-induced pneumonitis.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing pneumonitis include: * Age: Older adults (>65 years) are more susceptible to pneumonitis due to age-related declines in immune function. * Medical conditions: Individuals with underlying respiratory diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, or cystic fibrosis are at increased risk of developing pneumonitis. * Genetic predispositions: Certain genetic mutations, such as those affecting the surfactant protein D gene, can increase an individual's susceptibility to pneumonitis.
metadata.complications: If pneumonitis is not detected or not treated, you may gradually develop lung damage that cant be reversed. In healthy lungs, the air sacs stretch and relax with each breath. Ongoing inflammation of the thin tissue lining each air sac causes scarring and makes the air sacs less flexible. They become stiff like a dried sponge. This is called pulmonary fibrosis. In severe cases, pulmonary fibrosis can cause high blood pressure in the lungs, right-sided heart failure, respiratory failure or death.

metadata.causes: Poison ivy plant Enlarge image Close Poison ivy plant Poison ivy plant A poison ivy plant typically has three leaflets branching off a single stem. It may grow as a low plant or bush or as a vine. Low-lying poison ivy plants are usually found among groups of weeds and other plants. Unlike poison ivy and poison oak, it doesnt grow in a three-leaf-per-stem pattern. Poison ivy rash is caused by an allergic reaction to an oily resin called urushiol. Its found in poison ivy, poison oak and poison sumac. This oily resin is very sticky, so it easily attaches to your skin, clothing, tools, equipment and pets fur. You can get a poison ivy reaction from: Touching the plant. If you touch the leaves, stem, roots or berries of the plant, you may have a reaction. Touching contaminated objects. If you walk through some poison ivy and then later touch your shoes, you might get urushiol on your hands. You might then transfer it to your face or body by touching or rubbing. If the contaminated object isnt cleaned, the urushiol on it can still cause a skin reaction years later. Inhaling smoke from the burning plants. Even the smoke from burning poison ivy, poison oak and poison sumac can irritate or harm your nasal passages or lungs. Pus that oozes from blisters doesnt contain urushiol and wont spread the rash. metadata.symptoms: Nerve cell (neuron) Enlarge image Close Nerve cell (neuron) Nerve cell (neuron) The basic unit of communication in the nervous system is the nerve cell (neuron). Each nerve cell consists of the cell body, which includes the nucleus, a major branching fiber (axon) and numerous smaller branching fibers (dendrites). The myelin sheath is fatty material that covers, insulates and protects nerves of the brain and spinal cord. Most people infected with the virus that causes polio, called poliovirus, dont get symptoms.
metadata.causes: Polio is caused by the poliovirus. It mainly targets nerve cells in the spinal cord and brain stem that control muscle movement. Nerve cells controlling sensation are generally not affected. The naturally-occurring poliovirus, called the wild-type poliovirus, has been eliminated in most countries and causes few cases of polio. Another version of the virus, called the vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV), is more widespread and now causes most infections worldwide. VDPV exists mainly in a few countries that use an oral vaccine with a weakened poliovirus. The weakened virus in the oral vaccine doesnt itself cause polio, and vaccinated people rarely contract VDPV. Instead, VDPV is a new version of the virus that develops within a community or region where not enough people are vaccinated. Even though the weakened virus in the oral vaccine doesnt cause illness, it can spread. If most people in a community are vaccinated, the spread of the weakened virus is controlled. If many people arent vaccinated, the weakened virus can move through a community for a long time. This gives the virus the chance to change, or mutate, and behave like the wild-type virus that causes illness. Infections from VDPV have been reported in the United States. In each case, the person was either not vaccinated or had a significantly weakened immune system. One case in New York in 2022 was in a county with a lower-than-average polio vaccination rate. Samples from wastewater showed that VDPV was spreading in some communities. Since 2000, polio vaccination in the United States has used an injected vaccine with an inactivated poliovirus that doesnt create the risk for VDPV.
metadata.risk_factors: Polio mainly affects children. But anyone who hasnt been vaccinated is at risk of getting the disease. Polio mainly affects children. But anyone who hasnt been vaccinated is at risk of getting the disease.
metadata.complications: Severe disease that affects the ability to breathe can cause death. Long-term complications for people who recover may include: Permanent paralysis Muscle shortening that causes deformed bones or joints Chronic pain Post-polio syndrome Signs and symptoms of polio are similar to other viral diseases that affect the nervous system. Its important to get a timely and accurate diagnosis. If you had polio before, see your health care provider if you have new or worse signs or symptoms. Request an appointment

This is the most common type of ongoing kidney disease thats passed through families, also called inherited. Symptoms of ADPKD often start between the ages of 30 and 40. metadata.risk_factors: The biggest risk factor for getting polycystic kidney disease is getting the gene changes that cause the disease from one or both parents. metadata.complications: Complications linked to polycystic kidney disease include: High blood pressure. This is common in polycystic kidney disease. Not treated, high blood pressure can cause more damage to the kidneys and increase the risk of heart disease and strokes. Loss of kidney function. The kidneys losing their ability to do their work is one of the most serious complications of polycystic kidney disease. Nearly half of people with the condition have kidney failure by age 60. But for some people, it starts in the early 30s. Pain. Its common to have pain with polycystic kidney disease. Pain often is in the side or back. The pain can come and go or be ongoing. The pain may be linked to bleeding into a cyst, a urinary tract infection, a kidney stone or, less often, cancer. Cysts in the liver. The older people with polycystic kidney disease get, the more likely it is theyll get cysts in the liver. With cysts, the liver most often keeps working. Women tend to get larger cysts than do men. Hormones and pregnancies might be part of the reason. Brain aneurysm. A balloonlike bulge in a blood vessel, called an aneurysm, in the brain can cause bleeding if it bursts. People with polycystic kidney disease have a higher risk of aneurysms. People with a family history of aneurysms seem to be at highest risk. Ask your healthcare professional if you need screening. If screening doesnt show an aneurysm, your healthcare professional may suggest screening again in a few years. The timing of repeat screening depends on your risk. Pregnancy complications. Most people with polycystic kidney disease can have success with pregnancy. But sometimes, they can get a life-threatening condition called preeclampsia during pregnancy. Those most at risk have high blood pressure or a loss of kidney function before they become pregnant. Heart valve conditions. As many as 1 in 4 adults with polycystic kidney disease gets mitral valve prolapse. When this happens, the heart valve no longer closes well. This lets blood leak backward. Colon conditions. People with polycystic kidney disease may get weaknesses and pouches or sacs called diverticula in the wall of the colon. This condition is called diverticulosis. Diverticula most often dont cause symptoms, but they may bleed or get infected. People often have polycystic kidney disease for years without knowing it. If you have some of the symptoms of polycystic kidney disease, see your healthcare professional. If you have a parent, sibling or child with polycystic kidney disease, see your healthcare professional to talk about screening for the condition. Request an appointment

metadata.symptoms: Polycythemia vera (PV) is a rare blood disorder characterized by the excessive production of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets in the bone marrow. The main symptoms and signs of PV include: * **Excessive fatigue**: Due to an increased number of red blood cells, patients may experience persistent fatigue, weakness, and shortness of breath. * **Headaches**: Thrombosis (blood clots) can occur due to the high platelet count, leading to headaches, dizziness, and confusion. * **Bone pain**: PV can cause bone marrow expansion, which can lead to bone pain, particularly in the skull, pelvis, or spine. * **Dark urine**: The increased concentration of red blood cells can cause urine to appear dark yellow or tea-colored due to the high levels of bilirubin. * **Easy bruising and bleeding**: Thrombosis can also cause easy bruising, petechiae (small red spots), and bleeding gums. These symptoms are often accompanied by other signs such as an enlarged spleen, splenomegaly, and a palpable spleen.
metadata.causes: Polycythemia vera (PV) is a rare blood disorder characterized by an overproduction of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets in the bone marrow. The primary causative factors of PV are genetic mutations that affect the JAK2 gene, which regulates cell growth and division. These mutations lead to the production of a constitutively active form of the JAK2 protein, resulting in uncontrolled cell proliferation. Biological factors, such as an abnormality in the bone marrow stem cells, also play a role in the development of PV. Environmental factors, such as exposure to certain chemicals or radiation, may also contribute to the risk of developing PV. Lifestyle factors, such as smoking and obesity, have been linked to an increased risk of developing PV. It's worth noting that PV is often diagnosed after age 50, suggesting that it may be related to aging or cumulative genetic damage over time. However, the exact mechanisms underlying the development of PV are still not fully understood, and more research is needed to determine the specific factors that contribute to its pathogenesis.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing Polycythemia Vera (PV) include: 1. **Genetic predisposition**: Individuals with a family history of PV are more likely to develop the condition, particularly those with a first-degree relative affected. 2. **Age**: PV typically affects individuals over 60 years old, with the majority of cases occurring in people between 65 and 75 years old. 3. **Male sex**: Males are more likely than females to develop PV, with a male-to-female ratio ranging from 1.5:1 to 2.5:1. These demographic factors significantly increase an individual's likelihood of developing Polycythemia Vera.
metadata.complications: Polycythemia vera (PV) is a rare blood disorder characterized by an overproduction of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. If left untreated or poorly managed, PV can lead to several serious complications, including increased risk of thrombosis (blood clots), stroke, and bleeding due to excessive clotting. Additionally, PV can also increase the risk of organ damage, such as kidney failure and liver disease. The most significant complications of untreated or poorly managed PV include: * Thrombotic events: Blood clots in the legs, lungs, and brain can occur due to the increased viscosity of blood. * Bleeding risks: Excessive clotting can lead to uncontrolled bleeding, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract, which can be life-threatening. * Organ damage: PV can cause kidney failure, liver disease, and other organ damage due to the accumulation of abnormal red blood cells. It is essential to note that timely diagnosis and treatment with medications such as hydroxyurea or interferon-alpha can help manage PV and reduce the risk of these complications.

The primary causative factors of PMLE are genetic predisposition, ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun or artificial light sources, and individual differences in skin pigmentation. Biological factors such as defects in the skin's natural repair mechanisms and immune system dysfunction also play a role. This leads to the characteristic symptoms of PMLE, including erythema (redness), edema (swelling), and blistering.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Polymorphic Light Eruption (PMLE) include: * Genetic predisposition: Individuals with a family history of PMLE are more likely to develop the condition. * Age: PMLE typically affects individuals between the ages of 20-40, with peak incidence during adolescence and early adulthood. * Fair skin: People with fair skin, particularly those with a Fitzpatrick skin type I or II, are at increased risk of developing PMLE. These factors contribute significantly to the likelihood of developing PMLE.

metadata.symptoms: Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR) is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by muscle pain and stiffness, particularly in the neck, shoulders, and hips. The main symptoms of PMR include: 1. **Muscle pain and stiffness**: Patients typically experience widespread muscle pain and stiffness, especially in the neck, shoulders, and hips, which can be exacerbated by movement or activity. 2. **Morning stiffness**: Morning stiffness is a hallmark symptom of PMR, with patients often reporting that their muscles feel stiffer in the morning and improve as the day progresses. 3. **Fatigue**: Patients with PMR often experience persistent fatigue, which can impact daily activities and overall quality of life. These symptoms are typically accompanied by other signs such as: * Elevated inflammatory markers (e.g., erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP)) * Joint pain and stiffness * Weight loss * Loss of appetite It's essential to note that PMR can be asymptomatic in some cases, and not all patients will experience all of these symptoms. A diagnosis of PMR is typically made based on a combination of clinical presentation, laboratory tests, and imaging studies (e.g., X-rays or MRI).
metadata.causes: Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR) is a chronic inflammatory disorder characterized by muscle pain and stiffness, particularly in the neck, shoulder, and hip areas. The primary causative factors of PMR are thought to be autoimmune in nature, with an overactive immune response triggered by an abnormal interaction between genetic predisposition and environmental triggers such as infections or hormonal changes. Biological factors, including an imbalance of cytokines and other inflammatory mediators, contribute to the development of PMR. Genetic predisposition plays a role, with certain HLA haplotypes increasing the risk of developing the condition. Environmental factors, such as viral infections and hormonal fluctuations during menopause, may also trigger or exacerbate PMR in susceptible individuals. Lifestyle factors, including age and physical inactivity, are also thought to contribute to the development of PMR, although the exact mechanisms by which they do so are not fully understood.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR) include: 1. **Age**: PMR typically affects people over the age of 50, with the majority of cases occurring in individuals between 60-80 years old. 2. **Gender**: Women are more likely to develop PMR than men, with a female-to-male ratio of approximately 3:1. 3. **Family history**: Individuals with a family history of PMR or other rheumatic conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis, are at increased risk of developing the condition. These demographic factors significantly contribute to the likelihood of developing PMR, and individuals with these characteristics should be aware of the potential risks and seek medical attention if symptoms persist.
metadata.complications: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is a chronic inflammatory disorder that can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is increased risk of cardiovascular events, such as heart attacks and strokes, due to the systemic inflammation associated with PMR. Additionally, untreated PMR can also increase the risk of osteoporosis, fractures, and cognitive decline. Untreated PMR can lead to a range of secondary conditions, including osteoporosis, which can result in fractures and increased risk of falls. Poorly managed PMR can also lead to anemia, which can cause fatigue, weakness, and shortness of breath. Furthermore, the chronic inflammation associated with PMR can also increase the risk of developing other inflammatory conditions, such as atherosclerosis and peripheral artery disease. It's worth noting that while these complications are potential risks, they can often be mitigated with proper treatment and management of PMR. Regular monitoring by a healthcare provider and adherence to treatment plans can help minimize the risk of these complications and improve overall quality of life for individuals with PMR.

metadata.symptoms: The main symptom of popliteal artery entrapment syndrome, also called PAES, is pain or cramping in the back of the lower leg. The back of the lower leg is called the calf. The pain or cramping occurs during exercise and goes away with rest. Other symptoms of PAES may include: Cold feet after exercise. Tingling or burning in the calf. Numbness in the calf area. metadata.causes: Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome, also called PAES, is caused by an irregular calf muscle, usually the gastrocnemius muscle. The condition may be seen at birth, or it may occur later in life. When its present at birth, the calf muscle or nearby artery forms in the wrong place during pregnancy. People who get the condition later in life have a calf muscle that is bigger than usual. The changes in the calf muscle cause it to press on the main artery behind the knee. This reduces blood flow to the lower leg. The lack of blood flow causes pain and cramping in the back of the lower leg during times of activity.
metadata.risk_factors: Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome, also called PAES, is uncommon. The following things increase the risk of the condition: Younger age. The condition is most often seen in people who are in their late teens or 20s. Its rarely diagnosed in those over age 40. Male sex assigned at birth. PAES can occur in anyone, but its much more common in young men. Extreme athletic activity. Runners, bicyclists, and athletes who try to build muscle fast with weight training routines or high-intensity circuit training are at the highest risk. metadata.causes: Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern Enlarge image Close Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern In an autosomal dominant disorder, the changed gene is a dominant gene. Heme also plays a role in clearing drugs and hormones from the body. Heme is made in the bone marrow and liver. This process involves eight different enzymes that turn porphyrins into heme. metadata.complications: Possible complications depend on the form of porphyria: Acute porphyrias can be life-threatening if an attack isnt promptly treated. During an attack, you may experience dehydration from loss of fluids, breathing problems, seizures or high blood pressure. You may need a stay in the hospital for treatment. Long-term complications with repeat acute attacks may include long-term pain, chronic kidney failure, liver damage or liver cancer. Cutaneous porphyrias can result in permanent skin damage. Cutaneous porphyrias also increase the risk of liver damage or liver cancer. In rare cases, a bone marrow transplant or liver transplant may be needed. Many symptoms of porphyria are like those of other, more common conditions. This can make it difficult to know if youre having an attack of porphyria. metadata.symptoms: Post-Polio Syndrome (PPS) is a chronic condition that affects individuals who have had poliomyelitis (polio) in the past. The main symptoms of PPS are characterized by muscle weakness, fatigue, and joint pain, which can be debilitating and impact daily life. Three to five key symptoms that patients typically experience include: 1) progressive muscle weakness, particularly in the arms and legs, which can lead to difficulty with activities such as walking, climbing stairs, or performing everyday tasks; 2) persistent fatigue, which can range from mild to severe and interfere with sleep patterns and overall quality of life; 3) joint pain and stiffness, especially in the shoulders, elbows, hips, and knees, which can cause discomfort and limited mobility; 4) muscle wasting and atrophy, particularly in the facial muscles, which can lead to facial weakness and drooping; and 5) autonomic dysfunction, including symptoms such as orthostatic intolerance (dizziness upon standing), tremors, and abnormal heart rhythms. These symptoms can vary in severity and impact, but are commonly experienced by individuals with PPS.
metadata.causes: Post-Polio Syndrome (PPS) is a chronic condition that affects individuals who have had poliomyelitis (polio) in childhood. The primary causative factors of PPS are the residual muscle damage and inflammation caused by the virus, which can lead to progressive muscle weakness, fatigue, and joint pain over time. Additionally, genetic predisposition and environmental factors such as smoking and exposure to toxins may also contribute to the development of PPS. Biological factors play a significant role in the pathogenesis of PPS, as the poliovirus can cause persistent inflammation and damage to the motor neurons, leading to muscle atrophy and weakness. Genetic factors, such as mutations in genes involved in muscle function and repair, may also predispose individuals to developing PPS. Environmental factors, including exposure to toxins and smoking, have been linked to an increased risk of developing PPS. These substances can exacerbate muscle damage and inflammation, leading to the progression of symptoms. Lifestyle factors, such as physical inactivity and poor nutrition, may also contribute to the development of PPS by further weakening muscles and impairing muscle function. It's worth noting that not everyone who has had polio will develop PPS, and the exact mechanisms underlying the condition are still not fully understood. However, research suggests that a combination of biological, genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors may contribute to its development.

metadata.symptoms: Postpartum preeclampsia is a serious medical condition that can occur in women after childbirth. The main symptoms and signs of postpartum preeclampsia include: The most common and characteristic symptoms of postpartum preeclampsia are hypertension, proteinuria, and liver dysfunction. Patients typically experience high blood pressure (hypertension) that is not explained by other medical conditions, often accompanied by elevated levels of protein in the urine (proteinuria). Additionally, patients may exhibit signs of liver damage, such as elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin levels. Other symptoms may include headaches, visual disturbances, and abdominal pain. It's worth noting that postpartum preeclampsia can be a life-threatening condition if left untreated or if treatment is delayed. It's essential for healthcare providers to monitor women closely after childbirth, especially those with a history of preeclampsia or hypertension, to detect any signs of this condition early on. In terms of specific numbers, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) defines postpartum preeclampsia as: * Blood pressure ≥160/110 mmHg * Proteinuria ≥300 mg/24 hours Early detection and treatment are crucial to prevent complications and ensure the best possible outcomes for women with postpartum preeclampsia.
metadata.causes: Postpartum preeclampsia is a rare but life-threatening complication that occurs in some women after childbirth, characterized by high blood pressure and damage to organs such as the kidneys and liver. The primary causative factors of postpartum preeclampsia are believed to be related to the placental abruption, which can lead to an inflammatory response and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines that can cause endothelial dysfunction and hypertension. Additionally, genetic predisposition and hormonal changes during pregnancy may also contribute to the development of postpartum preeclampsia. Biological factors: * Placental abruption: The separation of the placenta from the uterine wall can lead to an inflammatory response, releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines that can cause endothelial dysfunction and hypertension. * Endothelial dysfunction: The release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and other mediators can damage the endothelium, leading to increased vascular resistance and hypertension. Genetic factors: * Family history: Women with a family history of preeclampsia or other cardiovascular diseases may be at higher risk of developing postpartum preeclampsia. * Genetic predisposition: Certain genetic variants, such as those involved in the renin-angiotensin system, may increase the risk of developing postpartum preeclampsia. Environmental factors: * Hypertension during pregnancy: Women who develop hypertension during pregnancy are at higher risk of developing postpartum preeclampsia. * Multiple gestations: Carrying twins or other multiples increases the risk of postpartum preeclampsia due to increased placental mass and blood flow demands. Lifestyle factors: * Obesity: Women with a body mass index (BMI) greater than 30 are at higher risk of developing postpartum preeclampsia. * Smoking during pregnancy: Smoking during pregnancy can increase the risk of postpartum preeclampsia due to its effects on placental function and blood flow. It is essential to note that postpartum preeclampsia can be a complex condition, and multiple factors may contribute to its development.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for postpartum preeclampsia include: 1. **Age**: Women over 35 years old are at higher risk of developing postpartum preeclampsia, with the risk increasing significantly after 40 years. 2. **History of hypertension or kidney disease**: Women with a history of hypertension, kidney disease, or preeclampsia in a previous pregnancy are more likely to develop postpartum preeclampsia. 3. **Genetic predisposition**: Women with a family history of preeclampsia or hypertension are at higher risk of developing the condition. These factors can increase a woman's likelihood of developing postpartum preeclampsia, which is a serious complication that requires prompt medical attention.
metadata.complications: Postpartum preeclampsia is a severe complication of pregnancy that can lead to significant morbidity and mortality for both mother and baby. If left untreated or poorly managed, postpartum preeclampsia can progress to eclampsia, which can cause seizures and coma, as well as stroke, kidney failure, and liver failure. Additionally, it can also lead to placental abruption, hemorrhage, and maternal mortality. In severe cases, postpartum preeclampsia can result in long-term complications such as: 1. Chronic kidney disease: Prolonged hypertension and renal impairment can lead to chronic kidney disease, requiring dialysis or transplantation. 2. Cardiovascular disease: Untreated preeclampsia can increase the risk of cardiovascular events, including heart attack, stroke, and cardiac arrhythmias. 3. Neurological damage: Seizures and coma can result in permanent neurological damage, affecting cognitive function, motor skills, and quality of life. It is essential to recognize the signs and symptoms of postpartum preeclampsia promptly and seek immediate medical attention if they occur.

A child with an error in one or more genes in chromosome 15 is at the highest risk of getting Prader-Willi syndrome. For example, one of the genes might be missing. This error may or may not be inherited. Those who have a child with Prader-Willi syndrome and would like to have another baby should think about getting genetic counseling. metadata.complications: In addition to being hungry all the time, people with Prader-Willi syndrome have low muscle mass. As a result, they need fewer calories, and they may not be physically active. These factors make them prone to obesity and the medical problems related to obesity, such as: Type 2 diabetes. High blood pressure. High cholesterol. Heart disease. Sleep apnea. Other complications, such as being more likely to have liver disease and gallstones. Regularly scheduled well-baby visits can help find early signs of poor growth and development that can be signs of Prader-Willi syndrome or other conditions. metadata.causes: To understand the causes of precocious puberty in some children, its helpful to know what happens at puberty. metadata.complications: Possible complications of precocious puberty include: Short height. Children with precocious puberty might grow quickly at first and be taller than others their ages. Children who begin puberty long before others of their age might be upset about the changes in their bodies. For example, dealing with early periods can cause distress. metadata.symptoms: Prediabetes doesnt usually have any signs or symptoms. One possible sign of prediabetes is darkened skin on certain parts of the body. Affected areas can include the neck, armpits and groin. Classic signs and symptoms that suggest youve moved from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes include: Increased thirst Frequent urination Increased hunger Fatigue Blurred vision Numbness or tingling in the feet or hands Frequent infections Slow-healing sores Unintended weight loss
metadata.causes: The exact cause of prediabetes is unknown. But family history and genetics appear to play an important role. What is clear is that people with prediabetes dont process sugar (glucose) properly anymore. Most of the glucose in your body comes from the food you eat. When food is digested, sugar enters your bloodstream. Insulin allows sugar to enter your cells  and lowers the amount of sugar in your blood. Insulin is produced by a gland located behind the stomach called the pancreas. Your pancreas sends insulin to your blood when you eat. When your blood sugar level starts to drop, the pancreas slows down the secretion of insulin into the blood. When you have prediabetes, this process doesnt work as well. As a result, instead of fueling your cells, sugar builds up in your bloodstream. This can happen because: Your pancreas may not make enough insulin Your cells become resistant to insulin and dont allow as much sugar in
metadata.risk_factors: The same factors that increase the odds of getting type 2 diabetes also increase the risk of prediabetes. These factors include: Weight. Being overweight is a primary risk factor for prediabetes. The more fatty tissue you have  especially inside and between the muscle and skin around your abdomen  the more resistant your cells become to insulin. Waist size. A large waist size can indicate insulin resistance. The risk of insulin resistance goes up for men with waists larger than 40 inches and for women with waists larger than 35 inches. Diet. Eating red meat and processed meat, and drinking sugar-sweetened beverages, is associated with a higher risk of prediabetes. Inactivity. The less active you are, the greater your risk of prediabetes. Age. Although diabetes can develop at any age, the risk of prediabetes increases after age 35. Family history. Your risk of prediabetes increases if you have a parent or sibling with type 2 diabetes. Race or ethnicity. Although its unclear why, certain people  including Black, Hispanic, American Indian and Asian American people  are more likely to develop prediabetes. Gestational diabetes. If you had diabetes while pregnant (gestational diabetes), you and your child are at higher risk of developing prediabetes. Polycystic ovary syndrome. Women with this common condition  characterized by irregular menstrual periods, excess hair growth and obesity  have a higher risk of prediabetes. Sleep. People with obstructive sleep apnea  a condition that disrupts sleep repeatedly  have an increased risk of insulin resistance. People who are overweight or obese have a higher risk of developing obstructive sleep apnea. Tobacco smoke. Smoking may increase insulin resistance and can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes in people with prediabetes. Smoking also increases your risk of complications from diabetes. metadata.symptoms: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy complication characterized by high blood pressure and damage to organs such as the liver and kidneys. The main symptoms and signs of preeclampsia include: High Blood Pressure: Elevated systolic blood pressure (≥140 mmHg) or diastolic blood pressure (≥90 mmHg). Proteinuria: Excessive protein in the urine, which can be detected through urinalysis. Headache: Severe headaches are a common symptom of preeclampsia. Visual Disturbances: Blurred vision, double vision, or loss of peripheral vision due to increased blood pressure on the eyes. Seizures: In severe cases, preeclampsia can cause seizures (convulsions).
metadata.causes: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy complication characterized by high blood pressure and damage to organs such as the liver and kidneys. The primary causative factors of preeclampsia are placental abnormalities, specifically abnormal placentation and inadequate trophoblast invasion, which disrupts normal communication between the mother's immune system and the developing fetus. This leads to an imbalance in angiogenic and anti-angiogenic factors, resulting in endothelial dysfunction and increased blood pressure. Biological factors play a significant role in preeclampsia, with genetic predisposition being a major contributor. Women with a family history of preeclampsia are more likely to develop the condition. Environmental factors, such as obesity and hypertension, can also increase the risk of developing preeclampsia. Lifestyle factors, such as a diet high in processed foods and sugar, can also contribute to the development of preeclampsia by increasing inflammation and oxidative stress. Additionally, certain medical conditions, such as diabetes and kidney disease, can also increase the risk of preeclampsia. It's worth noting that the exact mechanisms underlying preeclampsia are still not fully understood, but research suggests that it is a complex interplay between genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors.
metadata.risk_factors: Several studies have shown a greater risk of preeclampsia among Black women compared with other women. Theres also some evidence of an increased risk among indigenous women in North America. A growing body of evidence suggests that these differences in risk may not necessarily be based on biology. A greater risk may be related to inequities in access to prenatal care and health care in general, as well as social inequities and chronic stressors that affect health and well-being. Lower income also is associated with a greater risk of preeclampsia likely because of access to health care and social factors affecting health. For the purposes of making decisions about prevention strategies, a Black woman or a woman with a low income has a moderately increased risk of developing preeclampsia.
