metadata.complications: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy complication characterized by high blood pressure and damage to organs such as the liver, kidneys, and brain. If left untreated or poorly managed, preeclampsia can lead to severe complications, including stroke, kidney failure, and placental abruption, which can result in maternal mortality. Untreated preeclampsia also increases the risk of premature birth and low birth weight. In addition to these life-threatening complications, preeclampsia can also cause secondary conditions such as: * Seizures: due to high blood pressure causing damage to the brain * Liver failure: leading to jaundice, vomiting, and abdominal pain * Pulmonary edema: a condition where fluid accumulates in the lungs, making it difficult to breathe Untreated preeclampsia can also lead to long-term health consequences for both mothers and their babies, including increased risk of cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, and developmental delays.

metadata.causes: Pregnancy loss, also known as miscarriage, is a complex condition that can be caused by various factors, including biological, genetic, and environmental influences. The primary causative factors include hormonal imbalances, chromosomal abnormalities, and uterine anomalies, which can lead to the failure of the embryo to implant or grow properly in the uterus. Additionally, certain medical conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and thyroid disorders can also increase the risk of miscarriage. Biological factors, such as age, fertility issues, and underlying medical conditions, play a significant role in pregnancy loss. Genetic factors, including inherited genetic mutations, can also contribute to miscarriage. Environmental factors, such as exposure to toxins or certain medications, may also increase the risk of miscarriage. Lifestyle factors, such as smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, and stress, have been linked to an increased risk of miscarriage. However, it's essential to note that many cases of pregnancy loss are not preventable and can occur even in women with a healthy lifestyle and no underlying medical conditions. It's also worth noting that some cases of pregnancy loss may be due to a combination of these factors, rather than a single cause.
metadata.risk_factors: Various factors raise the risk of miscarriage, including: Age. If youre older than age 35, you have a higher risk of miscarriage than a younger person. At age 35, you have about a 20 risk. At age 40, the risk is about 33 to 40. And at age 45, it ranges from 57 to 80. Past miscarriages. If youve had one or more prior miscarriages before, youre at higher risk of pregnancy loss. Long-term conditions. If you have an ongoing health condition, such as uncontrolled diabetes, you have a higher risk of miscarriage. Uterine or cervical problems. Certain uterine conditions or weak cervical tissues, also called incompetent cervix, might raise the chances of a miscarriage. Smoking, alcohol, caffeine and illegal drugs. People who smoke have a greater risk of miscarriage than do nonsmokers. Heavy use of caffeine or alcohol use also raises the risk. So does using illegal drugs such as cocaine. Weight. Being underweight or being overweight has been linked with a higher risk of miscarriage. Genetic conditions. Sometimes, one of the partners may be healthy but carry a genetic problem that raises the risk of a miscarriage. For example, one partner could have a unique chromosome that formed when the pieces of two different chromosomes attached to each other. This is called translocation. If either partner carries a chromosome translocation, passing it to an unborn child makes a miscarriage more likely. Various factors raise the risk of miscarriage, including: Age. metadata.complications: Sometimes, pregnancy tissue that stays in the uterus after a miscarriage can lead to a uterine infection about 1 to 2 days later. The infection is called a septic miscarriage. Symptoms include: Fever higher than 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit more than two times. Chills. Pain in the lower stomach area. Foul-smelling fluid called discharge from the vagina. Vaginal bleeding. Call your health care professionals office or your local OB triage or emergency department if you have these symptoms. The illness can get worse fast and become life-threatening without treatment. Heavy bleeding from the vagina, called a hemorrhage, is another miscarriage complication. Along with the bleeding, a hemorrhage often happens with symptoms such as: Fast heartbeat. Dizziness from low blood pressure. Tiredness or weakness due low red blood cells, also called anemia. Get medical care at once. Some people who have a hemorrhage need blood from a donor or surgery.

metadata.symptoms: Prehypertension is a condition characterized by blood pressure levels that are higher than normal but not high enough to be classified as hypertension. The main symptoms and signs of prehypertension include: (1) elevated systolic blood pressure, typically between 120-139 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure between 80-89 mmHg; (2) increased pulse rate, often above 100 beats per minute; (3) headaches, which can be a result of the increased pressure on blood vessels in the brain; and (4) dizziness or lightheadedness due to decreased blood flow to the brain. Additionally, patients with prehypertension may experience (5) fatigue or weakness, possibly due to the heart working harder to pump blood through the body. It is essential for individuals with prehypertension to work closely with their healthcare provider to monitor and manage their condition, as it can progress to full-blown hypertension if left untreated. Note: The American Heart Association defines prehypertension as a systolic blood pressure between 120-139 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure between 80-89 mmHg.
metadata.causes: Prehypertension is a condition characterized by blood pressure levels that are higher than normal but not high enough to be classified as hypertension. The primary causes of prehypertension include genetic predisposition, lifestyle factors such as physical inactivity, obesity, and excessive sodium intake, as well as environmental factors like stress and smoking. Additionally, certain medical conditions, such as kidney disease or sleep apnea, can also contribute to the development of prehypertension. Biological factors play a role in the development of prehypertension, including genetic mutations that affect blood pressure regulation, hormonal imbalances, and changes in blood vessel function. Environmental factors, such as exposure to air pollution and high levels of caffeine consumption, can also contribute to increased blood pressure levels. Lifestyle factors are a significant contributor to the development of prehypertension, with regular physical activity, a healthy diet, and adequate sleep being essential for maintaining normal blood pressure levels.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for prehypertension include: * Age: Individuals over 40 years old are more likely to develop prehypertension due to age-related changes in blood pressure regulation. * Obesity: Being overweight or obese, particularly around the waistline, increases the risk of developing prehypertension due to insulin resistance and metabolic dysregulation. * Family history: A family history of hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or kidney disease can increase an individual's likelihood of developing prehypertension. These factors are interrelated, and addressing them through lifestyle modifications and medical interventions can help mitigate the risk of progressing to full-blown hypertension.
metadata.complications: Prehypertension, a condition characterized by blood pressure levels between 120/80 mmHg and 139/89 mmHg, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. If prehypertension is not addressed, it can increase the risk of developing cardiovascular disease, including heart attacks, strokes, and kidney damage due to high blood pressure's damaging effects on these organs. Untreated prehypertension also increases the risk of developing type 2 diabetes and peripheral artery disease. The most significant complications that may arise from untreated or poorly managed prehypertension include: 1. Cardiovascular disease: High blood pressure can cause the heart to work harder, leading to cardiac hypertrophy (enlargement) and increased risk of heart failure. 2. Kidney damage: Prolonged high blood pressure can lead to kidney damage, including chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease requiring dialysis or transplantation. 3. Stroke and cerebral vasospasm: Uncontrolled high blood pressure can cause blood vessels in the brain to rupture, leading to stroke or cerebral vasospasm (a temporary constriction of blood vessels). It is essential to work with a healthcare provider to manage prehypertension through lifestyle modifications and, if necessary, medication to lower blood pressure and reduce the risk of these complications.

metadata.causes: Premature birth, also known as preterm birth, is a medical condition where a baby is born before 37 weeks of gestation. The primary causes of premature birth are biological and genetic factors, including maternal infection, multiple pregnancy, and genetic disorders such as Down syndrome or sickle cell disease. Additionally, environmental factors such as smoking, substance abuse, and exposure to toxins during pregnancy can also increase the risk of premature birth. Other contributing factors include: * Uterine abnormalities or uterine rupture * Placental abruption or placenta previa * Maternal medical conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, or kidney disease * Exposure to certain medications or substances during pregnancy It's worth noting that many cases of premature birth are the result of a combination of these factors, rather than a single cause.
metadata.risk_factors: Often, the exact cause of premature birth isnt clear. But certain things can raise the risk. Some risk factors linked to past and present pregnancies include: Pregnancy with twins, triplets or other multiples. A span of less than six months between pregnancies. Its ideal to wait 18 to 24 months between pregnancies. Treatments to help you get pregnant, called assisted reproduction, including in vitro fertilization. More than one miscarriage or abortion. A previous premature birth. Some health problems can raise the risk of premature birth, such as: Problems with the uterus, cervix or placenta. Some infections, mainly those of the amniotic fluid and lower genital tract. Ongoing health problems such as high blood pressure and diabetes. Injuries or trauma to the body. Lifestyle choices also can raise the risk of a preterm pregnancy, such as: Smoking cigarettes, taking illicit drugs or drinking alcohol often or heavily while pregnant. Being underweight or overweight before pregnancy. Becoming pregnant before the age of 17 or after 35. Going through stressful life events, such as the death of a loved one or domestic violence. For unknown reasons, Black and Native people in the United States are more likely to have premature births than are women of other races. But premature birth can happen to anyone. metadata.symptoms: The main symptom of premature ejaculation is not being able to delay ejaculation for more than three minutes after penetration. But it might occur in all sexual situations, even during masturbation. Premature ejaculation can be classified as: Lifelong. Lifelong premature ejaculation occurs all or nearly all the time beginning with the first sexual encounter. Acquired. Acquired premature ejaculation develops after having previous sexual experiences without problems with ejaculation. Many people feel that they have symptoms of premature ejaculation, but the symptoms dont meet the criteria for a diagnosis. Its typical to experience early ejaculation at times.
metadata.causes: The exact cause of premature ejaculation isnt known. It was once thought to be only psychological. But health care providers now know that premature ejaculation involves a complex interaction of psychological and biological factors.
metadata.risk_factors: Various factors can increase the risk of premature ejaculation. They may include: Erectile dysfunction. You might be at increased risk of premature ejaculation if you have trouble getting or keeping an erection. Fear of losing an erection might cause you to hurry through sex. This may happen whether youre aware of it or not. Stress. Emotional or mental strain in any area of life can play a role in premature ejaculation. metadata.complications: Premature ejaculation can cause issues in your personal life. They might include: Stress and relationship problems. A common complication of premature ejaculation is relationship stress. Fertility problems. Premature ejaculation can sometimes make it hard for a partner to get pregnant. This may happen if ejaculation doesnt occur in the vagina. Talk with your health care provider if you ejaculate sooner than you wish during most sexual encounters. metadata.symptoms: Symptoms of primary ovarian insufficiency are like those of menopause or low estrogen. They include: Irregular or missed periods. This symptom might be present for years. It also could develop after a pregnancy or after stopping birth control pills. Trouble getting pregnant. Hot flashes and night sweats. Vaginal dryness. Anger, depression or anxiety. Trouble with focus or memory. Less sexual desire.
metadata.causes: Primary ovarian insufficiency may be caused by: Chromosome changes. Chromosomes are thread-like structures that contain genes. Most often, people assigned female at birth have two X chromosomes in their cells. But some people with primary ovarian insufficiency have one typical X chromosome and one altered X chromosome. This can be a sign of genetic conditions such as mosaic Turner syndrome. Other people with primary ovarian insufficiency have X chromosomes that are fragile and break. This is called fragile X syndrome. Toxins. Chemotherapy and radiation therapy are common causes of toxin-induced ovarian insufficiency. These treatments can damage genetic material in cells. Other toxins such as cigarette smoke, chemicals, pesticides and viruses might speed up ovarian insufficiency. An immune system response to ovarian tissue. This also is called autoimmune disease. In this rare form, the immune system makes protective proteins that attack ovary tissue by mistake. This harms sacs in the ovaries that each contain an egg, called follicles. It also damages the egg. What triggers the immune response is unclear. But being exposed to a virus may play a role. Unknown factors. Most often, the cause of primary ovarian insufficiency isnt clear. You might hear this called an idiopathic cause. Your health care professional may recommend more testing to try to find the cause. Video: Ovulation Show transcript for video Video: Ovulation Ovulation is the release of an egg from one of the ovaries. It often happens about midway through the menstrual cycle, although the exact timing may vary. In preparation for ovulation, the lining of the uterus, or endometrium, thickens. The pituitary gland in the brain stimulates one of the ovaries to release an egg. The wall of the ovarian follicle ruptures at the surface of the ovary. The egg is released. Finger-like structures called fimbriae sweep the egg into the neighboring fallopian tube. The egg travels through the fallopian tube, propelled in part by contractions in the fallopian tube walls. Here in the fallopian tube, the egg may be fertilized by a sperm. If the egg is fertilized, the egg and sperm unite to form a one-celled entity called a zygote. As the zygote travels down the fallopian tube toward the uterus, it begins dividing rapidly to form a cluster of cells called a blastocyst, which resembles a tiny raspberry. When the blastocyst reaches the uterus, it implants in the lining of the uterus and pregnancy begins. If the egg isnt fertilized, its simply reabsorbed by the body  perhaps before it even reaches the uterus. About two weeks later, the lining of the uterus sheds through the vagina. This is known as menstruation.
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that raise the risk of primary ovarian insufficiency include: Age. The risk goes up between ages 35 and 40. Primary ovarian insufficiency is rare before age 30. But younger people and even teens can get it. Family history. Having a family history of primary ovarian insufficiency raises the risk of getting this condition. Ovarian surgery. Surgeries that involve the ovaries raise the risk of primary ovarian insufficiency. Factors that raise the risk of primary ovarian insufficiency include: Age. The risk goes up between ages 35 and 40. Primary ovarian insufficiency is rare before age 30. But younger people and even teens can get it. Family history. Having a family history of primary ovarian insufficiency raises the risk of getting this condition. Ovarian surgery. metadata.complications: Primary ovarian insufficiency can lead to other health conditions, including the following: Infertility. Not being able to get pregnant can be a complication of primary ovarian insufficiency. Rarely, pregnancy is possible until the bodys supply of eggs runs out. Osteoporosis. This condition causes bones to become weak, brittle and more likely to break. Women with low levels of the hormone estrogen have a higher risk of getting osteoporosis. Thats because estrogen helps keep bones strong. Depression or anxiety. Some people with primary ovarian insufficiency become depressed or anxious. This can be due to the risk of infertility and other conditions that arise from low estrogen levels. Heart or blood vessel disease. Early loss of estrogen might raise the risk of heart conditions or stroke. Dementia. This is the term for a group of symptoms that affect memory, thinking and social skills. The dementia risk may be linked with getting both ovaries removed and not receiving estrogen therapy afterward in people under age 43. Parkinsons disease. This long-term condition affects the nervous system, which includes the brain and spinal cord. It also affects parts of the body controlled by nerves. The higher risk of Parkinsons disease also may be linked with surgery to remove the ovaries. Treatment for primary ovarian insufficiency helps prevent these other health conditions. If youve missed your period for three months or more, see your health care team to figure out the cause. You can miss your period for many reasons, such as pregnancy, stress, or a change in diet or exercise habits. But its best to get a health care checkup whenever your menstrual cycle changes. Even if you dont mind not having periods, see a health care professional to find out whats causing the change. Low estrogen levels can lead to a condition that causes weak and brittle bones, called osteoporosis. Low levels of estrogen also can lead to heart disease. Request an appointment

metadata.symptoms: Premature Ventricular Contractions (PVCs) are abnormal heart rhythms characterized by premature electrical impulses originating in the ventricles, leading to irregular heartbeat. The main symptoms of PVCs typically include: 1) palpitations or a feeling of skipping beats, where patients may feel a sudden, irregular beat or sensation that their heart is "skipping" a beat; 2) chest discomfort or pain, often described as a squeezing or tightness in the chest; and 3) shortness of breath or difficulty breathing. Additionally, some patients may experience lightheadedness, dizziness, or fainting spells due to decreased blood flow and oxygen delivery to the body's tissues. In rare cases, PVCs can also lead to more severe symptoms such as syncope (fainting), anxiety, or even cardiac arrhythmia. It is essential for individuals experiencing these symptoms to seek medical attention if they persist or worsen over time. Please note that not everyone with PVCs will experience all of these symptoms, and the severity of the condition can vary from person to person.
metadata.causes: Premature Ventricular Contractions (PVCs) are abnormal heart rhythms that originate in the ventricles, rather than the normal sinoatrial node. The primary causative factors of PVCs include genetic predisposition, electrolyte imbalances, and cardiac structural abnormalities, such as cardiomyopathy or coronary artery disease. Biological factors, such as an inherited tendency to develop arrhythmias, can also contribute to the development of PVCs. Additionally, environmental factors, such as exposure to certain medications or substances that disrupt heart rhythm, may trigger PVCs in susceptible individuals. Lifestyle factors, such as a sedentary lifestyle, poor diet, and stress, can also increase the risk of developing PVCs by contributing to underlying cardiac structural abnormalities or electrolyte imbalances.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) include: * Age: PVCs are more common in individuals over 40 years old, with a peak incidence between 60-80 years. * Family history: Individuals with a family history of cardiac arrhythmias or sudden cardiac death are at increased risk of developing PVCs. * Obesity and physical inactivity: Being overweight or inactive can increase the risk of developing PVCs, as it can lead to changes in heart function and structure. These factors contribute significantly to the development of PVCs, which can be a sign of an underlying cardiac condition that requires medical attention.
metadata.complications: Premature Ventricular Contractions (PVCs) are abnormal heartbeats that can increase the risk of various cardiovascular complications, particularly in individuals with underlying heart conditions. If left untreated or poorly managed, PVCs can lead to serious outcomes such as cardiac arrhythmia, which may result in decreased cardiac output, reduced blood pressure, and potentially life-threatening cardiac arrest. Additionally, frequent PVCs can also contribute to the development of atrial fibrillation, a type of irregular heartbeat that increases the risk of stroke and other cardiovascular events. In severe cases, untreated or poorly managed PVCs can lead to more significant complications, such as: * Cardiac failure: Repeated episodes of PVCs can put additional strain on the heart, leading to decreased cardiac function and potentially life-threatening cardiac failure. * Sudden cardiac death: Frequent PVCs can increase the risk of sudden cardiac death, particularly in individuals with underlying heart conditions or those who are already at high risk for cardiovascular events. It is essential to note that while PVCs are generally not a life-threatening condition, they can still pose significant risks if left untreated or poorly managed. Regular monitoring and management by a healthcare professional are crucial to prevent these complications and ensure optimal cardiac health.

metadata.causes: Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) is a complex medical condition characterized by physical, emotional, and behavioral symptoms that occur in the premenstrual phase of the menstrual cycle, typically occurring 1-2 days before menstruation. The primary causative factors of PMS are hormonal fluctuations, particularly the increase in levels of progesterone and estrogen, which can lead to changes in neurotransmitter levels, such as serotonin and dopamine, affecting mood regulation. Additionally, genetic predisposition, lifestyle factors, and environmental influences, including stress and diet, also play a role in the development of PMS. Biological factors: * Hormonal fluctuations: The increase in progesterone and estrogen levels can lead to changes in neurotransmitter levels, affecting mood regulation. * Serotonin and dopamine imbalance: Fluctuations in these neurotransmitters can contribute to symptoms such as depression, anxiety, and irritability. Genetic factors: * Family history: Women with a family history of PMS are more likely to experience the condition themselves. * Genetic predisposition: Certain genetic variants may affect hormone regulation and neurotransmitter function, increasing the risk of developing PMS. Environmental factors: * Stress: High levels of stress can exacerbate symptoms of PMS. * Diet: A diet high in processed foods, sugar, and saturated fats can worsen symptoms of PMS. Lifestyle factors: * Sleep patterns: Poor sleep quality and duration can contribute to symptoms of PMS. * Exercise: Regular exercise can help alleviate symptoms of PMS, but excessive exercise may exacerbate them. It's essential to note that each woman's experience with PMS is unique, and the underlying mechanisms can vary from person to person.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) include: 1. **Age**: Women between 20 and 40 years old are more likely to experience PMS, with symptoms typically worsening in the late teens to early twenties. 2. **Genetic predisposition**: Women with a family history of PMS or other hormonal disorders are more likely to develop the condition. 3. **Hormonal imbalance**: Irregularities in estrogen and progesterone levels, particularly those related to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), can increase the risk of developing PMS. These factors contribute significantly to the development of PMS, although other lifestyle and medical conditions may also play a role.
metadata.complications: Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) can lead to several potential complications, including mood disorders such as depression and anxiety, which can be severe enough to interfere with daily life if left untreated or poorly managed. Untreated PMS can also increase the risk of developing polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), a hormonal disorder that can lead to insulin resistance, weight gain, and increased risk of type 2 diabetes. Additionally, chronic stress and anxiety associated with PMS can contribute to cardiovascular disease. If left untreated or poorly managed, PMS can also lead to secondary conditions such as migraines, fibromyalgia, and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), which can significantly impact quality of life and overall health.

metadata.symptoms: Presbyopia develops gradually. You may first notice these signs and symptoms after age 40: A tendency to hold reading material farther away to make the letters clearer Blurred vision at normal reading distance Eyestrain or headaches after reading or doing close-up work You may notice these symptoms are worse if you are tired or are in an area with dim lighting.
metadata.causes: Anatomy of the eye Enlarge image Close Anatomy of the eye Anatomy of the eye Your eye is a complex and compact structure measuring about 1 inch (2.5 centimeters) in diameter. It receives millions of pieces of information about the outside world, which are quickly processed by your brain. Presbyopia Enlarge image Close Presbyopia Presbyopia With normal vision, an image is sharply focused onto the retina (top image). If you have presbyopia, your inflexible lens doesnt adjust to focus light properly, so the point of focus falls behind the retina (bottom image). This makes close-up objects appear blurry. To form an image, your eye relies on the cornea and the lens to focus the light reflected from objects. The closer the object, the more the lens flexes. The cornea is the clear, dome-shaped front surface of your eye. The lens is a clear structure about the size and shape of an MMs candy. Both of these structures bend (refract) light entering your eye to focus the image on the retina, located on the inside back wall of your eye. The lens, unlike the cornea, is somewhat flexible and can change shape with the help of a circular muscle that surrounds it. When you look at something at a distance, the circular muscle relaxes. When you look at something nearby, the muscle constricts, allowing the relatively elastic lens to curve and change its focusing power. Presbyopia is caused by a hardening of the lens of your eye, which occurs with aging. As your lens becomes less flexible, it can no longer change shape to focus on close-up images. As a result, these images appear out of focus.
metadata.risk_factors: Certain factors can make you more likely to develop presbyopia, including: Age. Age is the greatest risk factor for presbyopia. Almost everyone experiences some degree of presbyopia after age 40. Other medical conditions. Being farsighted or having certain diseases  such as diabetes, multiple sclerosis or cardiovascular diseases  can increase your risk of premature presbyopia, which is presbyopia in people younger than 40. Drugs. Certain drugs are associated with premature presbyopic symptoms, including antidepressants, antihistamines and diuretics. metadata.complications: See an eye doctor if blurry close-up vision is keeping you from reading, doing close-up work or enjoying other normal activities. He or she can determine whether you have presbyopia and advise you of your options. metadata.symptoms: Priapism is a rare and painful medical condition characterized by a prolonged erection of the penis that lasts for an abnormally long time, often without sexual stimulation or orgasm. The main symptoms and signs of priapism include: 1. Prolonged erections lasting more than 4 hours, which can be accompanied by pain, discomfort, and swelling of the penis. 2. Painful erections, which can range from mild to severe and may be accompanied by a feeling of burning or throbbing sensations in the penis. 3. Difficulty detuning, as the individual may experience difficulty relaxing the muscles in the penis to stop the erection. These symptoms can vary in severity and duration, but they are typically accompanied by significant discomfort and distress for the patient.
metadata.causes: Priapism is a rare and painful medical condition characterized by a prolonged erection of the penis that lasts for more than four hours, without sexual stimulation or orgasm. The primary causative factors of priapism are biological, specifically related to abnormal blood flow in the penis, which can be caused by conditions such as sickle cell disease, polycythemia vera, and dehydration. Additionally, certain medications, hormonal imbalances, and genetic disorders can also contribute to the development of priapism. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of priapism, particularly in individuals with underlying medical conditions that affect blood flow or hemoglobin levels. For example, sickle cell disease is a genetic disorder that affects the production of hemoglobin, leading to abnormal red blood cells that can cause priapism. Other biological factors, such as polycythemia vera, which involves an overproduction of red blood cells, can also contribute to the condition. Environmental and lifestyle factors may also play a role in the development of priapism, particularly in individuals who are dehydrated or have certain medical conditions that affect blood flow. For example, dehydration can cause a decrease in blood volume, leading to a reduction in blood flow to the penis, which can contribute to priapism. It's worth noting that priapism is a rare condition, affecting approximately 1 in 100,000 men, and most cases are idiopathic, meaning the exact cause is unknown. However, by understanding the underlying biological mechanisms and factors that contribute to the development of priapism, healthcare providers can provide more effective treatment options for affected individuals.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing priapism include: 1. **Age**: Priapism is more common in young males, with a peak incidence between 15 and 25 years old. 2. **Genetic predisposition**: Individuals with sickle cell disease or other hemoglobinopathies are at increased risk of developing priapism due to the abnormal shape of red blood cells that can cause vascular obstruction. 3. **Medical conditions**: Certain medical conditions, such as diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease, can increase the likelihood of priapism by affecting blood flow and vascular health. These factors contribute to an individual's increased risk of developing priapism, a painful and potentially debilitating condition characterized by prolonged erections without orgasm or resolution.
metadata.complications: Priapism, a prolonged and painful erection of the penis that lasts for more than four hours, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is tissue necrosis, where the prolonged ischemia (lack of blood flow) causes damage to the erectile tissue, leading to scarring and potentially permanent damage. Untreated priapism can also increase the risk of infection, abscess formation, and long-term erectile dysfunction. Secondary conditions that may develop if priapism is untreated or poorly managed include erectile dysfunction, urinary tract infections, and chronic pain in the penis. Additionally, repeated episodes of priapism can lead to fibrosis (scarring) of the penile tissue, making it more difficult to achieve an erection in the future. It's essential to seek medical attention immediately if symptoms persist or worsen over time, as prompt treatment can help prevent these complications and improve outcomes.

metadata.symptoms: More than half of people with primary biliary cholangitis do not have any noticeable symptoms when diagnosed. The disease may be diagnosed when blood tests are done for other reasons, such as routine testing. Symptoms eventually develop over the next 5 to 20 years. Those who do have symptoms at diagnosis typically have poorer outcomes. Common early symptoms include: Fatigue. Itchy skin. Later signs and symptoms may include: Yellowing of the skin and eyes, called jaundice. Dry eyes and mouth. Pain in the upper right abdomen. Swelling of the spleen, called splenomegaly. Bone, muscle or joint pain. Swollen feet and ankles. Buildup of fluid in the abdomen due to liver failure, called ascites. Fatty deposits, called xanthomas, on the skin around the eyes, eyelids or in the creases of the palms, soles, elbows or knees. Darkening of the skin thats not related to sun exposure, called hyperpigmentation. Weak and brittle bones, called osteoporosis, which can lead to fractures. High cholesterol. Diarrhea that may include greasy stools, called steatorrhea. Underactive thyroid, called hypothyroidism. Weight loss. Request an appointment
metadata.causes: Its not clear what causes primary biliary cholangitis. Many experts consider it an autoimmune disease in which the body turns against its own cells. Researchers believe this autoimmune response may be triggered by environmental and genetic factors. The liver inflammation seen in primary biliary cholangitis starts when certain types of white blood cells called T cells, also known as T lymphocytes, start to collect in the liver. Usually, these immune cells detect and help defend against germs, such as bacteria and viruses. But in primary biliary cholangitis, they mistakenly destroy the healthy cells that line the small bile ducts in the liver. Inflammation in the smallest ducts spreads and eventually damages other cells in the liver. As the cells die, theyre replaced by scar tissue, also known as fibrosis, that can lead to cirrhosis. Cirrhosis is scarring of liver tissue that makes it difficult for your liver to work properly.
metadata.risk_factors: The following factors may increase your risk of primary biliary cholangitis: Sex. Most people with primary biliary cholangitis are women. Age. Its most likely to occur in people 30 to 60 years old. Genetics. Youre more likely to get the condition if you have a family member who has or had it. Geography. Its most common in people of northern European descent, but primary biliary cholangitis can affect all ethnicities and races. Researchers think that genetic factors combined with certain environmental factors trigger primary biliary cholangitis. These environmental factors may include: Infections, such as a urinary tract infection. Smoking cigarettes, especially over long periods of time. Exposure to toxic chemicals, such as in certain work environments. The following factors may increase your risk of primary biliary cholangitis: Sex. metadata.complications: As liver damage worsens, primary biliary cholangitis can cause serious health problems, including: Liver scarring, called cirrhosis. Cirrhosis makes it difficult for your liver to work and may lead to liver failure. It means the later stage of primary biliary cholangitis. People with primary biliary cholangitis and cirrhosis have a poor medical outlook. They also have a higher risk of other complications. Increased pressure in the portal vein, called portal hypertension. Blood from your intestine, spleen and pancreas enters your liver through a large blood vessel called the portal vein. When scar tissue from cirrhosis blocks normal blood flow through your liver, blood backs up. This causes increased pressure inside the vein. Also, because blood doesnt flow correctly through your liver, drugs and other toxins arent filtered properly from your bloodstream. Enlarged veins, called varices. When blood flow through the portal vein is slowed or blocked, blood may back up into other veins. It usually backs up into those in your stomach and esophagus. Increased pressure may cause delicate veins to break open and bleed. Bleeding in the upper stomach or esophagus is a life-threatening emergency. It requires immediate medical care. Enlarged spleen, called splenomegaly. Your spleen may become swollen with white blood cells and platelets. This is because your body no longer filters toxins out of the bloodstream as it should. Gallstones and bile duct stones. If bile cannot flow through the bile ducts, it may harden into stones in the ducts. These stones can cause pain and infection. Liver cancer. Liver scarring increases your risk of liver cancer. If you have liver scarring, youll need regular cancer screening. Weak bones, called osteoporosis. People with primary biliary cholangitis have an increased risk of weak, brittle bones that may break more easily. Vitamin deficiencies. Not having enough bile affects your digestive systems ability to absorb fats and the fat-soluble vitamins, A, D, E and K. Because of this, some people with advanced primary biliary cholangitis may have low levels of these vitamins. Low levels can result in a variety of health problems, including night blindness and bleeding disorders. High cholesterol. Up to 80 of people with primary biliary cholangitis have high cholesterol. Decreased mental function, called hepatic encephalopathy. Some people with advanced primary biliary cholangitis and cirrhosis have personality changes. They also may have problems with memory and concentration. Increased risk of other disease. Primary biliary cholangitis is associated with other disorders, including those that affect the thyroid, skin and joints. It also can be associated with dry eyes and mouth, a disorder called Sjogrens syndrome.

metadata.symptoms: Primary Cough Headaches (PCH) are a type of headache disorder characterized by recurring headaches that are triggered or worsened by coughing. The main symptoms and signs of PCH include: 1. **Recurring headaches**: Patients typically experience frequent, recurrent headaches, often with a specific pattern or trigger, such as coughing, sneezing, or throat clearing. 2. **Pain location and quality**: Headaches in PCH are usually located on one side of the head, often behind the eye or temple area, and are described as sharp, stabbing, or piercing in nature. 3. **Cough-related exacerbation**: The headaches worsen or are triggered by coughing, sneezing, or throat clearing, which can be a significant factor in diagnosing PCH. It's worth noting that other symptoms may also occur, such as neck pain, facial tenderness, and sensitivity to light and sound. However, these three symptoms are the most common and characteristic of Primary Cough Headaches.
metadata.causes: Primary cough headaches (PCH) are a type of headache disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of coughing that trigger severe, unilateral headaches, often accompanied by autonomic symptoms such as nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and lacrimation. The primary causative factors of PCH include genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, and abnormal brain chemistry. Specifically, research suggests that PCH is associated with abnormalities in the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the trigeminal nerve system. The exact mechanisms underlying PCH are not fully understood, but it is thought to involve a complex interplay between genetic, environmental, and hormonal factors. For example, some studies have identified associations between PCH and mutations in genes involved in the regulation of pain perception and stress response, such as the TRPV1 gene. Additionally, environmental triggers such as respiratory infections, allergies, and stress can exacerbate or trigger PCH episodes. It's worth noting that PCH is often considered a variant of cluster headache, but it is distinct from other types of headaches in terms of its unique presentation and pathophysiology.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Primary Cough Headaches include: 1. **Genetic predisposition**: Family history plays a significant role in the development of primary cough headaches, with individuals having a first-degree relative (parent or sibling) with the condition being more likely to develop it. 2. **Age and gender**: Primary cough headaches are more common among young adults (20-40 years old), particularly females, who are 3-4 times more likely to develop the condition than males. 3. **Lifestyle factors**: Certain lifestyle habits, such as heavy caffeine consumption, smoking, and stress, may trigger or exacerbate primary cough headaches in susceptible individuals. These risk factors highlight the importance of considering both genetic and environmental factors when assessing an individual's likelihood of developing primary cough headaches.
metadata.complications: Primary Cough Headaches (PCH) are a type of headache disorder characterized by recurring, severe headaches that are often accompanied by coughing. If left untreated or poorly managed, PCH can lead to several serious complications, including increased intracranial pressure, which can cause brain damage, stroke, and even death. Untreated PCH can also lead to secondary conditions such as chronic pain syndrome, migraines, and tension headaches, which can significantly impact a person's quality of life. Additionally, the frequent coughing associated with PCH can lead to respiratory complications, including bronchitis, pneumonia, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The most significant complication of untreated or poorly managed PCH is increased risk of stroke, which can result in permanent disability, cognitive impairment, and even death.

metadata.symptoms: Primary immunodeficiency (PID) is a group of rare disorders characterized by impaired immune function, making individuals more susceptible to infections and diseases. The most common and characteristic symptoms of PID include recurrent severe infections, particularly those affecting the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts, such as pneumonia, bronchitis, sinusitis, and urinary tract infections. Additionally, patients with PID often experience chronic inflammatory conditions, such as arthritis, dermatitis, and nephritis, which can lead to joint pain, skin rashes, and kidney damage. Other common symptoms include recurring ear infections, sinusitis, and opportunistic infections, such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) and histoplasmosis. Furthermore, patients with PID may also experience autoimmune disorders, such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis, which can cause a range of systemic symptoms, including fever, fatigue, and joint pain. Please note that the specific symptoms and signs of PID can vary widely depending on the underlying immunodeficiency disorder and individual patient factors.
metadata.causes: Primary Immunodeficiency (PID) is a group of rare disorders characterized by impaired immune function, making individuals more susceptible to infections and diseases. The main causes of PID are genetic mutations that affect key components of the immune system, such as T cells, B cells, or complement proteins. These genetic defects can be inherited from one's parents or occur spontaneously due to random errors during DNA replication. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of PID, with genetic mutations being the primary cause. Environmental and lifestyle factors are less likely to contribute directly to the development of PID, but may exacerbate symptoms or increase the risk of infections in individuals with underlying immunodeficiency. Genetic factors account for approximately 90% of PID cases, with defects in genes involved in immune cell development, function, and regulation being common. Mutations in genes such as IL2RG, CD40LG, and BTK are particularly associated with PID.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Primary Immunodeficiency (PID) include: 1. **Genetic mutations**: Mutations in genes responsible for immune system function, such as those affecting B cell or T cell development, are a primary cause of PID. 2. **Family history**: Individuals with a family history of PID, particularly first-degree relatives, are more likely to develop the condition. 3. **Age**: PID can occur at any age, but it is most commonly diagnosed in childhood and adolescence. These genetic mutations and familial patterns increase an individual's likelihood of developing Primary Immunodeficiency.
metadata.complications: Primary Immunodeficiency (PID) is a group of rare disorders characterized by impaired immune function, making individuals more susceptible to infections and autoimmune diseases. If left untreated or poorly managed, PID can lead to severe complications, including increased risk of life-threatening infections, such as pneumonia, sepsis, and meningitis, which can be fatal if not promptly treated. Untreated PID can also result in the development of secondary conditions, including autoimmune disorders like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and type 1 diabetes, as well as cancers, such as lymphoma and leukemia. Additionally, PID can increase the risk of opportunistic infections, such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) and histoplasmosis, which can be debilitating and life-threatening. The most significant complications of untreated or poorly managed PID include increased mortality rates, organ damage, and long-term disability.

name: Primary Lateral Sclerosis
description: symptoms  symptoms of primary lateral sclerosis usually take years to develop and get worse. symptoms generally begin in the legs. rarely  pls begins with weakness in the tongue or hands. then weakness gradually moves down the spinal cord to the legs. however  symptoms vary from person to person. symptoms may include  stiffness  weakness and muscle spasms in the legs. this is known as spasticity. rarely  spasticity starts in only one leg and moves to the arms  hands  tongue and jaw. slowed movement. tripping  being clumsy and having trouble with balance. hand clumsiness. a hoarse voice  as well as slowed  slurred speech and drooling. trouble chewing and swallowing. sometimes  frequent  rapid and intense shifts in emotions. rarely  breathing problems and bladder problems late in the disease.. causes  in primary lateral sclerosis  the nerve cells in the brain that control movement slowly break down and stop working. these nerve cells are called upper motor neurons. as a result  the nerves are not able to activate the motor neurons in the spinal cord  which control voluntary muscles. this loss causes movement problems. people with pls may have problems with balance  weakness  slowed movement and clumsiness. pls also may cause problems with speech and swallowing.

metadata.symptoms: Symptoms of primary lateral sclerosis usually take years to develop and get worse. Symptoms generally begin in the legs. Rarely, PLS begins with weakness in the tongue or hands. Then weakness gradually moves down the spinal cord to the legs. However, symptoms vary from person to person. Symptoms may include: Stiffness, weakness and muscle spasms in the legs. This is known as spasticity. Rarely, spasticity starts in only one leg and moves to the arms, hands, tongue and jaw. Slowed movement. Tripping, being clumsy and having trouble with balance. Hand clumsiness. A hoarse voice, as well as slowed, slurred speech and drooling. Trouble chewing and swallowing. Sometimes, frequent, rapid and intense shifts in emotions. Rarely, breathing problems and bladder problems late in the disease.
metadata.causes: In primary lateral sclerosis, the nerve cells in the brain that control movement slowly break down and stop working. These nerve cells are called upper motor neurons. As a result, the nerves are not able to activate the motor neurons in the spinal cord, which control voluntary muscles. This loss causes movement problems. People with PLS may have problems with balance, weakness, slowed movement and clumsiness. PLS also may cause problems with speech and swallowing.
metadata.risk_factors: There are no established environmental risk factors for primary lateral sclerosis. There are no established environmental risk factors for primary lateral sclerosis.
metadata.complications: It can take as long as 20 years for primary lateral sclerosis to progress and become worse. Symptoms vary from person to person. Some people continue to walk, but others eventually need to use wheelchairs or other assistive devices. For most people, adult-onset PLS isnt thought to shorten life expectancy. But it can gradually affect the quality of your life as more muscles become disabled. Weaker muscles can cause you to fall, which can result in injuries. Problems with chewing and swallowing may result in poor nutrition. Performing activities of daily living, such as bathing and dressing, may become hard. People with PLS may develop problems with their thinking, known as cognitive decline. Or they may have changes in their behavior. For some people, their symptoms overlap with symptoms of frontotemporal dementia. Make an appointment to see a health care professional if you have persistent problems with stiffness or weakness in your legs or arms. Also see a health care professional if you have trouble swallowing or speaking. Take your child to a health care professional if your child develops muscle spasms or seems to be losing balance more often than usual. Request an appointment

metadata.causes: Primary progressive aphasia is caused by a shrinking of certain areas of the brain, known as lobes. In primary progressive aphasia, the frontal, temporal or parietal lobes are affected. When areas of the brain shrink, its called atrophy. The atrophy caused by primary progressive aphasia mainly happens on the left side of the brain. The areas affected are responsible for speech and language. Atrophy is linked to the presence of certain proteins in the brain. The proteins may reduce brain activity or function.
metadata.risk_factors: Risk factors for primary progressive aphasia include: Learning disabilities. People who had a childhood learning disability such as dyslexia may have a higher risk of developing primary progressive aphasia. Certain gene changes. Although primary progressive aphasia most often happens randomly, rare gene changes have been linked to the condition. If other members of your family have had primary progressive aphasia, consider genetic testing to see if you are more likely to develop it. metadata.complications: People with primary progressive aphasia eventually lose the ability to speak and write. This may take anywhere from 3 to 15 years. People with the condition also have trouble understanding written and spoken language. As the disease progresses, other mental skills such as memory, planning and organizing can be affected. Some people develop other symptoms such as problems with movement, balance and swallowing. With these complications, people with the disease eventually need help with day-to-day care. People with primary progressive aphasia also can develop depression as the disease progresses. Other complications might include blunted emotions such as not showing concern, poor judgment or social behavior thats not appropriate. See your healthcare professional if you have concerns about your ability to communicate. If you have a family member or friend who has symptoms of primary progressive aphasia, talk to the person about your concerns. Offer to go with the person to see a healthcare professional. If changes in speech or communication come on suddenly, call 911 or your local emergency number. Request an appointment

metadata.symptoms: About half of people with PSC do not have symptoms when they get a diagnosis. But symptoms appear at some point as damage to the liver worsens. Symptoms may include: Extreme tiredness. Itching. Pain in the upper belly. Diarrhea. Fever, related to repeat infections of the bile ducts. Yellowing of the whites of the eyes or yellowing of the skin, depending on skin color. This is called jaundice.
metadata.causes: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is an immune-mediated condition. This means the bodys immune system attacks its own tissues. Usually, inflammation is the bodys reaction to disease or injury. It increases blood flow, releases proteins that regulate defenses and brings in cells that fight germs. While this process usually helps the body heal, long-term inflammation from an immune-mediated condition can damage tissues. In PSC, it is not clear what triggers the inflammation of bile ducts. Research shows that PSC likely develops from a combination of factors rather than being passed directly from parent to child, known as simple inheritance. Some people may have a genetic tendency that makes them more vulnerable. On top of this, problems with the immune system and changes in the gut, such as the gut microbiome or environmental exposures, seem to play an important role. This means that instead of simple inheritance, PSC happens when genetic risk combines with environmental triggers. These may include immune system issues or digestive conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The connection with IBD is strong. About 70 to 80 of people with PSC also have IBD, most often ulcerative colitis. PSC also can occur in people with Crohns disease, though less commonly.
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that may increase the risk of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) include: Age. PSC can occur at any age, but its most often diagnosed in middle-aged adults. Sex. PSC occurs more often in men than women. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). About 5 to 7 of people with some form of IBD, such as ulcerative colitis or Crohns disease, also have PSC. Geographical location. The number of diagnoses of PSC is higher in Northern Europe and North America than in other parts of the world. Genes. Certain gene variations may play a role in the risk and development of the disease. Factors that may increase the risk of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) include: Age. metadata.complications: Complications of PSC may include: Liver disease and failure. Long-term inflammation of the bile ducts can lead to damage and scarring of liver tissues, also called cirrhosis. Cirrhosis associated with PSC causes progressive loss of liver function. Cancer. There is a significant risk of cancer of the bile ducts and gallbladder. There is less risk of cancer of the liver and pancreas. People with PSC and inflammatory bowel disease have an increased risk of cancer of the colon and rectum. Portal hypertension. The portal vein is the major route for blood flowing into the liver. High blood pressure in this vein is called portal hypertension. This complication can cause pressure on blood vessels throughout the digestive system that can lead to internal bleeding. Portal hypertension also can cause fluids from the liver to leak into the cavity holding the digestive organs. Bacterial infections. Bacterial infections of the bile ducts may occur, particularly after procedures used to manage the disease or when there is significant blockage of bile ducts. Thinning bones. People with PSC may experience thinning bones, also called osteoporosis. Vitamin deficiencies. Bile helps the intestines absorb vitamins A, D, E and K. PSC may result in the body not getting enough of these vitamins. This condition is called vitamin deficiency. Make an appointment with your healthcare professional if you have severe, persistent itching on much of your body with no obvious cause. Also, see your health professional if you feel extremely tired all the time, no matter how much rest you get. Its particularly important to talk with your health professional about extreme tiredness if you have ulcerative colitis or Crohns disease. metadata.symptoms: Proctitis is a medical condition characterized by inflammation of the rectum, which can be caused by various factors such as infection, irritation, or allergic reactions. The main symptoms and signs of proctitis include: The most common and characteristic symptoms of proctitis typically include: * Severe pain or discomfort in the rectal area, often described as a burning sensation or a feeling of urgency to have a bowel movement * Frequent diarrhea with blood or mucus present, which may be accompanied by abdominal cramps and fever * Rectal bleeding or spotting, which can be visible during bowel movements or after defecation * Urgency to have a bowel movement, often accompanied by a sudden need to pass stool * Abdominal pain or tenderness in the rectal area It's essential to note that proctitis can be caused by various underlying conditions, such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), infections like giardiasis or amoebiasis, or allergic reactions to certain foods or substances. A proper diagnosis and treatment plan should be established by a healthcare professional to effectively manage the condition and alleviate symptoms.
metadata.causes: Proctitis is a medical condition characterized by inflammation of the rectum, which can be caused by various factors. The primary causative factors include bacterial infections such as Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), sexually transmitted infections like chlamydia and gonorrhea, and inflammatory bowel diseases like ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. Additionally, environmental factors such as anal irritation from constipation or diarrhea can also contribute to the development of proctitis. Biological factors play a significant role in the pathogenesis of proctitis, as the rectal mucosa is sensitive to changes in pH, temperature, and bacterial load. Genetic predisposition may also increase an individual's susceptibility to certain types of proctitis, such as those caused by bacterial infections. Lifestyle factors, including poor hygiene, inadequate diet, and stress, can also exacerbate the condition. Environmental factors, such as exposure to toxins or chemicals, can also contribute to the development of proctitis. For example, anal irritation from constipation or diarrhea can lead to inflammation and infection in the rectum. Furthermore, certain medications, such as antibiotics, can disrupt the balance of gut bacteria, leading to an increased risk of proctitis. It's worth noting that proctitis can also be caused by other factors, including: * Trauma or injury to the rectum * Inflammatory bowel diseases like ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease * Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) * Anal fissures or hemorrhoids In conclusion, proctitis is a complex condition that can be caused by a combination of biological, genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors. Identifying the underlying causes of proctitis is essential for effective management and treatment.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for proctitis include: 1. **Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)**: Conditions such as ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease increase the likelihood of developing proctitis. 2. **Sexual activity**: Engaging in anal sex, particularly with multiple partners, can increase the risk of acquiring sexually transmitted infections (STIs) that cause proctitis, such as chlamydia and gonorrhea. 3. **HIV infection**: Individuals with HIV are more susceptible to developing proctitis due to their compromised immune system. These factors significantly contribute to the development of proctitis, highlighting the importance of preventive measures and early diagnosis.
metadata.complications: Proctitis, a condition characterized by inflammation of the rectum, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. If proctitis is not properly treated, it can increase the risk of developing anal fissures, hemorrhoids, and rectal cancer. Additionally, chronic proctitis can also lead to rectal bleeding, abdominal pain, and changes in bowel habits. In severe cases, untreated proctitis can cause significant complications such as: * Rectal perforation: a hole in the wall of the rectum that can lead to peritonitis (inflammation of the lining of the abdominal cavity) * Abscess formation: a collection of pus in the rectum or surrounding tissues * Fistula formation: an abnormal connection between the rectum and other organs or the skin It is essential to seek medical attention if symptoms persist or worsen over time.

name: Progeria
description: symptoms  usually within the first year of life  youll notice that your childs growth has slowed. but motor development and intelligence are not affected. symptoms of this progressive disorder cause a distinctive appearance. they include  slowed growth and poor weight gain  with below-average height and weight. lack of fat thats stored just beneath the skin. head that is large compared with the face. small jaw  chin and mouth and thin lips. thin  curved nose with a slight hook at the end  which may look like a birds beak. large eyes and eyelids that dont close completely. hair loss  including eyelashes and eyebrows. thin  spotty and wrinkled skin. veins easily seen through the skin. high-pitched voice. premature aging. symptoms also include health issues  severe progressive heart and blood vessel disease  also known as cardiovascular disease. hardening and tightening of skin. delayed tooth formation and tooth shape that is not usual. some hearing loss. loss of fat under the skin and loss of muscle. problems with the growth and development of bones. joint problems  including stiff joints. a hip thats forced out of the correct position  known as hip dislocation. dental problems. no significant progression of puberty. insulin resistance  which means the body doesnt respond well to insulin made by an organ called the pancreas.. causes  a change in one gene causes progeria. this gene  known as lamin a (lmna)  makes a protein thats needed to hold the center of a cell  called the nucleus  together. when the lmna gene has a change  a flawed lamin a protein called progerin is made. progerin makes cells unstable and appears to lead to progerias aging process. the changed gene that causes progeria is rarely passed down in families. in most cases  the rare gene change that causes progeria happens by chance.

metadata.symptoms: Usually within the first year of life, youll notice that your childs growth has slowed. But motor development and intelligence are not affected. Symptoms of this progressive disorder cause a distinctive appearance. They include: Slowed growth and poor weight gain, with below-average height and weight. Lack of fat thats stored just beneath the skin. Head that is large compared with the face. Small jaw, chin and mouth and thin lips. Thin, curved nose with a slight hook at the end, which may look like a birds beak. Large eyes and eyelids that dont close completely. Hair loss, including eyelashes and eyebrows. Thin, spotty and wrinkled skin. Veins easily seen through the skin. High-pitched voice. Premature aging. Symptoms also include health issues: Severe progressive heart and blood vessel disease, also known as cardiovascular disease. Hardening and tightening of skin. Delayed tooth formation and tooth shape that is not usual. Some hearing loss. Loss of fat under the skin and loss of muscle. Problems with the growth and development of bones. Joint problems, including stiff joints. A hip thats forced out of the correct position, known as hip dislocation. Dental problems. No significant progression of puberty. Insulin resistance, which means the body doesnt respond well to insulin made by an organ called the pancreas.
metadata.causes: A change in one gene causes progeria. This gene, known as lamin A (LMNA), makes a protein thats needed to hold the center of a cell, called the nucleus, together. When the LMNA gene has a change, a flawed lamin A protein called progerin is made. Progerin makes cells unstable and appears to lead to progerias aging process. The changed gene that causes progeria is rarely passed down in families. In most cases, the rare gene change that causes progeria happens by chance.
metadata.risk_factors: There are no known factors, such as lifestyle or environmental issues, that increase the risk of having progeria or giving birth to a child with progeria. But the age of the father has been described as a possible risk factor. Progeria is extremely rare. If youve had one child with progeria, the chances of having a second child with progeria are slightly higher than the general population but are still low. If you have a child with progeria, a genetic counselor can give you information about the risk of having other children with progeria. metadata.complications: Severe hardening of the arteries, known as atherosclerosis, is common in progeria. Arteries are blood vessels that carry nutrients and oxygen from the heart to the rest of the body. Atherosclerosis is a condition in which the walls of the arteries stiffen and thicken. This often limits blood flow. The condition especially affects arteries in the heart and brain. Most children with progeria die of complications related to atherosclerosis, including: Problems with blood vessels that supply the heart, resulting in heart attack and congestive heart failure. Problems with blood vessels that supply the brain, resulting in stroke. Other health problems frequently linked with aging  such as an increased cancer risk  usually dont develop as part of progeria. Progeria is usually found in infancy or early childhood. This often happens at regular checkups, when a baby first shows the distinctive signs of premature aging. If you notice changes in your child that could be symptoms of progeria, or you have any concerns about your childs growth or development, make an appointment with your childs health care provider. name: Progressive Supranuclear Palsy
description: symptoms  symptoms of progressive supranuclear palsy include  a loss of balance while walking. a tendency to fall backward can occur very early in the disease. an inability to aim your eyes properly. people with progressive supranuclear palsy may not be able to look downward. or they may experience blurring and double vision. not being able to focus the eyes can make some people spill food. they also may appear disinterested in conversation because of lack of eye contact. additional symptoms of progressive supranuclear palsy vary and may mimic those of parkinsons disease and dementia. symptoms get worse over time and may include  stiffness  especially of the neck  and awkward movements. falling  especially falling backward. slow or slurred speech. trouble swallowing  which may cause gagging or choking. being sensitive to bright light. trouble with sleep. loss of interest in pleasurable activities. impulsive behavior  or laughing or crying for no reason. trouble with reasoning  problem-solving and decision-making. depression and anxiety. a surprised or frightened facial expression  resulting from rigid facial muscles. dizziness.. causes  the cause of progressive supranuclear palsy isnt known. its symptoms result from the damage of cells in areas of the brain  especially areas that help you control body movements and thinking. researchers have found that the damaged brain cells of people with progressive supranuclear palsy have excess amounts of a protein called tau. clumps of tau also are found in other brain diseases  such as alzheimers disease. rarely  progressive supranuclear palsy occurs within a family. but a genetic link isnt clear. most people with progressive supranuclear palsy havent inherited the disorder.

metadata.symptoms: Symptoms of progressive supranuclear palsy include: A loss of balance while walking. A tendency to fall backward can occur very early in the disease. An inability to aim your eyes properly. People with progressive supranuclear palsy may not be able to look downward. Or they may experience blurring and double vision. Not being able to focus the eyes can make some people spill food. They also may appear disinterested in conversation because of lack of eye contact. Additional symptoms of progressive supranuclear palsy vary and may mimic those of Parkinsons disease and dementia. Symptoms get worse over time and may include: Stiffness, especially of the neck, and awkward movements. Falling, especially falling backward. Slow or slurred speech. Trouble swallowing, which may cause gagging or choking. Being sensitive to bright light. Trouble with sleep. Loss of interest in pleasurable activities. Impulsive behavior, or laughing or crying for no reason. Trouble with reasoning, problem-solving and decision-making. Depression and anxiety. A surprised or frightened facial expression, resulting from rigid facial muscles. Dizziness.
metadata.causes: The cause of progressive supranuclear palsy isnt known. Its symptoms result from the damage of cells in areas of the brain, especially areas that help you control body movements and thinking. Researchers have found that the damaged brain cells of people with progressive supranuclear palsy have excess amounts of a protein called tau. Clumps of tau also are found in other brain diseases, such as Alzheimers disease. Rarely, progressive supranuclear palsy occurs within a family. But a genetic link isnt clear. Most people with progressive supranuclear palsy havent inherited the disorder.
metadata.risk_factors: The only proven risk factor for progressive supranuclear palsy is age. The condition typically affects people in their late 60s and 70s. Its virtually unknown in people under the age of 40. The only proven risk factor for progressive supranuclear palsy is age. The condition typically affects people in their late 60s and 70s. Its virtually unknown in people under the age of 40.
metadata.complications: Complications of progressive supranuclear palsy result primarily from slow and difficult muscle movements. These complications may include: Falling, which could lead to head injuries, fractures and other injuries. Trouble focusing your eyes, which also can lead to injuries. Trouble sleeping, which can lead to feeling tired and excessive daytime sleeping. Not being able to look at bright lights. Trouble swallowing, which can lead to choking or inhaling food or liquid into the airway, known as aspiration. Pneumonia, which can be caused by aspiration. Pneumonia is the most common cause of death in people with progressive supranuclear palsy. Impulsive behaviors. For example, standing up without waiting for assistance, which can lead to falls. To avoid the hazards of choking, your healthcare professional may recommend a feeding tube. To avoid injuries due to falling, a walker or a wheelchair may be used. Make an appointment with your healthcare professional if you experience any of the symptoms listed above. Request an appointment

metadata.symptoms: Prolactinoma is a type of pituitary tumor that produces excess prolactin, leading to various symptoms. The most common and characteristic symptoms experienced by patients with prolactinoma include: (1) galactorrhea, which is the spontaneous flow of milk from the nipple unassociated with childbirth or nursing; (2) amenorrhea, or the absence of menstrual periods, due to high levels of prolactin suppressing gonadotropin-releasing hormone and subsequently estrogen and progesterone production; (3) infertility, as elevated prolactin can disrupt ovulation and sperm production; and (4) visual disturbances, such as double vision, blurred vision, or loss of peripheral vision, caused by compression of nearby optic nerves. Additionally, patients may experience headaches, fatigue, and weight gain due to the tumor's effects on hormone regulation. Note: These symptoms are not exhaustive, but they are among the most common and characteristic presentations of prolactinoma.
metadata.causes: Prolactinoma is a type of pituitary tumor that produces excess prolactin, leading to various symptoms such as galactorrhea (spontaneous milk production), amenorrhea (absence of menstruation), and infertility. The primary causative factors of prolactinoma are genetic mutations in the HIF1A gene, which can lead to uncontrolled cell growth and tumor formation. Additionally, environmental factors such as radiation exposure and certain medications can also contribute to the development of prolactinoma. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of prolactinoma, as it is often associated with an overproduction of prolactin due to a pituitary adenoma (a non-cancerous tumor) that secretes excessive amounts of this hormone. Genetic predisposition also plays a crucial role, as individuals with a family history of prolactinoma are more likely to develop the condition. Environmental factors such as radiation exposure, particularly in childhood and adolescence, have been linked to an increased risk of developing prolactinoma. Certain medications, including antipsychotic drugs, can also stimulate prolactin production and increase the risk of tumor formation.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing prolactinoma include: 1. **Age**: Prolactinomas are more common in women between the ages of 20 and 50, with a peak incidence in women aged 30-40. 2. **Genetic predisposition**: Family history plays a significant role, with approximately 10-15% of cases occurring in first-degree relatives of patients with prolactinoma. 3. **Hormonal influences**: Certain hormonal imbalances, such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), thyroid disorders, and pituitary tumors, can increase the risk of developing a prolactinoma. These factors highlight the importance of considering age, genetics, and hormonal imbalances when assessing an individual's risk for developing a prolactinoma.
metadata.complications: Prolactinoma, a type of pituitary tumor that produces excess prolactin, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. If left unaddressed, prolactinoma can cause hypogonadism (reduced sex hormone production), infertility, and menstrual irregularities in women, as well as decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and testicular shrinkage in men. Additionally, the tumor can also lead to visual disturbances due to compression of nearby nerves, potentially resulting in blindness or severe vision loss. Secondary conditions that may develop if prolactinoma is untreated or poorly managed include: 1. Hypogonadism: Reduced sex hormone production can lead to infertility, decreased libido, and erectile dysfunction. 2. Visual disturbances: Compression of nearby nerves can cause blindness or severe vision loss. 3. Neurological symptoms: Prolonged compression of the optic chiasm can lead to visual field defects, double vision, and other neurological symptoms. It is essential to seek medical attention if symptoms persist or worsen over time, as prompt treatment can help prevent these complications and improve quality of life.

It surrounds the top part of the tube that drains urine from the bladder, called the urethra. The prostates main job is to make the fluid that feeds and carries sperm, called seminal fluid. The prostate is part of the male reproductive system. Its often not clear what causes prostate cancer. Healthcare professionals have found some things that raise the risk of this cancer. These include older age, obesity and a family history of prostate cancer. The exact cause of prostate cancer often isnt known. Prostate cancer starts when cells in the prostate develop changes in their DNA. A cells DNA holds the instructions that tell the cell what to do. In healthy cells, the DNA tells the cells to grow and multiply at a set rate. The DNA also tells the cells to die at a set time. In cancer cells, the DNA changes give different instructions. The changes tell the cancer cells to grow and multiply quickly. Cancer cells can keep living when healthy cells would die. This causes too many cells. The cancer cells might form a mass called a tumor. The tumor can grow to invade and destroy healthy body tissue. In time, cancer cells can break away and spread to other parts of the body. When cancer spreads, its called metastatic cancer.
