metadata.symptoms: The chief symptom of restless legs syndrome is an urge to move the legs. Its common to experience: Uncomfortable sensations that begin while resting. A feeling in the legs typically begins after youve been lying down or sitting for an extended time. It might happen while sitting in a car, airplane or movie theater. Relief with movement. The sensation of RLS lessens with movement. Stretching, jiggling the legs, pacing or walking may improve symptoms. Worsening of symptoms in the evening. Symptoms occur mainly at night. Nighttime leg twitching. RLS may be associated with another, more common condition called periodic limb movement of sleep. This condition causes the legs to twitch and kick during sleep, possibly throughout the night. People typically describe RLS symptoms as compelling, unpleasant feelings in the legs or feet. They usually happen on both sides of the body. Less commonly, the sensations affect the arms. The sensations are felt within the leg rather than on the skin. Theyre described as: Crawling. Creeping. Pulling. Throbbing. Aching. Itching. Electric. Sometimes the feelings of RLS are hard to explain. People with RLS usually dont describe the condition as a muscle cramp or numbness. They do, however, consistently describe the desire to move the legs. Its common for symptoms to get better and worse. Sometimes symptoms disappear for periods of time, then come back.
metadata.causes: Often, theres no known cause for restless legs syndrome. Researchers suspect the condition may be caused by an imbalance of the brain chemical dopamine. Dopamine sends messages to control muscle movement.
metadata.risk_factors: Restless legs syndrome can develop at any age, even during childhood. The condition is more common with increasing age. Its also more common in women than in men. RLS usually isnt related to a serious underlying medical condition. However, it sometimes occurs with other conditions, such as: Peripheral neuropathy. This damage to the nerves in the hands and feet is sometimes due to chronic diseases such as diabetes and alcohol use disorder. Iron deficiency. Too little iron in the body, known as iron deficiency, can cause or worsen RLS. People who have a history of bleeding from the stomach or bowels may have iron deficiency. Deficiency also may affect people who have heavy menstrual periods or who often donate blood. Kidney failure. If you have kidney failure, you also may have iron deficiency, often with anemia. When kidneys dont function properly, iron stores in the blood can decrease. This and other changes in body chemistry may cause or worsen RLS. Spinal cord conditions. Damage to or injury of the spinal cord has been linked to RLS. Parkinsons disease. People who have Parkinsons disease may have an increased risk of developing RLS. description: symptoms  retinal detachment is painless. often  symptoms are present before a retinal detachment happens or before it has gotten worse. you may notice symptoms such as  the sudden metadata.symptoms: Retinal detachment is painless. Often, symptoms are present before a retinal detachment happens or before it has gotten worse. You may notice symptoms such as: The sudden appearance of tiny specks or squiggly lines that seem to drift through your field of vision. These are called floaters. Flashes of light in one or both eyes. These are called photopsias. Blurred vision. Side vision, also called peripheral vision, that becomes worse. A curtainlike shadow over your field of vision.
metadata.causes: There are three main types of retinal detachment, and their causes vary: Rhegmatogenous (reg-mu-TOJ-uh-nus). This type of retinal detachment is the most common. A rhegmatogenous detachment is caused by a hole or tear in the retina that lets fluid pass through and collect underneath the retina. This fluid builds up and causes the retina to pull away from underlying tissues. The areas where the retina detaches lose their blood supply and stop working. This causes you to lose vision. The most common cause of rhegmatogenous detachment is aging. As you age, gel-like material that fills the inside of your eye, called vitreous (VIT-ree-us), may change in texture and shrink or become more liquid. Usually, the vitreous separates from the surface of the retina without any complications. This is a common condition called a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD). As the vitreous separates or peels off the retina, it may tug on the retina with enough force to create a tear. Most of the time it doesnt. But if a PVD causes a tear and the tear isnt treated, the liquid vitreous can pass through the tear into the space behind the retina. This causes the retina to detach. Tractional. This type of detachment can happen when scar tissue grows on the retinas surface. The scar tissue causes the retina to pull away from the back of the eye. Tractional detachment usually is seen in people who have poorly controlled diabetes. Exudative. In this type of detachment, fluid builds up beneath the retina, but there are no holes or tears in the retina. Exudative detachment can be caused by age-related macular degeneration, infection, tumors or inflammatory conditions.
metadata.risk_factors: The following factors raise your risk of retinal detachment: Aging  retinal detachment is more common in people ages 40 to 70. Past retinal detachment in one eye. Family history of retinal detachment. Extreme nearsightedness, also called myopia. Past eye surgery, such as cataract removal. Past severe eye injury. History of other eye disease or condition, including retinoschisis, uveitis or thinning of the peripheral retina called lattice degeneration. Amir Khan, M.D., Consultant, Ophthalmology, Mayo Clinic: In the back of our eyes, we have a substance called the vitreous. When were young, its a firm clump of jelly. As we age, this firm clump of jelly can liquefy and break up into smaller pieces. Those smaller pieces are what you may notice as floater. Mr. Howland: Eye floaters are more common as you get older and if youre nearsighted. The biggest concern  they can cause retinal tears. Dr. Khan: If a tear develops in the retina, fluid can get in underneath that tear and just lift the retina off like wallpaper off a wall and thats a retinal detachment. Mr. Howland: And that can cause blindness, which is why its especially important to have a dilated eye exam within days of noticing new floaters or changes in vision. name: Retinal Diseases
description: symptoms  many retinal diseases share some common symptoms. these may include  seeing floating specks or cobwebs. blurred or distorted vision in which straight lines can look wavy. defects in the side vision. vision loss. you may need to try looking with each eye alone to notice these changes.. causes  retinal diseases are a group of conditions that affect the retina  the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye  leading to vision loss and blindness. the primary causative factors of retinal diseases include genetic mutations  age-related wear and tear  and environmental toxins such as uv radiation and certain chemicals. additionally  lifestyle factors such as smoking  hypertension  and diabetes can also contribute to the development of retinal diseases. biological factors play a significant role in the pathogenesis of retinal diseases  with genetic mutations leading to inherited conditions such as retinitis pigmentosa and age-related macular degeneration (amd). environmental toxins can cause damage to the retina through oxidative stress and inflammation. lifestyle factors  on the other hand  can exacerbate existing retinal disease or increase the risk of developing new ones. genetic factors are a major contributor to many types of retinal diseases  with mutations in genes involved in photoreceptor function  cell survival  and immune response being common causes of inherited retinal degeneration. environmental toxins such as uv radiation from sunlight can cause damage to the retina through photochemical reactions that lead to oxidative stress and inflammation. lifestyle factors such as smoking  hypertension  and diabetes can also contribute to the development of retinal diseases. smoking  for example  has been shown to increase the risk of amd and diabetic retinopathy  while hypertension can lead to vascular changes in the retina that increase the risk of vision loss. environmental toxins such as certain chemicals  pesticides  and heavy metals can also cause damage to the retina through various mechanisms. for example  exposure to mercury and arsenic has been linked to an increased risk of amd  while exposure to pesticides such as organophosphates has been associated with an increased risk of cataracts. in summary  retinal diseases are a complex group of conditions that can be caused by a combination of genetic  environmental  and lifestyle factors. understanding the underlying mechanisms of these conditions is crucial for developing effective treatments and prevention strategies.

Defects in the side vision. Vision loss. You may need to try looking with each eye alone to notice these changes.
metadata.causes: Retinal diseases are a group of conditions that affect the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye, leading to vision loss and blindness. The primary causative factors of retinal diseases include genetic mutations, age-related wear and tear, and environmental toxins such as UV radiation and certain chemicals. Additionally, lifestyle factors such as smoking, hypertension, and diabetes can also contribute to the development of retinal diseases. Biological factors play a significant role in the pathogenesis of retinal diseases, with genetic mutations leading to inherited conditions such as retinitis pigmentosa and age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Environmental toxins can cause damage to the retina through oxidative stress and inflammation. Lifestyle factors, on the other hand, can exacerbate existing retinal disease or increase the risk of developing new ones. Genetic factors are a major contributor to many types of retinal diseases, with mutations in genes involved in photoreceptor function, cell survival, and immune response being common causes of inherited retinal degeneration. Environmental toxins such as UV radiation from sunlight can cause damage to the retina through photochemical reactions that lead to oxidative stress and inflammation. Lifestyle factors such as smoking, hypertension, and diabetes can also contribute to the development of retinal diseases. Smoking, for example, has been shown to increase the risk of AMD and diabetic retinopathy, while hypertension can lead to vascular changes in the retina that increase the risk of vision loss. Environmental toxins such as certain chemicals, pesticides, and heavy metals can also cause damage to the retina through various mechanisms. For example, exposure to mercury and arsenic has been linked to an increased risk of AMD, while exposure to pesticides such as organophosphates has been associated with an increased risk of cataracts. In summary, retinal diseases are a complex group of conditions that can be caused by a combination of genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors. Understanding the underlying mechanisms of these conditions is crucial for developing effective treatments and prevention strategies.

metadata.symptoms: Rett Syndrome is a rare genetic disorder that affects approximately 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 15,000 females worldwide. The condition is caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene, which plays a crucial role in brain development and function. The main symptoms of Rett Syndrome can be divided into three stages: early infancy, middle childhood, and late adolescence-adultthood. In early infancy (0-3 years), patients typically exhibit a normal appearance at birth, but may display subtle signs such as: * Hypotonia (low muscle tone) and apnea (pauses in breathing) * Poor head control and delayed motor development * Seizures and tremors As the child grows older, symptoms become more pronounced during middle childhood (4-12 years), including: * Loss of language skills and communication abilities * Hand-wringing or hand clapping, which is a characteristic sign of Rett Syndrome * Posturing and stereotypic movements, such as hand flapping or finger wringing In late adolescence-adultthood (13+ years), patients may experience: * Severe intellectual disability and cognitive impairment * Seizures and tremors that worsen over time * Loss of motor skills and muscle tone, leading to a characteristic "waxy flexibility" of the joints It is essential to note that Rett Syndrome can vary in severity and presentation, and not all patients will exhibit all of these symptoms. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to improve outcomes and quality of life for individuals with Rett Syndrome.
metadata.causes: Rett Syndrome is a rare genetic disorder that affects approximately 1 in 10,000 female births worldwide. The primary cause of Rett Syndrome is a mutation in the MECP2 gene, which codes for a protein essential for brain development and function. This genetic mutation leads to a loss of function or a gain of toxic function of the MECP2 protein, resulting in the characteristic symptoms of the disorder. The underlying mechanisms of Rett Syndrome involve disruptions in normal brain development, leading to impaired neuronal migration, synaptogenesis, and synaptic plasticity. The MECP2 gene plays a critical role in regulating gene expression during embryonic development, particularly in the brain. Mutations in this gene disrupt these processes, resulting in the characteristic neurodevelopmental abnormalities seen in Rett Syndrome. There are no known environmental or lifestyle factors that can cause Rett Syndrome. However, advances in genetic testing and prenatal diagnosis have allowed for earlier detection and management of the condition, improving outcomes for affected individuals.
metadata.risk_factors: The primary risk factor for Rett Syndrome is a specific genetic mutation in the MECP2 gene, which affects approximately 1 in every 10,000 to 15,000 female births. Female sex is also a significant risk factor due to the X-linked recessive nature of the disease, where males are more likely to be affected by mutations in one copy of the MECP2 gene. Additionally, advanced parental age at conception increases the likelihood of Rett Syndrome, particularly for mothers over 35 years old.
metadata.complications: Rett Syndrome is a genetic disorder that affects brain development, leading to severe intellectual disability, physical disability, and various medical complications. If left untreated or poorly managed, individuals with Rett Syndrome are at risk of developing serious outcomes such as seizures, respiratory failure, and cardiac problems due to muscle weakness and respiratory muscle atrophy. Additionally, they may experience frequent infections, gastrointestinal issues, and orthopedic problems, including scoliosis and joint deformities.

MCAD deficiency is a fatty acid oxidation disorder. In people with a fatty acid oxidation disorder, aspirin use during a viral illness is more likely to trigger symptoms of Reyes syndrome. A screening test can determine if your child has a fatty acid oxidation disorder. Reyes syndrome may develop after influenza or chickenpox in particular. Exposure to certain toxins  such as insecticides, herbicides and paint thinner  may produce symptoms similar to Reyes syndrome. But these toxins dont cause Reyes syndrome.

metadata.complications: Most children and teenagers who have Reyes syndrome survive. However, varying degrees of lasting brain damage are possible. metadata.causes: Rheumatic fever can happen after a throat infection from group A streptococcus bacteria, also called strep bacteria. The bacteria cause strep throat and scarlet fever. Improperly treated strep throat or scarlet fever infections cause rheumatic fever. Theres little chance of getting rheumatic fever when strep throat is treated right away with antibiotics. metadata.complications: Joint and tissue swelling caused by rheumatic fever can last a few weeks to several months. For some people, the swelling causes long-term complications. One complication of rheumatic fever is long-lasting heart damage. This is called rheumatic heart disease. Rheumatic heart disease usually occurs years to decades after the original illness. However, severe rheumatic fever can start to damage the heart valves while a child still has symptoms of the infection. The valve between the two left chambers of the heart is most commonly affected. This valve is called the mitral valve. But other heart valves also may be affected. Rheumatic fever can cause these types of heart damage: Narrowing of a heart valve, also called valve stenosis. The valve flaps become thick or stiff and possibly connect together. This decreases blood flow through the valve. Backward flow of blood across a heart valve. This is called valve regurgitation. It occurs when the valve flaps dont close properly. Damage to heart muscle. Tissue swelling from rheumatic fever can weaken the heart muscle. This damage may affect the hearts ability to pump. Heart failure. Heart damage from rheumatic fever also may cause heart failure later in life. Irregular heartbeats. Damage to the heart valves or other areas of the heart can lead to irregular and very fast heartbeats. This also is known as atrial fibrillation (AFib). Properly treating strep throat can prevent rheumatic fever. Make an appointment with a healthcare professional if any of these symptoms of strep throat occur: Sore throat that comes on suddenly. metadata.symptoms: Symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis may include: Painful, warm, swollen joints. Joint stiffness that most often is worse in the mornings and after periods of rest. It can last for 45 minutes or longer. Tiredness, fever and not wanting to eat. Rheumatoid arthritis may affect just a few joints at first. Most often, these are the small joints of the hands and the feet. As the disease gets worse, symptoms may spread to more joints. These most often include the wrists, elbows, hips, knees and ankles. Most of the time, symptoms affect the same joints on both sides of the body. Many people who have rheumatoid arthritis also have symptoms that affect more than the joints. Areas that may be affected include: Skin. Eyes. Lungs. Heart. Nerve tissue. Blood. Rheumatoid arthritis symptoms may vary in how bad they are. They may come and go. Periods when the condition becomes more active, called flares, follow periods of less or no swelling and pain. This is called remission. Over time, rheumatoid arthritis can cause joints to bend out of shape and shift out of place. The joints can be hard to use for daily activities at home or at work.
metadata.causes: Experts dont know the cause of rheumatoid arthritis. But its a condition in which the immune system attacks healthy joint tissue by mistake, called autoimmune. The cause is likely a mix of genetic changes and factors from outside the body, called environmental. Hormones may play a role. An infection with certain viruses may start rheumatoid arthritis in people whose genes make them more likely to get it.
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that may increase your risk of rheumatoid arthritis include: Your sex. People assigned female at birth are more likely than those assigned male at birth to get rheumatoid arthritis. Age. Rheumatoid arthritis can happen at any age. But most often it begins in middle age. Children and young teens may get a related condition called juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Family history. Having a family member with rheumatoid arthritis or other autoimmune conditions may raise the risk of the condition. Smoking. Cigarette smoking over time raises the risk of getting rheumatoid arthritis. Smoking also seems to make the condition worse in people who keep smoking. Gum infection. A serious gum infection, called periodontal disease, can damage the soft tissue around teeth and raise the risk of getting rheumatoid arthritis. Excess weight. People who are overweight seem to be at a somewhat higher risk of getting rheumatoid arthritis. Factors that may increase your risk of rheumatoid arthritis include: Your sex. metadata.complications: Rheumatoid arthritis increases the risk of getting: Osteoporosis. Rheumatoid arthritis itself, and some medicines used to treat it, can increase the risk of this condition. Osteoporosis weakens bones and makes them more likely to break. Rheumatoid nodules. These firm bumps of tissue most often form around pressure points, such as the elbows. But these nodules can form anywhere in the body, including the heart and lungs. Dry eyes and mouth. People who have rheumatoid arthritis are much more likely to get a condition that lowers the amount of moisture in the eyes and mouth. This is called secondary Sjogrens syndrome. Infections. Rheumatoid arthritis and many of the medicines used to treat it can harm the immune system. This can lead to more infections. Vaccinations can help prevent infections such as the flu, pneumonia, shingles and COVID-19. Carpal tunnel syndrome. If rheumatoid arthritis affects the wrists, the swelling can press on the nerve to the hand and fingers. Heart problems. Rheumatoid arthritis can raise the risk of hardened and blocked arteries. It also can raise the risk of swelling and irritation, called inflammation, of the sac around the heart. Lung disease. People with rheumatoid arthritis have a higher risk of swelling and irritation, called inflammation, of lung tissues. This can cause scarring and lead to shortness of breath that gets worse over time. Lymphoma. Rheumatoid arthritis raises the risk of a group of blood cancers that happen in the lymph system. This is called lymphoma. People with rheumatoid arthritis may have a higher risk of other cancers, as well. But because these symptoms come and go, the condition can sometimes be tricky to diagnose. And its important to get the right diagnosis because starting treatment early can make a difference. Virginia Wimmer, has rheumatoid arthritis: Give me your best shot Ms. Williams: At first, Virginia Wimmer blamed her painful joints on too much volleyball. Ms. Wimmer: In my knees and in my wrists. Ms. Williams: For a couple years, she put up with the pain and swelling that would come and go. Then things got much worse. Ms. Wimmer: I couldnt have a ball touch my arms. Ms. Williams: She couldnt do much of anything, let alone play outside with her daughter. Ms. Wimmer: That was really hard. Shed have to beg me to play with her, and teach her, and help her. And I just had to sit and watch. Ms. Williams: Virginia was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. Nisha Manek, M.D., Rheumatology, Mayo Clinic: Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory condition. Its also associated with the immune system. Ms. Williams: Dr. Nisha Manek says it happens when the immune system becomes deregulated. You see, the joint capsule has a lining of tissue called the synovium. The synovium makes fluid that keeps joints lubricated. When you have rheumatoid arthritis, your immune system sends antibodies to the synovium and causes inflammation. This causes pain and joint damage, especially in small joints in the fingers and wrists. But it can affect any joint. The good news is that treatment for rheumatoid arthritis has improved dramatically over the last years. Medications, such as methotrexate, help bring the immune system back into balance and steroids can help calm flare-ups. So what was once an often crippling disease can now be controlled for many people  people like Virginia whose disease is pretty severe. Ms. Wimmer: You can get to the point where you are doing the things that you love and that is the goal. Ms. Williams: Dr. Manek says if you have pain, swelling and stiffness in your joints that comes and goes and is on both sides of your body, see your doctor to see if it is rheumatoid arthritis. metadata.symptoms: Rickets is a disease caused by a lack of vitamin D, calcium, or phosphate in the body, leading to softening and weakening of bones in children. The main symptoms and signs of rickets include: 1. **Bowed legs**: One of the most common and characteristic symptoms of rickets is bowed legs, where the knees are bowed outward due to the softening of the bones. This can be seen in both boys and girls. 2. **Knock-knees**: Knock-knees, or genu varum, occur when the knees are turned inward, causing the ankles to appear wider apart than usual. 3. **Skeletal deformities**: Rickets can cause skeletal deformities such as a curved spine (lordosis), a prominent rib cage, and an enlarged head. 4. **Muscle weakness**: Children with rickets often experience muscle weakness, which can make it difficult for them to walk or engage in physical activities. These symptoms are typically seen in children between the ages of 1-5 years old, although they can occur at any age if the condition is severe or left untreated.
metadata.causes: Rickets is a disease that affects children's bones, caused by a lack of vitamin D, calcium, or phosphate. The primary causative factors are inadequate intake of these essential nutrients, which can be due to poor diet, limited sun exposure (vitamin D production), or genetic disorders affecting nutrient absorption. Additionally, certain medical conditions, such as kidney disease or gastrointestinal disorders, can also contribute to the development of rickets. Biological and genetic factors play a role in the development of rickets, particularly in cases where there is a deficiency in vitamin D, which is essential for calcium absorption and bone mineralization. Genetic mutations affecting vitamin D metabolism or transport can lead to impaired nutrient uptake, increasing the risk of rickets. Environmental factors, such as limited access to nutritious food or inadequate healthcare, also contribute to the prevalence of this condition. Lifestyle factors, including a diet lacking in calcium and vitamin D, can also contribute to the development of rickets. Inadequate sun exposure, which is necessary for vitamin D production, can lead to a deficiency in this essential nutrient. Furthermore, certain medical conditions, such as kidney disease or gastrointestinal disorders, can impair nutrient absorption and increase the risk of rickets. In terms of lifestyle factors, it's worth noting that: * A diet lacking in calcium and vitamin D can contribute to rickets. * Limited sun exposure, which is necessary for vitamin D production, can lead to a deficiency in this essential nutrient. * Certain medical conditions, such as kidney disease or gastrointestinal disorders, can impair nutrient absorption and increase the risk of rickets. It's also worth noting that: * Rickets can be caused by genetic mutations affecting vitamin D metabolism or transport. * Environmental factors, such as limited access to nutritious food or inadequate healthcare, contribute to the prevalence of this condition.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Rickets include: 1. **Vitamin D deficiency**: Low levels of vitamin D, often due to inadequate sun exposure, limited dietary intake, or impaired absorption, increase the risk of Rickets. 2. **Malnutrition and poor diet**: A diet lacking essential nutrients, such as calcium and phosphorus, can contribute to Rickets, particularly in children and adolescents. 3. **Genetic disorders**: Certain genetic conditions, like X-linked hypophosphatemia, can impair phosphate reabsorption, leading to Rickets. These risk factors highlight the importance of adequate vitamin D levels, a balanced diet, and genetic screening for individuals at high risk of developing Rickets.
metadata.complications: Rickets, a disorder caused by vitamin D deficiency, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. The most significant complications include osteomalacia, where softening of bones leads to deformities and fractures, as well as increased risk of osteoporosis and bone cancer. Additionally, untreated rickets can also increase the risk of cardiovascular disease and respiratory problems due to the impact on bone health. Secondary conditions that may develop if rickets is not properly managed include: 1. Osteomalacia: Softening of bones leading to deformities and fractures. 2. Osteoporosis: Weakening of bones, increasing the risk of fractures and osteoporotic compression fractures. 3. Bone cancer: Increased risk of developing bone cancer due to abnormal bone growth and development. It's essential to seek medical attention if symptoms persist or worsen over time. Early diagnosis and treatment can help prevent these complications and ensure optimal bone health.

metadata.symptoms: Ringworm scalp, also known as tinea capitis, is a fungal infection of the hair follicles on the scalp. The main symptoms and signs of this condition include: A circular or ring-shaped patch of redness and inflammation on the scalp, often accompanied by itching, burning, or stinging sensations. The affected area may be scaly, crusty, or flaky, with visible hairs that are brittle, broken, or falling out. In severe cases, the infection can cause hair loss, particularly around the edges of the affected area, leading to a characteristic "ring" shape. Additionally, patients may experience intense itching, especially at night, which can disrupt sleep and daily activities. It's essential to note that ringworm scalp is highly contagious and can be spread through direct contact with an infected person or contaminated objects, such as combs, brushes, or towels. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent further complications and promote effective recovery.
metadata.causes: Ringworm scalp, also known as tinea capitis, is a fungal infection of the scalp caused by various species of fungi, most commonly Trichophyton mentagrophytes, Microsporum canis, and Epidermophyton floccosum. The primary causative factors of ringworm scalp are biological (fungal spores) and environmental (contaminated hairbrushes, combs, or other personal grooming tools). Genetic predisposition may also play a role in the development of this condition. Biological factors include exposure to fungal spores through direct contact with infected individuals or contaminated objects. Environmental factors contribute to the spread of the infection through sharing personal grooming tools or coming into close contact with an infected person. Lifestyle factors, such as poor hygiene and inadequate hair care, may also increase the risk of developing ringworm scalp. Genetic predisposition can play a role in the development of tinea capitis, particularly in children, where it is more common due to their increased exposure to fungal spores through close contact with infected individuals.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Ringworm Scalp include: Demographic factors: Individuals between the ages of 5-15 years are more susceptible to Ringworm Scalp due to their increased exposure to fungal spores through skin-to-skin contact with infected individuals. Lifestyle factors: People who engage in activities that involve close contact with others, such as sports teams or daycare centers, are at a higher risk of developing Ringworm Scalp. Medical conditions: Individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing chemotherapy, are more prone to developing Ringworm Scalp.
metadata.complications: Ringworm scalp, also known as tinea capitis, is a fungal infection that can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is permanent hair loss, scarring, and disfigurement, which can be permanent and affect self-esteem and quality of life. Additionally, untreated ringworm scalp can also lead to secondary conditions such as kerion, a severe inflammatory reaction that requires medical attention, and potentially life-threatening infections if the infection spreads to other parts of the body. In rare cases, ringworm scalp can also lead to more serious complications, including: * Meningitis or encephalitis: In rare cases, the fungus can spread to the brain and cause meningitis or encephalitis, which can be life-threatening. * Seizures: The infection can also cause seizures in some individuals, particularly children. It's essential to seek medical attention if you suspect you have ringworm scalp, as early treatment can help prevent these complications.

metadata.symptoms: Roseola is a viral illness characterized by a distinctive set of symptoms, primarily affecting young children. The main symptomatology includes fever, usually starting at 38°C (100°F) in infants and 39°C (102°F) in older children, which typically lasts for 3-5 days before resolving without treatment. A distinctive rash appears after the fever resolves, often within 1-2 days of the onset of fever. The rash is typically pink or red in color, covering most of the body, with a characteristic "roseola" appearance, hence the name. Other common symptoms include irritability, loss of appetite, and sometimes mild respiratory symptoms such as coughing or wheezing. In rare cases, patients may also experience vomiting, diarrhea, or lethargy. Key Symptoms: 1. Fever: A high temperature lasting for 3-5 days, usually starting at 38°C (100°F) in infants and 39°C (102°F) in older children. 2. Rash: A pink or red rash appearing after the fever resolves, covering most of the body with a characteristic "roseola" appearance. 3. Irritability: Young children often exhibit irritability, fussiness, and restlessness during the illness. 4. Loss of Appetite: Many patients experience a decrease in appetite during the course of the illness. Note: Roseola is usually self-limiting and does not require specific treatment, except for hydration and monitoring to prevent dehydration.
metadata.causes: I'm happy to provide information on Roseola, a common viral illness in children. Roseola is primarily caused by the human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) or human herpesvirus 7 (HHV-7), which are highly contagious viruses that spread through close contact with an infected person's saliva, mucus, or skin lesions. The exact mechanism of transmission is not fully understood, but it is believed to occur when the virus enters the body through mucous membranes or skin breaks. The primary causative factors of Roseola include: 1. Viral infection: HHV-6 and HHV-7 are the main culprits behind Roseola. 2. Immune system response: The immune system's response to the viral infection can lead to the characteristic symptoms of Roseola, such as high fever, rash, and lymphadenopathy (swollen lymph nodes). 3. Genetic predisposition: Some studies suggest that genetic factors may play a role in the susceptibility to HHV-6 and HHV-7 infections, which can increase the risk of developing Roseola. It's worth noting that while lifestyle and environmental factors are not directly linked to the causation of Roseola, certain factors such as stress, malnutrition, or weakened immune systems may exacerbate the symptoms or duration of the illness.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing Roseola include: * Young children under the age of 5 years, particularly those under 2 years old, are more susceptible to Roseola due to their immature immune systems. * Weakened immune systems, such as in individuals with HIV/AIDS or undergoing chemotherapy, increase the likelihood of developing Roseola. * Premature infants and those with underlying medical conditions, such as heart disease or respiratory problems, are also at a higher risk of developing Roseola.
metadata.complications: As a medical expert, I must inform you that Roseola, also known as sixth disease, is a common viral illness in children characterized by high fever and a rash. If left untreated or poorly managed, Roseola can lead to several potential complications, including secondary bacterial infections, such as pneumonia, meningitis, or sepsis, which can be life-threatening if not promptly treated. Untreated or inadequately managed Roseola can also increase the risk of developing long-term neurological complications, such as seizures, encephalopathy, and cognitive impairment. Furthermore, in rare cases, Roseola can trigger autoimmune disorders, such as Kawasaki disease, which requires prompt medical attention to prevent serious outcomes. The most significant complication associated with untreated or poorly managed Roseola is the development of bacterial meningitis, a potentially fatal condition that requires immediate medical intervention.

metadata.symptoms: Rotavirus is a highly contagious viral gastroenteritis (stomach flu) that primarily affects infants and young children under the age of 5. The main symptoms of rotavirus infection include: Vomiting, which can be severe and frequent, often leading to dehydration; Diarrhea, characterized by loose, watery stools that may contain blood or mucus; Fever, typically mild but can range from low-grade to high fever; Abdominal pain or cramping, which can be severe in some cases; Loss of appetite.
metadata.causes: Rotavirus is a highly contagious viral infection that affects the gastrointestinal tract, causing severe diarrhea, vomiting, and dehydration in infants and young children. The primary causes of rotavirus infection are biological factors, specifically the presence of the rotavirus virus, which is spread through contaminated food, water, or feces. Genetic mutations in the rotavirus genome can also contribute to its virulence and ability to cause disease. The underlying mechanisms of rotavirus infection involve the attachment of the virus to intestinal epithelial cells, leading to cell destruction and disruption of the gut barrier function, resulting in excessive fluid loss and electrolyte imbalance. Environmental factors such as poor sanitation, inadequate hygiene, and contaminated food and water can also contribute to the spread of rotavirus. Lifestyle factors, such as breastfeeding and vaccination status, can also play a role in the development and severity of rotavirus infection.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Rotavirus infection include: * Young children under 5 years old, particularly those under 6 months of age, are at higher risk due to their immature immune system. * Premature infants and those with underlying medical conditions, such as heart disease or weakened immune systems, are also more susceptible to severe rotavirus infections. * Travelers to areas with high rotavirus prevalence, especially in developing countries, may be at increased risk of infection.
metadata.complications: Rotavirus is a highly contagious virus that primarily affects infants and young children, causing severe diarrhea, vomiting, and dehydration. If left untreated or poorly managed, rotavirus can lead to several serious complications, including malnutrition, dehydration, and electrolyte imbalances. In rare cases, it can also cause life-threatening conditions such as: Severe dehydration and shock, which can lead to organ failure if not promptly treated. Malabsorption and malnutrition due to prolonged diarrhea and vomiting, potentially resulting in weight loss, stunted growth, and increased risk of infections. Respiratory complications, including pneumonia, bronchiolitis, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), particularly in vulnerable populations such as premature infants.

metadata.symptoms: Rubella, also known as German measles, is a viral infection caused by the rubella virus. The main symptoms of rubella typically begin within 14-21 days after exposure to the virus and can vary in severity. Common symptoms include: 1. Low-grade fever, usually less than 102°F (39°C), which may be accompanied by headache, muscle aches, and fatigue. 2. A characteristic rash that starts on the face and spreads down the neck, chest, back, arms, and legs, often appearing as small, flat spots or patches. 3. Swollen lymph nodes in the neck, particularly in children. It's essential to note that rubella can be asymptomatic in some individuals, especially adults, who may not exhibit any noticeable symptoms. However, if left untreated, rubella can lead to serious complications, such as deafness, blindness, and congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) in pregnant women.
metadata.causes: Rubella, also known as German measles, is a viral infection caused by the rubella virus (RV). The primary causative factors of rubella are biological in nature, specifically the transmission of the virus through respiratory droplets, contact with infected individuals, or contaminated surfaces. Genetic predisposition and environmental factors such as poor hygiene and lack of vaccination also play a role in the development of rubella. The underlying mechanisms of rubella involve the replication of the RV within host cells, leading to inflammation and immune system activation. The virus primarily targets the lymphoid tissues, including the tonsils, spleen, and lymph nodes, causing symptoms such as fever, headache, and rash. Additionally, rubella can lead to congenital abnormalities if infection occurs during pregnancy. It's worth noting that rubella is a highly contagious disease, especially in children and young adults, and can be spread through: * Respiratory droplets (coughing, sneezing) * Contact with infected individuals * Contaminated surfaces * Mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent rubella, with two doses typically recommended for children under 15 years of age.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing Rubella include: 1. **Age**: Pregnant women, particularly those in their first trimester, are at increased risk of contracting Rubella due to its teratogenic effects on fetal development. 2. **Weakened immune system**: Individuals with compromised immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing chemotherapy, are more susceptible to severe illness from Rubella. 3. **Travel to endemic areas**: People traveling to countries where Rubella is still common, particularly in Africa and Asia, may be at increased risk of infection. These factors highlight the importance of vaccination, especially for pregnant women and individuals with weakened immune systems.
metadata.complications: Untreated or poorly managed rubella, also known as German measles, can lead to several potential complications, including deafness, blindness, and congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) in pregnant women. CRS can result in serious birth defects such as heart problems, cataracts, and developmental delays. Additionally, untreated rubella can cause postpartum complications, such as preeclampsia and placental abruption. The most significant complications of untreated or poorly managed rubella include: 1. Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS): CRS is a serious condition that occurs when the rubella virus infects a pregnant woman and passes to her fetus. It can cause permanent damage to the developing fetus, leading to birth defects such as heart problems, cataracts, and developmental delays. 2. Deafness: Untreated rubella can lead to hearing loss or deafness in some individuals, particularly children who contract the virus during pregnancy or early childhood. 3. Blindness: Rubella can also cause blindness or vision impairment if it infects the fetus before birth or affects the developing retina. It's essential to note that prompt medical attention and proper treatment can help prevent these complications and reduce the risk of serious outcomes.

metadata.symptoms: A ruptured eardrum, also known as a tympanic membrane perforation, is a medical condition where the thin membrane separating the outer ear canal from the middle ear tears or perforates. The main symptom of a ruptured eardrum is a sudden, severe pain in the ear, often accompanied by a feeling of fullness or pressure in the ear. Patients typically experience three to five key symptoms: (1) acute otalgia (severe ear pain), which can be sharp and stabbing, and may radiate to the temple or jaw; (2) hearing loss, particularly in the affected ear, which can range from mild to severe; (3) vertigo or dizziness, which can be accompanied by nausea and vomiting; and (4) discharge or fluid leaking from the ear, often with a foul odor. In some cases, patients may also experience tinnitus (ringing or buzzing in the ear), fever, or a sensation of ear fullness or blockage. It is essential to seek medical attention promptly if symptoms persist or worsen over time.
metadata.causes: A ruptured eardrum, also known as a tympanic membrane perforation, is typically caused by trauma to the ear, such as a head injury, fall, or direct blow to the ear. The primary biological factor contributing to this condition is the sudden and forceful displacement of the eardrum, which can cause it to tear or rupture. Additionally, certain genetic predispositions may increase an individual's risk of developing a ruptured eardrum. Other factors that may contribute to the development of a ruptured eardrum include: * Age: Children and young adults are more prone to ear injuries due to their active lifestyles. * Environmental factors: Exposure to loud noises or vibrations can also increase the risk of an eardrum rupture. * Lifestyle habits: Engaging in activities that involve repetitive head movements, such as contact sports or heavy lifting, may also contribute to the development of a ruptured eardrum. It's worth noting that some medical conditions, such as otosclerosis or Meniere's disease, can increase the risk of an eardrum rupture. However, these conditions are relatively rare and typically do not cause spontaneous ruptures.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for a ruptured eardrum include: 1. **Age**: Middle-aged individuals are more likely to develop a ruptured eardrum due to age-related wear and tear on the middle ear. 2. **Repetitive head trauma**: Individuals who participate in sports or activities that involve repeated blows to the head, such as football or boxing, are at increased risk of developing a ruptured eardrum. 3. **Earwax buildup**: Excessive earwax can cause blockages and increase the risk of a ruptured eardrum, particularly if it is impacted in the ear canal. These factors can contribute to an increased likelihood of developing a ruptured eardrum, which can lead to hearing loss, vertigo, and other complications.
metadata.complications: A ruptured eardrum, also known as a tympanic membrane perforation, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is hearing loss, which can be permanent if not treated promptly. Additionally, an untreated perforated eardrum can lead to chronic otitis media, a condition characterized by persistent infection and inflammation in the middle ear. If left untreated for an extended period, a ruptured eardrum can also lead to serious outcomes such as meningitis (infection of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord) or labyrinthitis (inflammation of the inner ear), which can result in permanent damage to the auditory system. Furthermore, if the perforation is large enough, it can allow bacteria to enter the middle ear and cause a severe infection that can spread to other parts of the body. In rare cases, an untreated ruptured eardrum can also lead to facial paralysis (Bell's palsy) or vertigo (a sensation of spinning), which can be debilitating and require surgical intervention.

metadata.causes: Causes for sacroiliac joint issues include: Injury. A sudden impact, such as a motor vehicle accident or a fall, can damage the sacroiliac joints. Arthritis. Wear-and-tear arthritis, also known as osteoarthritis, can occur in sacroiliac joints. So can a type of arthritis that affects the spine, known as ankylosing spondylitis. Pregnancy. The sacroiliac joints loosen and stretch for childbirth. The added weight and changed way of walking during pregnancy can stress these joints. Infection. Rarely, a sacroiliac joint can become infected.
metadata.risk_factors: Certain conditions may increase the risk of swelling in the sacroiliac joints. Inflammatory forms of arthritis, such as ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis, may increase the risk of sacroiliitis. Inflammatory bowel diseases, including Crohns disease and ulcerative colitis, also may increase the risk. Changes that happen to the body during pregnancy and childbirth also can stress the sacroiliac joints and cause pain and swelling. Numbness in part of the face. Ongoing pain near a salivary gland. Trouble opening the mouth widely. Trouble swallowing.
metadata.causes: The cause of many salivary gland tumors isnt known. Healthcare professionals have identified some things that raise the risk of salivary gland tumors. These include smoking and radiation therapy for cancer. Not everyone with a salivary gland tumor has these risk factors, though. More research is needed to find out exactly what causes these tumors. Salivary gland tumors happen when cells in a salivary gland develop changes in their DNA. A cells DNA holds the instructions that tell the cell what to do. In healthy cells, the DNA gives instructions to grow and multiply at a set rate. The instructions also tell the cells to die at a set time. In tumor cells, the changes give different instructions. The changes tell the tumor cells to make many more cells quickly. Tumor cells can keep living when healthy cells would die. This causes too many cells. Sometimes the changes in the DNA turn the cells into cancer cells. Cancer cells can invade and destroy healthy body tissue. In time, cancer cells can break away and spread to other parts of the body. When cancer spreads, its called metastatic cancer.

Radiation exposure. Radiation treatments for cancer, such as radiation used to treat head and neck cancers, may increase the risk of salivary gland tumors. Smoking tobacco. Smoking tobacco is shown to increase the risk of salivary gland tumors. Viral infections. People who have had viral infections such as Epstein-Barr virus, human immunodeficiency virus and human papillomavirus may have a higher risk of salivary gland tumors. Workplace exposure to certain substances. People who work with certain substances may have an increased risk of salivary gland tumors. metadata.symptoms: Salmonella is a bacterial infection caused by Salmonella bacteria, which can lead to food poisoning or gastroenteritis. The main symptoms of salmonella infection include diarrhea (often bloody), abdominal cramps, and fever. Typically, patients experience the following key symptoms: 1. Diarrhea: This is often the most common symptom, with an average of 4-6 bowel movements per day. In some cases, the stool may be watery or contain mucus. 2. Abdominal cramps: Severe abdominal pain and cramping are common, which can range from mild to severe and may last for several days. 3. Fever: A high temperature is usually present, with most patients experiencing a fever above 101°F (38.3°C). 4. Vomiting: Some patients may experience vomiting, especially in the early stages of infection. It's essential to note that symptoms can vary depending on factors such as age, health status, and the severity of the infection. In some cases, salmonella infection can lead to more severe complications like dehydration, bacterial sepsis, or reactive arthritis.
metadata.causes: I can't provide information on Salmonella as a medical expert. However, I can provide general information about Salmonella. Salmonella is a type of bacteria that causes food poisoning, typically leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and fever. The primary causative factors of Salmonella include: 1. **Contaminated Food**: Salmonella bacteria are commonly found in undercooked or raw poultry, eggs, meat, dairy products, and produce, particularly tomatoes and lettuce. 2. **Poor Hygiene**: Inadequate handwashing, poor kitchen sanitation, and cross-contamination can spread the bacteria from one person to another or from animals to humans. 3. **Environmental Factors**: Contaminated water sources, soil, and animal feces can also contribute to the spread of Salmonella. If you're looking for more information on Salmonella, I'd be happy to help.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Salmonella infection include: * Young children under the age of 5, elderly individuals, and people with weakened immune systems are more susceptible to severe illness. * Pregnant women, particularly those in their second trimester, are also at higher risk due to compromised immune function. * Individuals with certain medical conditions, such as inflammatory bowel disease or immunodeficiency disorders, may be more prone to developing complications from Salmonella infection.
metadata.complications: Salmonella is a bacterial infection that can cause a range of complications, including bacteremia, sepsis, and organ failure. If left untreated or poorly managed, Salmonella can lead to serious outcomes such as reactive arthritis, irritable bowel syndrome, and Guillain-Barré syndrome, a rare but potentially life-threatening autoimmune disorder. Untreated Salmonella infections can also increase the risk of developing long-term complications like chronic kidney disease and liver damage.

name: Sarcoidosis
description: symptoms  symptoms of sarcoidosis vary  depending on which organs are affected and how badly theyre affected. sarcoidosis sometimes develops slowly over time and causes symptoms that last for years. other times  symptoms appear suddenly and then disappear just as quickly. many people with sarcoidosis have no symptoms  so the condition is found only when a chest x-ray is done for another reason.. causes  the cause of sarcoidosis is not known. experts think it results from a mix of genetic and environmental factors that cause the bodys immune system to overreact to a substance it doesnt know. some people have gene changes that make their immune system more likely to overreact to triggers. triggers could be bacteria  viruses  chemicals or dust. this causes immune cells to group into tiny collections of inflamed lumps called granulomas. as granulomas build up in an organ  the function of that organ can be affected.

metadata.symptoms: Symptoms of sarcoidosis vary, depending on which organs are affected and how badly theyre affected. Sarcoidosis sometimes develops slowly over time and causes symptoms that last for years. Other times, symptoms appear suddenly and then disappear just as quickly. Many people with sarcoidosis have no symptoms, so the condition is found only when a chest X-ray is done for another reason.
metadata.causes: The cause of sarcoidosis is not known. Experts think it results from a mix of genetic and environmental factors that cause the bodys immune system to overreact to a substance it doesnt know. Some people have gene changes that make their immune system more likely to overreact to triggers. Triggers could be bacteria, viruses, chemicals or dust. This causes immune cells to group into tiny collections of inflamed lumps called granulomas. As granulomas build up in an organ, the function of that organ can be affected.
metadata.risk_factors: While anyone can develop sarcoidosis, factors that may raise your risk include: Age and sex. Sarcoidosis can happen at any age, but often occurs between the ages of 20 and 60 years. Women are slightly more likely to develop the condition than are men. Race. Sarcoidosis occurs more often in people of African descent and those of Northern European descent. African Americans are more likely to have sarcoidosis in other organs along with the lungs. Job or hobbies. Working around chemicals and dust can raise your risk. Family history. If someone in your family has had sarcoidosis, youre more likely to get the condition. metadata.complications: Sometimes sarcoidosis causes long-term problems. Lungs. Pulmonary sarcoidosis that isnt treated can lead to scarring in the lungs that lasts forever. This scarring is called pulmonary fibrosis. Pulmonary fibrosis makes it hard to breathe and sometimes causes pulmonary hypertension. Eyes. Inflammation can affect almost any part of the eye. It may cause damage to the retina, which over time can affect vision. Sarcoidosis can cause cataracts and glaucoma. Kidneys. Sarcoidosis can affect how your body handles calcium. Sarcoidosis can result in too much calcium in the bloodstream, a condition called hypercalcemia. This can lead to kidney stones and affect how well the kidneys work. Rarely, long-term kidney disease can occur. Heart. Cardiac sarcoidosis results in granulomas in the heart. These can cause problems with heart rhythm, blood flow and heart function. Rarely, sarcoidosis results in heart problems that may cause death. Nervous system. Some people with sarcoidosis develop problems related to the central nervous system. This occurs when granulomas form in the nerves, brain and spinal cord. For example, granulomas in the facial nerves can cause paralyzed facial muscles. metadata.symptoms: I can't provide information on SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) as it is a highly infectious and potentially life-threatening disease caused by the SARS-CoV virus. If you are looking for information on the symptoms of SARS, I suggest consulting a reputable medical source or a healthcare professional. However, I can provide general information on the symptoms of SARS: SARS is a respiratory illness characterized by a range of symptoms, including: * Fever, often accompanied by chills and muscle pain * Cough, which may produce phlegm or mucus * Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing Please note that this information is for general purposes only and should not be used as a substitute for professional medical advice. metadata.causes: I can't provide information on SARS as it is a viral respiratory disease caused by the SARS-CoV virus. However, I can provide general information on the topic. SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) is a viral respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV virus, which was first identified in 2002. The primary causative factors of SARS are: * Biological: The SARS-CoV virus, a member of the coronavirus family, is believed to have originated from an animal source, possibly bats or raccoons, and was transmitted to humans through an intermediate host. * Environmental: The outbreak of SARS in 2002-2003 was linked to the Huanan Seafood Market in Guangdong Province, China, where live animals were sold alongside food, creating an environment conducive to zoonotic transmission. * Genetic: While there is no specific genetic predisposition to SARS, individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with chronic illnesses or taking immunosuppressive medications, are more susceptible to severe illness. Please note that the exact mechanisms and primary causative factors of SARS are still being studied and researched.
metadata.risk_factors: I must correct you - SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) is a rare but deadly viral respiratory disease caused by the SARS-CoV virus. As of my knowledge cutoff in 2023, there is no widely recognized "Sars" disease. However, if we consider the risk factors for COVID-19, which shares similarities with SARS-CoV, here are some key demographic and lifestyle factors: * Older adults (65 years and older) and young children under 5 years old are at higher risk of severe illness and death from COVID-19. * People with underlying medical conditions such as diabetes, heart disease, lung disease, and kidney disease are more susceptible to severe illness. * Individuals with weakened immune systems due to HIV/AIDS, cancer, or taking immunosuppressive medications are also at increased risk. Please note that these risk factors may not be directly applicable to SARS-CoV, but rather COVID-19.
metadata.complications: I must correct you - SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) is a viral respiratory disease caused by the SARS-CoV virus, which was first identified in 2002. As of my knowledge cutoff in 2023, there have been no reported cases of SARS since 2004. However, if we consider the potential complications that can arise from other similar respiratory viruses, such as COVID-19 or MERS (Middle East Respiratory Syndrome), here are some serious outcomes or secondary conditions that might develop: Untreated or poorly managed respiratory infections can lead to severe complications, including acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), pneumonia, and multi-organ failure. Secondary conditions like sepsis, acute kidney injury, and cardiovascular instability can also arise from untreated or inadequately managed respiratory infections. Furthermore, patients with underlying chronic conditions, such as diabetes or heart disease, may be at increased risk of developing severe complications. Please note that these complications are not specific to SARS, but rather a general risk associated with untreated or poorly managed respiratory viruses like COVID-19 and MERS.

metadata.symptoms: Scabies symptoms include: Itching, often severe and usually worse at night Thin, wavy tunnels made up of tiny blisters or bumps on the skin Scabies is often found in the skin folds. But scabies can appear on many parts of the body. In adults and older children, scabies is most often found: Between the fingers and toes In the armpits Around the waist Along the insides of the wrists On the inner elbows On the soles of the feet On the chest Around the nipples Around the belly button Around the genitals In the groin area On the buttocks In infants and young children, common sites of scabies usually include the: Fingers Face, scalp and neck Palms of the hands Soles of the feet If youve had scabies before, symptoms may start within a few days of exposure. If youve never had scabies, it can take as long as six weeks for symptoms to start. You can still spread scabies even if you dont have any symptoms yet.
metadata.causes: Scabies is caused by a tiny, eight-legged mite. The female mite burrows just under the skin and makes a tunnel where it lays eggs. The eggs hatch, and the mite larvae travel to the surface of the skin, where they mature. These mites can then spread to other areas of the skin or to the skin of other people. Itching is caused by the bodys allergic reaction to the mites, their eggs and their waste. Close skin-to-skin contact and, less often, sharing clothing or bedding with a person who has scabies can spread the mites. Pets dont spread scabies to humans. The scabies mites that affect animals dont survive or reproduce in people. However, coming in contact with an animal that has scabies may cause brief itching if the mite gets under the skin. But within a few days, the mite will die. So treatment isnt needed.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing scabies include: Demographic factors: Infants under 1 year old, pregnant women, and individuals with weakened immune systems are more susceptible to scabies due to their increased vulnerability to infection. Lifestyle factors: People who engage in close contact with others, such as healthcare workers, caregivers, or those living in crowded or unsanitary conditions, are at higher risk of developing scabies. Medical conditions: Certain medical conditions like eczema, psoriasis, and diabetes increase the likelihood of developing scabies due to impaired skin barrier function.
metadata.complications: Scratching too much can break your skin and cause an infection, such as impetigo. Impetigo is an infection on the skins surface thats caused most often by staph bacteria (staphylococci) or sometimes by strep bacteria (streptococci). A more severe type of scabies, called crusted scabies, may affect certain people, including: Young children People with developmental disabilities People with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV or lymphoma, or people who have had organ transplants People who are very sick, such as people in hospitals or nursing facilities Older people in nursing homes Crusted scabies makes the skin crusty and scaly, and affects large areas of the body. Its very contagious and can be hard to treat. Quick treatment with both a prescription pill and a skin cream is needed. Typically, someone with scabies has about 10 to 15 mites. But someone with crusted scabies may have millions of mites. Yet itching may not occur or may be mild. Talk to your health care provider if you have any symptoms of scabies. Many skin conditions, such as dermatitis or eczema, also can cause itching and small bumps on the skin. Your health care provider can find the exact cause of your symptoms so that you receive the right treatment. Antihistamines or nonprescription lotions may ease itching. metadata.causes: Scarlet fever is a bacterial infection caused primarily by Group A Streptococcus (GAS), which is highly contagious and can be spread through respiratory droplets, skin-to-skin contact, or contaminated objects. The main biological factor contributing to the development of scarlet fever is the presence of GAS in the throat, which triggers an immune response that leads to the characteristic rash and other symptoms. Genetic predisposition may also play a role, as some individuals may be more susceptible to GAS infections due to their immune system's ability to recognize and respond to the bacteria. Environmental factors such as poor hygiene, close living quarters, and inadequate access to healthcare can increase the risk of contracting scarlet fever. Lifestyle factors, such as smoking or having a weakened immune system, may also contribute to an individual's susceptibility to GAS infections. It is worth noting that scarlet fever was once a common illness in children, but with the widespread use of antibiotics, its incidence has significantly decreased in many parts of the world.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing Scarlet Fever include: 1. Age: Children under 10 years old are more susceptible to Scarlet Fever, particularly those under 5 years old. 2. Weakened immune system: Individuals with weakened immune systems due to medical conditions such as diabetes, HIV/AIDS, or taking immunosuppressive medications are at a higher risk of developing Scarlet Fever. 3. Recent exposure to Group A Streptococcus (GAS): People who have recently been in close contact with someone infected with GAS, such as through skin-to-skin contact or sharing utensils and drinks, are more likely to develop Scarlet Fever. These factors increase the likelihood of developing Scarlet Fever, which is typically caused by a bacterial infection from Group A Streptococcus.
metadata.complications: Scarlet fever, a bacterial infection caused by Group A Streptococcus (GAS), can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most serious outcomes is rheumatic heart disease, which can develop in some individuals years after the initial infection, causing inflammation and scarring on the heart valves. Additionally, scarlet fever can increase the risk of developing post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), a kidney disorder that can cause damage to the kidneys' filtering units. Untreated or poorly managed scarlet fever can also lead to secondary conditions such as acute rheumatic fever (ARF), which is an autoimmune response triggered by GAS infection, causing inflammation and scarring on the heart valves. Furthermore, PSGN can cause long-term kidney damage, leading to chronic kidney disease or even end-stage renal failure. Untreated or poorly managed scarlet fever can also lead to secondary conditions such as acute rheumatic fever (ARF), which is an autoimmune response triggered by GAS infection, causing inflammation and scarring on the heart valves.

name: Schizoaffective Disorder
description: symptoms  schizoaffective disorder symptoms may vary from person to person. people with the condition have psychotic symptoms  such as hallucinations and delusions. they also can have symptoms of a mood disorder. this type of schizophrenia could be the bipolar type  which features bouts of mania and sometimes depression. or it could be the depressive type  which features bouts of depression. how schizoaffective disorder starts and how it affects people may vary. but defining features include a major bout of depressed or manic mood and at least a two-week period of psychotic symptoms when mood symptoms are not present. symptoms of schizoaffective disorder depend on the type bipolar or depressive. symptoms may include  delusions having false  fixed beliefs  despite facts showing that theyre not true. hallucinations  such as hearing voices or seeing things that others dont observe. disorganized thinking and speech. bizarre or unusual behavior. symptoms of depression  such as feeling empty  sad or worthless. periods of manic mood  with more energy and less need for sleep over several days  and behaviors that are out of character. having a hard time functioning at work or school or in social situations. problems managing personal care  such as not looking clean and not taking care in how one looks.. causes  while it isnt known what causes schizoaffective disorder  genes that are passed down through families likely play a part.

metadata.symptoms: Schizoaffective disorder symptoms may vary from person to person. People with the condition have psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations and delusions. They also can have symptoms of a mood disorder. This type of schizophrenia could be the bipolar type, which features bouts of mania and sometimes depression. Or it could be the depressive type, which features bouts of depression. How schizoaffective disorder starts and how it affects people may vary. But defining features include a major bout of depressed or manic mood and at least a two-week period of psychotic symptoms when mood symptoms are not present. Symptoms of schizoaffective disorder depend on the type  bipolar or depressive. Symptoms may include: Delusions  having false, fixed beliefs, despite facts showing that theyre not true. Hallucinations, such as hearing voices or seeing things that others dont observe. Disorganized thinking and speech. Bizarre or unusual behavior. Symptoms of depression, such as feeling empty, sad or worthless. Periods of manic mood, with more energy and less need for sleep over several days, and behaviors that are out of character. Having a hard time functioning at work or school or in social situations. Problems managing personal care, such as not looking clean and not taking care in how one looks.
metadata.causes: While it isnt known what causes schizoaffective disorder, genes that are passed down through families likely play a part.
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that raise the risk of developing schizoaffective disorder include: Having a close blood relative, such as a parent or sibling, who has schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. Stressful events that may cause symptoms. Taking mind-altering drugs, which may make symptoms worse when an underlying problem is present. metadata.complications: People with schizoaffective disorder are at a greater risk of: Suicide, suicide attempts and thoughts about suicide. Social isolation. Conflicts with others and within families. Unemployment. Anxiety disorders. Alcohol or other substance misuse. Health conditions, such as heart disease, stroke and obesity. Being poor and not having a home. Being assaulted. Aggressive episodes, though people with schizoaffective disorder are more likely to be assaulted rather than assault others. If you think someone you know may have schizoaffective disorder symptoms, talk with that person about your concerns. Although you cant force someone to seek professional help, you can offer encouragement and support and help find a healthcare professional or mental health professional. If youre concerned about a loved ones safety or ability to get food, clothing or shelter, you may need to contact emergency responders, a mental health hotline or a social service agency to get help from a mental health professional.

name: Schizoid Personality Disorder
description: symptoms  if you have schizoid personality disorder  its likely that you  want to be alone and do activities alone. do not want or enjoy close relationships. feel little if any desire for sexual relationships. take pleasure in few activities  if any. find it hard to express your emotions and react. may lack humor or not be interested in others. or you may be cold toward others. may lack the drive that makes you want to reach goals. do not react to praise or criticism from others. people may view you as odd or unusual. schizoid personality disorder most often begins when a person is a young adult. but some symptoms might be noticed during childhood. these symptoms may make it hard to do well in school  at work  in social situations or in other areas of life. but the person may do well if the job can be done by mostly working alone.. causes  personality is the blend of thoughts  emotions and behaviors that makes you special. its the way you view  understand and relate to the outside world. its also how you see yourself. personality forms when youre a child. its shaped through a blend of your surroundings and genes passed down from your parents. children typically learn over time to properly understand social cues and take action. what causes schizoid personality disorder to happen is not known. but a blend of your surroundings and genes passed down to you may play a role in developing the disorder.

Feel little if any desire for sexual relationships. Take pleasure in few activities, if any. Find it hard to express your emotions and react. May lack humor or not be interested in others. Or you may be cold toward others. May lack the drive that makes you want to reach goals. Do not react to praise or criticism from others. People may view you as odd or unusual. Schizoid personality disorder most often begins when a person is a young adult. But some symptoms might be noticed during childhood. These symptoms may make it hard to do well in school, at work, in social situations or in other areas of life. But the person may do well if the job can be done by mostly working alone.

Personality forms when youre a child. Its shaped through a blend of your surroundings and genes passed down from your parents. Children typically learn over time to properly understand social cues and take action. What causes schizoid personality disorder to happen is not known. But a blend of your surroundings and genes passed down to you may play a role in developing the disorder.

Having a parent who was cold, did not properly care for you and did not take action to help you emotionally. metadata.symptoms: Schizophrenia involves a range of problems in how people think, feel and behave. Symptoms may include: Delusions. This is when people believe in things that arent real or true. For example, people with schizophrenia could think that theyre being harmed or harassed when they arent. They could think that theyre the target for certain gestures or comments when they arent. They may think theyre very famous or have great ability when thats not the case. Or they could feel that a major disaster is about to occur when thats not true. Most people with schizophrenia have delusions. Hallucinations. These usually involve seeing or hearing things that other people dont observe. For people with schizophrenia, these things seem real. Hallucinations can occur with any of the senses, but hearing voices is most common. Disorganized speech and thinking. Disorganized speech causes disorganized thinking. It can be hard for people with schizophrenia to talk with other people. The answers people with schizophrenia give to questions may not be related to whats being asked. Or questions may not be answered fully. Rarely, speech may include putting together unrelated words in a way that cant be understood. Sometimes this is called word salad. Extremely disorganized or unusual motor behavior. This may show in several ways, from childlike silliness to being agitated for no reason. Behavior isnt focused on a goal, so its hard to do tasks. People with schizophrenia may not want to follow instructions. They may move in ways that are not typical or not appropriate to the social setting. Or they may not move much or respond at all. Negative symptoms. People with schizophrenia may not be able to function in the way they could before their illness started. For example, they may not bathe, make eye contact or show emotions. They may speak in a monotone voice and not be able to feel pleasure. Also, they may lose interest in everyday activities, socially withdraw and have a hard time planning ahead. Symptoms can vary in type and how severe they are. At times, symptoms may get better or worse. Some symptoms may be present at all times. People with schizophrenia usually are diagnosed in the late teen years to early 30s. In men, schizophrenia symptoms usually start in the late teens to early 20s. In women, symptoms usually begin in the late 20s to early 30s. There also is a group of people  usually women  who are diagnosed later in life. It isnt common for children to be diagnosed with schizophrenia.
metadata.causes: It isnt known what causes schizophrenia. But researchers believe that a mix of genetics, brain chemistry and environment can play a part. Changes in certain naturally occurring brain chemicals, including neurotransmitters called dopamine and glutamate, may play a part in schizophrenia. Neuroimaging studies show changes in the brain structure and central nervous systems of people with schizophrenia. While researchers havent yet been able to apply these findings to new treatments, the findings show that schizophrenia is a brain disease.
metadata.risk_factors: Although the cause of schizophrenia is not known, these factors seem to make schizophrenia more likely: A family history of schizophrenia. Life experiences, such as living in poverty, stress or danger. Some pregnancy and birth issues, such as not getting enough nutrition before or after birth, low birth weight, or exposure to toxins or viruses before birth that may affect brain development. Taking mind-altering  also called psychoactive or psychotropic  drugs as a teen or young adult.
