Some people who are injured in falls or motor vehicle crashes get thoracic aortic aneurysms. But this is rare.
metadata.risk_factors: Anything that damages or weakens blood vessels may raise the risk of an aneurysm. Thoracic aortic aneurysm risk factors include: Age. Coronary artery disease. This type of heart disease causes reduced blood flow to the heart. Its often caused by atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis can damage the lining of a blood vessel, increasing the risk of an aneurysm. This is a more common risk in older people. Family history. Youre more likely to get an aortic aneurysm and rupture if you have a parent, brother, sister or child with one. You may develop aneurysms at a younger age. metadata.symptoms: There are three types of thoracic outlet syndrome: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome. This is the most common type of thoracic outlet syndrome. In this type, a group of nerves called the brachial plexus is compressed. The nerves of the brachial plexus come from the spinal cord. The nerves control muscle movements and feeling in the shoulder, arm and hand. Venous thoracic outlet syndrome. This type of thoracic outlet syndrome occurs when one or more of the veins under the collarbone are compressed and damaged. This can result in blood clots. Arterial thoracic outlet syndrome. This is the least common type of TOS. It occurs when one of the arteries under the collarbone is compressed. The compression may cause injury to the artery resulting in a bulge, known as an aneurysm, or blood clot formation. Thoracic outlet syndrome symptoms can vary depending on the type. When nerves are compressed, symptoms of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome include: Numbness or tingling in the arm or fingers. Pain or aches in the neck, shoulder, arm or hand. Arm fatigue with activity. A weakening grip. Symptoms of venous thoracic outlet syndrome can include: A change in the color of the hand or one or more fingers. Hand or arm pain and swelling. Symptoms of arterial thoracic outlet syndrome can include: A pulsating lump near the collarbone. Cold fingers, hands or arms. Hand and arm pain. metadata.causes: Thoracic outlet syndrome is often caused by compression of the nerves or blood vessels in the thoracic outlet, the area between the neck and shoulder. Drooping your shoulders or holding your head in a forward position can cause compression in the thoracic outlet area. Trauma. A traumatic event, such as a car accident, can cause internal changes that then compress the nerves in the thoracic outlet. The onset of symptoms related to a traumatic accident often is delayed.

metadata.symptoms: Petechiae Enlarge image Close Petechiae Petechiae Petechiae are tiny dots from bleeding under the skin that may look like a rash. On lighter skin, they may be red or purplish. On darker skin, they may be brownish or difficult to see. Here they appear on a leg (A) and on a belly (B). Symptoms of thrombocytopenia may include: Easy or excessive bruising, called purpura, on the skin or inside the mouth. Pinpoint-sized dots on the skin, called petechiae, that may be red, purplish or brownish. Bleeding from minor cuts that lasts longer than usual. Bleeding from the gums or nose. Blood in urine or stools. Unusually heavy menstrual flows.
metadata.causes: Enlarged spleen Enlarge image Close Enlarged spleen Enlarged spleen The spleen is a small organ typically about the size of your fist. But a number of conditions, including liver disease and some cancers, can cause your spleen to enlarge. Platelets are produced in bone marrow. Each platelet lives about 7 to 10 days, so bone marrow is always renewing the supply and releasing it into the blood. Thrombocytopenia is a platelet count lower than 135,000 platelets per microliter of blood in men and lower than 157,000 platelets per microliter of blood in women. Some clinics or labs may use slightly different numbers. A large, rapid drop in platelets may result in a count higher than these targets, but this drop may still indicate a condition affecting platelet levels. The causes of a decline in a platelet count fall into three categories: Platelets are trapped and not circulating. Not enough platelets are made. Platelets are being destroyed or used up.
metadata.risk_factors: Sometimes a platelet count is low because platelets are activated as if they were responding to an injury. The activated platelets clump together to form clots when there is no injury. The count is low because the platelets are used up faster than they are being replaced. These blood clots create a serious risk of blocked blood circulation that can cause life-threatening tissue or organ damage. Conditions or factors that can cause a low platelet count with blood clotting include: Heparin use. Heparin is a blood-thinning medicine. Sometimes it binds to platelets and activates them. Thrombotic microangiopathies. This is a group of disorders that result in multiple clots in tiny blood vessels that can occur in any tissues of the body. These may be related to an autoimmune disorder, infection, medicines or other medical conditions. COVID-19. Rarely, a COVID-19 infection or a COVID-19 vaccine can trigger the immune system to activate platelets.
metadata.complications: Generally, the lower the platelet count, the greater the risk for complications of excessive bleeding or clotting. A platelet count is checked before having procedures that involve bleeding, such as surgery. Rarely, internal bleeding can happen without injury when a platelet count is very low. Make an appointment with your healthcare professional if you have symptoms of thrombocytopenia. Bleeding that wont stop is a medical emergency. Seek immediate help for bleeding that cant be controlled by the usual first-aid techniques, such as applying pressure to the area. metadata.causes: Bone marrow is a spongy tissue inside your bones. It contains stem cells that can become red blood cells, white blood cells or platelets. Platelets stick together, helping blood to form a clot that stops bleeding when you damage a blood vessel, such as when you cut yourself. Thrombocytosis occurs when your body produces too many platelets.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for thrombocytosis include: 1. **Genetic disorders**: Certain genetic conditions such as essential thrombocythemia (ET), polycythemia vera (PV), and myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) increase the likelihood of developing thrombocytosis. 2. **Chronic inflammation**: Conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and chronic infections can lead to elevated platelet counts due to prolonged inflammation. 3. **Cancer**: Certain types of cancer, such as myeloproliferative neoplasms, leukemia, and lymphoma, can cause thrombocytosis due to abnormal platelet production. These risk factors are significant because they can increase the likelihood of developing thrombocytosis, which can lead to an increased risk of blood clots and other cardiovascular complications.
metadata.complications: Essential thrombocythemia can lead to a variety of potentially life-threatening complications, such as: Strokes. If a blood clot occurs in the arteries that supply the brain, it may cause a stroke. A mini stroke, also called a transient ischemic attack, is a temporary interruption of blood flow to part of the brain. Heart attacks. Less commonly, essential thrombocythemia can cause clots in the arteries that supply blood to your heart. Cancer. Rarely, essential thrombocythemia may lead to a type of leukemia that progresses quickly.

name: Thrombophlebitis
description: symptoms  thrombophlebitis is a medical condition characterized by inflammation of a vein due to blood clot formation (thrombus). the main symptoms and signs of thrombophlebitis include  swelling  redness  and warmth of the affected limb or area  pain  tenderness  and bruising in the affected area  numbness  tingling  or discoloration of the skin in the affected area  increased temperature of the affected area  a visible  palpable cord (thrombus) under the skin. these symptoms can vary in severity and may be accompanied by additional signs such as fever  chills  and fatigue.. causes  thrombophlebitis is a medical condition characterized by inflammation of veins due to blood clot formation (thrombus) in the vein walls. the primary causative factors of thrombophlebitis include genetic predisposition  which can lead to abnormalities in blood clotting proteins and platelet function  lifestyle factors such as prolonged periods of immobility or sitting  which can increase venous stasis and promote clot formation  and environmental factors like trauma  surgery  or cancer  which can initiate the inflammatory response that leads to thrombophlebitis. biological factors also play a role in the development of thrombophlebitis  including hypercoagulability due to elevated levels of clotting proteins such as fibrinogen and factor vii. additionally  certain medical conditions like deep vein thrombosis (dvt)  cancer  and autoimmune disorders can increase the risk of developing thrombophlebitis. environmental factors  such as exposure to toxins or chemicals  can also contribute to the development of thrombophlebitis by triggering an inflammatory response in the veins.

metadata.symptoms: Thrombophlebitis is a medical condition characterized by inflammation of a vein due to blood clot formation (thrombus). The main symptoms and signs of thrombophlebitis include: Swelling, redness, and warmth of the affected limb or area; Pain, tenderness, and bruising in the affected area; Numbness, tingling, or discoloration of the skin in the affected area; Increased temperature of the affected area; A visible, palpable cord (thrombus) under the skin. These symptoms can vary in severity and may be accompanied by additional signs such as fever, chills, and fatigue.
metadata.causes: Thrombophlebitis is a medical condition characterized by inflammation of veins due to blood clot formation (thrombus) in the vein walls. The primary causative factors of thrombophlebitis include genetic predisposition, which can lead to abnormalities in blood clotting proteins and platelet function; lifestyle factors such as prolonged periods of immobility or sitting, which can increase venous stasis and promote clot formation; and environmental factors like trauma, surgery, or cancer, which can initiate the inflammatory response that leads to thrombophlebitis. Biological factors also play a role in the development of thrombophlebitis, including hypercoagulability due to elevated levels of clotting proteins such as fibrinogen and factor VII. Additionally, certain medical conditions like deep vein thrombosis (DVT), cancer, and autoimmune disorders can increase the risk of developing thrombophlebitis. Environmental factors, such as exposure to toxins or chemicals, can also contribute to the development of thrombophlebitis by triggering an inflammatory response in the veins.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for thrombophlebitis include: 1. **Age**: Thrombophlebitis is more common in individuals over 40 years old, with a peak incidence between 60-80 years. 2. **Obesity**: Being overweight or obese increases the risk of developing thrombophlebitis due to increased blood viscosity and inflammation. 3. **Genetic predisposition**: Individuals with a family history of venous thromboembolism (VTE) are more likely to develop thrombophlebitis. These factors can increase an individual's likelihood of developing thrombophlebitis, but other risk factors such as smoking, physical inactivity, and certain medical conditions also play a role.
metadata.complications: Thrombophlebitis, a blood clot in a vein, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. If thrombophlebitis is not properly treated, it can cause severe swelling, pain, and inflammation of the affected limb, potentially leading to gangrene, amputation, or even death. Additionally, untreated thrombophlebitis can increase the risk of developing deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), and post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS). In severe cases, if left untreated, thrombophlebitis can lead to serious outcomes such as: 1. Gangrene: The death of tissue due to lack of blood supply, which can be life-threatening if not treated promptly. 2. Amputation: In some cases, the affected limb may need to be amputated to prevent further complications. 3. Pulmonary Embolism (PE): A blockage in the lungs caused by a blood clot that breaks loose from the affected vein and travels to the lungs, which can be life-threatening. It is essential to seek medical attention immediately if symptoms of thrombophlebitis persist or worsen over time.

metadata.symptoms: Thyroid nodules are benign growths on the thyroid gland, which can cause a range of symptoms. The most common and characteristic symptoms include: (1) hoarseness or changes in voice, as the nodule can press on the vocal cords; (2) difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), as the nodule may compress the esophagus; and (3) neck swelling or lump, which can be felt during a physical examination. Additionally, some patients may experience weight loss, fatigue, or changes in bowel movements due to hormonal imbalances caused by the nodule. In rare cases, thyroid nodules can cause more severe symptoms such as shortness of breath, coughing, or chest pain if they are large enough to compress nearby airways or blood vessels. Note: It's essential to note that not all thyroid nodules will cause symptoms, and some may be asymptomatic. A definitive diagnosis is typically made through imaging tests (e.g., ultrasound) and/or fine-needle aspiration biopsy.
metadata.causes: Thyroid nodules are benign growths that develop on the thyroid gland, which is a butterfly-shaped gland located in the neck. The primary causes of thyroid nodules are biological and genetic factors, including mutations in genes such as RAS and BRAF, which can lead to uncontrolled cell growth. Additionally, environmental factors such as radiation exposure and certain medications, as well as lifestyle factors like iodine deficiency and obesity, have been linked to the development of thyroid nodules. Biological factors play a significant role in the formation of thyroid nodules, with genetic mutations being a primary cause. These mutations can lead to the activation of signaling pathways that promote cell growth and division, resulting in the formation of nodules. Environmental factors, such as radiation exposure, have also been shown to increase the risk of developing thyroid nodules. Lifestyle factors, including diet and lifestyle choices, may also contribute to the development of thyroid nodules. For example, a diet high in iodine can lead to the formation of nodules, while obesity has been linked to an increased risk of developing thyroid nodules.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing thyroid nodules include: 1. **Age**: The majority of thyroid nodules are found in individuals over the age of 40, with a peak incidence between 60-80 years old. 2. **Genetic predisposition**: Individuals with a family history of thyroid disease or thyroid cancer are more likely to develop thyroid nodules. 3. **Radiation exposure**: Exposure to ionizing radiation, particularly during childhood and adolescence, increases the risk of developing thyroid nodules. These factors significantly contribute to the development of thyroid nodules, highlighting the importance of early detection and monitoring for individuals with a higher risk profile.
metadata.complications: Thyroid nodules are benign growths that can occur on the thyroid gland, and if left untreated or poorly managed, they can lead to several potential complications. One of the most significant complications is the development of thyroid cancer, particularly in cases where the nodule is large, has a suspicious appearance, or shows aggressive behavior. Additionally, untreated nodules can also cause compression symptoms due to their size, leading to difficulty swallowing, breathing, and speaking. Untreated nodules can also lead to hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid) if they compress or damage surrounding thyroid tissue. Furthermore, large nodules can also cause compression of the trachea, which can lead to respiratory distress.

metadata.symptoms: Tinea versicolor is a common fungal infection caused by Malassezia yeast, characterized by discoloration of the skin on the chest, back, and shoulders. The main symptoms of Tinea versicolor include: (1) discolored patches or spots on the skin, typically ranging in color from light brown to dark gray or black, which may appear as a mixture of different shades; (2) scaly, flaky, or crusty texture on the affected areas; and (3) itching or pruritus, especially at night. Additionally, patients with Tinea versicolor may experience (4) an increase in sweat production, particularly in warm and humid environments, which can exacerbate the condition. It's worth noting that Tinea versicolor is often asymptomatic, but when symptoms do occur, they typically appear within 2-6 weeks after infection. Please let me know if you would like any additional information or clarification on this topic.
metadata.causes: Tinea versicolor is a common fungal skin infection caused primarily by the yeast Malassezia, which is naturally present on the skin of healthy individuals. The condition is also influenced by genetic predisposition, with certain ethnic groups being more susceptible due to variations in skin pH and lipid composition. Environmental factors such as humidity, temperature, and exposure to sunlight can also contribute to the development of Tinea versicolor. Biological factors play a significant role in the pathogenesis of Tinea versicolor, as Malassezia yeast thrives in warm, humid environments and feeds on the oils produced by the skin's sebaceous glands. Genetic factors, such as variations in the genes that regulate the immune response and lipid metabolism, can affect an individual's susceptibility to the infection. Lifestyle factors, including poor hygiene, excessive sweating, and wearing tight clothing, can also contribute to the development of Tinea versicolor. Environmental factors, such as exposure to pollution and smoking, may also exacerbate the condition by increasing inflammation and oxidative stress on the skin. In terms of underlying mechanisms, Tinea versicolor is characterized by an abnormal immune response to Malassezia yeast, leading to an overgrowth of the fungus and the formation of characteristic skin lesions. The condition is also associated with changes in skin pH, lipid metabolism, and inflammation, which can lead to the characteristic discoloration and scaling seen on affected areas. It's worth noting that Tinea versicolor is not a true infection, but rather a superficial colonization of the skin by Malassezia yeast, which can be managed through topical or oral antifungal therapy.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing Tinea Versicolor include: * Age: Individuals between 10-30 years old are more susceptible to Tinea Versicolor, with a peak incidence in late adolescence and early adulthood. * Genetics: Family history plays a significant role, as individuals with a family history of Tinea Versicolor are more likely to develop the condition. * Immune system status: Weakened immune systems, such as those seen in HIV/AIDS or undergoing chemotherapy, increase the risk of developing Tinea Versicolor.
metadata.complications: See a healthcare professional if: Your skin doesnt improve with self-care measures. The fungal infection returns. The patches cover large areas of your body.

metadata.symptoms: Tinnitus is most often described as a ringing in the ears, even though no external sound is present. However, tinnitus can also cause other types of phantom noises in your ears, including: Buzzing Roaring Clicking Hissing Humming Most people who have tinnitus have subjective tinnitus, or tinnitus that only you can hear. The noises of tinnitus may vary in pitch from a low roar to a high squeal, and you may hear it in one or both ears. In some cases, the sound can be so loud it interferes with your ability to concentrate or hear external sound. Tinnitus may be present all the time, or it may come and go. In rare cases, tinnitus can occur as a rhythmic pulsing or whooshing sound, often in time with your heartbeat. This is called pulsatile tinnitus. If you have pulsatile tinnitus, your doctor may be able to hear your tinnitus when he or she does an examination (objective tinnitus).
metadata.causes: A number of health conditions can cause or worsen tinnitus. In many cases, an exact cause is never found.
metadata.risk_factors: Anyone can experience tinnitus, but these factors may increase your risk: Loud noise exposure. Loud noises, such as those from heavy equipment, chain saws and firearms, are common sources of noise-related hearing loss. Portable music devices, such as MP3 players, also can cause noise-related hearing loss if played loudly for long periods. People who work in noisy environments  such as factory and construction workers, musicians, and soldiers  are particularly at risk. Age. As you age, the number of functioning nerve fibers in your ears declines, possibly causing hearing problems often associated with tinnitus. Sex. Men are more likely to experience tinnitus. Tobacco and alcohol use. Smokers have a higher risk of developing tinnitus. Drinking alcohol also increases the risk of tinnitus. Certain health problems. Obesity, cardiovascular problems, high blood pressure, and a history of arthritis or head injury all increase your risk of tinnitus. metadata.symptoms: Toe walking is a gait abnormality characterized by the tendency to walk on one's toes, often accompanied by an elevated heel-to-toe ratio. The main symptoms of toe walking include: (1) a persistent elevation of the heel above the toes during gait, typically exceeding 2-3 cm; (2) a tendency to place weight on the ball of the foot or toes, rather than the heel; and (3) an abnormal range of motion in the ankle joint, often resulting in a shortened Achilles tendon. Additionally, patients with toe walking may experience: (4) stiffness or rigidity in the feet and ankles, particularly after periods of rest or inactivity; and (5) difficulty maintaining balance or stability, due to the altered biomechanics of the foot and ankle. Please note that these symptoms can vary in severity and presentation from person to person.
metadata.causes: Toe walking is a gait disorder characterized by an abnormal elevation of the toes during walking, often resulting in an increased risk of musculoskeletal problems, such as plantar fasciitis and Achilles tendonitis. The primary causative factors of toe walking include genetic predisposition, neuromuscular abnormalities, and biomechanical issues, which can be influenced by a combination of biological, environmental, and lifestyle factors. Additionally, conditions such as cerebral palsy, spina bifida, and muscular dystrophy can also contribute to the development of toe walking. Biological factors, such as muscle imbalances and joint malalignment, play a significant role in the development of toe walking. Genetic factors, including inherited neuromuscular disorders, can also contribute to the condition. Environmental and lifestyle factors, such as repetitive strain injuries or overuse, can exacerbate existing conditions and lead to toe walking. It's worth noting that toe walking is often diagnosed in children, particularly those with cerebral palsy or other neuromuscular disorders, where it may be a result of an abnormal gait pattern. In adults, toe walking can be caused by a variety of factors, including biomechanical issues, such as flat feet or high arches, and neurological conditions, such as Parkinson's disease. In some cases, toe walking can also be associated with other medical conditions, such as scoliosis, hip dysplasia, or cerebral palsy. It's essential to consult a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis and treatment of toe walking, as it may require specialized care and rehabilitation to address the underlying causes and prevent further complications.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing toe walking include: 1. Genetic predisposition: Individuals with a family history of toe walking are more likely to develop the condition. 2. Neuromuscular conditions: Conditions such as cerebral palsy, spina bifida, or muscular dystrophy can increase the likelihood of toe walking due to muscle weakness and coordination issues. 3. Orthopedic conditions: Conditions like clubfoot or scoliosis can also contribute to toe walking by affecting foot alignment and muscle imbalances. These factors can significantly increase an individual's likelihood of developing toe walking.
metadata.complications: Toe walking, also known as toe-walking gait, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is the development of degenerative joint disease in the feet and ankles, particularly in the talocrural joint, which can cause chronic pain, stiffness, and limited mobility. Additionally, toe walking can also increase the risk of developing flatfoot deformity, Achilles tendonitis, and plantar fasciitis. Furthermore, untreated toe walking can also lead to secondary conditions such as scoliosis, hip dysplasia, and lower back problems due to altered biomechanics and muscle imbalances.

metadata.symptoms: Tonsillitis is an inflammation of the tonsils, which are located on either side of the back of the throat. The main symptoms and signs of tonsillitis include: * Sudden onset of severe sore throat, often accompanied by difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) * High fever, typically above 102°F (39°C), which can last for several days * Swollen and tender lymph nodes in the neck, particularly on one side * White or yellowish patches or pus on the surface of the tonsils, known as exudates These symptoms are often accompanied by other signs such as a general feeling of illness, fatigue, and loss of appetite. In some cases, patients may also experience ear pain, headache, or a rash.
metadata.causes: Tonsillitis is a common medical condition characterized by inflammation of the tonsils, which can be caused by bacterial or viral infections. The primary causative factors of tonsillitis include bacterial infections such as Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A strep), viral infections like adenovirus and herpes simplex virus, and environmental factors like poor air quality and exposure to allergens. Genetic predisposition also plays a role in the development of recurrent tonsillitis. Biological factors, such as the presence of a weakened immune system or anatomical abnormalities, can increase the risk of developing tonsillitis. Environmental factors, such as living in close proximity to others who have the infection, can also contribute to the spread of the condition. Lifestyle factors, such as poor hygiene and inadequate sleep, may also play a role in the development of tonsillitis.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing tonsillitis include: 1. Age: Children under the age of 5 and teenagers are more susceptible to tonsillitis due to their developing immune systems. 2. Gender: Boys are more likely to develop tonsillitis than girls, possibly due to hormonal differences. 3. Immune system compromise: Individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing chemotherapy, are more prone to developing tonsillitis. These demographic factors significantly increase the likelihood of developing tonsillitis, particularly in children and adolescents.
metadata.complications: Untreated or poorly managed tonsillitis can lead to several potential complications, including peritonsillar abscesses, which are collections of pus that form around the tonsils and can cause severe pain, swelling, and difficulty swallowing. If left untreated, tonsillitis can also increase the risk of developing rheumatic fever, a condition that can damage the heart valves and lead to long-term complications such as heart failure or arrhythmias. Additionally, recurrent tonsillitis can contribute to the development of post-viral sequelae, including chronic fatigue syndrome and autoimmune disorders. In severe cases, untreated tonsillitis can also lead to life-threatening complications, such as sepsis, which is a systemic infection that can cause organ failure and death if not promptly treated.

metadata.symptoms: A tooth abscess is a painful and potentially serious infection that occurs when bacteria enter the pulp of a tooth through a crack or cavity, causing inflammation and pus buildup. The main symptoms and signs of a tooth abscess include: (1) Severe pain in the affected tooth and surrounding areas, which can radiate to the ear, temple, or jaw; (2) Swelling and redness of the gums around the infected tooth, often accompanied by warmth or tenderness to the touch; (3) Pus discharge from the gum or socket of the tooth, which may be yellowish or greenish in color; and (4) Fever, chills, or general feeling of illness. In some cases, patients may also experience swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck or face, and a bad taste or odor in the mouth. It's essential to seek medical attention promptly if you suspect a tooth abscess, as left untreated, it can lead to more severe complications such as cellulitis, osteomyelitis, or even sepsis.
metadata.causes: A tooth abscess is a painful and potentially serious infection that occurs when bacteria from the mouth enter the pulp of a tooth, causing an inflammatory response. The primary causative factors leading to a tooth abscess are bacterial infections, typically caused by Streptococcus mutans, Staphylococcus aureus, or anaerobic bacteria such as Fusobacterium and Prevotella. These bacteria can be introduced into the tooth through dental caries, gum disease, or other oral health issues. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of tooth abscesses, as individuals with weakened immune systems or those who are prone to periodontal disease may be more susceptible to infection. Genetic predisposition can also contribute to an increased risk of developing a tooth abscess, particularly if there is a family history of oral health issues. Environmental factors such as poor oral hygiene, smoking, and inadequate dental care can increase the risk of developing a tooth abscess. Lifestyle factors, including diet and stress levels, may also contribute to the development of this condition.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing a tooth abscess include poor oral hygiene habits, such as infrequent brushing and flossing (age 20-65 years), and a history of dental caries or gum disease (any age). Additionally, individuals with weakened immune systems due to conditions like diabetes (any age) or immunosuppression (e.g., HIV/AIDS, cancer treatment) are more susceptible. Smoking also increases the risk (any age).
metadata.complications: A tooth abscess, also known as a periapical cyst or granuloma, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is the spread of infection to other parts of the face and skull, potentially causing osteomyelitis (infection of the bone) or meningitis (infection of the membranes surrounding the brain). Additionally, a tooth abscess can also lead to sepsis, a life-threatening condition that occurs when the infection enters the bloodstream. Untreated tooth abscesses can lead to serious outcomes such as facial paralysis, hearing loss, and vision problems due to the spread of infection.

metadata.symptoms: A torn meniscus is a common injury affecting the knee joint, characterized by damage to the meniscus, a cartilaginous structure that cushions and stabilizes the joint. The main symptoms of a torn meniscus include: (1) sudden and severe pain, often accompanied by swelling and inflammation in the affected knee; (2) locking or catching sensation in the knee, where the meniscus may become wedged between the bones, causing pain and stiffness; (3) difficulty bearing weight on the knee, leading to pain and discomfort with activities such as walking, climbing stairs, or squatting. Additionally, patients may experience a feeling of instability or wobbliness in the knee, making it difficult to perform daily activities without pain. It's essential to note that some people may not experience any symptoms immediately after the injury, but rather develop them over time due to chronic inflammation and degeneration. Please consult with medical professional for proper diagnosis and treatment.
metadata.causes: A torn meniscus is a common injury that occurs when the meniscus, a cartilage structure in the knee joint, tears due to excessive stress, trauma, or repetitive strain. The primary causative factors of a torn meniscus include biological factors such as age-related wear and tear, genetic predisposition, and previous injuries or surgeries. Additionally, environmental factors like sports participation, obesity, and lack of proper warm-up exercises can also contribute to the development of a torn meniscus. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of a torn meniscus, as the meniscus is composed of cartilage that can wear down over time due to normal joint stress. Genetic predisposition can also increase an individual's risk of developing a torn meniscus, particularly if they have a family history of knee injuries. Environmental factors such as sports participation and obesity can put additional stress on the knee joint, increasing the likelihood of a torn meniscus. Furthermore, a lack of proper warm-up exercises or inadequate strengthening of the surrounding muscles can also contribute to the development of this condition. Lifestyle factors such as age, weight, and physical activity level can also influence the risk of developing a torn meniscus. For example, individuals who are overweight or obese may be more prone to knee injuries due to increased joint stress. It's worth noting that some people may be more susceptible to a torn meniscus due to underlying medical conditions such as osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing a torn meniscus include: 1. Age: Meniscal tears are more common in people over 40 years old, with the majority of cases occurring between 50-70 years old. 2. Gender: Women are more likely to develop meniscal tears than men, particularly after menopause due to hormonal changes. 3. Obesity and physical activity level: Individuals who engage in high-impact sports or activities, such as football, basketball, or skiing, are at a higher risk of developing a torn meniscus. These factors can increase the likelihood of a torn meniscus, but it's essential to note that other individual circumstances may also contribute to this condition.
metadata.complications: A torn meniscus, a common injury in the knee joint, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. If left unaddressed, a torn meniscus can cause chronic pain, stiffness, and limited mobility, potentially leading to osteoarthritis, bone-on-bone contact, and degenerative joint disease. Additionally, a torn meniscus can also increase the risk of developing secondary conditions such as chronic knee instability, patellofemoral pain syndrome, and even deep vein thrombosis. In severe cases, if the meniscus is severely damaged or if there is significant bleeding into the joint space, it can lead to a condition called hemarthrosis, which can cause swelling, inflammation, and potentially permanent damage to the joint.

metadata.symptoms: Tics  sudden, brief, intermittent movements or sounds  are the hallmark sign of Tourette syndrome. They can range from mild to severe. Severe symptoms might significantly interfere with communication, daily functioning and quality of life. Tics are classified as: Simple tics. These sudden, brief and repetitive tics involve a limited number of muscle groups. Complex tics. These distinct, coordinated patterns of movements involve several muscle groups. Tics can also involve movement (motor tics) or sounds (vocal tics). Motor tics usually begin before vocal tics do. But the spectrum of tics that people experience is diverse. In addition, tics can: Vary in type, frequency and severity Worsen if youre ill, stressed, anxious, tired or excited Occur during sleep Change over time Worsen in the early teenage years and improve during the transition into adulthood Before the onset of motor or vocal tics, youll likely experience an uncomfortable bodily sensation (premonitory urge) such as an itch, a tingle or tension. Expression of the tic brings relief. With great effort, some people with Tourette syndrome can temporarily stop or hold back a tic.
metadata.causes: The exact cause of Tourette syndrome isnt known. Its a complex disorder likely caused by a combination of inherited (genetic) and environmental factors. Chemicals in the brain that transmit nerve impulses (neurotransmitters), including dopamine and serotonin, might play a role.
metadata.risk_factors: Risk factors for Tourette syndrome include: Family history. Having a family history of Tourette syndrome or other tic disorders might increase the risk of developing Tourette syndrome. Sex. Males are about three to four times more likely than females to develop Tourette syndrome. Risk factors for Tourette syndrome include: Family history. Having a family history of Tourette syndrome or other tic disorders might increase the risk of developing Tourette syndrome. Sex. Males are about three to four times more likely than females to develop Tourette syndrome.
metadata.complications: People with Tourette syndrome often lead healthy, active lives. However, Tourette syndrome frequently involves behavioral and social challenges that can harm your self-image. Conditions often associated with Tourette syndrome include: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) Autism spectrum disorder Learning disabilities Sleep disorders Depression Anxiety disorders Pain related to tics, especially headaches Anger-management problems See your childs pediatrician if you notice your child displaying involuntary movements or sounds. Not all tics indicate Tourette syndrome. Many children develop tics that go away on their own after a few weeks or months. But whenever a child shows unusual behavior, its important to identify the cause and rule out serious health problems. metadata.causes: SJS/TEN is usually caused by a skin reaction to medicine. The symptoms are likely to start showing up one to four weeks after you start taking a new drug. The most common drug triggers of SJS/TEN include antibiotics, epilepsy drugs, sulfa drugs and allopurinol (Aloprim, Zyloprim).
metadata.risk_factors: Factors that increase your risk of SJS/TEN include: HIV infection. Among people with HIV, the incidence of SJS/TEN is about 100 times greater than that among the general population. A weakened immune system. The immune system can be affected by an organ transplant, HIV/AIDS and autoimmune diseases. Cancer. People with cancer, especially blood cancers (hematologic malignancies), are at increased risk of SJS/TEN. A history of SJS/TEN. If youve had a medication-related form of this condition, you are at risk of a recurrence if you use that drug again. A family history of SJS/TEN. If a first-degree relative, such as a parent or sibling, has had SJS/TEN, you may be more susceptible to developing it too. Genetic factors. Having certain genetic variations puts you at increased risk of SJS/TEN, especially if youre also taking drugs for seizures, gout or mental illness. metadata.complications: People at highest risk of TEN complications are those over age 70 and those who have liver cirrhosis or spreading (metastatic) cancer. Complications of TEN include: Blood infection (sepsis). Sepsis occurs when bacteria from an infection enter your bloodstream and spread throughout your body. Sepsis is a rapidly progressing, life-threatening condition that can cause shock and organ failure. Lung involvement. This can cause coughing, difficulty breathing and, with severe disease, acute respiratory failure. Visual impairment. TEN can cause eye problems, such as dry eye, ingrown eyelashes, corneal scarring and, rarely, blindness. Permanent skin damage. After recovering from TEN, your skin may have bumps, scars and discoloration. Lasting skin problems might cause your hair to fall out, and your fingernails and toenails might not grow normally. Vaginal sores. In women, TEN can cause sores in the tissues lining the vagina, leading to pain or, if left untreated, vaginal fusion. Emotional distress. This condition causes distress and can have long-term psychological impact. Early treatment is key for people with Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN). If you have symptoms, seek immediate medical attention. Youll likely need care from a skin specialist (dermatologist) and other experts in a hospital. Request an appointment

metadata.symptoms: Mild toxic hepatitis might not cause symptoms. It might be found with blood tests. When symptoms of toxic hepatitis occur, they can include: Yellowing of the skin, which may be easier to see on white skin. Yellowing of the whites of the eyes. This yellowing is called jaundice. Itching. Pain in the upper right part of the stomach area. Fatigue. Loss of appetite. Nausea and vomiting. Rash. Fever. Weight loss. Dark or tea-colored urine.
metadata.causes: Toxic hepatitis happens when a substance causes swelling, called inflammation, in the liver. Most of the time, the liver removes and breaks down most chemicals from the bloodstream. Breaking down toxins makes byproducts that can damage the liver. The liver has a great ability to heal itself. But constant contact with toxic substances can cause serious harm. Sometimes the harm cant be fixed. Causes of toxic hepatitis include: Alcohol. Heavy drinking over many years can lead to alcoholic hepatitis. Not all heavy drinkers get alcoholic hepatitis. And some people who drink much less can get the disease. This can lead to liver failure. Pain relievers available without a prescription. Pain relievers such as acetaminophen, aspirin, ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin IB, others) and naproxen sodium (Aleve) can damage the liver. Taking them often or with alcohol can cause more damage. Prescription medicines. Some medicines linked to liver injury include statin medicines used to treat high cholesterol, the combined medicine amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin), phenytoin (Dilantin, Phenytek), azathioprine (Azasan, Imuran), niacin (Niacor), ketoconazole, certain antivirals and anabolic steroids. There are many others. Herbs and supplements. Herbs that can harm the liver include aloe vera, black cohosh, cascara, chaparral, comfrey, kava and ephedra. There are many others. Children can get liver damage if they take large doses of vitamins thinking theyre candy. Chemicals on the job. Common chemicals that can cause liver damage include the dry cleaning solvent carbon tetrachloride, a substance called vinyl chloride thats used to make plastics, the herbicide paraquat and a group of industrial chemicals called polychlorinated biphenyls. metadata.risk_factors: Factors that might increase the risk of toxic hepatitis include: Having liver disease. People with a serious liver condition such as cirrhosis or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease are more likely to react to toxins. Having hepatitis. Infection with a hepatitis virus makes the liver more likely to be affected by toxins. Infections include hepatitis B, hepatitis C and infections caused by less common hepatitis viruses. Aging. With age, the liver breaks down harmful substances more slowly. So toxins stay in the body longer. Sex. Women seem to process, also called metabolize, certain toxins more slowly than men do. So their livers are in contact with higher amounts of harmful substances longer. This increases the risk of toxic hepatitis. Having certain gene changes, also called mutations. Inheriting certain gene changes that affect the liver enzymes that break down toxins might increase the risk of toxic hepatitis. metadata.complications: Typical liver versus liver cirrhosis Enlarge image Close Typical liver versus liver cirrhosis Typical liver versus liver cirrhosis A typical liver (left) shows no signs of scarring. In cirrhosis (right), scar tissue replaces healthy liver tissue. The swelling, called inflammation, of toxic hepatitis can lead to liver damage and scarring. Over time, this scarring, called cirrhosis, makes it hard for the liver to do its job. Toxic hepatitis, even without cirrhosis, can lead to liver failure. The only cure for ongoing liver failure is to replace the liver with a healthy one from a donor, called a liver transplant. See a healthcare professional right away if you have symptoms that worry you. Taking too much of some medicines, such as acetaminophen (Tylenol, others), may lead to liver failure. Pain in the upper stomach area. Coma. If you suspect an acetaminophen overdose, immediately call 911 or your local emergency services. In the United States, call a poison control center at 800-222-1222. Do not wait to see symptoms. An acetaminophen overdose can be fatal. But it can be treated soon after the acetaminophen is taken. metadata.symptoms: Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) is a life-threatening medical condition characterized by a sudden onset of severe illness, often caused by bacterial infections such as Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. The most common and characteristic symptoms of TSS include: Vasodilation, leading to widespread flushing and erythema (redness) of the skin, particularly on the face, neck, and trunk. This is often accompanied by a low-grade fever, typically ranging from 38°C to 40°C (100°F to 104°F). Additionally, patients with TSS often experience severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Furthermore, they may exhibit hypotension (low blood pressure), which can lead to shock and organ failure if left untreated. It's essential to note that the symptoms of TSS can progress rapidly, and prompt medical attention is crucial to prevent complications and mortality. If you suspect someone has TSS, it's vital to seek immediate medical care. Note: The key symptoms listed above are specific and medically accurate, but it's always best to consult a healthcare professional for an accurate diagnosis and treatment plan.
metadata.causes: Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) is a rare but life-threatening medical condition caused primarily by bacterial toxins produced by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. The primary causative factors of TSS are the use of superabsorbent tampons, particularly during menstruation, which can lead to bacterial growth and toxin production. Additionally, genetic predisposition and certain environmental exposures, such as exposure to endotoxins from gram-negative bacteria, can also contribute to the development of TSS. Biological factors play a crucial role in the pathogenesis of TSS, as the bacteria that cause the condition produce exotoxins that can lead to severe systemic inflammation and organ failure. The toxins stimulate the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, which can cause widespread tissue damage and disrupt normal immune function. Genetic predisposition may also contribute to an individual's susceptibility to developing TSS, with some studies suggesting that genetic variations in genes involved in the immune response or bacterial pathogenesis may increase the risk of developing the condition.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) include: 1. **Menstrual products**: Women who use tampons, especially during their menstrual period, are at higher risk due to bacterial contamination. 2. **Underlying medical conditions**: Individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with cancer, HIV/AIDS, or taking immunosuppressive medications, are more susceptible to TSS. 3. **Staphylococcus aureus infection**: The presence of Staphylococcus aureus bacteria on the skin or in the vagina increases the risk of developing TSS. These factors highlight the importance of proper hygiene, safe menstrual practices, and awareness of underlying medical conditions.
metadata.complications: Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) is a life-threatening medical condition that can arise from bacterial infections, particularly those caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. If left untreated or poorly managed, TSS can lead to severe complications, including multi-organ failure, respiratory distress, and cardiac arrest. Additionally, TSS can also cause secondary conditions such as sepsis, acute kidney injury, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

metadata.symptoms: Most people infected with toxoplasmosis do not have any symptoms. They often dont know theyre infected. Some people have flu-like symptoms, including: Fever. Swollen lymph nodes that may last for weeks. Headache. Muscle aches. Skin rash.
metadata.causes: Toxoplasma gondii is a parasite that can infect most animals and birds. It can only go through the entire cycle of reproduction in domestic and wild cats. These are the main hosts for the parasite. Immature eggs, a middle stage of reproduction, can be in the feces of cats. This immature egg allows for the parasite to make its way through the food chain. It can pass from soil and water to plants, animals and humans. Once the parasite has a new host, the reproduction cycle goes on and causes an infection. If youre in typical health, your immune system keeps the parasites in check. They stay in your body but are not active. This often gives you lifelong immunity. If youre exposed to the parasite again, your immune system would clear it out. If your immune system is weakened later in life, parasite reproduction can start again. This causes a new active infection that can lead to serious disease and complications. People often get a toxoplasma infection one of the following ways: Cat feces with the parasite. Cats that hunt or who are fed raw meat are more likely to carry toxoplasma parasites. You may get infected if you touch your mouth after touching anything that has been in contact with cat feces. This may be gardening or cleaning a litter box. Contaminated food or water. Undercooked beef, lamb, pork, venison, chicken and shellfish are all known carriers of the parasite. Unpasteurized goat milk and untreated drinking water also may be carriers. Unwashed fruits and vegetables. The surface of fruits and vegetables may have the parasite on them. Contaminated kitchen tool. Parasites may be on cutting boards, knives and other utensils that come into contact with raw meat or unwashed fruits and vegetables. Infected organ transplant or transfused blood. Rarely, toxoplasma parasites are passed through an organ transplant or blood transfusion.
metadata.risk_factors: The parasite is found throughout the world. Anyone can become infected. Risks of serious disease from toxoplasmosis include things that prevent the immune system from fighting infections, such as: Infection with HIV/AIDS. Chemotherapy treatment for cancer. metadata.symptoms: Symptoms can range from mild to severe. Symptoms may be seen at birth, but they may be mild and not noticed until an infant is about 4 to 8 weeks old. Symptoms may get worse when a child is eating. Symptoms include: Coughing often. The cough may sound like a barking seal. Noisy breathing, such as high-pitched wheezing or rattling sounds. Trouble getting enough air that gets worse with crying, coughing, eating or activity. Trouble clearing mucus from the airway. Frequent infections in the airway, such as pneumonia or bronchitis. Trouble swallowing or eating. Shortness of breath when active, for example, playing with other children or playing sports. Tracheomalacia may affect the whole windpipe or only a small section. When tracheomalacia includes the airways in the lungs, also known as the bronchi, its called tracheobronchomalacia (tray-key-oh-brong-koh-muh-LAY-shuh).
metadata.causes: Causes of tracheomalacia include: A trachea that is not fully developed. In newborns, the cartilage may not be developed enough. The soft cartilage causes the windpipe to be floppy. The windpipe doesnt stay open when breathing. Changes in how the trachea develops. In some infants the trachea doesnt develop in the typical way. For example, it might not have enough cartilage. Some infants are born with an opening between the esophagus  the tube that goes from the mouth to the stomach  and the trachea. This can cause tracheomalacia. Changes can make the windpipe more likely to collapse when breathing. Pressure on the trachea from a blood vessel. A blood vessel, such as the aorta or the main branches of the aorta, may press on the windpipe so it doesnt open enough with breathing. Damage to the trachea from injury or illness. For example, the windpipe can be damaged from surgery or medical procedures or from having a breathing tube for a long time. Examples of illnesses that can damage the windpipe include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and frequent lung infections.
metadata.risk_factors: Risk factors for tracheomalacia include: Being born too early. The windpipe may not be fully developed in infants born too early. The cartilage is not strong enough to hold the airway open. Differences in main blood vessels. These blood vessels bring blood from the heart to the rest of the body. Pressure on the windpipe from these blood vessels increases the risk of tracheomalacia. Being born with a passage between the trachea and the esophagus. The opening, called a tracheoesophageal fistula, can increase the risk of tracheomalacia. Injury to the windpipe. Surgery, medical procedures or having a breathing tube for a long time can injure the windpipe so that it collapses with breathing. Illnesses that affect the windpipe. Having frequent airway and lung infections, such as bronchitis and pneumonia, can irritate and weaken the windpipe. GERD also can irritate and weaken the windpipe. metadata.symptoms: Signs and symptoms of trachoma usually affect both eyes and may include: Mild itching and irritation of the eyes and eyelids Eye discharge containing mucus or pus Eyelid swelling Light sensitivity (photophobia) Eye pain Eye redness Vision loss Young children are particularly susceptible to infection. But the disease progresses slowly, and the more painful symptoms may not emerge until adulthood. The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified five stages in the development of trachoma: Inflammation  follicular. The early infection has five or more follicles  small bumps that contain lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell  visible with magnification on the inner surface of your upper eyelid (conjunctiva). Inflammation  intense. In this stage, your eye is now highly infectious and becomes irritated, with a thickening or swelling of the upper eyelid. Eyelid scarring. Repeated infections lead to scarring of the inner eyelid. The scars often appear as white lines when examined with magnification. Your eyelid may become distorted and may turn in (entropion). In-turned eyelashes (trichiasis). The scarred inner lining of your eyelid continues to deform, causing your lashes to turn in so that they rub on and scratch the transparent outer surface of your eye (cornea). Corneal clouding (opacity). The cornea becomes affected by an inflammation that is most commonly seen under your upper lid. Continuous inflammation compounded by scratching from the in-turned lashes leads to clouding of the cornea. All the signs of trachoma are more severe in your upper lid than in your lower lid. Without intervention, a disease process that begins in childhood can continue to advance into adulthood.
metadata.causes: Trachoma is caused by certain subtypes of Chlamydia trachomatis, a bacterium that can also cause the sexually transmitted infection chlamydia. Trachoma spreads through contact with discharge from the eyes or nose of an infected person. Hands, clothing, towels and insects can all be routes for transmission. In developing countries, eye-seeking flies also are a means of transmission.

In areas where the disease is active, its most common in children ages 4 to 6. Sex. In some areas, womens rate of contracting the disease is two to six times higher than that of men. This may be attributed to the fact that women have more contact with children, who are the primary reservoir of infection. Flies. People living in areas with problems controlling the fly population may be more susceptible to infection. Factors that increase your risk of contracting trachoma include: Crowded living conditions. metadata.symptoms: Transient Global Amnesia (TGA) is a rare neurological disorder characterized by sudden and temporary loss of memory, often accompanied by confusion, disorientation, and difficulty with speech and language. The most common and characteristic symptoms of TGA include: (1) sudden onset of severe amnesia, with patients often unable to recall their own name, address, or recent events; (2) profound disorientation, including confusion about time, place, and person; (3) difficulty with speech and language, including trouble finding words, speaking in a slow and labored manner, and difficulty understanding written or spoken language; and (4) impaired motor function, including weakness, numbness, or paralysis of the face, arm, or leg. In some cases, patients may also experience visual disturbances, such as blurred vision or double vision, and emotional lability, including anxiety, agitation, or depression. Please note that TGA is a rare condition, and not all patients will exhibit all of these symptoms. The exact duration of the amnesia can vary from hours to days, with most cases resolving within 24-48 hours without any long-term effects.
metadata.causes: Transient Global Amnesia (TGA) is a rare neurological disorder characterized by sudden and temporary loss of memory and cognitive function. The primary causes of TGA are thought to be related to abnormal blood flow to the brain, particularly in the hippocampus, which is responsible for forming new memories. This can occur due to a variety of factors, including atherosclerosis (narrowing of the arteries), vasculitis (inflammation of the blood vessels), or even a sudden increase in intracranial pressure. Biological and genetic factors may also play a role, as some cases of TGA have been linked to underlying conditions such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, or traumatic brain injury. Environmental factors, such as exposure to toxins or certain medications, can also contribute to the development of TGA. Lifestyle factors, such as smoking or hypertension, may also increase the risk of developing this condition. It's worth noting that TGA is often associated with a sudden and unexpected event, such as a car accident or a fall, which can cause a temporary disruption in blood flow to the brain.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Transient Global Amnesia (TGA) include: Age: Individuals over 50 years old are at a higher risk of developing TGA. Medical conditions: Hypertension, diabetes, and cardiac disease are associated with an increased risk of TGA. Lifestyle factors: A history of head trauma or stroke, as well as certain medications such as beta-blockers and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), can also increase the likelihood of developing TGA.
metadata.complications: Transient Global Amnesia (TGA) is a rare neurological disorder characterized by temporary loss of memory, confusion, and disorientation. If left untreated or poorly managed, TGA can lead to serious complications, including increased risk of stroke, seizures, and cognitive decline. Additionally, repeated episodes of TGA may result in long-term cognitive impairment, dementia, and even death. The most significant complications of untreated or poorly managed TGA include: 1. Increased risk of stroke: Repeated episodes of TGA can increase the risk of subsequent strokes, which can be devastating for patients. 2. Cognitive decline: Untreated or poorly managed TGA can lead to long-term cognitive impairment, including memory loss and decreased cognitive function. 3. Dementia: In severe cases, repeated episodes of TGA may result in the development of dementia, a condition characterized by progressive cognitive decline. It's essential to note that most people with TGA make a full recovery within 24-48 hours without any long-term consequences. However, prompt medical attention and proper management are crucial to minimize the risk of complications and ensure optimal outcomes.

name: Transient Ischemic Attack
description: symptoms  transient ischemic attacks usually last a few minutes. most symptoms disappear within an hour. rarely  symptoms may last up to 24 hours. the symptoms of a tia are similar to those found early in a stroke. symptoms happen suddenly and may include  weakness  numbness or paralysis in the face  arm or leg  typically on one side of the body. slurred speech or trouble understanding others. blindness in one or both eyes or double vision. dizziness or loss of balance or coordination. you may have more than one tia. their symptoms may be similar or different depending on which area of the brain is involved.. causes  the cause of a transient ischemic attack is similar to the cause of an ischemic stroke  which is the most common type of stroke. in an ischemic stroke  a blood clot blocks the blood supply to part of the brain. in a tia  unlike a stroke  the blockage is brief and there is no permanent damage. the blockage that occurs during a tia often results from a buildup of cholesterol-containing fatty deposits called plaques in an artery. this is known as atherosclerosis. the buildup also may occur in an arterys branches that supply oxygen and nutrients to the brain. plaques can decrease the blood flow through an artery or lead to the development of a clot. a blood clot that moves from another part of the body  such as the heart  to an artery that supplies the brain also may cause a tia.

metadata.symptoms: Transient ischemic attacks usually last a few minutes. Most symptoms disappear within an hour. Rarely, symptoms may last up to 24 hours. The symptoms of a TIA are similar to those found early in a stroke. Symptoms happen suddenly and may include: Weakness, numbness or paralysis in the face, arm or leg, typically on one side of the body. Slurred speech or trouble understanding others. Blindness in one or both eyes or double vision. Dizziness or loss of balance or coordination. You may have more than one TIA. metadata.causes: The cause of a transient ischemic attack is similar to the cause of an ischemic stroke, which is the most common type of stroke. In an ischemic stroke, a blood clot blocks the blood supply to part of the brain. In a TIA, unlike a stroke, the blockage is brief and there is no permanent damage. The blockage that occurs during a TIA often results from a buildup of cholesterol-containing fatty deposits called plaques in an artery. This is known as atherosclerosis. The buildup also may occur in an arterys branches that supply oxygen and nutrients to the brain. Plaques can decrease the blood flow through an artery or lead to the development of a clot. A blood clot that moves from another part of the body, such as the heart, to an artery that supplies the brain also may cause a TIA.

metadata.symptoms: Symptoms of transposition of the great arteries include: Blue or gray skin due to low oxygen levels. Depending on skin color, these color changes may be harder or easier to see. Pounding heartbeat. Weak pulse. Lack of appetite. Poor weight gain. Some people with the congenitally corrected type of TGA may not have symptoms for many years. Also, skin color changes may not be seen right away if a baby with TGA also has other heart changes that let some oxygen-rich blood move through the body. But as the baby becomes more active, less oxygen-rich blood flows through the body. The changes in skin color become more noticeable as oxygen levels drop.
metadata.causes: Transposition of the great arteries, also called TGA, happens during pregnancy when the unborn babys heart is forming. An unborn baby also is called a fetus. The cause is most often not known. To understand TGA, it may help to know how the heart usually pumps blood. The typical heart has four chambers. The two upper chambers are called the atria. The two lower chambers are called the ventricles. The artery that carries blood from the heart to the lungs is called the pulmonary artery. It connects to the hearts lower right chamber, called the right ventricle. The right side of the heart moves blood to the lungs. In the lungs, blood picks up oxygen and then returns it to the hearts left side. The left side of the heart then pumps the blood through the bodys main artery, called the aorta. The blood then goes out to the rest of the body.
metadata.risk_factors: Possible risk factors for congenital heart defects such as transposition of the great arteries include: Rubella, also called German measles. Having rubella during pregnancy can cause changes in an unborn babys heart development. A blood test done before pregnancy can determine if youre immune to rubella. A vaccine is available if you arent. Some medicines. Taking certain medicines during pregnancy can cause congenital heart defects and other health conditions present at birth. Always tell your healthcare team about the medicines you take. Alcohol use. Drinking alcohol during pregnancy raises the risk of congenital heart defects in the baby. Smoking. If you smoke, quit. Smoking during pregnancy can be harmful to the unborn baby, also called a fetus. Diabetes. Careful control of blood sugar before and during pregnancy can reduce the risk of congenital heart defects in the baby. Diabetes that develops during pregnancy is called gestational diabetes. metadata.complications: Complications depend on the type of transposition of the great arteries. Possible complications of complete transposition of the great arteries may include: Not enough oxygen to body tissues. Unless theres some mixing of oxygen-rich blood and oxygen-poor blood within the heart, this complication causes death. Possible complications of congenitally corrected transposition, also called l-TGA, may include: Complete heart block. Transposition of the great arteries can change the way electrical signals move through the heart and tell the heart to beat. A complete heart block occurs if all signals are blocked. Heart valve disease. In l-TGA, the valve between the upper and lower heart chambers, called the tricuspid valve, may not close all the way. Blood might flow backward. This condition is called tricuspid valve regurgitation. It can make it harder for the heart to pump blood. Heart failure. The heart cant pump enough blood to meet the bodys needs. Heart failure may happen over time in l-TGA because the right lower heart chamber is pumping under higher pressure than usual. The strain may make the muscle of the right lower chamber weak. Serious congenital heart defects are often diagnosed before or soon after a child is born. Get help right away if a child has trouble breathing. Also get emergency medical help for anyone who has blue or gray skin or nails. Low oxygen levels can cause this change in skin color. Depending on skin color, the changes may be harder or easier to see. Request an appointment

metadata.symptoms: Transverse Myelitis (TM) is a rare but serious medical condition characterized by inflammation of the spinal cord, which can lead to significant disability. The main symptoms and signs of TM include: 1. **Sudden onset of weakness or paralysis**: Patients typically experience sudden and severe weakness or paralysis in one or more segments of the body, often starting from the waist down and progressing upwards. 2. **Loss of sensation**: Affected individuals may experience numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation in the affected areas, which can be bilateral (affecting both sides) or unilateral (affecting only one side). 3. **Urinary retention or incontinence**: TM can cause urinary retention or incontinence due to damage to the spinal cord's autonomic nervous system, leading to bladder dysfunction. 4. **Muscle spasms and stiffness**: Patients may experience muscle spasms, stiffness, and rigidity, particularly in the back, arms, and legs. These symptoms can vary in severity and progression, but prompt medical attention is essential to prevent long-term damage and improve outcomes.
metadata.causes: Transverse Myelitis (TM) is a rare but serious medical condition characterized by inflammation of the spinal cord, leading to damage to the myelin sheath that surrounds nerve fibers. The primary causative factors of TM include viral infections, such as herpesvirus 6 or 7, and autoimmune disorders, where the immune system mistakenly attacks the healthy tissues in the spinal cord. Additionally, genetic predisposition and certain environmental exposures, such as exposure to toxins or radiation, have also been identified as potential triggers for TM. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of TM, with viral infections triggering an abnormal immune response that leads to inflammation and damage to the spinal cord. Genetic mutations can also contribute to the susceptibility to TM by affecting the regulation of the immune system. Environmental factors, such as exposure to toxins or radiation, may also trigger the onset of TM in susceptible individuals. Lifestyle factors are not typically considered primary causative factors for TM, but certain behaviors, such as excessive physical activity or exposure to extreme temperatures, may exacerbate the condition in individuals who already have a predisposition to it.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Transverse Myelitis (TM) include: 1. **Autoimmune disorders**: Conditions such as multiple sclerosis, lupus, and rheumatoid arthritis increase the likelihood of developing TM. 2. **Infections**: Certain viral infections like herpes simplex virus, enterovirus, and human parvovirus B19 can trigger TM. 3. **Neurological conditions**: Presence of neurological conditions like Guillain-Barré syndrome, encephalitis, or meningitis also increases the risk of developing TM. These factors highlight the importance of identifying underlying autoimmune, infectious, or neurological conditions in patients presenting with symptoms of TM.
metadata.complications: Transverse Myelitis (TM) is a rare but potentially life-threatening medical condition characterized by inflammation of the spinal cord, which can lead to various serious complications if left untreated or poorly managed. If TM is not treated promptly and effectively, it can result in significant neurological deficits, including paralysis, loss of bladder and bowel function, and chronic pain. Additionally, secondary conditions such as spinal cord compression, autonomic dysfunction, and seizures can also develop, potentially leading to long-term disability and decreased quality of life. In severe cases, TM can lead to: 1. Spinal cord infarction: A blockage in the blood vessels supplying the spinal cord, which can result in permanent damage or paralysis. 2. Autonomic dysfunction: Disruption of the autonomic nervous system, leading to abnormal heart rate, blood pressure, and bowel function. 3. Seizures: Convulsive episodes that can be caused by inflammation or compression of the brain and spinal cord. Early diagnosis and treatment with corticosteroids and immunosuppressive medications are crucial to prevent these complications and improve outcomes for patients with TM.

In a child with traumatic brain injury, you may observe: Change in eating or nursing habits Unusual or easy irritability Persistent crying and inability to be consoled Change in ability to pay attention Change in sleep habits Seizures Sad or depressed mood Drowsiness Loss of interest in favorite toys or activities
metadata.causes: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) is a complex medical condition caused by physical trauma to the brain, resulting in damage to brain tissue, disruption of normal brain function, and altered behavior. The primary causative factors of TBI include violent head injuries, such as those sustained from falls, motor vehicle accidents, or assaults, which can lead to concussions, skull fractures, or penetrating brain injuries. Additionally, repetitive blows to the head, such as in sports or military service, can also contribute to the development of TBI. Biological factors play a role in the pathophysiology of TBI, including the activation of inflammatory pathways, oxidative stress, and disruption of normal blood-brain barrier function. Genetic predisposition may also influence an individual's susceptibility to TBI, with certain genetic mutations affecting the brain's ability to withstand injury. Environmental factors, such as exposure to toxins or infections, can also contribute to the development of TBI. Lifestyle factors, such as substance abuse and poor sleep habits, have been linked to an increased risk of TBI, particularly in individuals who engage in high-risk behaviors. Furthermore, certain medical conditions, such as hypertension and diabetes, may increase the risk of TBI by affecting blood vessel function and increasing inflammation in the brain. It's worth noting that TBI can also be caused by non-violent means, such as falls from heights or drowning, which can lead to a similar pattern of injury and damage.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) include: * Age: Children under 5 years old and older adults over 65 are at higher risk due to decreased brain resilience and increased vulnerability. * Gender: Males are more likely to experience TBI, with a male-to-female ratio of approximately 1.4:1. * Lifestyle factors: Participation in contact sports, such as football, hockey, or soccer, increases the risk of TBI. These demographic and lifestyle factors can significantly increase an individual's likelihood of developing Traumatic Brain Injury.
metadata.complications: Seizures. Some people with traumatic brain injury will develop seizures. The seizures may occur only in the early stages, or years after the injury. Recurrent seizures are called post-traumatic epilepsy. Fluid buildup in the brain (hydrocephalus). Cerebrospinal fluid may build up in the spaces in the brain (cerebral ventricles) of some people who have had traumatic brain injuries, causing increased pressure and swelling in the brain. Infections. Skull fractures or penetrating wounds can tear the layers of protective tissues (meninges) that surround the brain. This can enable bacteria to enter the brain and cause infections. An infection of the meninges (meningitis) could spread to the rest of the nervous system if not treated. Blood vessel damage. Several small or large blood vessels in the brain may be damaged in a traumatic brain injury. This damage could lead to a stroke, blood clots or other problems. Headaches. Frequent headaches are very common after a traumatic brain injury. They may begin within a week after the injury and could persist for as long as several months. Vertigo. Many people experience vertigo, a condition characterized by dizziness, after a traumatic brain injury. Sometimes, any or several of these symptoms might linger for a few weeks to a few months after a traumatic brain injury. When a combination of these symptoms lasts for an extended period of time, this is generally referred to as persistent post-concussive symptoms. Traumatic brain injuries at the base of the skull can cause nerve damage to the nerves that emerge directly from the brain (cranial nerves). Cranial nerve damage may result in: Paralysis of facial muscles or losing sensation in the face Loss of or altered sense of smell or taste Loss of vision or double vision Swallowing problems Dizziness Ringing in the ear Hearing loss

metadata.symptoms: Travelers diarrhea may begin suddenly during your trip or shortly after you return home. Most people improve within 1 to 2 days without treatment and recover completely within a week. However, you can have multiple episodes of travelers diarrhea during one trip. The most common symptoms of travelers diarrhea are: Suddenly passing three or more looser watery stools a day. An urgent need to pass stool. Stomach cramps. Nausea. Vomiting. Fever. Sometimes, people experience moderate to severe dehydration, ongoing vomiting, a high fever, bloody stools, or severe pain in the belly or rectum. If you or your child experiences any of these symptoms or if the diarrhea lasts longer than a few days, its time to see a healthcare professional.
metadata.causes: Its possible that travelers diarrhea may stem from the stress of traveling or a change in diet. But usually infectious agents  such as bacteria, viruses or parasites  are to blame. You typically develop travelers diarrhea after ingesting food or water contaminated with organisms from feces. So why arent natives of high-risk countries affected in the same way Often their bodies have become used to the bacteria and have developed immunity to them.
metadata.risk_factors: Each year millions of international travelers experience travelers diarrhea. High-risk destinations for travelers diarrhea include areas of: Central America. South America. Mexico. Africa. South Asia and Southeast Asia. Traveling to Eastern Europe, South Africa, Central and East Asia, the Middle East, and a few Caribbean islands also poses some risk. However, your risk of travelers diarrhea is generally low in Northern and Western Europe, Japan, Canada, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand, and the United States. Your chances of getting travelers diarrhea are mostly determined by your destination. But certain groups of people have a greater risk of developing the condition. These include: Young adults. The condition is slightly more common in young adult tourists. Though the reasons why arent clear, its possible that young adults lack acquired immunity. They may also be more adventurous than older people in their travels and dietary choices, or they may be less careful about avoiding contaminated foods. People with weakened immune systems. A weakened immune system due to an underlying illness or immune-suppressing medicines such as corticosteroids increases risk of infections. People with diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, or severe kidney, liver or heart disease. These conditions can leave you more prone to infection or increase your risk of a more-severe infection. People who take acid blockers or antacids. Acid in the stomach tends to destroy organisms, so a reduction in stomach acid may leave more opportunity for bacterial survival. People who travel during certain seasons. The risk of travelers diarrhea varies by season in certain parts of the world.
