description: symptoms  uterine polyps are benign growths in the uterus that can cause various symptoms. the most common and characteristic symptoms experienced by patients with uterine polyps include  heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding  particularly in women who have not yet reached menopause. this excessive bleeding may be accompanied by clotting or passing of clots during menstruation. additionally  some women may experience irregular periods  including infrequent or prolonged periods  as well as a feeling of pressure or discomfort in the lower abdomen. in some cases  patients may also notice changes in their cervical mucus  such as an increase in its thickness and stickiness. please note that not all women with uterine polyps will exhibit these symptoms  and some may be asymptomatic altogether. however  if you suspect you have uterine polyps or are experiencing any of these symptoms  it is essential to consult a healthcare professional for proper evaluation and diagnosis.. causes  uterine polyps are growths in the uterus that can cause a range of symptoms  from heavy menstrual bleeding to infertility issues. the primary causes of uterine polyps are hormonal imbalances  particularly an excess of estrogen  which stimulates the growth of the polyp tissue. additionally  genetic factors and certain lifestyle habits  such as obesity and smoking  have been linked to an increased risk of developing uterine polyps. biological factors  including a family history of polyps or other gynecologic conditions  can also contribute to their development. environmental factors  such as exposure to endocrine disruptors or certain chemicals  may also play a role in the etiology of uterine polyps. lifestyle factors  such as obesity and smoking  have been associated with an increased risk of developing uterine polyps.

metadata.symptoms: Uterine polyps are benign growths in the uterus that can cause various symptoms. The most common and characteristic symptoms experienced by patients with uterine polyps include: heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, particularly in women who have not yet reached menopause. This excessive bleeding may be accompanied by clotting or passing of clots during menstruation. Additionally, some women may experience irregular periods, including infrequent or prolonged periods, as well as a feeling of pressure or discomfort in the lower abdomen. In some cases, patients may also notice changes in their cervical mucus, such as an increase in its thickness and stickiness. Please note that not all women with uterine polyps will exhibit these symptoms, and some may be asymptomatic altogether. However, if you suspect you have uterine polyps or are experiencing any of these symptoms, it is essential to consult a healthcare professional for proper evaluation and diagnosis.
metadata.causes: Uterine polyps are growths in the uterus that can cause a range of symptoms, from heavy menstrual bleeding to infertility issues. The primary causes of uterine polyps are hormonal imbalances, particularly an excess of estrogen, which stimulates the growth of the polyp tissue. Additionally, genetic factors and certain lifestyle habits, such as obesity and smoking, have been linked to an increased risk of developing uterine polyps. Biological factors, including a family history of polyps or other gynecologic conditions, can also contribute to their development. Environmental factors, such as exposure to endocrine disruptors or certain chemicals, may also play a role in the etiology of uterine polyps. Lifestyle factors, such as obesity and smoking, have been associated with an increased risk of developing uterine polyps.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing uterine polyps include: 1. **Age**: Women over 40 years old are more likely to develop uterine polyps, with the risk increasing after menopause. 2. **Hormonal influences**: Women with a history of irregular menstrual cycles or those taking hormone replacement therapy (HRT) are at higher risk due to the potential for hormonal imbalances. 3. **Family history**: Women with a first-degree relative (mother or sister) who has had uterine polyps are more likely to develop them themselves. These factors contribute significantly to the overall risk of developing uterine polyps, and it's essential to be aware of them to take preventive measures if necessary.
metadata.complications: Uterine polyps are growths in the uterus that can cause a range of complications, including heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pain, and infertility issues. If left untreated or poorly managed, uterine polyps can lead to serious outcomes such as anemia due to excessive blood loss, infection, and the development of endometrial hyperplasia, which increases the risk of cancer. Untreated uterine polyps can also increase the risk of miscarriage, preterm labor, and placental abruption. Additionally, large or multiple polyps can cause pressure on surrounding organs, leading to complications such as bowel obstruction or bladder damage. The most significant complication of untreated uterine polyps is an increased risk of endometrial cancer, which can develop if the polyp cells become malignant over time.

metadata.complications: Uterine prolapse often happens with prolapse of other pelvic organs. These types of prolapse can also happen: Anterior prolapse. Anterior prolapse results from weak connective tissue between the bladder and roof of the vagina. It can cause the bladder to bulge into the vagina. This is called a cystocele or prolapsed bladder. Posterior vaginal prolapse. Weak connective tissue between the rectum and the floor of the vagina can cause the rectum to bulge into the vagina. This might cause difficulty with bowel movements. Posterior vaginal prolapse is also called a rectocele. See a health care provider to talk about treatment options if symptoms of uterine prolapse bother you and keep you from doing daily activities. metadata.symptoms: Uveitis is a medical condition characterized by inflammation of the uvea, the middle layer of the eye. The main symptoms and signs of uveitis include: (1) Eye pain or discomfort, which can range from mild to severe; (2) Blurred vision, often accompanied by sensitivity to light; and (3) Flashes of light or floaters in the visual field, which are caused by vitreous hemorrhage or retinal detachment. Additionally, patients may experience redness of the eye, particularly in the iris and choroid, which can be accompanied by tearing and swelling of the eyelids. In some cases, uveitis can also cause decreased vision, double vision, or loss of peripheral vision. It's worth noting that the symptoms of uveitis can vary depending on the underlying cause, such as infection, injury, or autoimmune disorders. Prompt medical attention is essential to diagnose and treat uveitis effectively, as untreated inflammation can lead to permanent vision loss and other complications.
metadata.causes: Uveitis is a complex inflammatory eye disorder characterized by inflammation of the uvea, the middle layer of the eye. The primary causes of uveitis are autoimmune disorders, such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and Hashimoto's thyroiditis, which can lead to an abnormal immune response that attacks the eye tissues. Additionally, infections, trauma, and certain medications can also trigger uveitis. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of uveitis, with genetic predisposition being a major contributing factor. Some individuals may be more susceptible to developing uveitis due to their genetic makeup, which can affect the immune system's response to perceived threats. Environmental and lifestyle factors, such as exposure to certain medications or infections, can also trigger the onset of uveitis. Genetic factors are thought to contribute to the development of uveitis in approximately 20-30% of cases, with certain genetic mutations affecting the immune system's function and increasing the risk of developing uveitis. Environmental factors, such as exposure to ultraviolet radiation, can also trigger inflammation in the eye and increase the risk of developing uveitis. Lifestyle factors, such as smoking and poor diet, may also contribute to the development of uveitis, although the exact mechanisms by which these factors influence the condition are not fully understood.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for uveitis include: Age: Young adults and children under the age of 20 are more likely to develop uveitis, with a peak incidence in those between 10-30 years old. Genetic predisposition: Individuals with a family history of uveitis or other autoimmune disorders, such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus, are at increased risk. Medical conditions: Certain medical conditions, including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), psoriasis, and sarcoidosis, increase the likelihood of developing uveitis.
metadata.complications: Contact your healthcare team if you think you have the warning signs of uveitis. You may be referred to an eye specialist, called an ophthalmologist. If youre having significant eye pain and unexpected vision problems, seek immediate medical attention.

name: Vaginal Agenesis
description: symptoms  vaginal agenesis often goes unnoticed until females reach their teens  but dont menstruate (amenorrhea). other signs of puberty usually follow typical female development. vaginal agenesis may have these features  the genitals look like a typical female. the vagina may be shortened without a cervix at the end  or absent and marked only by a slight indentation where a vaginal opening would typically be located. there may be no uterus or one thats only partially developed. if theres tissue lining the uterus (endometrium)  monthly cramping or chronic abdominal pain may occur. the ovaries typically are fully developed and functional  but they may be in an unusual location in the abdomen. sometimes the pair of tubes that eggs travel through to get from the ovaries to the uterus (fallopian tubes) are absent or do not develop typically. vaginal agenesis may also be associated with other issues  such as  problems with development of the kidneys and urinary tract developmental changes in the bones of the spine  ribs and wrists hearing problems other congenital conditions that also involve the heart  gastrointestinal tract and limb growth. causes  its not clear what causes vaginal agenesis  but at some point during the first 20 weeks of pregnancy  tubes called the mullerian ducts dont develop properly. typically  the lower portion of these ducts develops into the uterus and vagina  and the upper portion becomes the fallopian tubes. the underdevelopment of the mullerian ducts results in an absent or partially closed vagina  absent or partial uterus  or both.

metadata.symptoms: Vaginal agenesis often goes unnoticed until females reach their teens, but dont menstruate (amenorrhea). Other signs of puberty usually follow typical female development. Vaginal agenesis may have these features: The genitals look like a typical female. The vagina may be shortened without a cervix at the end, or absent and marked only by a slight indentation where a vaginal opening would typically be located. There may be no uterus or one thats only partially developed. If theres tissue lining the uterus (endometrium), monthly cramping or chronic abdominal pain may occur. The ovaries typically are fully developed and functional, but they may be in an unusual location in the abdomen. Sometimes the pair of tubes that eggs travel through to get from the ovaries to the uterus (fallopian tubes) are absent or do not develop typically. Vaginal agenesis may also be associated with other issues, such as: Problems with development of the kidneys and urinary tract Developmental changes in the bones of the spine, ribs and wrists Hearing problems Other congenital conditions that also involve the heart, gastrointestinal tract and limb growth
metadata.causes: Its not clear what causes vaginal agenesis, but at some point during the first 20 weeks of pregnancy, tubes called the mullerian ducts dont develop properly. Typically, the lower portion of these ducts develops into the uterus and vagina, and the upper portion becomes the fallopian tubes. The underdevelopment of the mullerian ducts results in an absent or partially closed vagina, absent or partial uterus, or both.
metadata.risk_factors: I must correct you - Vaginal agenesis is a rare congenital condition where the vagina fails to develop during fetal development. The main risk factors for vaginal agenesis include: 1. **Genetic predisposition**: Individuals with a family history of vaginal agenesis or other congenital anomalies are more likely to develop the condition. 2. **Advanced maternal age**: Women over 35 years old at the time of conception are at increased risk due to higher rates of chromosomal abnormalities and genetic mutations. 3. **Fetal exposure to certain medications**: Exposure to certain medications, such as diethylstilbestrol (DES), during pregnancy has been linked to an increased risk of vaginal agenesis. These factors can increase the likelihood of developing vaginal agenesis, but it's essential to note that many cases are isolated and not associated with any specific risk factor.
metadata.complications: Vaginal agenesis may impact your sexual relationships, but after treatment, your vagina will typically function well for sexual activity. Females with a missing or partially developed uterus cant get pregnant. If you have healthy ovaries, however, it may be possible to have a baby through in vitro fertilization. The embryo can be implanted in the uterus of another person to carry the pregnancy (gestational carrier). Discuss fertility options with your health care provider. metadata.causes: Vaginal atrophy is a common gynecological condition characterized by thinning, drying, and inflammation of the vaginal walls, leading to symptoms such as pain during sex, vaginal bleeding, and decreased libido. The primary causes of vaginal atrophy are hormonal changes, particularly estrogen deficiency, which can occur due to menopause, premature ovarian failure, or surgical removal of the ovaries. Additionally, certain medications, such as hormone replacement therapy (HRT) inhibitors, and chronic conditions like diabetes and thyroid disorders can also contribute to vaginal atrophy. Biological factors play a significant role in the development of vaginal atrophy, as estrogen levels decline with age, leading to decreased vaginal elasticity and hydration. Genetic predisposition may also be a factor, as some women are more susceptible to hormonal imbalances due to their genetic makeup. Environmental and lifestyle factors, such as smoking and poor diet, can also exacerbate vaginal atrophy by reducing blood flow and increasing inflammation. It's worth noting that vaginal atrophy is often associated with the decline of estrogen levels, particularly after menopause, when the ovaries stop producing estrogen. This hormonal shift can lead to a range of symptoms, including vaginal dryness, pain during sex, and decreased libido.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for vaginal atrophy include: 1. **Age**: Vaginal atrophy is more common in postmenopausal women (ages 55+), as estrogen levels decline with age, leading to thinning and drying of the vaginal tissue. 2. **Hormonal changes**: Decreased estrogen levels due to menopause or premature ovarian failure can cause vaginal atrophy. 3. **Genetic predisposition**: Women with a family history of vaginal atrophy are more likely to develop the condition, suggesting a possible genetic component. These factors increase the likelihood of developing vaginal atrophy, which can lead to symptoms such as dryness, itching, and painful sex.
metadata.complications: Vaginal atrophy, also known as vaginal dryness, is a common condition characterized by thinning, drying, and inflammation of the vaginal walls due to decreased estrogen levels, often associated with menopause or hormone replacement therapy (HRT). If left untreated or poorly managed, vaginal atrophy can lead to several serious complications, including increased risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs), painful sex, and chronic pelvic pain. Additionally, untreated vaginal atrophy may also increase the risk of developing vulvovaginal candidiasis (yeast infections) and bacterial vaginosis. The most significant complication is the increased risk of UTIs, which can lead to more severe symptoms such as dysuria, hematuria, and pyelonephritis. Poorly managed vaginal atrophy may also increase the risk of developing vulvovaginal candidiasis (yeast infections), which can cause discomfort, itching, and burning sensations. Untreated vaginal atrophy may also lead to chronic pelvic pain, which can significantly impact a woman's quality of life and overall well-being.

Urine that has an unusual odor or contains blood. Vaginal fluid called discharge that looks or smells unusual. Pain during sex. metadata.causes: Vaginal fistulas have many possible causes, including certain medical conditions and problems that can happen because of surgery. These causes include the following: Surgery complications. Surgeries that involve the vaginal wall, anus or rectum can lead to vaginal fistulas. So can surgery on the area between the vagina and anus, called the perineum. Fistulas can form for reasons such as injuries during surgery and infections after surgery. Skilled surgeons can repair injuries while operating, which lowers the risk of fistula. But complications such as fistulas are more common after surgery in people with diabetes or in people who use tobacco. Surgery to remove the uterus, called a hysterectomy, is an example of an operation that can raise the risk of a vaginal fistula. The risk is higher if the hysterectomy is more complex. For example, the risk rises if the surgery takes longer than five hours, or if it involves larger blood loss or the removal of more surrounding tissue. Childbirth injuries. A vaginal fistula could stem from tearing that sometimes happens when a babys head comes through the opening of the vagina. Or a fistula might form due to an infection of a surgical cut made between the vagina and the anus to help deliver a baby. This cause is not common in developed countries. Being in labor a long time because the baby cant move into the birth canal can raise the risk of a vaginal fistula, mainly in developing countries. Thats partly because access to emergency delivery measures such as C-section may be limited. Crohns disease. This condition inflames tissue that lines the digestive tract. If you follow your Crohns treatment plan, youre not likely to get a vaginal fistula. Crohns is a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Another type of IBD called ulcerative colitis also may lead to vaginal fistulas, but the risk of that happening is even lower. Certain cancers and radiation therapy. Cancer of the anus, rectum, vagina or cervix can lead to a vaginal fistula. So can damage from radiation therapy for the treatment of cancer in the pelvic area. Diverticulitis. This condition involves small, bulging pouches in the digestive tract. Diverticulitis that leads to a vaginal fistula is more common in older people. A large amount of stool stuck in the rectum. This condition is known as a fecal impaction. It also is more likely to cause a vaginal fistula in an older person.
metadata.risk_factors: A vaginal fistula has no clear risk factors. A vaginal fistula has no clear risk factors.
metadata.complications: Vaginal fistulas can lead to other health conditions called complications. Complications of vaginal fistulas include: Fistulas that keep coming back. Ongoing pelvic infections. Narrowing of the vagina, anus or rectum. This also is called stenosis. Trouble becoming pregnant. Loss of a pregnancy after 20 weeks, also called stillbirth. Get a healthcare checkup if you think you have symptoms of a vaginal fistula. Tell your healthcare professional if you have symptoms that affect your daily life, relationships or mental health. metadata.causes: Vaginitis is a common vaginal infection characterized by inflammation of the vagina, cervix, and vulva. The primary causative factors of vaginitis include bacterial vaginosis (BV), caused by an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria such as Gardnerella vaginalis; yeast infections, typically caused by Candida albicans; and trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection caused by the parasite Trichomonas vaginalis. These conditions are often triggered by changes in hormonal balance, immune system function, or exposure to certain environmental factors. Biological factors such as hormonal fluctuations during menstruation, pregnancy, or menopause can disrupt the natural balance of vaginal flora, leading to an overgrowth of pathogenic microorganisms. Genetic predisposition may also play a role in some cases of vaginitis, particularly in individuals with weakened immune systems. Environmental factors, such as exposure to antibiotics, birth control pills, or certain chemicals, can also contribute to the development of vaginitis. Lifestyle factors, including poor hygiene, multiple sex partners, and smoking, can increase the risk of developing vaginitis. Additionally, certain medical conditions, such as diabetes, HIV/AIDS, and pelvic inflammatory disease, can also predispose individuals to vaginal infections.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for vaginitis include: 1. **Age**: Vaginitis is more common in women under the age of 25 and over the age of 60, as hormonal changes during puberty and menopause can disrupt vaginal pH and lead to infection. 2. **Sexual activity**: Women who are sexually active with multiple partners or have a new partner are at higher risk of developing vaginitis due to increased exposure to sexually transmitted infections (STIs). 3. **Hormonal imbalances**: Women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), thyroid disorders, or other hormonal imbalances may be more susceptible to vaginal infections. These demographic factors can increase a woman's likelihood of developing vaginitis, particularly bacterial vaginosis and yeast infections.
metadata.complications: Vaginitis, an inflammation of the vagina, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. If left untreated, vaginitis can increase the risk of developing pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), a serious condition that can cause infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pain. Additionally, recurrent or persistent infections can also lead to scarring, adhesions, and chronic vaginal discharge. Untreated vaginitis can also increase the risk of developing secondary conditions such as bacterial vaginosis, yeast infections, and trichomoniasis, which can be more difficult to treat and may require longer courses of antibiotics.

metadata.symptoms: Valley Fever, also known as coccidioidomycosis, is a fungal infection caused by Coccidioides immitis or Coccidioides posadasii. The main symptoms of Valley Fever typically include: (1) Pneumonia-like symptoms, such as coughing, chest pain, and difficulty breathing; (2) Fever, which can range from mild to severe; and (3) Headache, fatigue, and muscle aches. Additionally, some patients may experience lymphadenopathy (swollen lymph nodes), particularly in the neck and armpits, and skin lesions or rashes. In more severe cases, Valley Fever can lead to respiratory failure, meningitis, or other life-threatening complications. It is essential for individuals living in endemic areas to take preventive measures, such as avoiding dusty environments during peak fungal spore season (usually April-September), wearing protective clothing, and seeking medical attention promptly if symptoms develop. Note: These symptoms are typical of Valley Fever but may vary depending on the severity and individual case.
metadata.causes: Valley Fever, also known as coccidioidomycosis, is a fungal infection caused by Coccidioides immitis or Coccidioides posadasii, which are soil-dwelling fungi found in the southwestern United States, Mexico, and parts of South America. The primary causative factors leading to Valley Fever are biological, specifically exposure to the fungal spores through inhalation of contaminated soil, dust, or water. Genetic predisposition may also play a role, as some individuals with weakened immune systems are more susceptible to infection. The underlying mechanisms involve the inhalation of fungal spores, which can become airborne when disturbed by foot traffic, construction, or other activities that stir up soil particles. Once inhaled, the spores germinate and form spherules, which release arthroconidia that infect the lungs and cause inflammation. Lifestyle factors, such as living in areas with high fungal spore concentrations, may also contribute to the risk of infection. Environmental factors, like drought or flooding, can increase the spread of fungal spores, making it more likely for people to be exposed.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Valley Fever, also known as coccidioidomycosis, include: Demographic factors: Individuals living in endemic regions, particularly in the southwestern United States, are at higher risk due to exposure to contaminated soil. Young adults (20-40 years old) and older adults (60+ years old) are more likely to develop Valley Fever. Pregnant women and individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing chemotherapy, are also at increased risk. Lifestyle factors: People who engage in outdoor activities, such as hiking, gardening, or construction work, that involve disturbing soil or sand are more susceptible to infection. Individuals who live in areas with poor ventilation or air conditioning may be more likely to develop Valley Fever due to the spread of spores through airborne transmission. Medical conditions: Certain medical conditions, such as lung disease, diabetes, and rheumatoid arthritis, can increase an individual's susceptibility to Valley Fever. Additionally, individuals taking immunosuppressive medications or those with a history of fungal infections are more likely to develop the disease.
metadata.complications: Valley Fever, also known as coccidioidomycosis, is a fungal infection caused by Coccidioides immitis or Coccidioides posadasii. If left untreated or poorly managed, Valley Fever can lead to serious complications, including respiratory failure, which can be life-threatening if not promptly treated with antifungal medications. Untreated Valley Fever can also cause secondary conditions such as pneumothorax (collapsed lung), pulmonary hemorrhage, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). In rare cases, the infection can spread to other parts of the body, including the brain, heart, and bones, leading to serious outcomes like meningitis, endocarditis, and osteomyelitis.

metadata.symptoms: A varicocele usually occurs on the left side of the scrotum and often produces no signs or symptoms. Possible signs and symptoms may include: Pain. A dull, aching pain or discomfort is more likely when standing or late in the day. Lying down often relieves pain. A mass in the scrotum. If a varicocele is large enough, a mass like a bag of worms may be visible above the testicle. A smaller varicocele may be too small to see but noticeable by touch. Differently sized testicles. The affected testicle may be noticeably smaller than the other testicle. Infertility. A varicocele may lead to difficulty fathering a child, but not all varicoceles cause infertility.
metadata.causes: Male reproductive system Enlarge image Close Male reproductive system Male reproductive system The male reproductive system makes, stores and moves sperm. Testicles produce sperm. Fluid from the seminal vesicles and prostate gland mixes with sperm to make semen. The penis ejaculates semen during sexual activity. The testicles receive oxygen-rich blood from two testicular arteries  one artery for each side of the scrotum. Similarly, there are also two testicular veins that transport oxygen-depleted blood back toward the heart. Within each side of the scrotum, a network of small veins (pampiniform plexus) transport the oxygen-depleted blood from the testicle to the main testicular vein. A varicocele is the enlargement of the pampiniform plexus. The exact cause of a varicocele is unknown. One contributing factor may be the malfunction of valves inside the veins that are intended to keep blood moving in the right direction. Also, the left testicular vein follows a slightly different path than the right vein  a path that makes a problem with blood flow more likely on the left. When the oxygen-depleted blood gets backed up in the network of veins, they widen (dilate), creating the varicocele.
metadata.risk_factors: There dont appear to be any significant risk factors for developing a varicocele. There dont appear to be any significant risk factors for developing a varicocele.
metadata.complications: Having a varicocele can make it difficult for your body to regulate the temperature of the testicles. Oxidative stress and the buildup of toxins can result. These factors may contribute to the following complications: Poor testicular health. For boys going through puberty, a varicocele may inhibit testicle growth, hormone production, and other factors related to the health and function of the testicle. For men, a varicocele may result in gradual shrinkage due to tissue loss. Infertility. A varicocele doesnt necessarily cause infertility. An estimated 10 to 20 of men diagnosed with a varicocele experience difficulty fathering a child. Among men with fertility problems, about 40 have a varicocele. Annual wellness visits for boys are important for monitoring the development and health of testicles. Its important to schedule and keep these appointments. A number of conditions could contribute to pain, swelling or a mass in the scrotum. If you experience any of these, see your health care provider to get a timely and accurate diagnosis. metadata.symptoms: Spider veins Enlarge image Close Spider veins Spider veins Spider veins appear as thin, red lines or as weblike networks of blood vessels on the surface of the skin. Spider veins, a mild form of varicose veins, most often appear on the legs and feet. Varicose veins might not cause pain. Symptoms of varicose veins include: Veins that are dark purple, blue or the same color as the skin. Depending on skin color, these changes may be harder or easier to see. Veins that look twisted and bulging. They often look like cords on the legs. When there are painful symptoms of varicose veins, they might include: An achy or heavy feeling in the legs. Burning, throbbing, muscle cramping and swelling in the lower legs. Worse pain after sitting or standing for a long time. Itching around one or more of the veins. Changes in skin color around a varicose vein. Spider veins are like varicose veins, but theyre smaller. Spider veins are found closer to the skins surface and might look like a spiders web. Spider veins occur on the legs but also can be found on the face. They vary in size and often look like a spiders web.
metadata.causes: Weak or damaged valves can lead to varicose veins. Arteries carry blood from the heart to the rest of the body. Veins return blood from the rest of the body to the heart. To return blood to the heart, the veins in the legs must work against gravity. Muscles tighten in the lower legs to act as pumps. Vein walls help blood return to the heart. Tiny valves in the veins open as blood flows toward the heart, then close to stop blood from flowing backward. If these valves are weak or damaged, blood can flow backward and pool in the veins, causing the veins to stretch or twist.
metadata.risk_factors: The two main risk factors for varicose veins are: Family history. If other family members have varicose veins, theres a greater chance you will too. Obesity. Being overweight puts added pressure on veins. Other things that might increase the risk of varicose veins include: Age. Aging causes wear and tear on the valves in the veins that help control blood flow. Over time, that wear causes the valves to allow some blood to flow back into the veins, where it collects. Sex. Women are more likely to get the condition. Hormones tend to relax vein walls. So changes in hormones before a menstrual period or during pregnancy or menopause might be a factor. Hormone treatments, such as birth control pills, might increase the risk of varicose veins. Pregnancy. During pregnancy, the blood volume in the body increases. This change supports the growing baby but also can make the veins in the legs bigger. Standing or sitting for long periods of time. Movement helps blood flow. metadata.complications: Complications of varicose veins are rare. They can include: Ulcers. Painful ulcers can form on the skin near varicose veins, mostly near the ankles. A discolored spot on the skin often begins before an ulcer forms. See your healthcare professional right away if you think you have a leg ulcer. Blood clots. Sometimes, veins deep within the legs get larger. They might cause leg pain and swelling. Seek medical help for ongoing leg pain or swelling. This can mean a blood clot. Bleeding. name: Vascular Dementia
description: symptoms  vascular dementia is a progressive neurological disorder caused by reduced blood flow to the brain  often resulting from a series of small strokes or changes in the brain s blood vessels. the main symptoms and signs of vascular dementia include  1. memory loss and confusion  patients typically experience significant difficulties with short-term memory  such as forgetting recent events or conversations  and may exhibit disorientation and confusion. 2. mood changes  vascular dementia can lead to irritability  anxiety  depression  and mood swings  which can be distressing for both patients and caregivers. 3. difficulty with communication  patients may struggle to find the right words  use incorrect words  or have trouble understanding conversations. these symptoms can progress over time  affecting daily functioning and quality of life. early detection and treatment are crucial in managing vascular dementia  as they can help slow disease progression and improve outcomes.. causes  vascular dementia is a progressive neurological disorder caused primarily by reduced blood flow to the brain  resulting from a series of small strokes or changes in the brain s blood vessels. the underlying mechanisms involve damage to the brain s blood vessels  leading to impaired blood supply  inflammation  and oxidative stress  which ultimately disrupt normal brain function. lifestyle factors such as high blood pressure  diabetes  smoking  and physical inactivity are significant risk contributors. biological factors play a crucial role in the development of vascular dementia  including genetic predisposition  age-related changes in the brain s vasculature  and underlying medical conditions like hypertension and atherosclerosis. environmental factors  such as exposure to air pollution  may also contribute to the risk of developing vascular dementia.

metadata.symptoms: Vascular dementia is a progressive neurological disorder caused by reduced blood flow to the brain, often resulting from a series of small strokes or changes in the brain's blood vessels. The main symptoms and signs of vascular dementia include: 1. Memory loss and confusion: Patients typically experience significant difficulties with short-term memory, such as forgetting recent events or conversations, and may exhibit disorientation and confusion. 2. Mood changes: Vascular dementia can lead to irritability, anxiety, depression, and mood swings, which can be distressing for both patients and caregivers. 3. Difficulty with communication: Patients may struggle to find the right words, use incorrect words, or have trouble understanding conversations. These symptoms can progress over time, affecting daily functioning and quality of life. Early detection and treatment are crucial in managing vascular dementia, as they can help slow disease progression and improve outcomes.
metadata.causes: Vascular dementia is a progressive neurological disorder caused primarily by reduced blood flow to the brain, resulting from a series of small strokes or changes in the brain's blood vessels. The underlying mechanisms involve damage to the brain's blood vessels, leading to impaired blood supply, inflammation, and oxidative stress, which ultimately disrupt normal brain function. Lifestyle factors such as high blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, and physical inactivity are significant risk contributors. Biological factors play a crucial role in the development of vascular dementia, including genetic predisposition, age-related changes in the brain's vasculature, and underlying medical conditions like hypertension and atherosclerosis. Environmental factors, such as exposure to air pollution, may also contribute to the risk of developing vascular dementia.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Vascular Dementia include: Age: The risk of developing Vascular Dementia increases with age, with most cases occurring in people over 65 years old. Lifestyle Factors: A sedentary lifestyle, high blood pressure, diabetes, and smoking are significant risk factors that can increase the likelihood of developing Vascular Dementia. Medical Conditions: Presence of chronic conditions such as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and stroke, as well as history of transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) or previous strokes, also significantly increases the risk.
metadata.complications: Vascular dementia, also known as vascular cognitive impairment (VCI), is a progressive neurological disorder caused by reduced blood flow to the brain, typically resulting from a series of small strokes or changes in blood vessels. If left untreated or poorly managed, vascular dementia can lead to significant complications, including increased risk of stroke, heart attack, and death. The most significant complications associated with untreated or poorly managed vascular dementia include: 1. Increased risk of recurrent stroke: Vascular dementia increases the risk of future strokes, which can further damage brain tissue and worsen cognitive decline. 2. Cognitive decline and dementia progression: Untreated vascular dementia can lead to accelerated cognitive decline and increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease or other forms of dementia. 3. Depression, anxiety, and behavioral changes: Vascular dementia can also increase the risk of developing depression, anxiety, and behavioral changes, such as agitation and aggression, which can further impact quality of life. It is essential to note that early detection, treatment, and management of vascular dementia can help mitigate these complications and improve outcomes.

metadata.symptoms: Before you faint due to vasovagal syncope, you may experience some of the following symptoms: Change in skin color. Lightheadedness. Tunnel vision  your field of vision narrows so that you see only whats in front of you. Upset stomach. Feeling warm. A cold, clammy sweat. Blurred vision. During a vasovagal syncope episode, people around you may notice: Jerky movements. A slow, weak pulse. Dilated pupils. Recovery after a vasovagal episode generally begins in less than a minute. However, if you stand up too soon after fainting  within about 15 to 30 minutes  youre at risk of fainting again.
metadata.causes: Vasovagal syncope occurs when the part of your nervous system that regulates heart rate and blood pressure overreacts to a trigger. Common triggers include: Standing for long periods of time. Heat exposure. Seeing blood. Having blood drawn. Fear of bodily injury. Straining, such as to pass stool. Vasovagal syncope can happen without a trigger. During a vasovagal syncope episode, your heart rate slows, and the blood vessels in your legs widen. This allows blood to pool in your legs, which lowers your blood pressure. The drop in blood pressure and slowed heart rate quickly reduce blood flow to your brain, and you faint. metadata.symptoms: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is a life-threatening cardiac arrhythmia characterized by rapid, irregular heart rhythms originating in the ventricles. The main symptom of VF is sudden loss of consciousness or collapse, often accompanied by a feeling of impending doom or death. Patients typically experience: 1) Sudden and severe chest pain or discomfort, which may be mistaken for a heart attack; 2) Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing; 3) Pale or blue-tinged skin due to inadequate blood flow; and 4) Rapid heartbeat or palpitations, often with a sensation of pounding or fluttering in the chest. In some cases, patients may also experience confusion, disorientation, or seizures. It is essential to note that VF can progress rapidly, leading to cardiac arrest if not treated promptly and effectively. Note: The symptoms of ventricular fibrillation are often subtle and non-specific, making it crucial for healthcare professionals to recognize the condition through clinical evaluation and electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring.
metadata.causes: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is a life-threatening cardiac arrhythmia characterized by rapid, irregular electrical activity in the ventricles of the heart. The primary causative factors of VF include coronary artery disease, high blood pressure, and electrolyte imbalances, particularly potassium and magnesium deficiencies. Additionally, genetic predispositions, such as long QT syndrome, can also contribute to the development of VF. The underlying mechanisms of VF involve a disruption in the normal electrical conduction system of the heart, leading to chaotic and uncoordinated ventricular contractions. This can be caused by damage to the cardiac tissue, such as myocardial infarction (heart attack), or by abnormal electrical impulses that originate from the heart's natural pacemaker, the sinoatrial node. It is worth noting that VF is often a result of a combination of these factors, rather than a single cause.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for ventricular fibrillation include: * Advanced age (≥65 years): Age is a significant risk factor, as the heart's electrical conduction system becomes less efficient with increasing age. * Male gender: Males are more likely to develop ventricular fibrillation than females due to higher levels of testosterone, which can increase cardiac arrhythmias. * Pre-existing cardiovascular disease, such as coronary artery disease or heart failure, significantly increases the risk of ventricular fibrillation. These factors are not exhaustive, but they are among the most significant contributors to the development of ventricular fibrillation.
metadata.complications: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is a life-threatening cardiac arrhythmia that can lead to severe complications if left untreated or poorly managed. If VF is not promptly treated, it can result in cardiac arrest, brain damage due to lack of oxygen, and death. Additionally, VF can also cause significant long-term consequences, including heart failure, stroke, and chronic kidney disease. The most significant complications of untreated or poorly managed ventricular fibrillation include: 1. Cardiac arrest: The sudden loss of cardiac function can lead to a decline in blood pressure, organ perfusion, and ultimately, death. 2. Brain damage: Prolonged lack of oxygen supply to the brain can cause irreversible damage, leading to cognitive impairment, seizures, or even coma. 3. Organ failure: The prolonged period of VF can result in multi-organ failure, including kidney and liver failure, which can be life-threatening. It's essential to note that prompt recognition, defibrillation, and appropriate medical treatment are crucial in managing ventricular fibrillation to prevent these complications.

metadata.symptoms: A Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) is a congenital heart defect characterized by an abnormal opening in the septum between the left and right ventricles of the heart. The main symptoms and signs of VSD include: * **Shortness of breath**: This is one of the most common symptoms, as the heart has to work harder to pump blood through the defect, leading to increased pulmonary congestion. * **Cyanosis**: A bluish discoloration of the skin, particularly on the hands and feet, due to decreased oxygen levels in the blood. * **Fatigue**: Patients may experience persistent fatigue or weakness, as the heart is not able to pump enough blood to meet the body's needs. * **Rapid or irregular heartbeat (palpitations)**: The abnormal flow of blood through the VSD can cause an increase in heart rate or arrhythmias. These symptoms can vary in severity and may be accompanied by other signs, such as a loud "machinery" murmur heard during auscultation.
metadata.causes: A Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) is a congenital heart defect characterized by an abnormal opening in the septum between the two ventricles of the heart, allowing blood to flow from one ventricle to the other. The primary causative factors of VSD are genetic mutations that affect the development of the heart during fetal growth, with approximately 75% of cases being due to a single gene mutation. Additionally, environmental factors such as maternal smoking and exposure to certain toxins have been linked to an increased risk of VSD. The underlying mechanisms of VSD involve disruptions in the normal process of cardiac septation, which is the formation of the dividing wall between the ventricles during fetal development. This can be caused by a variety of genetic mutations that affect the expression of genes involved in heart development, such as those related to the Notch signaling pathway or the TGF-β signaling pathway. It's worth noting that VSD is often diagnosed at birth or shortly after, and while it may not cause symptoms immediately, it can lead to complications such as heart failure, arrhythmias, and increased risk of pulmonary hypertension if left untreated.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) include: 1. **Genetic predisposition**: Family history of VSD or other congenital heart defects, particularly in first-degree relatives. 2. **Premature birth**: Babies born prematurely are at a higher risk of developing VSD due to incomplete fetal development and increased risk of genetic mutations. 3. **Maternal diabetes**: Women with pre-existing diabetes during pregnancy have an increased risk of having a child with VSD. These factors highlight the importance of prenatal screening, family history, and maternal health in identifying individuals at high risk for VSD.
metadata.complications: A Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) is a congenital heart defect where there is an abnormal opening in the septum between the two lower chambers of the heart, allowing blood to flow from one chamber to another. If left untreated or poorly managed, VSD can lead to serious complications such as pulmonary hypertension, heart failure, and arrhythmias. Additionally, untreated VSD can also increase the risk of endocarditis, stroke, and sudden cardiac death. In particular, the most significant complications that can arise from untreated or poorly managed VSD include: * Pulmonary hypertension: High blood pressure in the lungs can lead to right-sided heart failure and respiratory distress. * Heart failure: The increased workload on the heart can lead to fatigue, shortness of breath, and swelling in the legs and feet. * Arrhythmias: Abnormal heart rhythms can increase the risk of stroke and other cardiovascular complications. It's essential to note that with proper medical care and treatment, most children with VSD can lead normal lives and have a good prognosis.

name: Ventricular Tachycardia
description: symptoms  when the heart beats too fast  it may not send enough blood to the rest of the body. so the organs and tissues may not get enough oxygen. symptoms of ventricular tachycardia are due to a lack of oxygen. they may include  chest pain  called angina. dizziness. pounding heartbeat  called palpitations. lightheadedness. shortness of breath. ventricular tachycardia can be a medical emergency even if your symptoms are minor. ventricular tachycardia  sometimes called v-tach or vt  is grouped according to how long an episode lasts. nonsustained v-tach stops on its own within 30 seconds. brief episodes may not cause any symptoms. sustained v-tach lasts more than 30 seconds. this type of ventricular tachycardia can cause serious health problems. symptoms of sustained v-tach may include  fainting. loss of consciousness. cardiac arrest or sudden death.. causes  ventricular tachycardia is caused by faulty heart signaling that makes the heart beat too fast in the lower heart chambers. the lower heart chambers are called the ventricles. the fast heart rate doesnt allow the ventricles to fill and squeeze to pump enough blood to the body. many things can cause or lead to problems with heart signaling and trigger ventricular tachycardia. these include  prior heart attack. any heart condition that caused scarring of heart tissue  called structural heart disease. poor blood flow to the heart muscle due to coronary artery disease. heart problems present at birth  including long qt syndrome. changes in levels of body minerals called electrolytes. these include potassium  sodium  calcium and magnesium. side effects of medicines. use of stimulants such as cocaine or methamphetamine. sometimes  the exact cause of ventricular tachycardia cant be determined. this is called idiopathic ventricular tachycardia.

metadata.symptoms: When the heart beats too fast, it may not send enough blood to the rest of the body. So the organs and tissues may not get enough oxygen. Symptoms of ventricular tachycardia are due to a lack of oxygen. They may include: Chest pain, called angina. Dizziness. Pounding heartbeat, called palpitations. Lightheadedness. Shortness of breath. Ventricular tachycardia can be a medical emergency even if your symptoms are minor. Ventricular tachycardia, sometimes called V-tach or VT, is grouped according to how long an episode lasts. Nonsustained V-tach stops on its own within 30 seconds. Brief episodes may not cause any symptoms. Sustained V-tach lasts more than 30 seconds. This type of ventricular tachycardia can cause serious health problems. Symptoms of sustained V-tach may include: Fainting. Loss of consciousness. Cardiac arrest or sudden death.
metadata.causes: Ventricular tachycardia is caused by faulty heart signaling that makes the heart beat too fast in the lower heart chambers. The lower heart chambers are called the ventricles. The fast heart rate doesnt allow the ventricles to fill and squeeze to pump enough blood to the body. Many things can cause or lead to problems with heart signaling and trigger ventricular tachycardia. These include: Prior heart attack. Any heart condition that caused scarring of heart tissue, called structural heart disease. Poor blood flow to the heart muscle due to coronary artery disease. Heart problems present at birth, including long QT syndrome. Changes in levels of body minerals called electrolytes. These include potassium, sodium, calcium and magnesium. Side effects of medicines. Use of stimulants such as cocaine or methamphetamine. Sometimes, the exact cause of ventricular tachycardia cant be determined. This is called idiopathic ventricular tachycardia.
metadata.risk_factors: Any condition that puts a strain on the heart or damages heart tissue can increase the risk of ventricular tachycardia. Lifestyle changes such as eating healthy and not smoking may lower the risk. Its also important to get proper medical treatment if you have any of the following conditions and events: Heart disease. Side effects of medicines. Severe changes in the level of body minerals, called electrolyte imbalances. A history of using stimulant drugs such as cocaine or methamphetamine. A family history of tachycardia or other heart rhythm disorders also makes a person more likely to get ventricular tachycardia. metadata.complications: Complications of ventricular tachycardia depend on: How fast the heart is beating. How long the rapid heart rate lasts. Whether there are other heart conditions. A life-threatening complication of V-tach is ventricular fibrillation, also called V-fib. V-fib can cause all heart activity to suddenly stop, called sudden cardiac arrest. Emergency treatment is needed to prevent death. V-fib happens most often in people with heart disease or a prior heart attack. Sometimes it occurs in those who have high or low potassium levels or other changes in body mineral levels. Other possible complications of ventricular tachycardia include: Frequent fainting spells or unconsciousness. Heart failure. Sudden death caused by cardiac arrest. Many different things can cause ventricular tachycardia, sometimes called V-tach or VT. Its important to get a fast, accurate diagnosis and appropriate care. Even if you have a healthy heart, you should get prompt medical help if you have symptoms of V-tach. Make an appointment for a health checkup if you think you have an irregular heartbeat. Sometimes, urgent or emergency care is needed. Call 911 or your local emergency number for these symptoms: Chest pain that lasts more than a few minutes. Difficulty breathing. Fainting. name: Vertebral Tumor
description: symptoms  signs and symptoms of vertebral tumors include  back pain in the area of the tumor. back pain that radiates or shoots from the back to a nearby area. back pain thats worse at night. changes in sensation  such as numbness or a feeling of pins and needles. loss of the ability to move part of the body. loss of control over the bladder and bowels. muscle weakness.. causes  most vertebral tumors are caused by cancer that starts somewhere else in the body. cancer that spreads from an organ to somewhere else in the body is called metastatic cancer. any cancer can spread to the spine. most vertebral tumors are caused by cancer that spreads from the breasts  lungs or prostate. other cancers that tend to spread to the spine include kidney cancer and thyroid cancer. cancers that affect the blood cells and bone marrow also can cause vertebral tumors. these cancers include multiple myeloma and lymphoma. vertebral tumors that start in the spine are rare. its not clear what causes them. vertebral tumors that start in the spine happen when cells in the bones of the spine develop changes in their dna. a cells dna holds the instructions that tell the cell what to do. in healthy cells  the dna gives instructions to grow and multiply at a set rate. the instructions tell the cells to die at a set time. in the tumor cells  the dna changes give different instructions. the changes tell the tumor cells to make many more cells quickly. tumor cells can keep living when healthy cells would die. this causes too many cells. sometimes cells develop changes in their dna that turn them into cancer cells. cancer cells can invade and destroy healthy body tissue. they can break away and spread to other parts of the body. examples of vertebral tumors that start in the spine and arent cancerous include  hemangioma. osteoid osteoma. osteoblastoma. aneurysmal bone cyst. osteochondroma. enchondroma. chondroblastoma. examples of vertebral tumors that start in the spine and metadata.symptoms: Signs and symptoms of vertebral tumors include: Back pain in the area of the tumor. Back pain that radiates or shoots from the back to a nearby area. Back pain thats worse at night. Changes in sensation, such as numbness or a feeling of pins and needles. Loss of the ability to move part of the body. Loss of control over the bladder and bowels. Muscle weakness.
metadata.causes: Most vertebral tumors are caused by cancer that starts somewhere else in the body. Cancer that spreads from an organ to somewhere else in the body is called metastatic cancer. Any cancer can spread to the spine. Most vertebral tumors are caused by cancer that spreads from the breasts, lungs or prostate. Other cancers that tend to spread to the spine include kidney cancer and thyroid cancer. Cancers that affect the blood cells and bone marrow also can cause vertebral tumors. These cancers include multiple myeloma and lymphoma. Vertebral tumors that start in the spine are rare. Its not clear what causes them. Vertebral tumors that start in the spine happen when cells in the bones of the spine develop changes in their DNA. A cells DNA holds the instructions that tell the cell what to do. In healthy cells, the DNA gives instructions to grow and multiply at a set rate. The instructions tell the cells to die at a set time. In the tumor cells, the DNA changes give different instructions. The changes tell the tumor cells to make many more cells quickly. Tumor cells can keep living when healthy cells would die. This causes too many cells. Sometimes cells develop changes in their DNA that turn them into cancer cells. Cancer cells can invade and destroy healthy body tissue. They can break away and spread to other parts of the body. Examples of vertebral tumors that start in the spine and arent cancerous include: Hemangioma. Osteoid osteoma. Osteoblastoma. Aneurysmal bone cyst. Osteochondroma. Enchondroma. Chondroblastoma. Examples of vertebral tumors that start in the spine and are cancerous include: Chondrosarcoma. Ewing sarcoma. Osteosarcoma. Chordoma.
metadata.risk_factors: The risk of vertebral tumors is higher in people who have cancer or have been treated for cancer. Most vertebral tumors are caused by cancer that starts somewhere else in the body and spreads to the spine. Cancer that spreads to the spine most often starts in the breasts, lungs or prostate. metadata.complications: Complications caused by vertebral tumors include: Spinal cord compression. Spinal cord compression happens when a tumor grows to press on the spinal cord or nearby nerves. It often causes back pain at first. Later it can cause weakness and numbness in the part of the body controlled by the affected nerves. There may be difficulty walking and a loss of control of the bladder and bowels. Spinal instability. Spinal instability can happen if a vertebral tumor weakens the bones in the spine. Bones weakened by tumors can break or go out of alignment. This can make it hard for the spine to hold the body upright. Spinal instability typically causes pain and can lead to weakness. Treatments may help prevent or treat these complications. Make an appointment with a doctor or other healthcare professional if you have any symptoms that worry you. Some vertebral tumor symptoms are similar to symptoms caused by other conditions. For example, back pain is very common, and most back pain isnt caused by a tumor. Sometimes its hard to decide whether to see a healthcare professional when you have back pain. Make an appointment if: The pain is constant and is getting worse. The pain doesnt seem to be caused by a certain activity. The pain is worse at night. You have a history of cancer and the back pain is something new. Seek immediate medical care if you have back pain along with: Muscle weakness in the arms or legs. Loss of control of the bowel or bladder. Numbness or tingling in the genital area. name: Vertigo

Episodes of BPPV can disappear for some time and then recur. Activities that bring about the signs and symptoms of BPPV can vary from person to person, but are almost always brought on by a change in head position. Some people also feel out of balance when standing or walking. Abnormal rhythmic eye movements usually accompany the symptoms of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
metadata.causes: Inner ear and balance Enlarge image Close Inner ear and balance Inner ear and balance Semicircular canals and otolith organs  called the utricle and saccule  in your inner ear contain fluid and fine, hairlike sensors. These sensory hair cells help you keep your eyes focused on a target when your head is in motion. They also help you keep your balance. Often, theres no known cause for BPPV. This is called idiopathic BPPV. When there is a known cause, BPPV is often associated with a minor to severe blow to your head. Less common causes of BPPV include disorders that damage your inner ear or, rarely, damage that occurs during ear surgery or long periods positioned on your back, such as in a dentist chair. BPPV also has been associated with migraines.
metadata.risk_factors: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo occurs most often in people age 50 and older, but can occur at any age. BPPV is also more common in women than in men. A head injury or any other disorder of the balance organs of your ear may make you more susceptible to BPPV. name: Vesicoureteral Reflux
description: symptoms  vesicoureteral reflux symptoms often are due to a urinary tract infection (uti). a uti doesnt always cause symptoms  but most people notice some. these symptoms can include  a strong  constant urge to urinate. a burning feeling when urinating. the need to pass small amounts of urine often. cloudy urine. fever. pain in the side  groin or stomach area. babies and some small children with utis cant tell adults what their symptoms feel like. but they may have  a fever for no clear reason. lack of hunger. fussiness. as a child gets older  vesicoureteral reflux that doesnt get treated can lead to  bed-wetting. constipation or loss of control over bowel movements. high blood pressure. protein in urine. urgent need to urinate or urinating more often than usual. leaking urine by accident  also called urinary incontinence. another symptom of vesicoureteral reflux is swelling of one or both kidneys. this swelling is called hydronephrosis. its caused by the backup of urine into the kidneys. an imaging test called an ultrasound often finds this swelling before a baby is born.. causes  there are two main types of vesicoureteral reflux  and they have different causes. primary vesicoureteral reflux. children are born with this more common type of reflux. its caused by a problem with the valve that usually keeps urine from flowing backward from the bladder. the valve doesnt close well. this lets urine flow back up tubes called ureters that carry urine from the kidneys down to the bladder. as children grow  the ureters lengthen and straighten. that may metadata.symptoms: Vesicoureteral reflux symptoms often are due to a urinary tract infection (UTI). A UTI doesnt always cause symptoms, but most people notice some. These symptoms can include: A strong, constant urge to urinate. A burning feeling when urinating. The need to pass small amounts of urine often. Cloudy urine. Fever. Pain in the side, groin or stomach area. Babies and some small children with UTIs cant tell adults what their symptoms feel like. But they may have: A fever for no clear reason. Lack of hunger. Fussiness. As a child gets older, vesicoureteral reflux that doesnt get treated can lead to: Bed-wetting. Constipation or loss of control over bowel movements. High blood pressure. Protein in urine. Urgent need to urinate or urinating more often than usual. Leaking urine by accident, also called urinary incontinence. Another symptom of vesicoureteral reflux is swelling of one or both kidneys. This swelling is called hydronephrosis. Its caused by the backup of urine into the kidneys. An imaging test called an ultrasound often finds this swelling before a baby is born.
metadata.causes: There are two main types of vesicoureteral reflux, and they have different causes. Primary vesicoureteral reflux. Children are born with this more common type of reflux. Its caused by a problem with the valve that usually keeps urine from flowing backward from the bladder. The valve doesnt close well. This lets urine flow back up tubes called ureters that carry urine from the kidneys down to the bladder. As children grow, the ureters lengthen and straighten. That may help the valve work better and correct the backflow of urine over time. This type of vesicoureteral reflux tends to run in families. So it may be genetic. But the exact cause isnt known. Secondary vesicoureteral reflux. This type of reflux most often happens because the bladder doesnt empty properly. There can be many reasons for this. For example, a fold of tissue may block urine from fully leaving the bladder. Or muscles that connect the bladder to another tube called the urethra may become too narrow. Or the nerves that control the bladders ability to empty may become damaged.
metadata.risk_factors: Risk factors for vesicoureteral reflux include: Bladder and bowel dysfunction (BBD). Children with BBD hold their urine and stool. They also get repeated urinary tract infections. That can contribute to vesicoureteral reflux. Race. White children appear to have a higher risk of vesicoureteral reflux than do Black children. Sex assigned at birth. In general, girls have a much higher risk of having this condition than boys do. The exception is for vesicoureteral reflux thats present at birth. This is more common in boys. Age. Infants and children up to age 2 are more likely to have vesicoureteral reflux than older children are. Family history. Primary vesicoureteral reflux tends to run in families. Children whose parents had the condition are at higher risk of it. Siblings of children who have the condition also are at higher risk. So your healthcare professional may recommend screening tests for siblings of a child with primary vesicoureteral reflux. metadata.complications: Kidney damage is the main health concern, also called complication, that can happen with vesicoureteral reflux. The worse the reflux, the more serious the complications are likely to be. Complications may include: Kidney scarring. Without treatment, UTIs can lead to lasting damage to kidney tissue known as scarring. Extensive scarring may lead to high blood pressure and kidney failure. High blood pressure. The kidneys filter waste from the bloodstream. So damage to the kidneys can cause waste to build up. That in turn can raise blood pressure. Kidney problems. Scarring can cause an affected kidney to have trouble filtering blood. This may lead to kidney failure, meaning the kidney loses its filtering ability. This life-threatening condition can happen quickly, also known as acute kidney injury. Or it can develop over time, also called chronic kidney disease. metadata.causes: Viral gastroenteritis is a highly contagious and common gastrointestinal illness caused primarily by viral infections, such as norovirus, rotavirus, and adenovirus. The main biological factor contributing to this condition is the presence of a viral agent that invades the lining of the small intestine, leading to inflammation and damage to the epithelial cells. This results in symptoms such as diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, and fever. The primary causative factors of viral gastroenteritis include: 1. **Viral transmission**: The virus is typically spread through the fecal-oral route, where contaminated food or water is ingested, or through close contact with an infected individual. 2. **Weakened immune system**: Individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with underlying medical conditions or taking immunosuppressive medications, are more susceptible to severe illness and complications from viral gastroenteritis. 3. **Hygiene and sanitation**: Poor hygiene practices, inadequate handwashing, and contaminated food and water can contribute to the spread of the virus. These factors highlight the importance of good hygiene practices, proper handwashing, and safe food handling to prevent the transmission of viral gastroenteritis.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing viral gastroenteritis include: 1. Young children under 5 years old, as their immune systems are still developing and they may not be able to fight off viral infections effectively. 2. Older adults (65+ years), who may have weakened immune systems due to age-related decline in immune function or underlying medical conditions. 3. People with compromised immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS, cancer, or taking immunosuppressive medications. These demographic factors increase the likelihood of developing viral gastroenteritis, making them more susceptible to severe symptoms and complications.
metadata.complications: Viral gastroenteritis, also known as stomach flu, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is dehydration, which can progress to severe electrolyte imbalances, kidney damage, and even death if not promptly treated. Additionally, viral gastroenteritis can increase the risk of developing secondary conditions such as bacterial infections, malnutrition, and long-term gastrointestinal problems. In rare cases, untreated or poorly managed viral gastroenteritis can lead to more serious complications, including: * Severe diarrhea that can cause dehydration and electrolyte imbalances * Kidney failure due to prolonged dehydration and electrolyte disturbances * Malnutrition and weight loss due to severe vomiting and diarrhea It's essential to seek medical attention if symptoms persist or worsen over time.

metadata.symptoms: Vitamin deficiency anemia is a condition characterized by a decrease in the production of red blood cells or the amount of hemoglobin in the blood, leading to a reduction in oxygen delivery to tissues and organs. The main symptoms and signs of vitamin deficiency anemia include: fatigue and weakness, which are often described as persistent and unexplained tiredness that worsens with physical activity; pale skin, which is due to the reduced amount of red blood cells or hemoglobin; shortness of breath, also known as dyspnea, which occurs when the body's tissues do not receive enough oxygen; and dizziness or lightheadedness, which can be triggered by standing up quickly or changing positions. Additionally, some patients may experience headaches, irritability, and a general feeling of malaise or illness.
metadata.causes: Vitamin deficiency anemia is a medical condition characterized by a decrease in red blood cells or hemoglobin due to inadequate intake of essential vitamins, particularly vitamin B12 and iron. The primary causative factors include genetic predisposition, dietary deficiencies, and environmental exposures such as malabsorption disorders, gastrointestinal surgery, or chronic diseases like celiac disease or Crohn's disease. Additionally, certain medications, age-related decline in absorption, and poor nutrition can also contribute to the development of vitamin deficiency anemia. The biological mechanism underlying this condition involves impaired DNA synthesis and cell division, leading to a decrease in red blood cell production and function. The lack of essential vitamins disrupts normal hematopoiesis (the process by which blood cells are produced), resulting in anemia. It's worth noting that there are different types of vitamin deficiency anemia, including: * Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia: caused by inadequate dietary intake or impaired absorption due to genetic disorders, gastrointestinal surgery, or certain medications. * Iron deficiency anemia: caused by inadequate iron intake, increased iron loss through menstruation, pregnancy, or chronic bleeding, and impaired iron absorption. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent complications such as fatigue, weakness, and shortness of breath.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for Vitamin Deficiency Anemia include: 1. **Age**: Older adults are more susceptible to vitamin deficiency anemia due to decreased dietary intake, impaired absorption, and increased requirements. 2. **Pregnancy and lactation**: Women who are pregnant or breastfeeding have higher demands for certain vitamins, such as iron and folate, which can lead to deficiencies if not adequately supplemented. 3. **Vegetarian or vegan diet**: Individuals following a plant-based diet may be at risk of vitamin B12 deficiency due to limited dietary sources and potential impaired absorption. These factors highlight the importance of monitoring and addressing nutritional deficiencies in vulnerable populations.
metadata.complications: Vitamin Deficiency Anemia, also known as megaloblastic anemia, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is neurological damage, which can result in numbness, weakness, and paralysis in the extremities, as well as cognitive impairment and seizures. Additionally, untreated vitamin deficiency anemia can also increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, including heart failure and stroke. Furthermore, if left untreated, vitamin deficiency anemia can lead to a range of secondary conditions, including fatigue, weakness, pale skin, shortness of breath, and dizziness. In severe cases, it can also cause malnutrition, weight loss, and impaired immune function, making individuals more susceptible to infections and other illnesses. Untreated vitamin deficiency anemia can also increase the risk of developing certain cancers, such as colon cancer, due to the accumulation of toxic compounds in the body.

metadata.causes: Vitiligo is a chronic autoimmune skin disorder characterized by the loss of pigment-producing cells (melanocytes), leading to white patches on the skin. The primary causative factors of vitiligo are believed to be genetic predisposition, immune system dysregulation, and environmental triggers such as ultraviolet radiation, stress, and certain medications. Additionally, hormonal imbalances, thyroid disorders, and autoimmune diseases may also contribute to the development of vitiligo. Biological mechanisms underlying vitiligo involve an abnormal response of the immune system to melanocytes, leading to their destruction and subsequent loss of pigment production. This results in the characteristic white patches on the skin, which can be accompanied by other symptoms such as skin sensitivity and inflammation.
metadata.risk_factors: The main risk factors for developing vitiligo include: 1. **Genetic predisposition**: Individuals with a family history of vitiligo are more likely to develop the condition, suggesting a strong genetic component. 2. **Autoimmune disorders**: Presence of other autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, and rheumatoid arthritis increases the risk of developing vitiligo. 3. **Skin trauma or injury**: Physical damage to the skin, such as burns, cuts, or scrapes, can trigger the onset of vitiligo in susceptible individuals. These factors highlight the importance of genetic and autoimmune predispositions in the development of vitiligo.
metadata.complications: Vitiligo, a chronic autoimmune skin disorder, can lead to several potential complications if left untreated or poorly managed. One of the most significant complications is the development of secondary infections, such as bacterial or fungal infections, which can occur due to the loss of pigment in the affected skin areas. Additionally, vitiligo can also increase the risk of skin cancer, particularly in individuals with a history of sun exposure and fair skin. Untreated vitiligo can also lead to emotional distress, anxiety, and depression due to the visible appearance of white patches on the skin. Furthermore, the condition can also cause scarring and disfigurement if it progresses to more severe stages, leading to significant cosmetic concerns for affected individuals. In rare cases, vitiligo can also be associated with other autoimmune disorders, such as thyroid disease or diabetes, which can increase the risk of developing serious complications if left untreated.
